events.title: Fox-Roku deal poised to clear Justice Department scrutiny under consent decree, despite conservative pressure
events.summary: The Scoop Fox’s $22 billion acquisition of Roku is poised to clear Justice Department scrutiny and move forward under a consent decree, according to people familiar with the deliberations, despite efforts from a right-wing ally of President Donald Trump to hold up the deal. It’s unclear what a consent decree would entail, or what terms are being considered. It’s possible the DOJ could change course, the people said. Fox declined to comment. Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward also declined to comment on the deal. “However, we can affirm that this DOJ under President Trump’s leadership will continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy,” he said in a statement. The deal, which would unite Fox’s content empire of news and sports with Roku’s dominant connected-TV operating system, had worried rivals who fear that Fox will favor its own content. Roku’s free, ad-supported channel also competes for viewers and content with Tubi, which Fox owns. Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch has said his “expectation” is to run the two businesses separately while selling advertising across them. Semafor first reported in September that antitrust regulators were widening the inquiry into the deal, days before the two companies confirmed the deeper probe, known as a “second request.” That enhanced scrutiny came in part because of pressure from Newsmax majority owner Chris Ruddy, who bills himself as a Trump confidant and has had a long-running spat with Fox owner Rupert Murdoch, Semafor later reported. Rohan’s view Ruddy, briefly a reporter for Murdoch’s New York Post in the 1990s, has been feuding with Fox for more than a year over streaming access to his media assets. Murdoch’s camp has previously dismissed Newsmax’s efforts as a bid to “sue their way out of their own competitive failures,” and Murdoch himself has dined with Trump more than once. But it’s clear that Ruddy has been a headache for the Murdoch clan. Investors have fretted about the possibility that Fox’s deal for Roku could get tied up as a result of Ruddy’s efforts. Those worries were exacerbated after Fox ousted business anchor Maria Bartiromo following an internal investigation into allegations she leaked internal network information and communications to the Trump administration, a claim her lawyers have disputed. But if the deal goes through, it’s more evidence that the Murdoch name still carries a fair amount of weight in Washington.

events.title: North Korea denies role in Binance heist as customers withdraw billions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts North Korea dismisses Binance heist allegations as 'absurd' US rhetoric Kim Jong Un is the leader of North Korea, which has been accused of orchestrating the largest crypto heist in history. ( KCNA via Reuters ) North Korea has denied FBI allegations accusing the country of stealing $US6.3 billion from crypto exchange platform Binance. Ruling party official Kim Yo Jong dismissed the allegations as "absurd rhetoric and nothing new" from the US. Binance customers have withdrawn $US4.64 billion after the company lifted a temporary suspension on withdrawals. North Korea has denied US allegations that it was behind the $US6.3 billion ($9 billion) heist of cryptocurrency exchange platform Binance as "absurd rhetoric" and proof that Washington remained hostile towards the country. In a statement published by North Korean state media, Kim Yo Jong , the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, denied the country was responsible for carrying out last week's hack, thought to be the largest financial heist in history. Who is behind world's largest crypto heist? Almost $9 billion in cryptocurrency was hacked from exchange company Binance, but who was behind the attack? Ms Kim also warned the country had "issues to reconsider" over US hostility. "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state,' claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," she said in the statement. "But the US assertion is absurd rhetoric and nothing new. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds." On Saturday, the FBI accused a North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor of carrying out the hack and stealing billions in crypto. The FBI says North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor is behind the heist. ( Pexels: Tibe De Kort ) The US bureau said it had observed TraderTraitor converting stolen assets into a cryptocurrency called Ethereum and expected it to launder the assets further. "The FBI maintains its commitment to protecting the virtual asset community by identifying, mitigating, and disrupting North Korea's illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities," a statement read. Cybersecurity experts said North Korean hackers were among the world's most prolific crypto thieves, with the proceeds used to help fund the country's weapons programs. North Korea has denied all allegations of its links to cryptocurrency theft and other cybercrimes. Ms Kim said North Korea would reconsider unspecified issues in light of the "very unpleasant US hostile attitude". It comes as Pyongyang remains silent on US President Donald Trump's offers to resume US-North Korea summit diplomacy. Experts have indicated Pyongyang may be weighing its options. Binance customers withdrew about $US4.64 billion ($6.6 billion) worth of assets after the company lifted its temporary suspension on Sunday. Zhao Changpeng is the founder and CEO of Binance, which has moved to reassure its users following the hack. ( Reuters: Benoit Tessier ) "Between 06:00 and 15:30 UTC on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion," the company said on X. "Our team continues testing rigorously the remaining networks and assets. "Rest assured that market conditions are stable." The company said it had recovered 90 per cent of the stolen assets by using company money. events.title: What we know so far about the Learjet 60 private plane that crashed in Florida
events.summary: Roads are closed after a jet crashed on November 1. Saul Martinez/Getty Images A private jet crashed in South Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard. Weather data at the time of the crash shows thunderstorms and moderate turbulence in the area. NTSB officials said there is evidence of the jet breaking apart before impact. Nine people aboard a private jet were killed when it crashed and exploded in a fireball near Palm Beach, Florida , Sunday afternoon. The plane, a Learjet built in 2004 and registered as N722BD, had departed from Austin and was en route to the Bahamas. Tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson and his wife Helen Sharp died in the crash, as did their children, their nanny Anita Maria Cetina, and their friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, the victims' families shared. The plane's two pilots also died. Authorities have not said what caused the crash. "Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote on X on Sunday. National Transportation Safety Board Member Tom Chapman said during a press conference on Monday that access to the crash site is challenging because of the bad weather on the ground, causing the impact crater to fill with water. Officials also said crash debris was scattered across fields, homes, and businesses. The crash occurred less than 10 miles from President Donald Trump's Mar-A-Lago resort . Trump left West Palm Beach around noon aboard Air Force One to attend a rally in Iowa, according to White House pool reports. What we know about the flight Aviation-tracking data from FlightRadar24 showed the plane descending from 41,000 feet to about 35,000 feet as it entered Florida, then crossed the state before plummeting about 27,000 feet in about a minute to the ground near Palm Beach. The plane was about two hours into the flight to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when it crashed. In the minutes before the crash, a pilot can be heard on air traffic control recordings reporting the air temperature outside as -47 degrees Celsius (about -52 degrees Fahrenheit), as well as icing, precipitation, and moderate turbulence. The pilot later said "mayday," saying the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute, and moments later, reported an overspeed condition before impact. Video footage shared online of the crash shows that part of the Learjet's T-tail may have separated from the plane. Chapman said there is "some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact" and the NTSB is "still seeking to determine that." He also said the agency hopes to recover the cockpit voice recorder, but it's unclear if the particular jet had one installed. NTSB investigator Timothy Monville said during the briefing that the Federal Aviation Administration and the manufacturer Learjet, which is now a part of Bombardier, will assist the NTSB with the investigation. "We at Bombardier are deeply saddened by this tragic event and extend our sincerest sympathies to all those affected," Bombardier said in a statement. "We cannot comment on the potential cause of this accident until the investigation is complete and we will fully support the investigating authorities and cooperate as needed." What we know about the weather Widespread thunderstorms moved through South Florida on Sunday afternoon. Aviation weather data for the area showed heavy rain, low visibility, and turbulence around the time of the crash. "The weather conditions are a major focus of the investigation," Chapman said. "You all saw what the weather was like here at the surface; what we have to determine is what the weather conditions were like at altitude." There were thunderstorms in the area at the time of the crash. Saul Martinez/Getty Images It's not yet known what caused the crash, but retired Delta Air Lines pilot Mark Stephens told Business Insider that icing can occur at any altitude and, in some circumstances, cause a wing to lose lift and an aircraft to stall. "If there was a failure on one wing, meaning that wing iced up, then the good wing would still fly, but the other would lose lift," he said. "You'd have such an uneven lift that it would basically do close to exactly what the Learjet did; it can flop out of the sky." Stephens warned against immediately placing blame on the pilots, adding that anti-ice and weather radar systems can fail and that a number of factors beyond human error could have contributed. 'She was doing her job' Jared Isaacman, the NASA administrator and pilot, shared his personal thoughts on the crash on X and urged the public not to criticize the woman pilot in the ATC calls. "She was the second-in-command (SIC), and while she was empowered to point out mistakes as part of good crew resource management, she was doing her job, communicating with ATC right to the end in a terrifying situation," he wrote. He added that she "likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die," and the public does not know factors such as the jet's maintenance history, or whether there was structural failure and why. Isaacman also said that charter companies often hire commercial pilots "very early in their careers to gain experience," alongside airline-qualified captains. "She would still have the appropriate training, qualifications, and checkouts by an FAA examiner or designee," he said. "Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts. Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories." This is a developing story. Check back for updates. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Before the tragic Learjet crash, Adam Robinson had a message for startup founders: You don't need VCs to get rich
events.summary: Adam Robinson, right, poses with his wife Helen Sharp and the couple's two young children. Courtesy of the Robinson family Adam Robinson, who died in the Florida Learjet crash on Sunday, was a serial entrepreneur. Robinson's career in finance ended with a spiritual upheaval and a pivot into tech startups. An evangelist for bootstrapping, he leaves mourners in Aspen, Austin, and across the internet. Before this weekend's tragedy, Adam Robinson was carving out a picture-perfect life and a contrarian lane in tech entrepreneurship. The 45-year-old tech founder died in a private plane crash on Sunday near Greenacres and Palm Beach, Florida, along with his wife, their two young children, their nanny, and two friends. They were flying from Austin to the Bahamas when the plane went down. All nine occupants of the Learjet died, including the two pilots . "It's an unspeakable tragedy," Brett Hurt, a friend and mentor of Robinson's from Austin, told Business Insider on Monday. Robinson was an "amazing conscious capitalist," Hurt said, and a "beacon" for other startup founders learning how to bootstrap their own businesses. Robinson leaves behind a career that carried him from the halls of Wall Street during the 2008 financial crisis to serial entrepreneurship in Austin's post-2020 tech wave. In recent years, he has relocated to Aspen, Colorado, and crystallized an ideology that runs counter to Silicon Valley's VC-friendly ethos. On social media and in podcasts, Robinson evangelized for the idea that startups should run lean and earn their own keep . His companies, Retention.com, RB2B, and MoltSets, released a joint statement on Monday calling Robinson "a friend, a mentor and a bold, outspoken leader who lived life to the fullest." "His loss is deeply felt across our team and the tech community, as we collectively mourn," the statement said. Robinson's journey from Wall Street to tech Robinson grew up in the Houston suburbs and attended Rice University, where he was a guard on the basketball team. After college, he moved to New York City to work as a credit trader at Lehman Brothers. He stuck around until the 2008 financial crisis and then beyond, when Barclays absorbed much of Lehman after its bankruptcy. The Wall Street gigs made Robinson millions of dollars, he said on the ProfitLed podcast earlier this year. After around a decade, he'd also realized the lifestyle wasn't what he wanted and that he didn't have the invigorated energy of someone who truly loves their work. New York had given him another lesson, with a window into the tech startup world. His original roommates in the city had started Vimeo in their Tribeca apartment. "These guys were making just as much money, and it just appeared like they loved it," Robinson said on ProfitLed. "Everything they were dealing with just seemed so interesting to me." In his early 30s, unmarried, and with money in the bank from Wall Street, Robinson went through a bit of spiritual upheaval, he said on the Fulfillionaire podcast last year. He read Zappos CEO Tony Hsieh 's "Delivering Happiness," various Buddhist texts, and John Mackey and Rajendra Sisodia's "Conscious Capitalism." He said he realized that money shouldn't be the end-all, be-all motivator; he needed to start working with more purpose. He made the leap into startups. Robinson's early days in tech were a slog At the time of his death, Robinson was a bona fide serial entrepreneur, with a cluster of businesses — Retention.com, RB2B, and MoltSets. The same group of 32 people runs those businesses, and Robinson has said they bring in $35 million in annual revenue. They offer products for identifying website visitors and accessing contact information. It'd taken a bit of grind. Robinson's first startup, an email service provider called Robly, burned through his and his brother's money for its first few years. On ProfitLed, he said he had to lay off 27 of the company's 35 workers at one point; after paying severance, the company was profitable, yet its customer count was slowly shrinking. Thankfully for Robinson, they were on to an idea. A feature built at Robly to snag people's email addresses became popular with customers, and Robinson and the other founders spun the business off into a company called GetEmails. He described the tactic in a 2023 interview with Practical Ecommerce as "email laundering" — placing a pixel on customers' sites and then collecting email addresses from their anonymous web traffic. Robinson said on ProfitLed that he realized the product would be "10 times better of a business." From there, the business grew. GetEmails became Retention.com, and the team launched other companies. The day Robinson's plane crashed, he'd posted on LinkedIn that RB2B had hit $10 million in  annual recurring revenue  and MoltSets had nearly reached $1 million in ARR. Robinson explained the split between firms in characteristically bombastic style: "I think all-in-one platforms ALWAYS turn into garbage." He wrote that he would host a debate about keeping the companies separated on Tuesday. Robinson was an evangelist for bootstrapping More so than for his actual businesses, Robinson's star rose on the internet with a canny content-creation strategy and a no-holds-barred embrace of bootstrapping companies, or building them without outside capital. He accumulated 13,000 followers on X, and more than 160,000 on LinkedIn, presenting as a techie, brand-building thought leader. He often posted and spoke about the merits of the bootstrapping approach , arguing that it led companies to waste less on extraneous bets, keep their ambitions in scope, and more quickly identify the actual value of their product. This mindset contrasts with tech's typical embrace of venture capitalists, who Robinson often poked at in posts and interviews. "Bootstrapping to $10M ARR is easier and less risky than creating a VC-backed unicorn, with a far higher probability-weighted outcome," he wrote on X in January. In April, he posted: "You don't need to crash a plane to learn to fly ... and you don't need VC to build a business." And he often tied bootstrapping to an exhortation for founders to seek true financial freedom . "If you can hold out on investment long enough, the freedom you will have as a bootstrapper will give you the life you wanted when you started on this path in the first place," Robinson wrote on X in September. "VC will not." A wave of heartbreak in tech Figures in the tech world who'd interacted with Robinson or admired his bootstrapping enthusiasm expressed their grief on Monday. Hurt told Business Insider that when he visited Robinson in Aspen a few months ago, he was taken with how happy his friend seemed about his children, wife, and community in the Colorado mountain town. "He was a genuinely good, loving guy that just loved his family and loved the community so much, and did so much for everyone around him," Hurt said. "It's just absolutely tragic." Larry Kim, th

events.title: Indonesia’s severe drought threatens to disrupt China’s vast battery industry
events.summary: A severe drought in Indonesia is slowing output of a crucial material used to make electric vehicle batteries A severe drought in Indonesia is slowing output of a crucial material used to manufacture electric vehicle batteries, creating risks across China’s vast electric car supply chain. Indonesia is a vital link in the global electric car supply chain. The Southeast Asian nation is the world’s biggest production hub for nickel, a metal that is converted into a component used in lithium-ion batteries. But a sharp drop in rainfall in the country is causing local nickel refineries to reduce output, a move that could “add uncertainty … across the battery materials value chain”, according to market analysis firm CRU Group.

events.title: North Korea denies links to Binance hack as researchers trace stolen billions
events.summary: North Korea denied U.S. allegations linking it to the $6.3 billion Binance hack, calling it a "grave political provocation." Hackers moved stolen funds through roughly 12,000 wallets and 40,000 transactions across 11 blockchains, with about $2.85 billion frozen or seized, according to Elliptic. North Korea-linked actors began moving stolen funds onto Solana after draining $500 million from Tron staging wallets, according to Chainalysis. North Korea rejected U.S. allegations linking Pyongyang to the estimated $6.3 billion Binance hack, calling the accusation a “grave political provocation,” according to state media. Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denounced the FBI's attribution of the attack to North Korea-linked hacking group TraderTraitor, Yohnap reported Tuesday, citing the state-run Korean Central News Agency. "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state', claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," Kim said, according to KCNA. She accused Washington of misleading international public opinion by portraying cybercrimes around the world as the work of North Korea. The denial comes as blockchain analytics firms trace billions of dollars in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance through thousands of wallets across multiple blockchains. Elliptic and Chainalysis said hackers linked to North Korea have used increasingly complex techniques to obscure the trail of the funds. In the first four days after the attack, the hackers used roughly 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains and conducted more than 40,000 transactions, Elliptic said in a report Monday. The activity appeared highly complex and automated, with an average of one new wallet used every 25 seconds. Much of the laundering activity initially took place on the Tron blockchain, where stolen funds were distributed across about 7,700 addresses before being moved to Ethereum through cross-chain bridges, according to Elliptic. At least $147 million had been transferred out of Tron through such bridges. The hackers also used decentralized exchanges to swap stolen stablecoins into cryptocurrencies that cannot be frozen by their issuers, including ether. Elliptic said roughly $786 million in stablecoins was converted before issuers including Tether and Circle froze the remaining assets. The laundering operation has since expanded to other blockchains, including Solana. Chainalysis said North Korea-linked actors had begun a new phase of laundering after moving more than $500 million through intermediary wallets on Tron. Elliptic also identified the first signs of bitcoin mixing, a technique designed to make transactions harder to trace. About 28 bitcoin, worth $2.2 million, had passed through 18 mixing transactions as of early Monday, the firm said. Despite the extensive movement of funds, about $2.85 billion — or 44% of exactly $6.43 billion stolen as reported by Elliptic — has been frozen or seized, while roughly $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly in bitcoin and ether. The firm said only a negligible amount of stolen funds appeared to have been cashed out, with most of the activity involving transfers or conversions between cryptocurrencies rather than exchanges into spendable funds. Elliptic said the laundering has moved slower than after the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, when North Korean hackers moved all the stolen ether within 10 days. It expects the remaining funds to be gradually converted into bitcoin and potentially cashed out through over-the-counter brokers and exchanges over several months. Binance, meanwhile, said withdrawals were resuming in phases and warned users against scammers offering to expedite transactions or help claim compensation. The exchange added it has covered about 95% of the affected amount, with the remaining 5% consisting of less liquid tokens that take longer to source. Binance said it was working with industry partners to acquire the remaining assets.

Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it’s facing growing pressure . The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth . However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear. When discussing how AI could potentially “contribute to revenue growth over time,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said: “On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.” Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate. Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business. During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple’s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company’s service business could expand into new territory. “We’ve also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store, and during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store,” Parekh said. “At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we’ve talked about before, and expect to see those continue into the summer quarter.” Parekh added: “As we move ahead, we expect services growth to to be between 8 to 9% [in the December quarter]. This outlook contemplates our best estimates on sequential headwinds, primarily from third-party licensing and the additional half percentage point of foreign exchange I just mentioned.” TechCrunch has reached out to Apple for more information and will update this story if it responds. events.title: Oil rises after report of US strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island
events.summary: Earlier, US and Iran signalled that diplomatic talks are continuing. Oil prices rose after a Wall Street Journal report said the US struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, lifting fears of wider conflict and oil supply disruption. Brent crude rose 0.5% to US$105.25 and WTI rose 0.5% to US$96.93, after Brent had fallen 7.63% the day before. Tehran said talks with the US continue, while Trump said a deal may still happen and the US-Iran war keeps pressure on Strait of Hormuz traffic and petrol prices. Oil prices rose in early Asian trade on Nov 3 after a report that the United States had struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, raising concerns about an escalation of the eight-month conflict and prolonged disruptions to Middle East oil supplies. Brent crude futures rose 48 US cents, or 0.5%, to US$105.25 a barrel by 1.04am GMT (9.04am Singapore time) while US West Texas Intermediate crude was up 47 US cents, or 0.5%, at US$96.93 a barrel. Brent crude futures settled US$8.66, or 7.63%, lower to US$104.77 a barrel on Nov 2. The United States struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing US officials. Some of the officials described the assaults as defensive in nature to prevent Iran from having the freedom to attack commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. “The report added a degree of risk premium back into the oil price. Just when markets were starting to price in a more diplomatic path, this reminder of ongoing military activity has flipped the tone,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. Meanwhile, Tehran said on Nov 3 that contacts between Iran and the US to end their war are continuing, after days of Iranian talks with Qatari mediators ended with altered proposals but no breakthrough. Trump raised doubts on Nov 3 about whether he would follow through on a threatened resumption of military strikes against Iran and said a deal with Tehran could happen. The US-Iran conflict began in late February has sharply reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which previously carried about a fifth of global crude oil and natural gas supplies. The Iran war is a leading cause of high petrol prices that are weighing on voters, and Trump is under pressure to end the conflict. Brent ended October at its highest in six months on concerns that the Middle East conflict could escalate again after the US midterm elections on Nov 3. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had granted the government certain authorities for peace talks. Additionally, the US will bring together delegations from Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10 and Nov 11 to discuss ending Moscow’s war against Ukraine, post-war security agreements and de-escalation. events.title: Torrens-to-Darlington labour company's contract terminated
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Torrens to Darlington Alliance terminates Career Boss contract Topic: Infrastructure Construction Industry A labour hire company has had its previously suspended contract on the Torrens to Darlington project terminated. ( Supplied: SA government ) The South Australian government has confirmed the Torrens to Darlington Alliance, tasked with delivering the $15.4 billion road upgrade, has cancelled its contract with Career Boss. SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said the dismissal was made on grounds that Career Boss have not "proactively disclosing" its involvement in a civil legal suit. State parliament's budget and finance committee has summoned the Alliance to answer questions over its due diligence processes. A labour hire company at the centre of a controversy surrounding alleged bikie threats has had its contract for the $15.4 billion Torrens-to-Darlington project terminated, the South Australian government has confirmed. Career Boss Australia, which had an agreement to supply workers to the South Road upgrade, had its contract suspended last month after it was revealed to be the subject of a civil dispute in the Supreme Court. The civil claim, lodged by businessman Robert Cammarano , alleged that motorcycle gang member Jamie Brown attempted to "coerce the transfer" of shares in the company, without Mr Cammarano's authority, by making "express threats of physical harm". The state government confirmed Career Boss's contract has been terminated by the T2D Alliance, a consortium of companies selected to deliver the major infrastructure project. A watered down ICAC gets called up for a full-bodied political scandal The government asking the state's anti-corruption watchdog to look at the $15.4 billion South Road project has been spun as a proactive step against potential bikie infiltration, but there is devil is in the detail. "The T2D Alliance wrote to Career Boss on October 18 to advise of the indefinite suspension of its labour hire agreement," an SA government spokesperson said. "Based on its legal advice, and as previously foreshadowed, the Alliance has terminated the contract." On Tuesday morning, SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said the dismissal was made on grounds that Career Boss have not "proactively disclosing" its involvement in a civil legal suit. "Point being that even though it's a civil dispute that's enough to give us grounds to be able to terminate them," he told ABC News Breakfast. The state treasurer Tom Koutsantonis said any contractors who had not declared changes to its management structures would also be terminated. He said the Department for Infrastructure and Transport would conduct integrity checks on contracts. "If we find any sudden changes in directorships, sudden changes in shareholdings, if there is controversy around the country, we will terminate for convenience," Mr Koutsantonis told 891 ABC Adelaide. Tom Koutsantonis says other companies would have their Torrens-to-Darlington contracts cancelled if shareholder or directorship changes are not disclosed. ( ABC News ) Alliance to appear before parliamentary committee On Monday, parliament's budget and finance committee passed a motion compelling the T2D Alliance, led by construction company John Holland, to appear before it on November 16. Opposition treasury spokesperson Ben Hood, who chairs the cross-party budget and finance committee, said on Monday the Alliance would be asked "what they knew and when, and when did the government alert them to this serious issue". Ben Hood says the parliamentary budget and finance committee will press the T2D Alliance on its due diligence processes. ( ABC News ) A representative of Mr Cammarano notified Transport Minister Joe Szakacs's chief of staff and Child Protection Minister Alice Rolls about the allegations at a meeting on September 11. Mr Szakacs's office passed on the claims to the South Road project team, which investigated the claims and found "no red flags" in the shareholdings. Police Minister Michael Brown last week told a press conference that all matters discussed in Ms Rolls's office were "already in the hands of police". Today, Mr Hood called on the government to sack Mr Szakacs and Ms Rolls. The premier and treasurer have both supported the decision to call the Alliance before the committee. The civil matter lodged by Mr Cammarano will return to court on November 16.

events.title: Supreme Court rejects DOJ's bid to block California from counting disputed ballots
events.summary: The Supreme Court denied the Department of Justice's bid to temporarily block California from counting the mail-in ballots of about 20,000 voters whom it suggested may not be U.S. citizens. The DOJ's petition to the Supreme Court came three days after the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals rejected the department's bid to overturn a federal district court judge's ruling that allowed the ballots to be counted. The petition comes a day before Nov. 3, Election Day. The Supreme Court could act on the petition at any time, but there is no deadline. The Supreme Court , in an order Monday evening, denied the Department of Justice's last-minute request to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from about 20,000 voters who it suggested may not be U.S. citizens. The one-sentence order came hours after the DOJ sought the injunction, and on the eve of Election Day. The Supreme Court did not explain its reason for the denial, and it did not note any dissents. The order came after Justice Elena Kagan presented the DOJ's request to the full court, which includes three appointees of President Donald Trump . The swift ruling was the latest courtroom blow to the Trump administration, which is engaged in multiple other legal fights related to the midterm elections. Those contests will determine which political party holds majorities in the House and Senate. Pollsters and analysts widely predict Democrats will make significant gains. On Sunday, a federal judge dismissed a DOJ lawsuit that sought to block Alaska election officials from immediately certifying the result of the U.S. Senate election there if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses that race by a margin that could be attributable to voter confusion about another candidate with his name. California Attorney General Rob Bonta told CNBC that Monday's denial by the Supreme Court was "completely appropriate, very expected." "This was a Hail Mary. It was baseless," Bonta said in a phone interview. "And the U.S. Supreme Court's response showed just how baseless it was." The attorney general noted both the speed of the Supreme Court's order and the fact that it was issued without the court first asking California to respond to the DOJ's request. "That is very rare," Bonta said, adding that, "We haven't seen this type of order where they didn't even ask for a response since 2018." The DOJ's application to the Supreme Court came three days after the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals rejected the department's attempt to overturn a federal district court judge's ruling that allowed the California ballots to be counted. That same day, another federal district judge in a separate case in California barred DOJ from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution for refusing to stop processing ballots or resisting other demands. During a hearing Monday in that second case, a DOJ lawyer admitted to Judge Trina Thompson that the lists of purported noncitizens on California's voter rolls had a "high error rate," MS NOW reported. But that lawyer also argued the errors are evidence of why election officials need to examine those rolls and make sure that everyone on them is a U.S. citizen. Trump focuses on Reflecting Pool in final public speech before midterms How the 2026 midterms could affect defense, healthcare, crypto and AI stocks DOJ asks Supreme Court to block California counting disputed mail-in ballots Solicitor General D. John Sauer, in his application Monday morning asking the Supreme Court to enjoin counting of the mail ballots, said, "In this case, this Office has been informed that the United States has identified more than 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered to vote in California based on publicly available information at the time that information was received, but who, in the United States' view, are likely not U.S. citizens." Sauer said "the United States is likely to succeed on the merits of its appeal" of the lower court ruling denying the DOJ's request. "The district court concluded that the United States lacks Article III standing to bring this suit, but the United States suffers a judicially cognizable 'injury to its sovereignty' from the 'violation of its laws,'" Sauer said in the petition. "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back." The DOJ sued California on Oct. 15 in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles. The complaint sought to prevent state election officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined." The DOJ previously gave Los Angeles County officials a thumb drive containing names of voters the department suggested could be noncitizens, who by law are barred from voting in federal elections.

events.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
events.summary: Kim Yo-jong, the sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un Published 3 November 2026, 00:56 GMT North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations an "absurd rhetoric". Kim Yo-jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage the country's public image. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack - which has been described as the largest in history. Pyongyang has also been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks - accusations that it has consistently denied. Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor. The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group. "The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said. Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack Published 2 days ago Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far Published 3 days ago The incident is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its economy. The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025. Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said. The country has consistently denied such claims. Kim Yo-jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace". Kim Yo-jong: North Korea's heir apparent? Published 16 June 2020 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Video, 00:02:32 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Published 16 June 2020 The BBC has contacted Binance for comment. Since the hack, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users. The company said initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals. Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack. Binance said on Sunday that its customers pulled out more than $3.6bn of assets from its exchange as it reopened after suspending all transactions in the wake of the hack. The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach. events.title: GOP's midterm blame game starts early
events.summary: Republicans don't know if they'll lose big or small on Tuesday, but they're already bracing for an epic blame game. Why it matters: Privately, Republicans acknowledge it's not a complicated version of Clue. The leading suspect: Mr. President, in the Oval Office, with an assortment of weapons — and one war. Returning Republican senators are unlikely to blame President Trump publicly. There's a price for that. And don't expect Trump to shoulder the responsibility. But do expect departing GOP lawmakers to take shots at Trump or his team, and Trump to fire back at Senate Republicans, whom he's never been shy about torching. The irony of Trump's second midterm: With Republicans privately resigned to losing the House, Trump can still credibly claim victory if they hold the Senate. "It's Donald Trump's midterms. He gets all the credit if we win. He gets all the credit if we lose," one national GOP strategist told Axios. The Iran war: From Alaska to Maine, Trump's decision to go to war with Iran — and the resulting spike in gas and diesel prices — has become a major political liability for Republican Senate nominees. "It's not tariffs … it's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said at a closed-door fundraiser in September, Axios reported last month . Tariffs: Trump's trade policies have compounded Republicans' affordability problems, particularly in farm country, where producers have faced higher costs and uncertainty over export markets. "We need to end this tariff war now," former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) , the GOP Senate nominee, said in an October campaign ad, breaking with Trump over his tariffs on Canada. Bad candidates: Trump's preferred nominees are also drawing blame, GOP strategists tell Axios. Paxton in Texas and Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina have forced Republicans to spend heavily defending races that should have been easier — and where the party had other options. Complacent incumbents: Sens. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) are facing accusations of "arrogance" and "laziness" from Republicans frustrated that their once-safe seats have become late-breaking battlegrounds — exactly the complacency NRSC Chair Tim Scott warned against. Weak governors: Underperforming gubernatorial nominees in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio threaten to drag down Republican Senate candidates. Vivek Ramaswamy, for example, saw his polling crater in the final weeks . Recruitment failures: Republicans couldn't persuade Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp to run for Senate, and in New Hampshire settled for their second-choice Sununu — former Sen. John Sununu — instead of his brother, former Gov. Chris Sununu. Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) landed marquee candidates in Alaska, Ohio and Iowa — though Michigan and Maine proved more difficult. MAGA money: Trump's political operation amassed an enormous war chest, but some Republicans complain the money arrived too late to rescue vulnerable candidates. Distractions: Trump's focus on D.C. construction projects, the Kennedy Center, Sen. Jon Husted's (R-Ohio) backside and the SAVE Act has frustrated Republicans desperate for a closing message focused on the economy. "Reflecting Pool presser was an interesting choice for closing message," another national GOP strategist said of Trump's Monday news conference.

events.title: Dodge announces return to NASCAR Cup Series beginning at Daytona 500
events.summary: Dodge is returning to the NASCAR Cup Series in 2027, a year earlier than initially expected LAS VEGAS -- Dodge is returning to the NASCAR Cup Series in 2027, a year earlier than initially expected. The Stellantis-owned Dodge brand announced its return at the SEMA Show in Las Vegas on Monday. Dodge will once again give the Cup Series four manufacturers, joining Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota in fielding entries to compete in a 36-race schedule that begins in mid-February and crowns a champion in early November. Kaulig Racing will use the Dodge Charger to field a two-car team beginning at the Daytona 500. AJ Allmendinger and Ty Dillon are expected to fill those seats. “Dodge’s return to the NASCAR Cup Series is a significant milestone for the sport,” NASCAR CEO Steve O’Donnell said in a statement. “This commitment speaks to Dodge’s belief in our sport and gives fans another reason to be excited about what’s ahead. “The partnership between NASCAR, (Ram CEO) Tim Kuniskis and the entire team at Stellantis has been nothing short of phenomenal. They have a deep passion for NASCAR and its ability to showcase the world’s top brands, and we can’t wait to see Dodge on the racetrack for the Daytona 500 and beyond.” Dodge raced in NASCAR through the 2012 season and left the same month it celebrated the Cup title with Brad Keselowski and Penske Racing. It was Dodge’s first Cup championship since Richard Petty’s sixth of seven titles in 1975. Dodge re-entered the NASCAR Truck Series with its Ram brand in 2026, with eyes on expanding to the premier Cup Series in 2028. Kuniskis vowed to be disruptive while doing it “unlike anyone else.” Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Kuniskis said Ram planned to tap into NASCAR’s estimated fan base of 20 million “and turn it into 80 or 100 million.” Kaulig had five trucks race this season, all of which are outside the top 10 in the series standings heading to the season finale at Homestead, Florida, this weekend. Normally, it would have taken Dodge two years to get ready for the Cup Series. But Dodge bypassed part of the timeline required to develop a new engine by partnering with Earnhardt Childress Racing to build Dodge-spec powerplants alongside its regular Chevrolet operations. Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota allowed that unique partnership in part because they believed a fourth manufacturer in NASCAR would be good for the overall health of the racing series. Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen. Those drones send their video over the air without any scrambling, so anyone with the right receiver can watch along. A Ukrainian unit can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before it hits. According to Defense News , the device is light, at about 10 ounces, which is less than half the weight of competing Ukrainian models, one of which weighs a couple of pounds. It also listens on the radio channels Russia’s newer Molniya drones started using for video in June. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine’s president, said in a June Facebook post cited by Defense News that “most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly.” He warned that putting too much trust in a detector could prove fatal. Beskrestnov has also warned that digital video could one day replace analog, which would blind receivers like this one. The New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, using Nvidia chips and emitting no signals . events.title: Asian stocks fall after US losses, oil holds drop
events.summary: In a sign some investors are looking to buy on dips, US stock futures gained. Japan is closed for a holiday. Asian stocks opened lower after a sell-off in US chipmakers deepened, overshadowing a plunge in oil prices on optimism over diplomatic progress towards ending the war in Iran. The MSCI Asia Pacific gauge dropped 0.5% with South Korea’s Kospi Index dropping more than 3%. In the United States, a gauge of chipmakers extended a three-day rout to 12% and the Nasdaq 100 sank 10% from its peak, entering a technical correction. In a sign some investors are looking to buy on dips, US stock futures gained. Japan is closed for a holiday. In Asia, attention will also turn to Chinese equities after the central bank said it will encourage financial institutions to make greater use of stock-support tools and optimise their terms as the authorities seek to bolster market stability. Apple’s shares fell in late US trading after the company delivered a mixed outlook to investors in its first quarterly report under chief executive John Ternus, with narrower profit margins overshadowing an upbeat sales forecast. Elsewhere, Anthropic disclosed a 12-fold increase in quarterly revenue while outlining plans to spend more than US$895 billion (S$1.14 billion) in the coming years. US oil held its losses early on Nov 3 after global benchmark Brent crude slumped 7.6% to close at US$104.77 a barrel as traders assessed signs of progress toward ending the conflict, a day before Americans vote in the midterm elections . A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar weakened on Nov 2 and longer-maturity Treasuries outperformed. Easing geopolitical tensions are lowering energy prices and inflation risks, yet the drop in crude has so far failed to revive appetite for technology shares as concerns over AI spending and stretched valuations persist . “Lower oil should be a tailwind for tech, but the fact that stocks could not hold the open even with crude plunging shows how little conviction is left even after last week’s carnage,” said Dave Mazza, chief executive at Roundhill Financial. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government had been granted more authority by the country’s supreme leader to pursue peace talks, while US President Donald Trump hinted at progress in negotiations. “They want to make a deal, and that could happen,” Trump told reporters in Washington. He added that oil prices had fallen because “it looks like that’s coming together very nicely” and “people found out about it”. Moments later, Trump mouthed “no” when a reporter shouted a question about whether he would resume military strikes on Iran after the Nov 3 midterm elections. Concerns over AI spending were also in focus as big technology companies returned to US bond markets to fund their investment plans. After an almost three-month borrowing drought, they are flooding back in. Oracle is selling US$10 billion of bonds alongside an equal amount of equity, while Meta Platforms is eyeing at least US$20 billion from a potential sale in multiple currencies. Microsoft sold US$25 billion of bonds on Nov 29 , its first US offering since 2017, while Alphabet tapped Europe’s bond market on Nov 2 for the second time in 2026 . The economic calendar adds another potential catalyst for the markets. US manufacturing activity picked up in October, supported by the strongest increase in production in nearly five years, while investors are looking ahead to a series of labour market reports. US job openings data due on Nov 3 are expected to show that listings edged higher in September, while weekly jobless claims due on Nov 5 are seen remaining near historically low levels. Economists expect the Nov 6 payrolls report to show job growth more than doubled to 65,000 in October, with the unemployment rate holding at 4.2%. “It’s going to be an extremely interesting week in the markets,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak. “We’ll have political issues to decipher as well as geopolitical ones. And growing doubts about AI investment returns will likely matter much more than historical patterns in determining the market’s direction going forward.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: Ebola outbreak kills more than 5,300 people in DR Congo
events.summary: The current Bundibugyo strain has spread to Kenya and Uganda, while two in Nigeria returned negative results. The death toll from the latest Ebola outbreak in Africa has surpassed 5,300, with the majority of cases recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC). The DRC is the epicentre of the latest outbreak, having declared its 17th – and largest – Ebola outbreak in mid-May. list 1 of 3 Uganda orders 21-day Ebola quarantine for citizens returning from DR Congo list 2 of 3 Attackers kill nurse, injure health worker responding to DRC Ebola case list 3 of 3 Incredible celebrations as last patient leaves a DRC Ebola centre According to data from the Africa CDC on Monday, the outbreak has killed 5,376 people: 5,372 in the DRC and two each in Kenya and Uganda. The Bundibugyo strain of the virus, responsible for the current outbreak, has infected some 10,444 people in the DRC, Uganda and Kenya, with a death rate of more than 50 percent. The virus has crossed borders several times in recent months. Neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 cases, almost all involving people who had travelled from the DRC, before being declared Ebola-free in August. Kenya recorded two deaths and nine infections in October, marking the first recorded cases of Ebola in the country. In Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, health authorities said two rounds of testing of two suspected cases in the northeast region confirmed the samples were negative. Abuja reported its first imported case in October, the first in more than a decade. It has no recorded deaths. In France, a single case involving a health worker returning from the DRC was reported in July. There are no approved treatments or vaccines to combat the rare Bundibugyo strain. In recent weeks, clinical trials have begun with the Ervebo vaccine, which has proved effective against the more common Zaire strain.

events.title: Apple says it's 'really hard' to predict when iPhone Duo supply will catch up to demand
events.summary: Apple said it can't predict when the iPhone Duo supply will catch up with demand, as customers who placed orders online face a long wait time. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Apple said it can't predict when the iPhone Duo supply will catch up with demand. Online delivery estimates for the iPhone Duo were pushed to late January 2027 after preorders opened. Memory shortages spurred by AI demand are constraining Apple's product supply and raising costs. If you're considering Apple’s first foldable iPhone , know that getting your hands on it could take a while. During Monday's earnings call , Sabih Khan, Apple's chief operating officer, told investors that the company couldn’t say when supply of its new iPhone Duo will catch up with demand. “So we're thrilled with the initial response on the iPhone Duo. iPhone Duo is constrained as of today,” Khan said in response to questions from a JPMorgan analyst. “The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible," Khan added. "But at this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance." The Duo was released on October 23, following preorders on October 16. The folding phone starts at $1,999 and opens like a book to reveal a 7.6-inch screen. Customers ordering online quickly faced a long wait, with delivery estimates slipping into late January 2027 shortly after preorders opened. The supply squeeze extends beyond Apple’s newest phone. Khan said that while strong demand constrained supplies of iPhones, Macs, and iPads during the September quarter, the biggest bottleneck was access to the advanced chipmaking technology used to produce Apple’s processors. “For the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory , as demand has been higher than what we expected,” Khan said. Apple is competing for memory with tech giants who are pouring money into AI data centers. Business Insider previously reported that Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron supply chips for both consumer gadgets and AI infrastructure , and as manufacturers shift production toward the booming AI market, device makers face tighter supplies and higher costs. The costs are already weighing on Apple. CFO Kevan Parekh said during the earnings call that, excluding tariff refunds, company and product gross margins would each have fallen about one percentage point sequentially, primarily because of higher memory costs. The shortages accompanied an otherwise strong quarter. Apple reported $114.5 billion in revenue, beating Wall Street’s estimates, with iPhone sales reaching $57.58 billion. events.title: Disney eyes thousands of layoffs, with managers asked to cut 20%
events.summary: The 20% in annual cost savings could come from job eliminations as well as from expense reductions. Disney is planning thousands of job cuts, with some managers told to find 20% annual cost savings through layoffs and lower spending. Chief executive Josh D’Amaro wants to use some savings for film and TV content, technology, theme parks and cruise ships. The cuts follow years of cost reductions across Disney, as traditional TV weakens and streaming growth slows; Disney had 231,000 staff worldwide last year. BURBANK, California – Walt Disney is moving towards thousands of job cuts, with the entertainment giant asking some managers to target 20% in annual cost savings, according to sources familiar with the matter. The savings could come from job eliminations as well as from expense reductions, said the sources, who asked to not be identified because the discussions are private. Some of Disney’s operations, from theme parks to TV network to the movie studio, will be affected disproportionately. Chief executive Josh D’Amaro aims to reinvest a portion of the savings into film and TV programming, technology, and the theme parks and cruise ship businesses, the sources said. The company has promised double-digit growth in adjusted earnings per share in the current fiscal year. A representative for Disney declined to comment. Disney has cut billions of dollars worth of costs and eliminated thousands of positions in recent years, with reductions impacting every division including ABC, Pixar, ESPN, the film studio and the experiences unit. The company had 231,000 people worldwide at the end of the last fiscal year. The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 1 that Disney was planning a restructuring of its TV division, and cuts at the company’s legal and global affairs unit. Other entertainment companies including Netflix, Sony Pictures Entertainment, and Skydance’s Paramount and Warner Bros. divisions have also cut jobs as revenue from traditional television declines and streaming subscriber growth slows. They also have to cope with more viewers tuning to social media, online videos and streaming services backed by tech giants like Amazon.com and Apple. At the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles in October, Disney president Dana Walden said: “There is a need to constantly evaluate how you’re structured and how big is the organisation. Technology set their sights on our business and we must survive and thrive and grow, and that’s what we’re going to do.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
events.summary: 'I've always looked in bins for clothes' Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket. On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters. Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it. Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come. During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist. Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor." Darryl Baker takes the clothes for herself and her children, and to sell In addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket. Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three. Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years. "I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever." Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds. "Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says. Jeff Ferrell sells some of what he finds, and gives away other items Jeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay. Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year". 'If something catches my eye, I'll grab it' While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online. Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on TikTok of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells. Millie Diamond turns dumped textiles and clothes into new outfits She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600. "I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it." Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes." 'I haven't bought shampoo for years' For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them. This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money." Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items. Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says. Charlotte Bayford gives some of her finds to charity But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law? Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita. "Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges. In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land , external . In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances. "In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says. "But there is no general rule that something is free to take simply because it has been put in a skip or bin.

events.title: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders , set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion. “I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack , on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said. On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life. “It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said. He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.” As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said. For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.” Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down. “It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.” But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out
events.summary: The new head of Apple says the company is working to get its new foldable iPhones available to more people after the $1,999 smartphone quickly sold out when it was released just over a week ago. John Ternus, who in September took over the role as Apple's chief executive from Tim Cook, said on Monday that he was "thrilled" at the early reaction to the iPhone Duo. While the costly phone, which sells for £1,999 in the UK, immediately sold out, some buyers have seen their screens crack . The phones are still in high demand and Sabhi Kahn, Apple's new chief operating officer, said the technology giant did not know when more Duos would be available. "At this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance," Kahn said during a call with financial analysts to discuss Apple's latest financial results. Apple executives did not mention during the call any issues with the iPhone Duo. But last week, the company said it would replace any phones that were impacted by an issue that caused a "small number" of the new phones to crack along the inside fold. Nevertheless, Apple said on Monday that over the last year it sold more iPhones globally than it ever has before. During the three months to 26 September, which did not include sales of the iPhone Duo that went on sale toward the end of October, Apple saw iPhone sales rise 17% to $57bn. Apple has boasted throughout the year that iPhone sales have been surging, despite the company's warnings that crucial components for the device, along with Mac computers and iPads, were constrained to the point of weighing down sales. Sales of Mac computers also grew during the quarter by 27%, hitting $10.7bn, another record for Apple. Overall sales at the company rose by 15% for the year, to $479bn. However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and Watch fell by 10% and 7%, respectively. Kahn noted during the call that most Apple devices are still seeing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with "advanced nodes." Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allows Apple's devices to operate more quickly, most of which Apple has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan. Khan said that such supply constraints are expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products. Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of Apple devices to store data like apps, photos, and text messages. Much of that memory storage runs through data centres which have seen a huge boom in demand for space as artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots and platforms, including those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, have become popular. As demand for memory has grown, storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple. Cook had earlier this year referred to the sudden increase in data centre costs that Apple was seeing as a "thousand year flood." It has led to the company raising prices on essentially all of its hardware products by around 20%. events.title: Hinge tests a cheaper plan as users become more fed up paying for dating apps
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Hinge is testing a cheaper subscription plan as its parent company Match Group looks for new ways to get users to pay for dating apps at a time when people are increasingly tired of subscriptions and, in some cases, dating apps altogether. During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call on Monday, Match Group said the new Hinge tier will include features such as additional filters and custom location boundaries, giving users more control over who they see and where they meet people. “It’s designed for women in particular, but also for price-sensitive users,” said Steve Bailey, chief financial officer of Match Group. “Remember that Hinge is one of the highest-priced products we have. The revenue per payer, for example, at Hinge is almost twice that of Tinder, around $30. It also has one of the lower payer penetrations. Its payer penetration is only slightly more than half that of Tinder.” Match Group didn’t share how much the new subscription will cost. TechCrunch has reached out to the company for more details. The move comes as dating apps continue to struggle to convince people to pay for services they’re growing tired of using. Between subscription fatigue, endless swiping, and frustration with the overall dating experience, users are increasingly questioning whether premium dating features are worth the money. Interestingly, Hinge is making this move despite being one of Match Group’s strongest performers. The app had a much better quarter than Tinder, with global monthly active users growing 12% year over year, direct revenue increasing 19%, and paying users rising 23% to 2.3 million. The app generated $221 million in direct revenue and had 2.3 million paid subscribers as of the end of the quarter. Direct revenue is money earned from subscriptions and in-app purchases. By comparison, Tinder brought in $480 million in direct revenue but experienced a slight 2% decline year-over-year, although it has 8.9 million paid users, a 4% decline from a year earlier. The lower-priced subscription could help Hinge build on that momentum by converting more users into paying customers without requiring them to spend as much upfront. The move also marks a shift in Hinge’s subscription strategy. In 2023, the company experimented with a more expensive tier aimed at users willing to pay extra for features designed to help them get more out of the app. Now, it’s testing whether a more affordable option could appeal to a broader audience. Still, cheaper subscriptions alone are unlikely to solve the bigger problem facing dating apps: user fatigue. Match Group says it’s seeing some signs of improvement, partly thanks to efforts to make its platforms feel less like traditional dating apps. Recent initiatives include Group Hangouts and Events , which offer users alternative ways to connect beyond the usual one-on-one matching experience. Match Group plans to ramp up those efforts in the fourth quarter. Another initiative on the horizon is real-time adaptive recommendations, which the company plans to begin testing in the fourth quarter. Announced during its CEO Connection presentation in September, the feature will allow Tinder to respond to user actions within seconds rather than hours, with the goal of making recommendations more relevant and personalized.
