events.title: Feeling isolated? Half of in-office workers describe their desk jobs as 'remote,' NY Fed survey finds
events.summary: Corporations have made the case that in-office work is critical to the collaboration and productivity that fuels business growth, but new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York pokes holes in this push, citing a "staggering share" of office-based workers who describe isolated roles. Researchers at the New York Fed find in a survey of college-educated workers that roughly half say in-office days are dominated by Zoom calls, Slack threads, and few actual interactions with colleagues. There are multiple reasons, the NY Fed research indicates, including fully remote colleagues, teams that are geographically sprawling, the technology tools that isolate workers, worker failure to comply with mandates, and employer failure to force adherence. Many workers across the U.S. are now back in-office a majority of the time, and they are feeling more isolated than ever. A recent survey from researchers at the New York Fed finds that roughly half of workers based in-office don't describe a daily experience on the job that matches the goal many corporate employers stated in upping in-person mandates. Whether three-, four- or five-day mandates , companies have cited the importance of creative collaboration for business productivity and growth, as well as mentorship opportunities. Yet workers surveyed by the NY Fed describe endless Zoom calls and Slacks, and little actual face time. "Days in the office often lack human contact," the researchers write. Specifically, 48.8% of survey respondents said they had no in-person meetings, either with teammates or non-teammates, on the days they were most recently in the office. There are a variety of reasons for the disconnect between in-office work mandates and actual experience. Roughly one in four workers are now fully remote, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data cited by the NY Fed, but they say that alone likely "understates the explosion in the experience of remoteness from colleagues." With teams being spread across more offices — an effect they say has become more pronounced in the post-Covid organization structure — many workers "no-showing" on mandates, and employers not enforcing mandates strictly, the result for in-office workers, according to the researcher, is that "they commute in just to take Zoom calls and answer Slack messages from their cubicles." The NY Fed paper, by NY Fed research economist Natalia Emanuel and University of Virginia economics professor Emma Harrington, concludes that "a staggering share of the workforce experiences this form of in-office remote work." The survey was conducted in September among a final sample of 1,835 college-educated workers. The researchers chose September, they say, to generate a "conservative estimate," since many companies push in-office attendance after summer ends, and the period between Labor Day and Thanksgiving has less remote work than holiday periods. The survey found that on in-office days, 70.6% of workers had at least one teammate who was not in the office; while half had no in-person meetings with all participants present, and over a third had neither in-person or hybrid meetings. "Amazingly, 37% of respondents reported that they had at least one meeting that was virtual, even though all the participants were in the same office that day. In short, many workers' commutes are simply yielding a new background for their Zoom calls," they write. They cite the example of Zoom CEO Eric Yuan , who said in 2023, "On Zoom, it's really hard. We cannot have a great conversation. We cannot debate each other well." But the researchers conclude, "if the debates in the office are also happening over Zoom, the benefits of the office may not be so large." The authors say that separate data on a Fortune 500 company employee base to which they had personnel data and badge swipe data shows that nearly half of corporate employees have at least one teammate who is out of the office on their in-office days. They say additional data from the BLS's American Time Use Survey similarly show that "Americans now spend more time physically alone on days they go into the office than they did before the pandemic." Other recent polling data from Gallup found worker sentiment to be at a 15-year low . The NY Fed authors caution that their research does not capture relationships with non-teammates, or worker's in-person interactions with clients, often outside the office. They also stress that workers who come to the office often cite seeing colleagues as a major draw. "But since the rise of remote work, the office increasingly fails to deliver this benefit," they write. They contend that the research has practical implications for both employers and employees. For one, the experience of remote work is much more widespread than understood, which could have many repercussions, including mental health issues. Second, organizational structure post-pandemic may not be optimal for making in-office mandates work.

events.title: 12 Skydance org charts reveal the execs who gained power in streaming, tech, and more after the Paramount-WBD merger
events.summary: Skydance has built a leadership team that includes David Ellison (center left), Ynon Kreiz (center right), and Andy Gordon (right). Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images Skydance CEO David Ellison has chosen which executives will help him take on Netflix and Disney. Paramount bought Warner Bros. Discovery in October, forming a Hollywood giant. Here are 12 organizational charts showing who holds power at Skydance. David Ellison has assembled a leadership team that he hopes will help Skydance compete with media powerhouses like Netflix and Disney. Skydance has unveiled the executives who will oversee its streaming, tech product, TV, sports, and advertising teams, weeks after completing the mega-merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery . Ellison's media giant informed employees of changes to their teams in recent weeks and sent a companywide email on Friday evening with links to memos detailing Skydance's new leadership. Business Insider previously reported on the new leaders for Skydance's product and tech teams under product chief Dane Glasgow , as well as its advertising unit under Jay Askinasi , the chief revenue officer for advertising. We're now publishing org charts for each of the teams outlined in Skydance's email blast to employees, some of which haven't been previously reported. It's the clearest picture yet of Ellison's leadership team as the media mogul tries to turn the new-look Skydance into a streaming leader — armed with content from HBO, studios Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures, CNN, CBS, and cable networks like HGTV, TNT, and MTV. Several top executives are out amid Skydance's leadership shake-up, including former Paramount streaming chief Cindy Holland and Warner Bros. film co-chairs Pam Abdy and Mike De Luca. Skydance's product and tech teams will be led mostly by Paramount execs, as former WBD leaders such as tech chief Avi Saxena and streaming product chief Tyler Whitworth will exit the company. However, Skydance's streaming business is headlined by longtime HBO chief Casey Bloys and a number of leaders from the WBD side. events.title: Latest national scam more sophisticated and 'just the tip of the iceberg'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Scammers target Kimberley travellers after international hotel booking data breach Travellers to the tourist town of Broome have been sent phishing scams. ( ABC Kimberley: Tom Forrest ) Customers across Australia are receiving scam messages following a data leak involving third-party booking provider RMS. Travellers to Western Australia's north say they were initially fooled by the phishing scams, as they included accurate details about upcoming accommodation bookings. RMS says investigations are continuing to assess the full scope and impact of the incident. A cybersecurity expert says scammers are using fear and "weaponising urgency", as holiday-makers and hotels in Western Australia's Kimberley are caught up in a global data breach. The breach, involving third-party booking provider RMS , saw hackers access names, booking information and contact details from across the country. Cameron Craig received a WhatsApp message regarding his upcoming booking at Cable Beach Club in Broome last week. The WhatsApp message sent to Cam Craig regarding his upcoming booking was a phishing scam. ( Supplied: Cam Craig ) The Sydney resident said the text requested him to provide his payment details through a link, or risk losing his booking. The message included details including the correct dates of his planned trip and his full name. Mr Craig said he clicked on the link and entered some of his credit card information but the session timed out. Cam Craig has been travelling to different destinations around Australia with his son. ( Supplied: Cam Craig ) He later realised the message was sent by an international number and the reservation code was different. Mr Craig said he alerted Cable Beach Club, which then notified guests. The resort has been contacted for comment. Kimberley Accommodation Group, which also uses RMS Cloud as its third-party reservation system, received reports from guests who had received similar phishing messages. Managing director Dannielle Hart said hackers used genuine booking details and asked customers to confirm card details or make a payment. Kimberley Accommodation Group owns venues across the region including the Kimberley Hotel in Halls Creek. ( Supplied: Facebook ) Ms Hart said the company was not able to comment on the number of customers impacted, or any customer financial losses at this stage. "Our advice to guests is not to respond to unexpected messages, click links, provide card details or make payments in response to communications about their booking," she said. RMS confirmed the unauthorised activity identified within the RMS environment had been contained yesterday. The provider said investigations were continuing as it assessed the full scope and impact of the incident. Rising costs approaching 'scary' levels for WA home owners Outback helicopter firm grounded over 'serious and imminent risk to safety' Serial rapist to be released despite 'high risk' to WA community Western Australia experienced a roller-coaster of weather in October Chief executive Adam Seskis said scams had become "increasingly sophisticated" in a statement, but confirmed credit card and payment details were not involved in the breach. Cybersecurity lecturer Brianna O'Shea said phishing scams had evolved over time to become more convincing. "Early attempts relied on generic mass emails with obvious spelling errors, poorly designed fake logos and simple web links," she said. Brianna O'Shea says more accommodation providers could be affected. ( Supplied: Brianna O'Shea ) The Murdoch University academic said third-party systems were a "lucrative target" for hackers. She said the breach could also have implications for FIFO workers and independent bed and breakfasts, where RMS was used to support bookings in temporary accommodation. "This is just the tip of the iceberg," Dr O'Shea said. "It'll be up to the owners to reach out to their customers and provide them with that support.

events.title: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date
events.summary: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Whether you intend to put its many tracking features to the test, or you simply want the longest battery life of any Apple Watch, it’s currently on sale for $699.99 ($100 off) in multiple colors at Amazon , matching its all-time low price. Apple Watch Ultra 4 Where to Buy: $799 $699 at Amazon Powered by Apple’s new S11 chip (also in the Series 12), the Apple Watch Ultra 4 delivers faster performance than the last-gen version, plus a handful of new Apple Intelligence features. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. An upcoming Siri Recap feature will be able to create summaries of conversations for later reference. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12 . Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon , just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot . The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off) , while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off) . You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off) . Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon . The versatile tool can help with repairing stuff, or putting together decorations. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it. The stapler comes with 1,200 fasteners.

events.title: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1A on Monday, (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print. The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI). RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals. To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more. Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’” When the term RSI became popular earlier this year , many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove. But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own internal definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below): In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified , and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred. For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data. However, Anthropic also said in the filing that none of its models have crossed this RSI threshold yet and that it is promising to keep humans in the R&D process for the foreseeable future. “We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.” Skeptics might point out that an S-1 functions as both disclosure and marketing, and that claims of being close to a model so powerful that it can build itself could fall into the latter category. Nevertheless, there’s no question that Claude’s capabilities, especially in terms of coding, math, and cybersecurity, have grow in leaps and bounds this year. If Anthropic thinks the possibility of RSI is close, maybe we should believe it and act — perhaps govern — accordingly. events.title: Sweetgreen managers could earn more than $200,000 a year under a new pay plan, as the salad chain bets higher pay will lift sales
events.summary: A fast-casual chain favored by the office lunch set is sweetening compensation packages for managers at its restaurants. Starting next year, Sweetgreen managers will be eligible to earn more than $200,000 a year if they meet certain milestones set by the company. The new offering, which will be paid through a mix of base salary and equity, is intended to empower managers who contribute to the business’s success, and “[share] those wins with those that are driving it,” co-founder and CEO Jonathan Neman said. Under the new incentive plan, Sweetgreen managers (known as “head coaches”) will see their base pay increase by up to 45% if they work at restaurants with higher sales volume. The company declined to specify how high sales need to be to meet this threshold. When restaurants outperform their sales goals, managers will get a revenue share bonus from the upside, with the percentage increasing based on their tenure in the business. Managers can also continue to receive equity in the company based on their performance. Base salary increases will go into effect in Q1 of 2027, while head coaches will start to receive bonuses based on store performance on a quarterly basis from Jan. 1, 2027, according to Sweetgreen. How Sweetgreen is making the case for higher pay. Higher labor and related costs cut into Sweetgreen’s earnings for the quarter ending in June, accounting for 29% of revenue, up from 28% the year prior. Same-store sales and restaurant profits also declined that quarter compared to 2025. (Sweetgreen will report Q3 earnings on Nov. 5.) Amid such economic pressures, Neman recognized that investing in additional compensation for managers “is definitely a bet.” “But the data supports that if we’re able to attract, retain, and incentivize better head coaches, that they will drive higher sales and better margins,” he added. Neman noted that while Sweetgreen is investing some money upfront to raise managers’ base salaries, most of the investment is contingent on their stores meeting certain performance targets. “Typically the company would take more of that upside. Now we’re sharing in that upside with our team, but…we think that’s a good trade,” he said. Zoom out. Sweetgreen isn’t the first fast-casual chain to bet big on its managers. Chipotle announced in 2021 that workers in its highest general manager position could earn $100,000, on average, as it sought to hang onto workers in a tight labor market. The burrito business doesn’t appear to have taken a financial hit from this move, as its restaurant operating margins have stayed between 23% and 26% in recent years. More than 85% of general managers at Chipotle were promoted internally in 2025, according to its 2026 proxy statement. Neman said Sweetgreen took inspiration from chains like In-N-Out Burger, which recently confirmed that store managers can earn more than $200,000 on average, and Raising Cane’s, which grants monthly bonuses to managers based on sales, and said in 2024 it paid managers up to $175,000 annually. In addition to business performance, Sweetgreen will be looking at metrics like team member turnover, “head coach stability” (i.e. whether managers stay in their stores), quality and experience scores, and internal mobility to determine whether this incentive program is working, Neman said. events.title: NASA administrator tells the internet to stop criticizing copilot of crashed Learjet 60
events.summary: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman defended the woman copilot in the private plane crash in Florida. Oliver Contreras/AFP/Getty Images NASA chief Jared Isaacman defended the copilot in the Learjet crash in South Florida. A recording of the copilot's mayday calls preceding the crash sparked reactions online. "She was doing her job, communicating with ATC right to the end in a terrifying situation," he said. The leader of NASA is standing up against online criticism of the copilot in the Learjet 60 private plane that crashed in South Florida on Sunday. Jared Isaacman , the NASA administrator who is also a pilot, said he was speaking out in a personal capacity to address some of the reactions to the crash, which killed nine people. Authorities have not said what caused the crash, and the identities of the pilots and the passengers have not been released, but a recording of a female copilot's mayday calls in the moments preceding the crash sparked reactions online. "I feel compelled to post after seeing commentary about the Lear 60 crash, from missile strikes to DEI to critiquing this poor woman's final radio calls," Isaacman wrote in an X post on Monday. "That last part is what I find most troubling." "She was the second-in-command (SIC), and while she was empowered to point out mistakes as part of good crew resource management, she was doing her job, communicating with ATC right to the end in a terrifying situation. She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die," he continued. Isaacman said he understood the public interest but that many factors remained unknown, including "the aircraft's maintenance history, whether there was a structural failure, if any failure was induced by turbulence, overspeed, or overcontrol, or everything happening in that cockpit." He also said that the charter industry often hires early-career commercial pilots who need to gain experience alongside airline-qualified pilots, adding the copilot would still have the necessary training and qualifications. "Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts. Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories," he added. Roads are closed after a jet crashed in Florida on Sunday. Saul Martinez/Getty Images The plane had departed from Austin and was en route to the Bahamas when it entered Florida on Sunday. It descended 27,000 feet in about a minute before crashing into the ground, data from FlightRadar24 showed. Officials from the National Transportation Safety Board have said that weather is a major focus of the investigation into the crash. South Florida experienced widespread thunderstorms on Sunday, with aviation weather data showing heavy rain, low visibility, and moderate turbulence. Mark Stephens, a retired Delta Air Lines pilot , told Business Insider that weather could have played a role and warned against jumping to place blame on the pilots. "Everybody's jumping to conclusions about the pilot; it's like Monday morning quarterbacking. 'Oh, it's her fault,'" Stephens said. "Well, that's a load of crap. And she wasn't even the captain." events.title: Claude's new AI report card tool gives companies a closer look at costs — and flags 'inefficiencies'
events.summary: Anthropic has launched "smart reports" for Claude Enterprise. Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Companies using Claude Enterprise can get a closer look at their employees' AI usage with a new tool. Claude's "smart reports" not only show how teams use AI — including flagging "off-topic" sessions — but also what it costs. Anthropic says the reports "should not be used for evaluating individual performance." Anthropic is giving corporate customers a new way to scrutinize how their employees use its artificial intelligence chatbot Claude — and how much the AI work is costing them. The AI giant announced "smart reports" for Claude Enterprise users last week. The interactive chart tool is designed to analyze a sample of a team's AI session transcripts and group work into categories, including the types of tasks employees use Claude for, the outputs it generates, and the cost. The reports can also — and this is the part that is undoubtedly making teams sit up straight — flag "inefficiencies" to employers, including sessions that produced "no work value" or were "personal or off-topic," according to a Claude support webpage. Anthropic's "smart reports" tool Anthropic In effect, the smart reports tool offers companies equipped with Claude Enterprise something of an AI report card. Each organization can run up to 10 reports a month at no charge. One caveat that Anthropic highlighted as "important" in its support documentation: "Smart reports help you understand adoption and plan your investment in Claude. They aren't designed and should not be used for evaluating individual performance or making employment decisions." To produce a report, bosses can select a team, a time range of up to the last 28 days, the Claude products to include, focus areas for analysis, and any custom questions they want Claude to answer while analyzing the transcripts. "Claude then reads a sample of transcripts in that scope, groups them into workstreams and types of outputs, attaches spend to each group, and writes up what it found," the Claude support page says. According to Anthropic, sessions involving "restricted topics" — including personal conversations related to race, ethnicity, health, legal issues, union activity, and political or religious views — are "used only for aggregate analysis and don't include summaries." "Personal conversations also don't include individual sessions or names," the Claude support page says. An Anthropic spokesperson told Business Insider on Monday that smart reports do not show employees' names by default, but those settings can be changed. "A report groups a team's work with Claude into workstreams and shows what each one cost. Opening a workstream shows short session summaries, not transcripts," the spokesperson said. The spokesperson added, "An organization's owner can turn on a setting that allows names to be shown with those summaries. When that setting is turned on, names remain hidden until someone viewing the report chooses to reveal them, and each reveal is logged." Sessions Claude identifies as personal or off-topic won't appear with names, the spokesperson said. The launch of smart reports comes as many companies are trying to get a handle on AI costs and measure any productivity gains. Some are wrestling with how broadly to let employees use AI tools . Bloomberg reported Monday that Goldman Sachs recently limited access to Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub coding tools to engineers only after assessing productivity and risk concerns. The move reportedly rankled some Goldman traders who used the tools for their work. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Pentagon is investigating if rogue freezers are tied to cyberattacks in France. Another wave of hacks is hitting supermarkets across Europe
events.summary: Lightning may not strike the same place twice, but hackers appear to be targeting the same systems, as refrigeration becomes the next frontier for cyberattacks. About 20 refrigerator systems in supermarkets Delhaize, Carrefour and Spar experienced outages late Sunday night into Monday morning, Stephan Moelans, CEO of refrigeration installer Sabcobel, told Belgium’s Belga News Agency on Monday. Swedish daily newspaper Aftonbladet reported similar outages in Swedish chains ICA and Coop, with outages also reported in Luxembourg and Estonia. “We began mobilizing technicians at 1 a.m. to get the situation under control,” Moelans said. “We’ve been working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network.” He noted this wave of suspected cyberattacks mirrored the hacking of hundreds of French supermarkets last month, when the temperature of grocery stores’ refrigerators and freezers was raised, spoiling food and causing small fires. Those supermarkets included 80 Carrefour locations, about 24 Monoprix locations, and 150 Intermarche locations. Hackers left the same calling card in the latest attacks. One location of a Swedish grocery store, ICA Kvantum Sjöbo , said in a Facebook post that its refrigerators and freezers were hacked overnight, and the temperature of the devices were set to 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 degrees Fahrenheit. As a result of the rising temperatures, the location has to throw away the stored food. “We are extremely sorry to have to throw out all this food, but we see no other way,” the store wrote. “Now we are focusing on getting everything back on track.” ICA told Fortune the outages were in a limited number of stores using an external supplier with networks outside of ICA’s main network, but the company’s central systems were unaffected. The European Commission did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment but said in a statement that the incident shows how much cyberattacks can “disrupt services, affect businesses and directly affect citizens’ daily lives.” In August, half a dozen U.S. military commissaries experienced a similar refrigeration system outage , and the Pentagon is now investigating both the French supermarket outages as well as the commissary outages as a potential cyberattack. Why refrigeration systems are hackers’ next big target Cybersecurity experts said it was only a matter of time before refrigerators and freezers became the target of hackers. As more appliances become internet-connected, they become more accessible to outside agents, and therefore more susceptible to potential network breaches, Nadiya Kostyuk, an assistant professor at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy and Technology, told Fortune. “A lot of these devices have a lot of really cool features, but the security is not the first priority for them,” Kostyuk said. “Hopefully future inventions will come with more security in mind when it comes to the design, and the existing ones also will be revisited to incorporate all the potential vectors of the cyberattacks.” Refrigerators in particular tend to use the same devices across commercial chains, meaning finding a weak point in one can expose vulnerabilities across other systems, according to Christopher Whyte, an associate professor of homeland security and emergency preparedness at Virginia Commonwealth University. The practical features of refrigerators and freezers also make them a target because outages can result in direct and immediate financial consequences, Whyte said. After the cyberattacks in France, two supermarkets, Intermarché and E.Leclerc, reported about €270,000, or $300,000, in combined damages , according to local news outlet Sud Ouest . “You can’t unspoil food or other products from these freezers. It’s just euros and dollars down the drain,” Whyte told Fortune . While there’s no official proof these outages are connected, Whyte noted the proximity of the French and U.S. outages to one another as well as the similarities in the systems impacted. “You’d be silly not to be suspicious,” he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Apple outpaces sales expectations as it continues to battle surging memory chip costs
events.summary: Apple beat its quarterly financial expectations in Chief Executive John Ternus’s first earnings report since taking over Tim Cook’s post in September, though the company continues to be pressured by a surge in memory chip costs. The iPhone maker posted revenue of $114.5 billion in its fiscal fourth-quarter, up 12% year-over-year and above Wall Street targets of $113.4 billion. Its profit was $30.7 billion, or $2.10 per share. Ternus extolled the company’s expanding lineup of products during a conference call with analysts, including the all-important iPhone business, which grew 17%, to $57.58 billion, in the three months ending on Sept. 26. Apple said that it expects overall revenue to grow between 7% and 10% year-over-year in the current, holiday quarter, seasonally Apple’s strongest quarter of the year. The forecast suggests a range of $153.8 billion to $158.2 billion, compared to the $153.2 billion that analysts were expecting. But the outlook for profit margins seems to have left investors cold. Shares of the $4.9 trillion company fell as much as 4% in after hours trading on Monday, before recovering some ground to trade down 2.7%. Many investors have been watching the impact of rising memory chip prices on Apple and how it will weigh on profit margins. To help offset what Ternus described on Monday’s call as an “unprecedented” situation in the memory market, Apple has raised prices across its product line. Apple’s gross margin weighed in at 47.9% in the recently ended quarter, landing near the high end of its forecast range and above the 47.2% gross margin it posted in the year-ago period. But Apple’s chief financial officer, Kevan Parekh, said tariff refunds lifted the gross margin by roughly one percentage point; without them, it would have been lower. For the current, holiday quarter, Apple said it expects gross margins to decline, ranging between 45% and 46% due to rising memory costs and some costs associated with ramping up its Siri AI service. Ternus has marked his first couple of months at Apple with a slew of product releases that have helped the engineer savant show off Apple’s latest innovations and ease into the new job. That has included the September launch of the foldable iPhone Duo, followed by new home products, and last week’s unveiling of Apple’s first touch screen MacBook Pro. Ternus said in a written statement that iPhone revenue reached a September quarter record and Services posted an all-time high, “capping off our best fiscal year ever.” “We’re closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet,” he said. “Together with the all-new Siri AI, it’s an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season.” Apple’s Services revenue, which includes iCloud, the App Store, and other services, was $31.57 billion, up roughly 10% year-over-year. But sales in the company’s iPad business and its wearables business both declined. Apple’s earnings followed financial reports from its Big Tech peers. Meta , Microsoft , Google, and Amazon all revealed their latest earnings in the last two weeks. While the companies generally had positive results, shares in the Nasdaq Composite have sunk in recent days as investors have weighed Big Tech’s positive growth, especially in cloud-computing demand for AI services, against the hundreds of billions Microsoft, Amazon, and others are spending in AI infrastructure. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: S&P 500 ends down; Apple dips ahead of quarterly report
events.summary: Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City on Oct 30, 2026. The S&P 500 ended lower on Nov 2 as oil prices tumbled on optimism about a potential US-Iran peace agreement, while Apple shares dipped ahead of the iPhone maker’s quarterly report and investors awaited the US midterm elections on Nov 3. Longer-dated US Treasury yields moved lower and Brent crude prices fell as Iran indicated it was open to peace talks after eight months of war in the Middle East that have kept energy prices elevated and stoked inflation. Apple closed down by 1.5% ahead of its quarterly report. After the closing bell, Apple posted results that beat expectations, driven by early demand for its iPhone 18 Pro line-up and price increases that helped offset rising memory-chip costs. The shares were close to flat after the report. Amazon rallied 2.2%, while Tesla climbed 1%. The Dow finished higher on Nov 2, and early in the session, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq gained on the first day of trading in November. In October, the Nasdaq fell 5.3% for the month following a sell-off on Oct 30 related to worries that massive spending on AI infrastructure is outpacing near-term cash generation. Jake Dollarhide, chief executive of Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma, warned that investors remain concerned about the pace of AI spending. “Companies have to realise there’s a limit to how much they spend and what it means in terms of enhanced shareholder value. At some point, there is no additional value-add, just expense,” he said. The S&P 500 declined 0.51% to end the session at 7,541.40 points. The Nasdaq dropped 1.07% to 25,164.32 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.41% to 51,983.98 points. Seven of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes rose, led by consumer discretionary, up 2.25%, followed by a 1.83% gain in materials. The energy index fell 4%. Volume on US exchanges was relatively heavy, with 18.8 billion shares traded, compared to an average of 17.3 billion shares over the previous 20 sessions. Oracle dropped almost 9% after regulatory filings showed the cloud infrastructure provider plans to raise US$20 billion (S$26 billion) through a debt and share sale, highlighting investor concerns that debt-funded spending could become harder to justify as borrowing costs rise. Sentiment towards AI-related companies remained shaky after an amended IPO filing showed Anthropic’s net loss narrowed sharply in the third quarter, while revenue jumped ahead of a potential listing. Marvell Technology tumbled 13% after the chipmaker said it was buying optical components maker Lumentum in a US$115 billion all-stock deal, including debt. Lumentum dropped 18.6%. Intel fell 8.8%, adding to a 29% drop on Oct 30 after it forecast quarterly revenue below market estimates and said it did not expect positive cash flow this year. Palantir dipped 3.1% ahead of its quarterly report after the bell. Chipmaker AMD fell 7.5% ahead of its quarterly report on Nov 3. S&P 500 third-quarter earnings are on track to climb over 30% year-over-year, with AI heavyweights accounting for much of that jump, according to LSEG data. Following Wall Street’s recent decline, the S&P 500 is valued at about 19 times expected earnings, its lowest valuation since 2023. Investors were also focused on US midterm elections on Nov 3, which will determine whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress away from President Donald Trump’s Republican Party. Polls suggest Democrats are likely to win the House of Representatives . The outcome in the Senate is less clear. Republicans controlled both chambers of Congress during the first two years of Trump’s latest term. Meanwhile, data showed that US manufacturing activity picked up in October amid solid domestic demand. Advancing issues outnumbered falling ones within the S&P 500 by a 2.2-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 35 new highs and one new low; the Nasdaq recorded 112 new highs and 323 new lows. REUTERS

events.title: In-N-Out may expand to these 3 states next, owner Lynsi Snyder says, as the 445-location burger chain pushes farther east
events.summary: In-N-Out may be putting a little extra mustard on its expansion plans . The California-based burger chain is considering putting down palm tree roots in three new states—Arkansas, Mississippi, and Oklahoma—potentially expanding the pool of people who insist on explaining “Animal Style” to you. The burger wars’ eastern theater: In-N-Out, which got its start just outside of Los Angeles in 1948, may be as synonymous with the West Coast as surfboards and clean IPAs, but: It has 445 restaurants in 10 states (including 289 in CA). It went farther east than ever last year, moving into Tennessee. It plans to open a New Mexico location next year. Because the Tennessee In-N-Outs get supplies shipped from Texas, it could make sense to also open locations in Arkansas, Mississippi, and Oklahoma, since they’re already in the path of the distribution network, Lynsi Snyder, the chain’s owner and president , told actor Terry Crews in a dream we had an interview recently posted to the company’s website. The chain also plans to expand in California. Appetite for regional burger chains: In-N-Out saw domestic sales grow about 10% last year compared to 2024, trailing only New York-based Shake Shack among US burger chains, the Wall Street Journal reported in June, citing Technomic.— BC This report was originally published by Morning Brew . events.title: Intel foundry push faces critical test after stock's 45% plunge in October
events.summary: Intel's 29% drop on Friday left the stock down 45% in October, its worst month on record, according to FactSet. Intel sees the global market for server CPUs growing fivefold to $200 billion in the next five years, but the softening PC market is hurting legacy revenue. Intel is redirecting some 18A capacity in Oregon fabs to make Intel 3 chips for its server CPUs As Intel comes off its steepest stock drop since the 1970s due to a worsening outlook for the PC market, the chipmaker is facing intensifying pressure to get its flailing foundry business off the ground. It's been an elusive task for Intel. The company has spent half a decade, and a good chunk of its $108 billion in capital expenditures over that stretch, trying to challenge Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. But it still has no marquee customer for its most advanced chips and is primarily manufacturing chips for its own products. Wall Street is losing patience. After the U.S. government took a 10% stake in Intel in August 2025, and Nvidia followed with a $5 billion investment, the stock started to shoot up, ultimately rising sixfold over 10 months before peaking in June. Intel was finally finding its niche in the artificial intelligence boom, delivering central processors used for agentic AI, while optimism simultaneously grew over its fab aspirations. Intel's story took a dramatic turn for the worse on Thursday, when the company said revenue this quarter will be between $1 billion and $2 billion shy of analysts' estimates as the PC market continues to suffer from soaring costs for memory and other components. Intel still counts on its PC segment for roughly half of its revenue, and consumers are increasingly choosing not to upgrade. The stock plummeted 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s, capping off a 45% plunge in October, the steepest monthly drop on record, according to FactSet. It's down another 8% in Monday trading. Intel's investments in the future are supposed to be paying off. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said he sees the global market for server processors increasing as much as five times over the next five years to about $200 billion. Intel's data center business recorded 78% growth in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.3 billion. However, Intel said it can't make enough chips to fill demand, pointing to industrywide supply constraints for wafers, substrates and memory, many of the same factors hurting PC sales. That's forcing Tan to make some hard choices. In response to the capacity shortage, Intel said it's shifting some Oregon factory capacity away from making wafers for its advanced 18A chips to make more wafers on an older node, known as Intel 3, used for its data center products. Intel is counting on 18A to attract outside foundry customers, so the shift in resources could complicate that effort. David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who previously spent almost three decades on Intel's board, said the latest moves are hardly welcoming to prospective foundry customers. "They're concerned that if Intel doesn't actually have excess capacity beyond its own demand, that they're just not a very credible supplier," Yoffie said. If it doesn't find a large-scale foundry customer within a year, "then the stress on Intel's economics are going to start to show even more dramatically," he said. An Intel spokesperson said in a statement that "customer confidence in Intel Foundry is built on execution." "We're delivering against our technology roadmap, demonstrating strong performance with 18A and progress on 14A," the spokesperson said, referring to the company's forthcoming chips. "We continue to see strong engagement with customers and remain focused on earning their business through consistent execution." Intel is best known for its industry-leading central processing units, or CPUs. Graphics processing units from Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices ruled the early AI boom because they excel at handling large workloads for training models and inference for chatbots, while CPUs like Intel's are crucial for running the virtual machines used by agentic apps like Meta 's Muse. As one of the only companies in the world capable of manufacturing and packaging the advanced chips it needs for its own products, Intel has "more control over their destiny" than most chipmakers, Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities, said in an interview. "If you don't have enough capacity, you leave revenue and money on the table," Klein said. Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, who was ousted in late 2024, spent his four-year tenure at the company aggressively pursuing foundry investments to catch up after delays on its 7- and 10-nanometer technologies, advanced process nodes that aim to fit more transistors on each chip. Tan has taken a more cautious approach, limiting spending until customer demand is locked in. He said on Thursday that "a couple customers" would be announced in the coming two quarters.

events.title: Nine engineers, 1,211 code updates in a day: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork
events.summary: Nine engineers, 1,211 pull requests in a day: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork Plus a case study where we put everything together by moving our runtime from Python to Rust while live. In January of this year, a small team at Microsoft set out to build Copilot Cowork , an agentic execution layer that performs multi-step workflows on a user’s behalf. That result brings the powerful AI-assisted tools and capabilities developers have today to everyday knowledge workers, all with Work IQ , Microsoft 365 security and governance, cloud execution, and Microsoft’s multi-model architecture. This is the story of how the team took Copilot Cowork from an empty repo to worldwide GA in about four and a half months, then moved its runtime from Python to Rust while it was live. Agents wrote most of the code. Ways of working changed along the way, and the practices other teams can adapt to build like a frontier development team: moving fast while keeping reliability, security, and cost in view. On October 21, nine engineers merged 1,211 pull requests into the main branch of the Copilot Cowork backend. That number would have sounded absurd to the team in January, when a handful of us made the first commit to an empty repo. Agents wrote most of the code, but engineers remained responsible for defining the work and judging the results. Our small team wrote clearer specs, set architecture and security boundaries, and focused its review on higher-risk changes, production impact, and cases where checks or reviewers disagreed. Automated checks and agent reviewers examined every change. Agents could propose changes, but they could not decide what was allowed to happen. We didn’t plan on working this way. But every few weeks, the agents got better, part of our process stopped working, and we adapted. Six practices emerged from those changes. They cover how we specify work, run agents within clear boundaries, test our checks, preserve what the team learns, shape the codebase for parallel work, and set limits on automated loops. They aren’t a recipe for matching our PR count. They are lessons other teams can adapt to build like a frontier development team while keeping reliability, security, and cost in view. We’ll end with the project that puts those practices to the test together: moving the live runtime from Python to Rust. Lesson 1: Write the spec before the code The first commit was made on January 13. From the start, agents wrote the code. In the first weeks, we learned that the agent was rarely what slowed us down. The bottleneck was not knowing exactly what we wanted. A vague request got us code that looked reasonable, survived a quick read, and then did the wrong thing. Fixing it took longer than writing a proper request would have in the first place. So we adopted a rule that still stands today: no code without a markdown spec written first. The spec covers three things: A good spec saves far more time than it costs upfront. But a weak one leads to rework a few days later. The faster agents became at implementation, the more important it became for us to be precise about intent, requirements, and what good looked like. Many of our specs start out spoken. Someone talks through a feature, and an agent turns that into a first draft of the spec, which the human then edits. I think this did more for our speed than any single model upgrade. We launched Copilot Cowork to our first enterprise customers in the Frontier program on March 30. Lesson 2: Run narrow agents inside clear boundaries The next step was running more than one agent at a time. Each works in its own copy of the repo, on one task, from one spec. One agent became five, and five became dozens. Merged PRs per month went from 257 in January to 2,754 in May. Our busiest week before GA had 783. Parallel work went better than we expected for two reasons: Narrow tasks: An agent with one well-defined task makes fewer mistakes than one asked to do a lot at once. Picking the model per task: We treated model choice as a quality-and-cost tradeoff, not a race to use the cheapest model. Some tasks warranted stronger reasoning; for others, a faster, less expensive model gave us the right balance. In Copilot Cowork, the model runs in a container without user credentials. A trusted host outside the container handles identity, policy, approvals, and tools, and every Microsoft 365 operation goes through the host. We didn’t want to limit what the agent could attempt, because a heavily restricted agent isn’t very useful . With our architecture, the model can plan and ask for anything, and the host decides what actually happens. That separation lets us increase the number of agents working in parallel without giving the model credentials or direct authority over operations. The host still applied identity, policy, approvals, and audit at the point of execution. Building that in at the start was much easier than adding it later would’ve been. It also helped in a way we didn’t plan for. The agent only talks to the host through a defined interface, so we could later replace the entire host without changing the agent—which we did when we migrated to Rust. We reached worldwide general availability on June 16, about four and a half months after the first commit, with several models and 16 plugins. Lesson 3: Make checks prove they checked something With agents writing most of the code, nine people couldn’t read every change, and waiting for a human review was becoming the slowest step for every PR. Several engineers each built their own review bot, modeled on how they review code themselves, and the bots competed. When one bot caught a problem another had missed, the bot that missed it got a new rule. Over time, each reviewer built up a large set of rules learned from its own misses. Each one has now been through at least10,000 generations; in each generation, the reviewer runs reviews, then reflects on what it missed and gets better at reviewing code. Today, a useful first review usually arrives within several minutes of a pull request being opened. On a sample of recent merged PRs, the median was about four and a half minutes. Slower, more specialized passes follow: One walks the call graph, looking for code that isn’t wired up and for tests that would still pass if the change were reverted One looks at operational problems like restart safety, metrics, and stale docs One reads every changed file end to end One checks behavior against the code being replaced The author gets quick feedback while the change is still fresh, and the detailed reading still happens. Of course, reviewer agents can still miss things. Once, a group of reviewer agents read a change in one of the most sensitive parts of the product. Each had been told to try to break it, and none found a problem. People on the team then read the same diff and found four blocking issues, all of which were fixed before it merged.

events.title: Palantir posts ‘highest-ever’ revenue growth rate of 96% as investors’ patience rests on a hair trigger
events.summary: Palantir Technologies said Monday that third quarter revenue rose 96% year over year to $2.3 billion, surpassing last year’s 63% growth and $1.2 billion in revenue. Chief financial officer David Glazer called it the “highest-ever” reported year-over-year growth rate as well as the highest ever sequential revenue growth rate of 20%. Moreover, quarterly revenue crossed the $2 billion milestone marker for the first time. It raised its full-year revenue forecast to between $8.53 billion and $8.534 billion, roughly 91% growth, from as high as $8.2 billion a quarter ago. However, investors didn’t seem swayed immediately. In after-hours trading shares began to climb, rising about 1.5% immediately after the figures were published, before dropping 3.6%. In the third quarter, Palantir reported adjusted and GAAP earnings per share of 44 cents. That compares to third quarter 2025 , when adjusted EPS was 21 cents and GAAP EPS was 18 cents. Analysts were expecting revenue of $2.18 billion and adjusted earnings of 41 cents per share. In his quarterly letter to investors, CEO Alex Karp touted the firm’s results, writing “it would be an understatement” to say Palantir’s results in Q3 “were extraordinary.” He said the company’s growth rate of 96% was “absolutely striking.” Palantir had guided revenue to roughly $2.16 billion to $2.164 billion. Palantir’s quarterly results came after last week’s bloodbath in certain tech stocks, and served as something of a temperature read on the AI trade. Karp made no bones about the change he sees on the horizon and how it could demolish certain sectors. “Every industry in the world—from banks to insurers to hospitals and even once-storied law firms —will either be remade or set briskly aside,” wrote Karp. He continued his aggressive optimism about the company he helped found in 2003 with investor Peter Thiel and others as the quarterly call with analysts got underway. Karp said Palantir’s quarterly earnings calls have grown beyond its financial results to serve as “the focal point of tech, society, and general trends.” He said Palantir’s earnings calls, streamed on YouTube, are “by far the most-watched earnings calls in the world.” The software maker has become a bellwether for public market confidence in AI software converting into revenue growth. Its latest financials come days after Alphabet suffered its worst one-day drop on record in its 22-year history as a public company. Disappointing reception to Amazon and Intel last week deepened concerns that relentless spending on AI—which is approaching $2 trillion in two years, according to S&P Global research—is sprinting well ahead of returns for investors. Google parent Alphabet lost $505 billion in market value since it published third-quarter figures last week and Intel’s stock dropped about 29% last week. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 1% Monday and the benchmark is down 4% over the past five days. At Palantir, investors keep a gimlet eye on U.S. commercial revenue as evidence that companies as well as governments are willing to pony up for AI software. That business grew 148% to $984 million, compared to $397 million a year ago.  And for the first time, U.S. commercial revenue skipped ahead of U.S. government revenue, clocking in at $984 million versus $953 million. U.S. government revenue grew to $953 million, up 96% from $486 million a year ago.  Meanwhile, total contract value rose 6% to $2.9 billion and U.S. commercial contract value grew 11% to $1.5 billion.  For the current quarter, Palantir forecast revenue of roughly $2.64 billion to $2.65 billion, or about 88% growth at the midpoint. Analysts expected about $2.46 billion. Fiscal year 2026 revenue guidance also rose to 91% year over year growth, and U.S. commercial revenue guidance rose to 143%. The backdrop for Palantir is markedly different from its second quarter results in August even though Karp’s tone this quarter is just as ebullient as he was three months ago. This quarter, as last quarter, the $430 billion tech firm’s own quarterly release to investors said its results were “ crushing consensus expectations .” Karp maintained the same tone throughout the call and in response to a question for tech bull Dan Ives, said potential clients seek out Palantir because they’re concerned about their intellectual property and getting value from it. He compared it in various ways to types of romantic relationships. He said “warm leads” now turn quicker into “hot leads” the way a first date can progress further romantically. It’s a “very different jam,” said Karp. “We’ve gone from being the most attractive person in the physics department to being the captain of the football team kind of thing,” he continued. “I mean, not that I did that.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump cuts South Africa, Rwanda from AGOA trade program
events.summary: The News US President Donald Trump plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from African Growth and Opportunity Act eligibility next year, stripping both countries of duty-free access to the US market under Washington’s flagship Africa trade program. Trump formally notified Congress and both governments of his decision, the Office of the US Trade Representative said Monday, after an annual review determined Pretoria and Kigali have been engaging in “concerning and pervasive” practices inconsistent with AGOA’s eligibility criteria. These include “barriers that undermine American trade and investment” and practices that “pose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests in the region,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said. The statement also cited corruption in South Africa, while its concerns about Rwanda extended to the rule of law, political pluralism, and human rights. The decision follows months of US tension with both governments. Washington has clashed with Pretoria over Trump’s claims of a “genocide” against white South Africans, which experts have dismissed, and is ending PEPFAR aid to the country. South Africa hoped to use its critical mineral resources as leverage in trade talks. South African Trade Minister Parks Tau said the “decision does not define the broader relationship” between the countries and that South Africa would continue pursuing trade, investment and shared economic opportunities with the US. The trade ministry said it had offered additional concessions and called it “unfortunate that the US is now raising new issues that have not been the basis for discussions.” With Rwanda, the dispute centers on the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo: The US sanctioned Rwanda’s military in March and its defense ministry last week, accusing them of backing M23 rebels and using minerals from rebel-held territory in their supply chains. Know More South Africa has the most to lose as AGOA’s largest beneficiary, exporting about $1.7 billion worth of goods under the program in 2025, including vehicles and agricultural products. Rwanda’s exposure is far smaller, with US imports from the country totaling about $44 million last year. Standard trade will continue, but affected exports could become more expensive, and the damage may spread across southern Africa and impact thousands of jobs . “The loss of AGOA will reverberate through the SADC region as several countries, including Lesotho and Botswana, are part of the South African supply chain that provides goods and products for the US under AGOA,” said Witney Schneidman, a former US deputy assistant secretary of state for African affairs. AGOA, established in 2000, is authorized only through the end of 2028, and Schneidman said this episode highlights the need to modernize it. “China, the EU and South Africa’s other partners don’t turn their trade relations ‘on and off’ as the US does,” he said.

events.title: After topping 2024’s donor list, Elon Musk said he’d do ‘a lot less.’ Since then, he’s given more than George Soros has personally in his lifetime
events.summary: In May 2025, Elon Musk said he was pulling back from political spending. “I think in terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” Musk said in an interview with Bloomberg at the Qatar Economic Forum. “I think I’ve done enough.” He then left room to change course: “Well, if I see a reason to do political spending in the future, I will do it,” he said. “I don’t currently see a reason.” He had just finished the 2024 election cycle as the country’s biggest political donor , according to OpenSecrets . That year, he gave $291.5 million, all to Republicans. The next-largest donor, Timothy Mellon, gave $197 million. In the 17 months since, Musk has given $427.5 million to federal political committees, according to a Fortune analysis of Federal Election Commission filings through Oct. 14. That’s nearly $200 million more than George Soros, the man Musk has claimed “astroturfed” anti-Tesla protests . Soros, the Democratic megadonor, has given personally $243.2 million to federal committees in 47 years of FEC records . How much has Musk contributed? Most of Musk’s money arrived after July 1 of this year. SLF PAC, the flagship super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, reported a $75 million check from Musk on Sept. 9 and an $83 million check on Sept. 23. Musk has spent more than $200 million to help elect Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, to the Senate, according to a New York Times analysis. America PAC, the super PAC Musk funds, reported $165.6 million from him between July 1 and Oct. 14, in its October quarterly and pre-general reports. That includes $8 million in in-kind support from United States of America Inc., one of his companies, which America PAC attributed to Musk. He also gave $20 million on Sept. 4 to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republican candidates. And on Aug. 21, his trust gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Paxton , who is running against Democrat James Talarico. Other counts put him higher. The Times and OpenSecrets rank Musk as the top donor of the 2026 midterms, at $445.6 million for the full cycle (outside of the FEC, a Fortune analysis of IRS filings found he gave $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association on July 6). The Brennan Center for Justice, which counts his company alongside him, puts the total at $483 million . How much has Soros contributed? Soros’s largest personal checks came before July 2026. He gave Democracy PAC II, one of his family’s two super PACs, $125 million in September 2021 and $50 million in November 2022. In the 2024 cycle, he gave $4.2 million personally to federal committees, FEC records show. Soros has also given $67.8 million to political groups that report to the IRS, including $24.2 million to Justice & Public Safety PAC, according to IRS filings. FollowTheMoney, which compiles state campaign finance records, lists about $70 million more in state and local contributions. Together, that comes to about $381 million, still less than Musk has given since May 2025. The comparison changes if groups Soros funds are counted. The Fund for Policy Reform, a nonprofit, has given $210.5 million to Democracy PAC since 2020, including $60 million in January 2024 and $50 million in January 2026, but the nonprofit doesn’t disclose its donors. The Times describes it as a channel for Soros family money and notes that Alex Soros, George’s son, is a director. Counting the fund, Soros’s federal total is $453.7 million, more than Musk has given since his remarks. The Times counts George and Alex Soros together at $103.4 million this cycle and reports that the family’s two super PACs held about $173 million in cash as of mid-October. Over his lifetime, Musk has given $723.8 million to federal committees, about three times Soros’s personal federal total, according to Fortune’ s analysis of FEC filings. Fortune’ s analysis counts contributions each man made to federal political committees as reported to the FEC, including in-kind gifts that recipients attributed to them, and excludes duplicate memo entries. Musk’s totals run through Oct. 14, 2026; Soros’s run through Sept. 9, 2026. Musk’s totals exclude donations to groups that don’t disclose their donors, as well as any money given after Oct. 14. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump touts DC renovations ahead of tough midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump started off his last public speech before tomorrow’s midterms by highlighting one of his biggest second-term focuses: beautifying Washington, DC. Speaking in front of the Reflecting Pool, Trump went into the renovations in depth before turning to the campaign. “The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history,” Trump said as he listed off his administration’s accomplishments. But even as he addressed the upcoming election, Trump returned at times to his Washington projects. Trump has turned his gaze back to the capital as Republicans face a steep climb to hang onto their congressional majorities, with voters unhappy about the Iran war and the economy. Trump at one point acknowledged that reality, noting that “the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms.” But, he added, “we gave this a very strong shot.” — Shelby Talcott

events.title: Anthropic's colossal pay packages cost the company more than $100,000 a month per employee
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei speaks on a video at a conference. Giuliano Berti/Bloomberg via Getty Images Anthropic keeps a relatively small head count, with 5,300 workers, its IPO filing says. New numbers show Anthropic's personnel expenses topped $322,000 per worker last quarter. Anthropic's IPO will be a multimillionaire minter, giving workers liquidity. America has a classic salary milestone: six figures a year. Anthropic's average employee has cost their employer that much every month. Anthropic's personnel expenses topped $1.7 billion for its 5,300 workers from July through September, according to an amended S-1 filing the AI company released Monday morning ahead of its initial public offering later this month. That means the expenses averaged over $322,000 per worker over the three-month span. The total indicates how a seat inside Anthropic became one of the 21st century's quickest pathways to extraordinary wealth. Its coming IPO will mint a new cohort of multimillionaires. Even employees who've only been around for a couple of years have seen their stock options multiply in value several times over. The AI juggernaut has used high salaries and a rapidly growing valuation to recruit skilled engineers, researchers, and other specialists. Over the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic's personnel costs totaled $4.8 billion, according to the S-1. The last quarter's $1.7 billion tally included cash salaries and bonuses, benefits, and employer payroll taxes. The largest chunk of the total came from Anthropic's stock-based compensation expenses, an accounting measure of the equity it recognized for employees — that came out to $1.1 billion in the three-month span. Against the high employee expenses, Anthropic's revenue has raced far ahead. Back in 2023, the company spent more than twice as much on personnel as it made in revenue. In the first nine months of 2026, personnel costs tallied just 15% of total revenue. The numbers could fluctuate. Anthropic wrote in its S-1 that, as of the end of September, it had more than $32 billion in stock-based compensation expenses that it had not yet included in its accounting. A successful listing on the stock market would increase Anthropic's personnel costs in the coming quarters. Anthropic quintupled in head count from the end of 2024 to the end of September 2026. It's still much smaller than its tech-industry peers. Meta is valued at around $1.6 trillion, a possible target for Anthropic's IPO. The social media giant has around 67,000 employees. Broadcom, worth about the same, has more than 30,000. This trim size makes Anthropic look especially efficient , as Business Insider reported last week. The company tallied $6.6 million in annual revenue per employee, compared with estimates that put Meta at $3.2 million per employee and Google at $2.5 million. events.title: Anthropic says revenue surged 1,100% ahead of IPO
events.summary: According to several media outlets, Anthropic aims to raise around US$100 billion through an initial public offering at a valuation of US$1.5 trillion to US$2 trillion. WASHINGTON - Anthropic, one of the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies, on Nov 2 reported a more than 1,100 per cent surge in quarterly revenue and nearly US$900 billion (S$1.1 trillion) in spending commitments as it counts down to its Wall Street listing later in November . The San Francisco-based company was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers led by chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela, now its president, with AI safety as its focus. The listing comes amid growing nervousness among investors about the huge sums being poured into AI. Revenue reached US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from US$1.4 billion a year earlier, though sales growth slowed from previous quarters amid fierce competition from ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and cheaper models, many of them from China. The company, whose stock market debut is seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom lifting the US economy can last, said in an amended filing that its net loss reached US$23.3 billion in the July-September period. The loss stemmed mostly from non-cash accounting charges linked to the company’s rising valuation, the filing showed. Anthropic also posted an operating loss of US$567 million in the third quarter as it paid more for short-term computing capacity. The filing said the company has committed to spend about US$895 billion, mostly on computing power, with US$70 billion of that due before September 2027. The IPO will be a major test of the market’s faith in the AI boom, with the pool of potential investors set to widen as retail traders get their first chance to buy shares directly in a standalone AI giant. According to several media outlets, the five-year-old company plans to raise around US$100 billion in its initial public offering, at a valuation of between US$1.5 trillion and US$2 trillion. That would surpass the record set in June by SpaceX, which raised US$86 billion. Last week, concerns about AI spending triggered a sharp sell-off in big tech stocks after the latest earnings showed massive investment without clear signs of a return. Anthropic’s roughly 400-page filing devotes more than 90 pages to risks, including those facing an industry that has seen a string of reports in recent months of AI systems behaving in unexpected and harmful ways. Anthropic’s focus on safety is built into its corporate structure. It is a public benefit corporation, legally required to weigh its mission of developing AI safely alongside shareholder returns. The co-founders, meanwhile, will hold 50.1 per cent of shareholder voting power through a single special share, leaving investors who buy on the market little say over the company’s direction. The IPO comes as more major companies involved in the AI spending bonanza turn to the markets to finance their ambitions. Meta and Google parent Alphabet have launched their own fundraising plans on the public markets, and Oracle said on Nov 2 it was going ahead with a US$20 billion plan despite doubts about its financial exposure. events.title: Trump focuses on Reflecting Pool in final public speech before midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump began his final scheduled in-person speech before Election Day with lengthy remarks about the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Trump first mentioned the election more than 20 minutes into the speech, calling it "the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime." Later in the speech he continued discussing the pool, at which he spoke, as well as his push to erect a massive triumphal arch in Washington and his plans to build a promenade along the Potomac River. President Donald Trump began his final scheduled in-person speech before Tuesday's Election Day with a lengthy disquisition about his efforts to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other sites in Washington . "Today I'm thrilled to announce the official opening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool," Trump said Monday afternoon in front of the water feature, which was fenced off for months amid a problem-plagued renovation the president had ordered. The speech, which lasted nearly an hour, was expected to serve as Trump's "closing argument" on the midterms before millions of voters head to the polls to determine which party will control the House and Senate in the next Congress. How the 2026 midterms could affect defense, healthcare, crypto and AI stocks DOJ asks Supreme Court to block California counting disputed mail-in ballots But Trump kicked off his remarks with more than 20 minutes of commentary that focused largely on the Reflecting Pool, along with his administration's work on refurbishing other Washington-area monuments and cracking down on crime in the nation's capital. "The pool is now better and more beautiful than it's ever been before, and we're very proud of it," Trump said, before repeating unfounded claims that vandals were responsible for damaging the pool and delaying repairs. U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro told a court July 31 that the damage was caused by a contractor's botched installation. Trump lashed out at Pirro over the admission and has continued to claim vandals were to blame. Trump's first explicit reference to the midterms came around the 23-minute mark. "As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime," Trump said. "The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history," he said. He touted his administration's record and lashed out at some Democratic candidates by name, including Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. He also repeated his controversial claim that if Republicans win, "everybody is going to get $5,000." "We have to keep our Congress strong, free," Trump said. "America is ready to go. They're ready to vote. I hope they're ready to do the right thing." But Trump, as he has done in other recent remarks, seemed to acknowledge that Democrats had an advantage — at least when looking to historical trends that show the president's party tends to underperform in midterm elections. "For some reason, the sitting president doesn't win the midterms. But we gave this a very strong shot," he said. Later in the speech, Trump continued discussing the pool, as well as his push to erect a massive triumphal arch in Washington and his plans to build a promenade along the Potomac River. He also said the government planned to build a "National Garden of American Heroes," comprising "250 to 500 great American heroes in statue form." And he talked about ongoing efforts to renovate a public golf course in Washington that is subject to legal challenges.
