( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Residents living near the new Western Sydney International Airport are reporting increasing aircraft noise linked to the new Western Sydney airport. Blue Mountains resident David Lysiak says he worries about not being able to sleep at night as flights ramp up. An expert in air traffic managements says there are "no perfect options" when determining flight routes. Residents living in the Blue Mountains say they fear an end to the area's peace and quiet following last week's opening of the Western Sydney International Airport (WSI). The airport officially opened to domestic and international passengers on October 25 amid much fanfare. But a week later, concerns are being raised about aircraft noise. David Lysiak has lived in Warrimoo, a village in the lower Blue Mountains, for 44 years. Sydney's second airport officially opened on October 25. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) The retired grandfather and his wife raised four children there, and they have always loved the tranquillity. "It's just beautiful, quiet. Not many people. We have one shop, a general store," he said. "I just wander into the bush and go for a bushwalk, and take your bike down the trails … You ride through a blue gum forest and it's all accessible right from here." But he fears the serenity of the last four decades could be a thing of the past because his beloved town falls under the WSI flight path. Mr Lysiak is concerned for the future of Warrimoo. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Freight flights began operating from the airport around the clock in July. Mr Lysiak said he has heard the noise of some freight aircraft "quite distinctly". That sound is only going to become more frequent . International airlines Air New Zealand, Singapore Airlines, Fiji Airways, Qatar Airways and Vietjet Air have so far signed up with WSI, with flights expected to ramp up over the next couple of years. The airport has one active runway. ( Supplied: Australian government ) WSI has one runway, designated as Runway 05 or Runway 23, depending on the direction of use. Flights on Runway 23 arrive from the north-east and depart to the south-west over areas in the city's west and Blue Mountains. Flights on Runway 23 arrive from the north-east and depart to the south-west. ( Supplied: Australian government ) When Runway 05 is used, flights take off to the north-east and land from the south-west. Flights take off to the north-east and land from the south-west when Runway 05 is operational. ( Supplied: Australian government ) Weighing up if a trip from Sydney's new airport is for you The doors to Western Sydney International Airport are set to soon welcome commercial passengers. Airservices Australia has previously said that, where possible, Runway 23 would be prioritised during the day to minimise overflight and noise over residential suburbs to the north-east of the airport. Marek Bekier, a lecturer in air traffic management at the University of New South Wales School of Aviation, said there were always "trade-offs" when deciding on the best flight paths. "An air route connecting an airport to the wider airway system is not just a straight line in the sky," he said. "You have to think about it as a kind of three dimensional corridor that has to fulfil certain requirements. "No option is perfect. You will never find a new route that will basically satisfy the wishes and demands of everyone, so you always have to make some trade-offs." Community treated as 'collateral damage' Julius Timmerman, who moved to the Blue Mountains town of Lawson with his wife in 1996, said people in his community had been treated as "collateral damage". "I'm worried about not being able to sleep at night, just the effect on my amenity because we bought a house in the mountains in good faith that the area would remain quiet and peaceful," he said. "It's completely unfair that the people of Western Sydney and the Blue Mountains should be just treated as collateral damage for the sake of the airline industry." Julius Timmerman says he bought his house in the area thinking it would be quiet. ( Supplied ) He is one of hundreds of people in the community who want a rethink of the flight paths and have signed the Western Sydney Airport Community Impacts Alliance petition calling for a night-time curfew. "The main thing that we want is, as mentioned in the petition, a curfew from 11pm to 6am, which lines up with Kingston Smith Airport," he said.

Squarespace, the web company that helps customers build and host their own websites, is laying off about one-fifth of its workforce, in a move that will affect hundreds of jobs. Jeff Seedman, a public relations specialist representing Squarespace, confirmed the layoffs to TechCrunch. The Verge initially reported the layoffs. “Squarespace is restructuring its organization and reducing its global workforce by approximately 19%, representing around 300 employees,” said Seedman. “The changes are intended to simplify how we operate, sharpen our priorities and enable the company to move faster as we position Squarespace for its next phase of growth.” Website building has changed immensely over the last few years as a result of the generative AI boom. “Vibe-coding” website builders, which only require simple prompts from users to spin up functional front-end designs, have largely upended the industry, making it possible for users to create sites with significantly less effort. These kinds of sites have become an increasingly central part of the website-building business. Last year, web host rival Wix bought Base44 for $80 million . Similar offerings, like Lovable, have generated significant investor interest; Lovable raised a $400 million Series C round in August that valued the company at $13.3 billion. Google also recently launched Stitch , a feature that allows users to swiftly generate user-interface designs. Squarespace has also begun a big push into AI. In 2024, the company launched an AI tool called Blueprint. The company also recently announced Forma, an upcoming AI native platform, whose waitlist users can join . Squarespace was founded in 2004 and went public in 2021 at a $10 billion valuation. However, the company struggled in the ensuing years to generate enthusiastic public market interest. Squarespace ultimately decided to go private again by way of a $7 billion private equity deal in 2024. events.title: Fed will vote on rates less often. What that could mean for borrowers
events.summary: After the Federal Reserve meeting in October, Chairman Kevin Warsh unveiled changes that would reduce the number of rate-setting votes. The move could mean consumers wait longer for their borrowing costs to come down. Economists say consumers may be even more affected by the lack of transparency, as Warsh also implements measures to curtail so-called forward guidance. After the Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady last week, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced plans to reduce the number of rate-setting votes over the next two years. That move could potentially extend the timeline for everyday Americans to see borrowing costs adjust, some experts say. "Fewer Fed meetings in 2027 could mean consumers wait longer to see relief when borrowing costs are elevated," said James Vrachas, executive director at advisory firm Post Oak Group. Americans may feel somewhat removed from the Fed, but the central bank's moves have a ripple effect on many types of consumer products, including the borrowing rates for credit cards , home loans and auto financing. Midterm election: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisions These Senate races may help determine the fate of Social Security Social Security: How much money beneficiaries may lose if Congress does nothing Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 For example, most credit cards have variable rates tied to the prime rate, which moves with the Fed's benchmark. However, even with the central bank holding rates unchanged, credit card rates are edging higher as issuers protect themselves from risk, according to LendingTree. Card issuers are mitigating their exposure from borrowers who may fall behind on payments or default in the face of stubborn inflation in everyday expenses, said Matt Schulz, LendingTree's chief credit analyst. Generally, card issuers are slow to bring rates down, unless prompted by the Fed's actions, said Schulz: "Issuers will tinker with rates a bit at the margins at other times, but the big moves tend to only come when issuers are pushed." On Oct. 28, the central bank voted to keep the benchmark borrowing rate at the current target range of 3.75% to 4% as policymakers deliberated next steps with inflation remaining well above the Fed's 2% goal. The Fed will keep meeting eight times a year, Warsh said at the news conference following the October meeting, but next year, one of the eight meetings will not entail a vote on interest rates or include a post-meeting statement. The "strategy" meetings will increase to two the following year, leaving just six opportunities to adjust rates — with the exception of emergency meetings, if necessary. "For consumers, that could mean longer periods of uncertainty around borrowing costs," said Jordan Ricciardi, a senior wealth strategy associate at UBS. "Our clients looking to buy a home, refinance a mortgage or finance a business could be impacted as fewer scheduled opportunities means the Fed isn't as quickly responding to changing economic conditions." Borrowing rates may stay elevated for longer With fewer scheduled opportunities to adjust rates, that means borrowing rates could remain stubbornly high even if economic conditions begin to improve, Post Oak Group's Vrachas also said. As it stands, financial institutions can adjust rates whenever market conditions warrant, regardless of the Fed's meeting schedule, he said. In the meantime, though, many consumers may continue to face elevated borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans and credit card debt, among other financial products. "For consumers, the bigger concern isn't necessarily fewer meetings, but whether lenders pass along lower borrowing costs as quickly as they pass along increases," Vrachas said. 'Warsh keeps his proverbial cards closer to his chest' Consumers may be even more impacted by the lack of transparency, economists say, as Warsh implements measures to curtail so-called forward guidance, or how the Fed signals its future rate moves. Although economic conditions have become more complicated and information is more widely available, "Warsh keeps his proverbial cards closer to his chest than his recent predecessors have," said Mark Hamrick, an economic analyst and founder of The Hamrick Brief, a weekly newsletter. "I wouldn't expect consumers to see the universe of market rates change simply because the Fed votes less often," he said. "But the public may have less opportunity to hear from the source about how and why the Fed is making the decisions that shape what they pay to borrow and what they earn on their savings." In the interim, "the best protection for consumers remains shopping around, particularly for the highest yields among savings accounts and [certificates of deposit]," Hamrick said.

events.title: Judge tosses DOJ case against ex-FBI officials accused of lying about Hunter Biden probe
events.summary: A federal judge in Washington dismissed the Department of Justice's case accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress about investigations into Hunter Biden. The judge reportedly blasted the Justice Department, saying the situation "cannot be described as anything other than weaponization." He accused the DOJ of a "slapdash job" prosecuting ex-officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, suggesting it rushed the case ahead of the midterm election. A federal judge on Monday blasted the Department of Justice for "weaponization" as he dismissed its case accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress about investigations into Hunter Biden , multiple news outlets reported. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, in a hearing in U.S. District Court in Washington, reportedly tore into the DOJ over its "slapdash job" prosecuting ex-officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, saying he was "deeply troubled by what has happened here." Faruqui said the government lacked probable cause and failed to present evidence that the officials' statements before the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 were knowingly false, MS NOW reported. He also accused the DOJ of wrongly rushing the case ahead of the midterm election . The situation "cannot be described as anything other than weaponization," he said, according to MS NOW. Trump focuses on Reflecting Pool in final public speech before midterms How the 2026 midterms could affect defense, healthcare, crypto and AI stocks DOJ asks Supreme Court to block California counting disputed mail-in ballots The judge even apologized to the government's lawyers, calling it "incredibly unfair" that they were assigned to defend the flawed case. "This does not feel like an investigation," Faruqui reportedly added. "It feels like a broken one-wish willow obsession." The DOJ, in response to an email sent to its press office, said it "disagrees" with the decision. "We are evaluating all options but cannot comment further on an ongoing criminal investigation," the agency said in response to CNBC. "The Department's actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law – not politics." Attorneys for Floris and Benavides praised the judge's decision outside the courthouse later Monday morning. "This case should never have been brought. The government had no case, as the judge just laid out," a lawyer for Floris said, slamming the prosecution as a "spaghetti-at-the-wall, Hunter-Biden-conspiracy fever dream." A lawyer for Benavides said they hope the DOJ will not try to keep the case alive by seeking an indictment before a grand jury "where they get to be behind closed doors and get to shape the narrative, and we are unable to present our side." The DOJ did not take that step when they unveiled the allegations against Floris and Benavides on Oct. 23. Rather, despite the alleged misconduct taking place years earlier, prosecutors acquired a criminal complaint, which only requires a judge's signature. Criminal complaints are often used to obtain arrest warrant in situations where prosecutors need to move quickly . Faruqui had flagged that circumstance as unusual, and last week refused to sign off on a superseding complaint that added an obstruction charge against the two ex-officials. "I'm concerned with your view as to what the law is," the judge told the prosecutors in a hearing last Tuesday. "Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?"

events.title: Lindsay Clancy back in court seeking to have murder charges dismissed
events.summary: Defence argues juror misconduct and judge’s questioning impacted Clancy’s trial for strangling of her three children. Lindsay Clancy, the American mother facing murder charges for killing her three young children, has returned to court in a bid to get the charges dropped. Clancy’s lawyers urged Judge William Sullivan on Monday to dismiss the first-degree murder charges against her in the state of Massachusetts in the United States, saying retrying her for killing her three young children would violate ⁠⁠her constitutional rights. list 1 of 4 Thousands gather at final student-led rally ahead of Serbia election list 2 of 4 Suwayda remains in stasis as US signals differences with Israel on Syria list 3 of 4 Man targeted Muslims, Africans and North Africans, French prosecutors say list 4 of 4 Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy children’s murder case Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy if the case moves forward but have not decided if she would face the same first-degree murder charges. Monday’s hearing was her second time in court since September, when jurors were unable to reach a verdict at her trial. Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands in 2023 at her home in Duxbury, a suburb of Boston in Massachusetts. Clancy then attempted to take her own life by cutting herself with a knife and was paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window. At Monday’s hearing, defence lawyer Martin G Weinberg argued that the judge should have investigated further after the jury foreperson sent two notes indicating that a juror was not following the rules. Further questioning could have revealed grounds to remove the juror, identified as Michael Desronvil, and continue deliberations, he said. After receiving the notes, Sullivan spoke with each juror, reminding them of their duties and explaining what constitutes reasonable doubt in a court case. He asked whether they could apply the law to the case, and all said yes. But Weinberg argued that Sullivan had not gone far enough. A juror who said he could follow the law could have been lying, Weinberg said, and the situation warranted questioning the foreperson separately to learn more about what was happening during deliberations. Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague argued there was no indication the holdout juror’s disagreement stemmed from personal bias or an inability to deliberate, rather than a different assessment of the evidence. Sprague said the judge handled the ⁠⁠jury impasse appropriately, saying the fact that one juror dug in his heels did not mean Sullivan should risk interfering with the deliberations by questioning him. “It is clear from the record this ⁠⁠juror did not refuse to deliberate,” Sprague said. “He refused to agree.” Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington accused the lone holdout juror of using a mobile phone to research terms related to the case and questioned whether he had been truthful during jury selection. Clancy has never disputed killing her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behaviour. Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy, now 36, had mental health problems but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong. Sullivan did not immediately rule on the motion to dismiss. He scheduled another hearing for November 16 and suggested a retrial could begin in March. Another motion expected to be discussed is the state of Massachusetts’s request for a gag order barring lawyers and their supporters “from making extrajudicial statements to the media that would have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceeding”.

events.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump request to set aside California ballots
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms Top court declines to block California from counting ballots of voters Trump administration claims are not US citizens. The United States Supreme Court has declined to intervene on behalf of President Donald Trump’s administration in its bid to force California not to count the ballots of more than 20,000 voters it claims are not citizens. The Department of Justice had filed an emergency request earlier in the day, just one day before the US midterm elections . It is the latest development in a legal battle between the administration and California, a Democratic stronghold and the most populous US state. California says the move could disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters. The Justice Department wanted the Supreme Court to step in immediately and force California to set aside ballots from voters who appear on a list compiled by the Department of Homeland Security until their citizenship status can be verified. The department argues that once the ballots are mixed in with others, there would be no way to identify and remove them if the voters were later found to be ineligible. But California says the list is unreliable and could include thousands of US citizens. Voting has been under way since early October, with ballots mailed to about 23 million registered voters and hundreds of thousands already processed. State officials say it would be nearly impossible to separate the ballots in question. Last week, a federal judge rejected the administration’s request, raising concerns about the reliability of the data on the US Department of Homeland Security’s list. “If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Judge David Carter wrote. The administration turned to the Supreme Court after a federal appeals court also rejected the request on Friday. In September, the Supreme Court rejected an earlier effort to restrict mail-in voting. The dispute comes as Republicans fight to retain control of the US Congress in Tuesday’s elections. Trump has repeatedly made false claims about widespread voter fraud, but studies and state audits have shown that ineligible voting, including by non-citizens, is rare.

events.title: Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlash
events.summary: Exception for care workers will allow an estimated 280,000 people and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years Shabana Mahmood rowed back on her most hardline plans to make care workers wait 15 years for settlement in the UK, but told MPs on Monday that many migrants would still face retrospective rule changes to make them wait a decade. Under pressure from a cabinet backlash and health unions, the home secretary has offered a carve-out for care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years. But most of the rigorous new rules drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain, including plans to force those who arrived in the UK by irregular means such as small boats to face up to 30 years before being able to apply for settlement. The changes drew cries of betrayal from the Conservatives and the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, who said it was “the beginning of the capitulation”. But Mahmood told the Commons she would still enact sweeping changes that will mean many migrant workers will wait double the time they had expected for settlement. She said settlement was “one of most valuable rights this country can offer. Until now it has been given almost automatically. From today it must be earned. Those who contribute will settle fastest. Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait much longer.” In particular, the wait for those earning under £50,000 will double to 10 years. This was criticised by some Labour MPs who said vital workers such as research scientists and chefs would be caught by the changes. The Law Society said the changing rules could threaten the rule of law, saying it “retrospectively undermines the legal certainty that individuals, families and employers rely on”. Some MPs suggested they would continue to press the home secretary to rethink the retrospective nature of the changes – though the new policies do not require a vote in parliament, so MPs have limited means to block them. Abtisam Mohamed, the Labour MP for Sheffield Central, said: “Retrospectively uprooting someone’s plans, sometimes made at the most vulnerable time in their lives, is unfair. I’ll be pressing for those already here to be protected.” The former shadow home secretary Diane Abbott also criticised the retrospective changes. “You can come in legally, you can work legally and then have your residency rights turned upside down,” she said, warning of another potential Windrush scandal. The Walthamstow MP Stella Creasy said there was a “partial recognition” of the contribution migrants made but there were thousands of people “facing 10 years of limbo with many businesses unclear if talent will stay or not as a result”. She said: “The economic consequences of those people walking away from the UK will far outweigh any savings in entitlement to benefits, given many of them don’t claim anyway, so the home secretary still has work to do to make these reforms work for our national interest.” Refugees will also face a longer wait of 10 years, with an additional 10-year penalty for those who do not enter legally – and those who do not find employment will face a wait of up to 30 years. Andy Burnham, who promised voters in his Makerfield byelection that he would support Mahmood’s migration agenda, endorsed the plans and said the home secretary was “gripping this problem” by introducing the earned element. “People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” the prime minister said. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier. Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.” But migrant rights organisations accused the government of “moving the goalposts” for those who had played by the rules. “People who have built their lives around the government’s requirements deserve better than decisions that turn their own and their families’ lives upside down,” said Amnesty International. The key climbdown from the home secretary was an exemption for care workers – something which the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had explicitly criticised. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, also repeatedly refused to say she backed proposals to prolong the qualifying period for settlement. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Under pressure from health unions to make an exception for care workers, the home secretary has moved to allow an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependents to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years. In the revised set of proposals, care workers earning more than £25,000 will be able to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years, a third of the time that was announced last year.

events.title: Defense, healthcare, crypto and AI: How the midterm election could affect stocks
events.summary: The midterm election could reshape the outlook for companies heavily exposed to Washington, especially in defense, healthcare, crypto and artificial intelligence. Democratic control of either chamber could bring more investigations and oversight, while giving the party leverage over federal spending and must-pass legislation. Even without control of the White House, Congress could influence billions of dollars in government funding and determine whether Trump-era regulatory changes become lasting law. Lockheed Martin gets about 70% of its sales from the U.S. government. Medicaid accounts for three-quarters of Molina Healthcare's premium revenue . Coinbase is waiting on Congress to finish writing the rules for cryptocurrency . For some of the biggest U.S. companies, Washington is part of the business model. Now, the midterm election could change who holds the leverage. A Democratic victory in either or both chambers of Congress would grant the party new leverage to investigate companies , challenge federal spending and demand legislative concessions. But their reach would have limits: President Donald Trump would retain his veto and broad authority over tariffs, immigration and federal regulation. Historically, stocks have performed well under divided government. Under Republican presidents, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 23% in the year after midterms when Congress was split, compared with 16% when Democrats controlled both chambers, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis published Thursday. Analysts often attribute the pattern in part to congressional gridlock limiting sweeping policy changes. Still, some analysts caution against assuming that pattern will repeat. "We don't think that blueprint holds up this time around, and we still see plenty of reasons to be constructive on the U.S. equity market," said Ariana Salvatore , head of U.S. public policy research at Morgan Stanley. For investors, the midterm election could reshape which businesses preserve their advantages in Washington, particularly in industries such as defense , healthcare , banking and artificial intelligence . "There are some policy changes that might be market moving, at least for certain segments," said Jeff Buchbinder , chief equity strategist at LPL Financial. Congressional oversight and investigations Control of either the House or Senate would give Democrats committee gavels and subpoena power, allowing them to demand documents, compel testimony and haul executives before public hearings. Companies are already getting a preview. On Oct. 21, Sen. Richard Blumenthal , D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sought records tied to Trump's White House ballroom from donors including Cisco , Salesforce , ServiceNow and Kraken . Apple and Nvidia each committed $25 million to the project, according to records obtained by The Washington Post . Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., has separately sought records involving tariff exclusions, including communications involving Apple's former CEO, Tim Cook , as Democrats investigate whether Trump used trade policy to reward political allies and donors. While donations do not prove wrongdoing or favorable treatment, congressional probes still carry risks: subpoenas consume executive bandwidth, reveal internal communications and generate unpredictable news coverage. Few CEOs relish the idea of sitting at a witness table before lawmakers and television cameras. "It creates volatility because you get a negative headline," said Monica Guerra , Morgan Stanley's head of policy and geopolitical strategy, who expects Democrats to cast a wide net for their probes. Democrats have signaled interest in Trump family businesses, government contractors, firms tied to Donald Trump Jr.'s 1789 Capital , and companies associated with Elon Musk and the so-called Department of Government Efficiency . Then there is the most basic power Congress has: deciding where the money goes. Trump's 2025 tax cuts and spending law, known as One Big Beautiful Bill , is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion through 2034, according to a KFF analysis of Congressional Budget Office estimates. KFF is a nonpartisan nonprofit that provides health policy information. Meanwhile, new work requirements for Medicaid enrollees are scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, or earlier in some states, while tighter state budgets could mean fewer people are covered and greater pressure on provider payments. Molina Healthcare generated $32.2 billion , or 75% of its 2025 premium revenue, from Medicaid, according to the company's annual Securities and Exchange Commission filing. In the same filing, Molina warned that losing government contracts or failing to renew them on favorable terms could materially reduce premium revenue.

events.title: I used to be a supermarket cake decorator. Here are 9 of my best tips for ordering a cake.
events.summary: Many supermarkets offer the option to walk in and grab a cake from their bakery case, as well as the option to order a custom cake. Molly Allen I worked as a supermarket cake decorator for two years before opening my own bakery . Ask for whipped cream if you want a less-sweet cake, or for two cake flavors to please more guests. It could be worth asking about free smash cakes or using your own toys for kids' birthday cakes . Supermarket cakes can be an easy, more affordable way to celebrate any occasion. However, not all of these cakes are served and created equally. Take it from me: I worked in the bakery section of a popular supermarket for two years, prepping treats and decorating cakes, before opening my own bakery. Here are my go-to tips for ordering the best cake from your local supermarket.  Place your order long before your party Some supermarkets bake cakes on-site, but many work with prebaked, frozen cakes. In these cases, the bakery will keep a stock of common cake flavors (vanilla, chocolate) on hand, and maybe a more limited selection of additional flavor choices (carrot, red velvet, marble).  To make sure you get the flavor you want, order your custom cake with two to three weeks' notice. This can help give the decorator and the bakery time to ensure your desired flavor is in stock. Ask for whipped cream if you think grocery-store cakes are too sweet Ask for whipped cream if the frosting on supermarket cakes is usually too sweet for you. Jasmin Merdan/Getty Images If you've stayed away from grocery-store cakes because the typical buttercream frosting is a bit too sweet for you, check if the bakery has other options.  Vanilla buttercream is often a default choice, but it's usually not the only one. Some supermarket bakeries can use fresh whipped cream for topping a cake. Other choices might include cream-cheese frosting , chocolate frosting, coconut-pecan frosting typically used for German chocolate cakes, and even chocolate ganache. Generally, you won't know for sure unless you ask. Check if the bakery can do half-and-half flavors You may not have to choose between chocolate or vanilla cake. When ordering, ask about doing half vanilla and half chocolate so everyone at your party can enjoy a slice of their preferred flavor. This is often possible with half-sheet cakes and two-layer round cakes. (And it might also work with other cake flavors, too.) Order with the cake decorator if you want something very specific Cake decorators can sometimes work early hours. gerenme/Getty Images You can generally speak with any bakery employee to order a cake, but if you have a specific or out-of-the-box request for decorations, ask when you can speak with the cake decorator by phone or in person. In my experience, they often work early shifts so they can begin preparing orders and items for the display case. Decorating is their specialty, and they can be the best person to tell you if tackling the specific design you're hoping for is achievable. And, if not, they may be able to help brainstorm an alternative. Consider bringing in your own toys for kids' cakes Supermarket bakeries usually have a look book of designs that cake decorators are trained to make, and children's cakes often include character toys from popular movies and shows. If the bakery doesn't have your child's favorite character, don't be afraid to ask staff what's possible. Depending on the store and decorator, you may be able to bring in small, washed figurines for the decorator to incorporate into the design. Or you can try asking the decorator to leave space for a specific toy when creating the design. Don't be afraid to order a plain cake if you want to dress it up yourself Remember that cake decorators don't have to dress up your cake with a border, sprinkles, and writing if you don't want them to. If you want a semi-customized dessert, just order a plain, frosted cake in your desired size. That way, you can take it home and turn it into anything you want. Add edible flowers to dress it up for a more formal occasion, or top it with candy and sprinkles in your desired shades. You can even try adding your own fun candles, toys, and knickknacks on top. Request a plastic cake container instead of a bakery box Premade birthday cakes can usually be customized. iStock / Getty Images Plus At many bakeries, custom cake orders are packaged in cardboard boxes for pickup. If you anticipate you'll have leftover cake, ask for a plastic cake container instead. This will provide an airtight solution for easily storing leftovers. Keep in mind that this tip may not work for every bakery, and it could depend on the supplies they have on hand. Ask about a free smash cake for kids If you're planning to order a birthday cake for a young child, ask if your supermarket bakery also offers free smash cakes. A smash cake is tiny, typically 4 inches in diameter, meant just for a kid to dig into on their birthday. These are usually served alongside a larger sheet cake meant for guests. Some bakeries will give you a free smash cake when you order a larger decorated cake or meet a minimum order size. Check last-minute options if you forgot to order ahead Even if you forgot to order a few weeks in advance, there may still be options the store's cake decorator can pull together for you. If it's a few days before your event, or the morning of, it doesn't hurt to ask. The decorator may be able to put together a simple design while you shop for other items in the store. Or you can grab a premade option from the bakery case and ask for writing on top and extra sprinkles along the edges to spruce it up. Just keep in mind that your options may depend on how busy the bakery is when you visit. This story was originally published on March 25, 2023, and most recently updated on November 2, 2026. events.title: Senegal hosts Africa’s first Olympics
events.summary: More than 2,000 athletes from around the world are in Senegal for the Youth Olympic Games to compete in Africa’s first Olympic event. The head of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), Kirsty Coventry, says this is a milestone, not just for Senegal but for the continent, which has the largest youth population. The games, postponed four years ago because of the COVID-19 pandemic, are being viewed as a test for Africa to see whether it can handle major international sports events. She says this is a chance for Africa to show the world what it is capable of hosting such big events. Herself an Olympic gold medallist in swimming, Coventry tells Al Jazeera she hopes the games will empower young people and inspire them to dream big. But as the Olympic flame burns bright in Senegal – the future of the youth games is uncertain. Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye says hosting the event is a proud moment. However, the country is facing economic challenges, and some critics say the money could have been better spent elsewhere. Coventry says the IOC is re-evaluating its direction and examining how to reduce the costs of hosting. events.title: Approval of cheap version of HIV-prevention shot raises hopes in low-income countries
events.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a generic version of the world’s only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a generic version of the world’s only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV — a big step toward making the drug available inexpensively and more quickly in 120 low- and middle-income countries. The announcement was made on Monday morning by the manufacturer and organizations that helped to speed up development of the medication, called lenacapavir. The drug is expected to cost $40 a year per person in the countries where it will be available, the same price as daily preventive pills available now. But the shots are much more convenient than the pills because they’re needed much less frequently and they nearly eliminated new infections in two groundbreaking studies of people at high risk . People don’t always take their daily dose of medication, “and if you do not take it, you cannot get protected against HIV,” said Carmen Pérez Casas, HIV lead for the grant-making organization Unitaid, a global health agency. “With lenacapavir, we are much more hopeful.” Ultimately, advocates said, the medication should help drive down cases of HIV and AIDS — and deaths. According to the World Health Organization, 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year. With an affordable, high-quality generic medication now available, “we could help to scale this to the 20 million people around the world who need PrEP,” prescription medicine taken by people at risk of HIV before being exposed to the virus, said Carolyn Amole, who leads the HIV program for the Clinton Health Access Initiative, a global health organization. “And if we scale to those levels,” she added, “we can actually begin to bring an end to the HIV epidemic.” Generic lenacapavir can’t be sold in the U.S. because a brand-name version, Yeztugo, made by Gilead Sciences and approved last year, is still protected by a patent. The U.S. list price for that version, meaning the cost before insurance, is $28,218 a year. Gilead officials say that’s similar to some other types of PrEP, which stands for pre-exposure prophylaxis. The new generic was approved by the FDA under a longstanding practice designed to ensure the quality of HIV-related drugs provided to other countries by the U.S. government. Approval of a drug by the U.S. FDA can speed regulatory approval in many other countries. The approval is considered “tentative,” the FDA's standard designation for generics while the originator remains under patent. Until now, Gilead has been the sole supplier of lenacapavir, and demand has outstripped supply in low- and middle-income countries. Last year, Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable production. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America. “We share the sense of urgency around expanding access to lenacapavir for HIV prevention,” a Gilead spokesperson said in a statement. “We believe we have enabled the fastest and most sustainable path to expanding access for communities most affected by HIV.” The generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI, a health research institute in Africa. The partners sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Common side effects with lenacapavir include injection site reactions, headache and nausea. People also must be tested for HIV prior to starting the drug and with each injection; drug-resistant HIV has been identified when used by people with an undiagnosed HIV infection. “For any kind of PrEP … you need to have HIV testing in advance,” said Saiqa Mullick, director of implementation science with Wits RHI. “For many of the low- and middle-income countries, that is a rapid test.” Generic lenacapavir should start to become available in some places within weeks, those helping with the effort said, although it could take a bit longer in countries that require the drug to go through their own approval processes before people can start taking it. Generic versions made by the other manufacturers have yet to be approved by FDA. “The work is not done. Now, we need the funding to actually buy it for everyone who needs it and then we need to do the hard work of getting it to the millions of people who need it and want it,” Amole said. “But this is a great milestone.” Casas said she’s optimistic that scientific advances — along with political will and funding — can help the world curb HIV. “Now,” she said, “we have the tools.

events.title: John Deere built an AI assistant to stop farmers from drowning in decades of field data
events.summary: John Deere announced its new AI assistant at the Farm Progress Show in Iowa. Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images John Deere's AI assistant, unveiled in September, helps farmers analyze data quickly. JD is embedded in John Deere's Operations Center, a digital farm management system. Farmers are warming to AI, but accuracy and data privacy remain concerns. Farmers have more data than ever about their fields, equipment, and crops. But turning it into a decision could take weeks. John Deere says its new AI assistant, JD, can do it in minutes. The agricultural manufacturing company announced the tool in September at the Farm Progress Show in Iowa. JD is integrated within John Deere's Operations Center, which is a digital farm management system that connects farmers' field and machine data into one platform. Farmers can ask JD questions on their mobile devices, such as the best time to harvest based on past trends, or which sprayer covers the most acres per hour. Melissa Neuendorf, the principal product manager for customer AI solutions at John Deere, told Business Insider that JD came about because farmers consistently said they were struggling to manage their abundant data. "We're now at a point where farmers have so much data that they have a difficult time finding the insights manually themselves," Neuendorf said. While smaller agricultural tech companies such as OneSoil, VisorPro, Arable, and AgZen are developing generative AI tools to give insights on specific equipment or crop metrics, Deere is among the first major agricultural-equipment makers to put a large language model AI assistant directly inside a platform that combines farmers' field, machine, and operational data. JD's launch shows how generative AI is becoming a central part of crop management. "Prior to John Deere's announcement, this didn't exist in the industry," said Matt Darr, a professor in the agricultural and biosystems engineering department at Iowa State University, who was in the room when Deere announced JD. Why farmers are considering AI tools more than ever Farmers have been collecting data for decades. But now, modern farm equipment is outfitted with additional technology and sensors, creating large volumes of data that are difficult to keep up with. It can be stressful for farmers who must also navigate tight margins, unpredictable weather , and limited planting windows. Plus, "most farmers aren't data scientists on the side," Darr said. Neuendorf said dissecting vast datasets is complex and time-consuming, sometimes requiring weeks. That's where AI can help farmers: "AI provides them the capability to do a lot of that analysis in minutes," she said. Before coming up with JD, Deere launched an AI tool last August that allowed farmers to ask questions in natural language about Deere's help documentation and operator manuals. This replaced the manual task of farmers flipping through pages of operator manuals. The tool received positive feedback, prompting Deere to broaden its application and launch JD to answer specific questions on the spot. Farmers can input data into the Operations Center from non-John Deere equipment if they use machinery from other manufacturers. Then, if they query JD, it can analyze all of that data to deliver answers. The Operations Center and JD are free to use, Neuendorf said. The AI assistant is available through an early access program, in which interested customers sign up for a waitlist and are considered for participation. John Deere will make JD broadly available in mid-November Neuendorf told Business Insider that the feedback from farmers so far has been positive. Neuendorf said she recently spoke to a farmer who was driving past a field and noticed it had lower weed pressure, or fewer weeds present, than other fields. Through JD, the farmer was able to open John Deere's mobile app right away, ask the assistant about previous years, and understand how he managed the field differently. Winning farmer trust in AI technology A McKinsey global survey of 5,500 farmers, published in September, found that 72% expect generative AI to impact operations within five years, but only 17% use the tech right now. One reason only a minority of farmers use AI is because they're worried about data privacy and how their information could impact commodity prices, Darr said. "These are competitive businesses," Darr added. "How information is used can influence global markets and what happens to global commodity pricing." John Deere said in its release announcing JD that it doesn't sell farm data or use it for agriculture commodity trading or speculation. Katya Kheistver, the chief product and operating officer of OneSoil, an agricultural technology company, said farmers won't trust AI if it delivers generic advice rather than insights tied to specific, real field data. Farmers often start their use of AI by checking the tech's outputs against what they already know. The farmer "watches whether the answer lines up with reality," and if it does so consistently, trust grows, Kheistver said. The stakes are high if farmers make decisions based on AI-generated answers because they have "one chance a year to grow a crop," Darr said. They need to be able to trust that an AI tool is accurate. JD meshes high-quality datasets with advanced LLMs, Darr added, which sets the AI tool apart and promises a high degree of accuracy. Neuendorf said JD is configured to notify farmers when field data is missing, rather than making inaccurate assumptions or generating false advice. This configuration also encourages farmers to input additional data, so JD can derive more insights and help farmers "make better decisions for the next season," Neuendorf said. events.title: The internet's latest obsession: The end of the world
events.summary: The world seems convinced the end is near — and social media is amplifying that belief, convincing people to stock up on food, water, generators and other items. Why it matters: Online chatter is fueling viral predictions of societal collapse amid growing unease about the future. But you're probably not going to die tomorrow. What they're saying: Michael Mills, a researcher at the University of Kent who has studied doomsday prepping for more than a decade, told Axios that modern doomsday fears aren't necessarily about a specific apocalyptic scenario. "It's an overall reaction to uncertainty in most cases," Mills said. He noted that whereas Cold War-era survivalists were often focused on nuclear conflict, modern preppers worry about terrorism, climate disasters, geopolitical threats and emerging technologies. He described the modern mindset as a "multifaceted concern with uncertainty." State of play: Viral posts have repeatedly urged people around the world to stock up on food and water, following similar recommendations from various governments and warnings from former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino. The situation has gotten so buzzy that President Trump was asked about it in an interview Monday. He said Americans don't need to stock up because the U.S. is "in good shape. We're strong. We have a great military and we will not have those kind of problems." Separately, conservative commentator Tucker Carlson — a man with 17.9 million followers on X alone — published a lengthy post Sunday evening alleging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressuring Trump to launch renewed attacks on Iran after the midterms, potentially with a nuclear weapon. For what it's worth, Carlson has been predicting similar doomsday scenarios for a while, and he's been wrong before. And the Pentagon's newly reported plan calls for U.S. military bases to prepare to operate without outside support for at least 90 days, terrifying some people into asking , "What's the government know that they're not telling us?" The big picture: Worries about financial insecurity , skyrocketing health care costs , a lack of rainy-day savings and younger generations' perceived inability to buy a house all contribute to the feeling that life is not okay. Then you've got AI , which could cut thousands of jobs, enable a cyberattack or help engineer a dangerous, and potentially deadly, biological disease. And then there's the geopolitical situation: wars, genocide and the possibility of global warfare as China continues to threaten Taiwan and rumors abound that the U.S. and Israel will reignite the Iran war with a fresh round of attacks. Zoom in: Political uncertainty can also fuel doomsday prediction culture, particularly around major elections . Mills described the prepper movement as historically right-leaning, with fears increasing during the Obama and Biden administrations and subsiding among some preppers after Trump's 2016 victory. During elections, "where it can often seem that everything is at stake... we don't know which way those contests are going to go and so naturally that uncertainty kind of flares up," Mills said. Reality check: Preparing for a catastrophe doesn't make you a conspiracy theorist. Governments commonly warn people about potential disasters, like advising them to evacuate before a hurricane. Mills distinguishes ordinary emergency readiness from prepping, which typically involves preparing for disasters lasting weeks or months, sometimes longer. The bottom line: Nobody knows what catastrophe, if any, might come next. But feeling prepared and stocking up for a couple of days without power can make sitting in the dark a little less scary. events.title: Owner of private Serbian bank detained and accused of siphoning money
events.summary: Serbian authorities have detained the owner of a private bank on suspicion he was siphoning money from the lender BELGRADE, Serbia -- BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbian authorities Monday detained the owner of a private bank on suspicion he was siphoning money from the lender that was used for some public utility payments during the previous government of former President Aleksandar Vucic. Alta Bank rose to prominence under the rule of Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party that was ousted from power in a parliamentary election last week. The bank has handled all electricity payments by millions of users in the capital Belgrade, as well as public parking accounts. On Saturday, Serbia’s Central Bank revoked Alta Bank’s operating license and launched bankruptcy proceedings to protect the bank’s depositors, saying that its liquidity “has deteriorated significantly” and “could worsen further." Serbia’s Deposit Insurance Agency, which guarantees deposits of up to 50,000 euros ($56,000), will act as Alta Bank's bankruptcy administrator, the central bank said. Davor Macura, the bank owner who initially owned an exchange office before becoming a prominent banker, was given a 48-hour detention on Monday, prosecutors said. Macura’s lawyers told local media he was present at the bank headquarters in Belgrade and fully cooperated during an hourslong police search over the weekend. Lawyers added that Macura will be questioned by the public prosecutor on Tuesday. Macura, whose businesses also span retail and construction, is suspected of illegally moving 45 billion dinars ($428 million) out of Alta Bank’s vault. Two other persons were also held for aiding and abetting the crime. The moves against Alta Bank and its owner came as part of a wave of changes triggered by Vucic’s defeat in the Oct. 25 election that also included resignations in the state-run media, arrests of several officials and an announced review of long-standing corruption cases. Former central bank governor Kori Udovicki on Sunday criticized the Serbian Central Bank moves as too slow. She said on RTS television that the central bank “lost a week in which it could have limited the bank’s ability to transfer the money abroad or to the connected individuals.” Alta Bank is a rare Serbian lender that allowed tens of thousands of Russian émigrés to open personal and business accounts. Scores of Russians have moved to Russia-friendly Serbia since the start of the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Alta Bank's troubles resonated outside Serbia. The Central Bank of North Macedonia put Alta Bank’s subsidiary into temporary administration and limited cash withdrawals to 160 euros ($179) per week, while Montenegro's banking regulator shut down payment processing company Alta Pay. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say In Serbia, armed police could be seen guarding the bank's offices in Belgrade after dozens of customers stood in long lines over the weekend trying to withdraw their savings. Serbian investigative outlets in the past have described Macura as a tycoon whose political connections to Vucic and his SNS helped him win lucrative contracts with state agencies and public enterprises. In 2024, Macura’s Alta Group came under scrutiny by the European Central Bank, or ECB, when it attempted to acquire a 20% stake in Austria’s Addiko Group through two connected firms to avoid triggering the ECB’s approval requirement. The ECB spotted this and stopped the deal. It also questioned the anti-money laundering controls and the source of funds in Macura's network. The Association of Serbian Banks called Alta Bank's collapse “an individual issue” and said it would not affect other banks. The SNS, which has governed Serbia since 2012, lost the parliamentary election to the student-led Student List movement. The outgoing authorities remain in control until a formal transition of power, expected to take several weeks. Critics say the SNS has steadily taken control of state institutions since it came to power. It has been accused of corruption, cronyism, links to organized crime and pressure on the judiciary, police and media. The party has denied the accusations. events.title: Control of Britain’s 39m smart meters passes to non-profit startup
events.summary: The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence for Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, after years of spiralling costs and delays Control over Great Britain’s 39m smart meters has passed to a non-profit startup after its former owner presided over more than a decade of spiralling costs and delays in the troubled network. The company owned by crisis-hit outsourcing firm Capita has promised a “seamless transition” to its not-for-profit successor, which will take over running the data network connecting the smart meters from this week. The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence granted to Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, to set up the country’s first smart meter data network, a process that has been dogged by costly delays while millions of households faced billing issues . Industry sources said Capita’s subsidiary was effectively blocked from tendering for a new licence to manage the smart meter network after Whitehall officials decided to replace the commercial framework established in 2013 with a not-for-profit public-interest model governed by an independent board. Instead, the network underpinning Britain’s smart meters will become a wholly owned subsidiary of the Smart Energy Code Company (SECCo) with “a greater focus on cost, transparency and customer and consumer needs”, the new operator said. Its board will include veteran energy and telecoms industry executives as well as Dame Gillian Guy, the former chief executive of Citizens Advice, which claimed in 2024 that households had been “let down” by the rollout because almost a third of smart meters weren’t working properly. Ministers had initially hoped that all households would have a smart meter before 2020 to help modernise Britain’s outdated energy system and make better use of renewable energy and innovative data-led energy tariffs . But the rollout has faced “serious reputational obstacles” , according to the government’s spending watchdog, which meant that three in 10 households still do not have a meter and another £1.7bn may be required to complete the rollout. The tender process for a new smart network operator ran last summer, at around the same time that the industry regulator opened an investigation into Smart DCC’s procurement contracts, which included deals that were awarded without a competitive process and one which was granted to its parent company, Capita. Smart DCC agreed in July to pay £200,000 into a consumer redress fund, in the same week that its parent company was forced to apologise for its role in administering the crisis-hit Civil Service Pension Scheme, which kept thousands of retired civil servants waiting for payments. Capita’s market value has plunged by 97% in the last decade after the outsourcing company once in charge of administering a string of government schemes revealed severely strained finances and mounting debts before undertaking an emergency restructuring of the business. A Capita spokesperson said: “Capita is proud of its 13-year stewardship of DCC. What began as an ambitious programme is now critical national infrastructure, connecting more than 39.2m smart meters across 23m homes and small businesses, with network availability of 99.6%. “We hand over a secure and resilient network that millions of consumers rely on every day and have been working with stakeholders to ensure an orderly transition to DCC’s next chapter.” A spokesperson for Ofgem said Smart DCC had “played a critical role” in delivering “an efficient and secure digital communication structure”, and that the new licence holder would be expected to “build on that solid foundation”.

events.title: Trump administration turns to SCOTUS in California ballot case
events.summary: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to mandate that California separate ballots of more than 20,000 voters the government suspects are "likely" non-citizens. The big picture: A federal appeals court rejected the administration's bid to set aside mail ballots last week, erecting another roadblock in the DOJ's pre-election quest to demand the state root out claims of voter fraud in the final days of the midterm elections. Driving the news: "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," the DOJ wrote in an application filed to the high court. "The only way to preserve the district court's ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now," the application, signed by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, continued. The DOJ's initial lawsuit came after the administration threatened California officials with emergency court action unless it probed potential ineligible voters over 48 hours and set aside ballots. Catch up quick: A federal appeals court and a federal judge stymied the administration's bid. U.S. District Judge David Carter cast doubt on the government's voter lists in a late October order denying the administration's request for a temporary restraining order, citing the "vagueness" of the government's "descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states." And in last week's 2–1 ruling, a federal appeals court found that granting the request "would provoke catastrophic change, upending the administration of the election." What they're saying: "We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a statement shared to X. The California Secretary of State's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: Virgin Australia apologises after breaking girl's $33,000 wheelchair
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Virgin Australia apologises after breaking young girl's $33,000 wheelchair Adelaide Tuimalealiifano relies on her specialised wheelchair for mobility. ( Supplied: KZ Photography ) A six-year-old could not use her wheelchair after it was damaged on a flight she was taking for medical treatment. The incident is the latest involving wheelchairs on Virgin Australia flights. Advocates want mandatory reporting for airlines on incidents involving damaged or missing mobility equipment. A girl with a rare bone disease was left without the use of her specialist wheelchair after it was damaged by an airline while she travelled to medical appointments. Adelaide Tuimalealiifano is one of about 60 people in the world diagnosed with multicentric carpotarsal osteolysis syndrome (MCTO), a genetic disorder that leads to the loss of the wrist and ankle bones. She can walk short distances but mostly relies on her wheelchair, which is worth $33,000. The damage to the wheelchair meant it couldn't be used. ( Supplied: Amanda Tuimalealiifano ) But during a flight from Townsville to Brisbane this week, the wheelchair was broken when a bracket was twisted. "It actually took quite a significant force for that bracket to twist," Adelaide's mother Amanda said. The family discovered the damage when they arrived at Brisbane Airport. Without a working wheelchair, Adelaide's father Jaster carried his six-year-old daughter through the Queensland Children's Hospital. He later fixed the chair after buying some hardware tools, but Ms Tuimalealiifano said not everyone was so fortunate. Jaster Tuimalealiifano pushing his daughter in her wheelchair. ( Supplied: KZ Photography ) "If our daughter was an adult and she was travelling solo and she couldn't walk any more … she wouldn't be able to leave the airport and she would be stranded. "It can be absolutely detrimental for people with disabilities." Ms Tuimalealiifano posted about the ordeal in a social media video that has been watched almost 100,000 times. She received many comments from people sharing similar experiences. The Tuimalealiifano family have shared their story of learning to live with disability on social media. ( Supplied: KZ Photography ) "Some people with disabilities completely refuse to travel on public transportation like airlines because their chairs are so complex … and they are so reliant on it that they can't even chance it getting damaged," Ms Tuimalealiifano said. "It is a systemic issue in the airline industry." The family received multiple apologies from Virgin Australia. In a statement, a Virgin Australia spokesperson said the airline extended immediate support and assistance to the family. "Virgin Australia is committed to improving our processes to provide an accessible and inclusive travel experience for all our guests," the spokesperson said. Ms Tuimalealiifano hopes the incident is a catalyst and "stepping stone" for conversations and meaningful change in the travel industry. The incident is the latest in a number involving wheelchairs on Virgin Australia flights, including in 2017 , two in 2023 , including when a former Queensland Australian of the Year was tipped out of a wheelchair , and another two in 2024 . In August this year, Shane Hryhorec was removed from a Virgin Australia flight in the Whitsundays because of issues with storing his portable wheelchair motor. Megan Spindler-Smith says incidents with personal mobility devices are far too common. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) People With Disability Australia (PWDA) chief executive Megan Spindler-Smith said damage to personal mobility equipment such as wheelchairs was a "long-standing issue". "It's so common that I'm not sure how it can continue to happen," they said. "How are airlines not sorting this out? "When equipment is actually damaged, passengers need more than just a 'sorry, we'll try and do this better'." Former Queensland Australian of the Year tipped out of wheelchair Dr Dinesh Palipana says a ground crew member at Brisbane Airport ignored his carers and manoeuvred his wheelchair sharply, tipping him onto the ground. They want mandatory reporting for airlines on incidents involving damaged or missing personal mobility equipment to better understand the scale of the problem and common causes. PDWA has been working with the federal government on proposed aviation disability standards. Public consultation closed on the draft standards earlier this month. Spindler-Smith wants the standards to become "practical, enforceable requirements" that change procedures at airports. "What really needs to change is the prevention of it happening," they said.

Custom chip designer Marvell has signed a deal to acquire optical chip and networking equipment maker Lumentum in an all-stock deal with an enterprise value of $115 billion (including debt) and an equity value of about $80 billion . Marvell will provide 4.5 shares of its common stock for each share of Lumentum. This makes the deal one of the biggest acquisitions in tech history. It compares to Microsoft buying Activision Blizzard for $68.7 billion in 2022 and Dell buying EMC for $67 billion in 2016. Interestingly, the two companies have one major shareholder in common: Nvidia. In March, as part of a multi-year agreement to purchase Lumentum’s advanced laser components, the GPU giant invested $2 billion to support Lumentum’s R&D efforts and fab expansion. Later that same month, Marvell announced that Nvidia invested $2 billion in an effort to beef up Marvell’s optical networking and chips portfolio. With Lumentum, Marvell says it will become a leader in AI connectivity, with products that range from chips to data centers. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of calendar year 2028, should both companies’ shareholders, and regulators, agree. events.title: Ruby on Rails creator has a warning for 'cantankerous' coders: Learn some people skills
events.summary: David Heinemeier Hansson said engineers will need to "learn some basic people skills" in the age of AI. LAT Images/Getty Images David Heinemeier Hansson said that AI agents will bring hard times for "cantankerous" engineers. "Best learn some basic people skills," Hansson wrote. Engineers on X chimed in to wave goodbye to engineers with bad attitudes. Don't be cantankerous. David Heinemeier Hansson has some advice for engineers as they adjust to AI. Often referred to as DHH, Hansson created the webapp framework Ruby on Rails and has fashioned himself into a software sage. On Monday, Hansson shared his prediction on X: "The age of agents is going to be amazing for most programmers, but it'll be hard times for the cantankerous ones." Hansson wrote that special abilities won't save those who are difficult to work with. That would be a dramatic shift in software engineering, where some so-called "cracked" coders can get away with large egos or social awkwardness. "Best learn some basic people skills," Hansson wrote. The prediction sparked a conversation among engineers about their social habits and professionalism. One pointed out the irony: agents "don't care how cantankerous you are," but your human coworkers do. One user wrote a eulogy to the "guy whose whole job security was 'only I know how this works.'" Dart cofounder Zack Swafford wrote that teams only tolerated bad attitudes because the staffers had "arcane tribal knowledge." Others questioned how new the change was. People skills have long been valuable, from networking your way into a job to landing that big promotion. "Been true in every company forever," one X user commented. "Skills get you hired, being easy to work with keeps you around. Agents just make it obvious faster." Hansson is committed to the future of AI coding. In September, he declared " pencils down " on handwritten code. Hansson explained that writing code was an "exceptional state," performed only when something went wrong with the AI-generated code. For some engineers, Hansson's post was a vocabulary lesson. "I had to search the definition of 'cantankerous,'" one engineer commented. "First time reading that word." For the record: cantankerous means bad-tempered and uncooperative. Read the original article on Business Insider

(NASDAQ: MSFT) on Monday announced an expanded co-selling collaboration to help enterprises overcome a critical challenge in AI adoption: connecting the data, applications and infrastructure that power AI workloads. As AI initiatives expand, organizations need to use data and applications distributed across public clouds, private data centers, offices and partner environments. Yet the networks connecting these environments often remain fragmented and complex. Lumen’s capabilities help customers align network transformation with Microsoft Azure modernization plans earlier, so connectivity, security, data movement and AI infrastructure decisions are planned as part of one enterprise architecture. Lumen’s extensive network and on-demand control capabilities provide Azure customers with the simplified connectivity and resilient, high-performance network foundation needed to put AI to work. As part of the expanded collaboration, Lumen intends to bring its full suite of cloud networking and application connectivity capabilities to Azure, expanding how customers can access and deploy Lumen capabilities through Microsoft’s cloud and AI ecosystem. “AI is reshaping where applications run and how organizations use and move data,” said Katy Brown, Corporate Vice President, Americas Markets and Industries at Microsoft. “Microsoft is committed to giving customers choice as they connect existing environments to Azure. Our work with Lumen is focused on helping customers align their broader network transformation with their Azure cloud and AI priorities, while taking advantage of Azure’s native networking, security, scale and innovation.” “Enterprises are moving quickly to adopt AI, but many are still figuring out how to connect the data, applications and infrastructure behind it,” said Ryan Asdourian, chief strategy and marketing officer at Lumen. “Together with Microsoft, we’re bringing cloud, network and AI planning together earlier and putting AI to work more effectively.” Expanding enterprise access to cloud-native networking Through expanded co-sell efforts, Microsoft and Lumen intend to extend joint account planning engagement around enterprise opportunities where network modernization, Azure cloud platform migration and AI transformation increasingly converge. The companies also plan to identify opportunities to bring additional Lumen capabilities to Azure and Microsoft Marketplace over time. Alkira, a Lumen Connect ® solution available through Microsoft Marketplace, provides customers with an established purchasing option for its cloud-native networking capabilities. The collaboration supports several enterprise priorities: Connect distributed data for AI: Link enterprise sites, data centers and clouds to support Azure-based AI initiatives. Simplify hybrid and multi-cloud networking: Apply consistent policies and visibility across distributed environments. Adapt as needs change: Connect new clouds, partners and applications without treating each as a separate networking project. events.title: A National Geographic photographer taught me one easy tip for taking better nature photos with my phone
events.summary: Business Insider's reporter has been practicing photography for more than a decade, and now she wants to learn to shoot with her phone. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I used to focus on the background when taking photos of natural landscapes on my phone. A National Geographic photographer taught me to look closer. What's in front of a landscape matters as much as what's behind it, he said. Nowadays, people are "drowning in photographs," National Geographic photographer Kiliii Yüyan told me. But there are ways to make yours stand out — even if you're just shooting on your phone. Yüyan tells visual stories about how different cultures relate to the environment, from the Amazon to the Arctic seas. He gave me four useful tips for taking pictures with my phone , and one of them made me think about photographing nature in a whole new way. Put something between your camera and the scenery The author photographs a shoreline in Belfast, Maine. Joey Hadden/Business Insider When it comes to making phone photos stand out, Yüyan said natural landscapes are especially challenging since they've been photographed so much. His best advice is to find a foreground subject.  "Great backgrounds, such as mountains or waterfalls, are easy to find because we're always looking for them," Yüyan said. "On the other hand, a good foreground subject, such as blooming wildflowers or a craggy tree, can be much harder to find in the right location." Yüyan recommended searching for an interesting foreground subject and framing your shot so you can see the scenery in the distance.  The author photographs Jackson Hole, Wyoming. Joey Hadden/Business Insider "It'll give your images depth, intimacy, and make your photos unique," he said. I had never thought about foreground in this way before, but his tip reminded me of when I photographed a beach across the street from mountains in Santa Cruz, California. I started by photographing the beach from the shore. I thought the mountains looked nice, but the foreground was just sand, which made the bottom half of my image look boring.  Then I took my phone across some ocean rocks and into the tide pools. The rocks and the reflecting water spruced up my foreground, giving my image more layers. To me, this made my second picture feel more interesting and dynamic. The author photographs a beach in Santa Cruz, California. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I also thought about a time I took some photos on my phone during a hike in Prescott, Arizona. When I first arrived at the Watson Lake parking lot for my hike, I thought it looked stunning with rock formations I hadn't seen before. But photographing the scene from the lot didn't seem to do it justice.  Once I immersed myself in the landscape by hiking the trails, I found foreground subjects such as shrubs and trees that better framed the lake scene. The inclusion of these elements in the second image gave a better sense of what it was really like to be there because it had more layers showing what actually surrounds the lake. The author photographs Prescott, Arizona, in 2022. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Some images in my camera roll already seemed to support Yüyan's tip, but the National Geographic photographer helped me identify what makes certain pictures stronger than others. I'll go into my next nature trip feeling more inspired to shoot from my phone and scout for interesting foregrounds. Read the original article on Business Insider
