events.title: Readwise takes on Amazon’s Kindle and Goodreads with its new app for book lovers
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Readwise , the maker of a read-it-later app and digital reading companion that keeps track of your highlights across services, is now taking on Amazon’s e-book empire with its latest app, Readwise Books . The app is an e-book store and helps you track what you’ve read, similar to Amazon’s Goodreads. The bootstrapped startup described the new app as “a cross between Kindle and the Goodreads apps,” as it offers a single place to buy, read, and track books. However, Readwise Books aims to offer more detailed reading stats than the dates you read a book and whether you finished it. It lets readers visualize richer reading data like words read, pace, depth, immersion, and sessions. Meanwhile, its new store offers “millions” of e-books from the big five publishers and others, initially in the U.S., with more countries to come. Print books (fulfilled by Bookshop.org’s distributor) and some audiobooks are available as well, the company notes. The launch comes at a time when there’s been an explosion of new reading apps and book trackers , all hoping to challenge Goodreads by introducing new features like book clubs, widgets, improved discovery features, goal-setting, better lists and organizational tools, habit-tracking, and more. However, few indie developers have gone so far as to launch an alternative to Amazon’s Kindle e-books store, which remains the industry leader, with an 83% share of the market when Kindle+ (formerly Kindle Unlimited) is included in the stats. One of Kindle’s bigger advantages is that it offers an end-to-end solution for everything related to reading e-books, from the hardware devices to the book-tracking log. Readwise isn’t selling its own e-readers, but it is attempting to create its own community around reading, complete with tools for reading purchased and uploaded e-books, tracking them (like on Goodreads), sharing your reading progress with friends, and more. It also offers a number of ways to track books outside its ecosystem. This includes a way to track reading sessions by using Kindle’s browser-based Cloud Reader and a feature that lets you snap photos of physical books to mark your progress. Plus, you can upload any DRM-free EPUBs (a common e-book file format without copy protection). The app can read your e-books aloud via text-to-speech. Readwise believes its more in-depth metrics could be a big selling point, too, likening them to a “Strava for reading” — a reference to the metrics-heavy exercise app. “The desire to read books, like exercising and eating well, is laden with guilt,” the company explained in a blog post penned by co-founders Daniel Doyon and Tristan Homsi. “Many people feel like they should be reading more, but feeling bad about it tends to change nothing. The session tracking taps into a different psychological mechanism. It makes the reading you’re doing legible and, as the adage goes, that which is measured is improved.” The company adds that the most consistent feedback from users is that the app has led them to read more without willpower tricks like goal-setting, streaks, or scheduling. With publishers’ permission, the app will support AI-powered features as well, like session recaps, definitions and term lookups, word and phrase translations, and a location-aware ability to ask questions about the part you’re reading. (So far, only HarperCollins has opted in, though.) Unlike Goodreads’ locked-down ecosystem, Readwise is embracing open technology. This includes a public API and an MCP server. The latter supports AI agents that could be used to research book recommendations on your behalf, use your Readwise data to create a books page on your personal website, or even wire up your hackable e-reader to log your sessions automatically, depending on how involved your AI use cases may be. The new Readwise Books app will remain free, with some AI features later going behind a paywall. Its prior apps for reading and tracking highlights are either $7.99 per month each or $9.99 per month for both. The Books app is currently in beta and requires an invite , unless you’re already a Readwise subscriber. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Europe's fridges are getting hacked. Could America be next?
events.summary: Cyberattacks are wreaking havoc on an unlikely target across Europe: supermarket refrigerators. Why it matters: Hackers are turning everyday, internet-connected equipment into physical hazards, spoiling food and causing costly damage. U.S. supermarkets use similar technology, and the Pentagon is already investigating suspected cyberattacks involving refrigeration systems at six military commissaries. Driving the news: Suspected cyberattacks sent refrigerator and freezer temperatures soaring at dozens of European supermarkets overnight, spoiling food and threatening costly losses. Grocery chains Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt reported incidents affecting stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar disruptions, per Reuters . A Belgian company that operates Delhaize's refrigeration systems said hackers switched the units into defrost mode. Here's what to know. Supermarkets hacked in Europe Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported cyberattacks or IT disruptions, forcing some stores to discard spoiled food. Dozens of stores were affected, including an ICA supermarket in Sweden that said hackers set its refrigerator and freezer temperatures to 122°F, per ABC News . Authorities haven't shared who specifically is behind the attacks, per NBC News . Empty refrigerated shelves at a Proxy Delhaize supermarket in Maleizen, Belgium, following a refrigeration outage. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images Flashback: The incidents follow similar attacks in France last month, when hackers seized control of hundreds of refrigeration units, causing fires and spoiling food. It's unclear whether the attacks are connected. What they're saying: France's finance minister Roland Lescure said at the time that the attack "touches the heart of our food security." "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said. How fridges get hacked How it works: Hackers aren't opening up each individual fridge and setting new temperatures. Instead, they target computer systems that control the temperatures of multiple refrigerated units remotely. Many stores use internet-connected controllers — small computer-like devices, sometimes with touchscreens — that allow maintenance workers to remotely monitor temperatures without having to visit every store. Hackers can exploit software flaws or stolen login credentials to change temperatures or activate defrost functions. Case in point: Danish manufacturer Danfoss said it identified security flaws last year and had long recommended customers install updates, according to The Guardian . In the Netherlands, some affected refrigeration systems used default passwords and were connected to unsecured networks. A supermarket manager discards spoiled food following a refrigeration outage linked to suspected cyberattacks across Europe on Nov. 2 in Belgium. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images The cost of hacked refrigerators Spoiled food: If temperatures rise overnight, the stores end up finding ruined meat, dairy and frozen products the next morning. In some French supermarkets, the soaring hot temperatures lasted for six hours, per Reuters. Spoiled food becomes unsafe to sell. Overheating and fires: Refrigerators can also overheat and cause fires. French prosecutors confirmed that the October attacks caused fires and food losses. Supermarkets lose money: Some stores lost more than €130,000. Two markets in the French region of Alsace reported combined losses of €270,000, per The Guardian . Intermarché's parent company estimated its nationwide losses in the tens of millions of euros. Yes, but: Not every attack causes extensive damage. In Estonia, a refrigeration company said technicians responded to the breach within minutes and halted any massive losses, per AP . Fridge attacks in the U.S. Zoom out: Many U.S. supermarkets use refrigeration technology similar to that found in Europe. Danfoss markets refrigeration monitoring and management systems in the U.S. Copeland, a U.S.-based refrigeration technology company, sells controllers that manage the grocery store display cases and walk-in refrigerators. What we're watching: The Pentagon is investigating whether cyberattacks caused freezer malfunctions at at least six U.S. military commissaries in August.

events.title: After ProPublica Investigation, House Democrats Demand Answers on U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
events.summary: Photo illustration by ProPublica. Source images: Congress and videos obtained by ProPublica. What Happened: Citing ProPublica’s recent investigation , House Democrats are again asking the Trump administration to explain why hundreds of U.S. citizens have been held by immigration agents and how the government verifies citizenship during immigration operations. In an October letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, California Rep. Lou Correa and 39 other legislators demanded the administration share the number of citizens that immigration agents have detained and how the government is tracking such encounters. They also asked for more information about how agents are trained to verify citizenship and legal status. Why It Matters: ProPublica counted more than 500 Americans detained by immigration agents — almost certainly an undercount since the government is not transparently tracking the cases. Experts told us the cases collectively show federal agents running roughshod over the constitutional rights of citizens. We found more than 100 Americans who were questioned about their citizenship, 63 Americans detained while recording, 36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or their family and roughly a dozen citizens deported, mostly children. What They Said: “We remain concerned that the Department’s actions are violating American citizens’ constitutional rights to due process, equal protection, and freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, and request transparency regarding the Department’s actions,” the representatives wrote in their letter to DHS. DHS has long insisted it is not arresting U.S. citizens, and it defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.” “These members of Congress have shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who’ve broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than they ever have for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray, and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America,” a spokesperson wrote to ProPublica. Background: Democrats have been pushing the second Trump administration for more details about how immigration agents are interacting with U.S. citizens since early 2025 . Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens in response to our earlier reporting that found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents . Last month, Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, a New Mexico Democrat, introduced a bill, Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act, that would make it easier for citizens to sue immigration agents for wrongful arrests. events.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
events.summary: 'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers. Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland. Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets. Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time. Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network". He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates. Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely. "The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added. The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F). It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack. In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked. Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK. In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce. The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop. Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open. A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked. Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected". An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit. A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network". "ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said. One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees." The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers. Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC. In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores. The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem. The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia. In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator. A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores. A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

events.title: How Walmart heiress Alice Walton, the world's richest woman, spends her $135 billion fortune
events.summary: Alice Walton is the world's wealthiest woman. Wesley Hitt/Getty Images Walmart heiress Alice Walton is the richest woman in the world. She spends some of her fortune collecting art and opened a museum in 2011. Here's a look at her life, career, and fortune. Alice Walton, the daughter of Walmart founder Sam Walton, is the richest woman in the world. As of November 2026, Forbes estimates her net worth at about $135 billion, largely because of her inherited stake in Walmart. Including Walton's brothers Jim and Rob, Walmart is listed as the source of wealth of eight people in Forbes' 400 ranking of the wealthiest people in America. The 77-year-old Walton's fortune had grown $33 billion in the preceding 12 months as Walmart's stock rose 30%, Forbes estimated in March. She's the 14th richest person in the world. Despite the Waltons' high status, their personal lives remain largely private. Here's what we know about how Alice Walton spends her fortune, from collecting expensive art to building a medical school. Alice Walton, the only daughter of Walmart founder Sam Walton, is the world's richest woman. Rick T. Wilking/Getty Images Walton overtook L'Oréal heiress Françoise Bettencourt Meyers as the world's richest woman on Forbes' 2025 list, retaining the title this year. Unlike her brothers, Rob and Jim, Alice Walton has not played a major role in running Walmart and has instead become a patron of the arts. Members of the Walton family (L-R) Rob, Alice, and Jim speak during the annual Walmart shareholders meeting event on June 1, 2018 in Fayetteville, Arkansas. Rick T. Wilking/Getty Images Walton fell in love with the arts at a young age, according to a New Yorker profile. When she was around 10 years old, she bought her first work of art: a reproduction of a Picasso painting for about $2, she told the publication. After graduating from Trinity University in San Antonio in 1971, Walton briefly entered the family business, working for Walmart as a buyer of children's clothes, she told The New Yorker. But her career really began in finance, which led her to founding Llama Company , an investment bank, in 1988. She has been married and divorced twice and has no children. Walton has an immense private art collection that includes original works by legendary American artists. Alice Walton attends the American Federation of Arts 2017 Gala and Cultural Leadership Awards at The Metropolitan Club on October 26, 2017 in New York City. Sylvain Gaboury/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images "Collecting has been such a joy, and such an important part of my life in terms of seeing art, and loving it," she told The New Yorker in 2011. In 2011, she opened the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, with her private art collection. The Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in 2024. Hasan Akbas/Anadolu via Getty Images Walmart is also headquartered in Bentonville. Before the museum opened, it had four times the endowment of the famous Whitney Museum in New York, according to the New Yorker profile. In 2014, the Walmart heiress paid $44.4 million for a piece of artwork by Georgia O'Keeffe. 'Jimson Weed/White Flower No.1' by American artist Georgia O'Keeffe was briefly on display at Tate Modern in London in 2016. Rob Stothard/Getty Images At the time, it was the most expensive sale of a work of art by a female artist in history, the Observer reported. Walton later put it on display at her museum in Arkansas. Crystal Bridges underwent a major expansion this year. Crystal Bridges in 2024. Hasan Akbas/Anadolu via Getty Images The expansion grew Crystal Bridges' footprint by 50%, according to a press release. Walton has committed billions of dollars to philanthropy. Jim Walton, Alice Walton, and Rob Walton cheer at the annual shareholders meeting for Walmart in Fayetteville, Arkansas. REUTERS/Rick Wilking Walton has contributed more than $6 billion to five family charitable foundations, which had distributed an estimated $2 billion of her funds through 2024, Forbes reported. In 2017, the Walton Family Charitable Support Foundation gifted $120 million to the University of Arkansas to establish a School of Art . Walton also has her own charitable organization, the Alice L. Walton Foundation , which donates to causes including the arts, education, and health, according to its website. Walton has also put some of her money into politics. Justin Sullivan/Getty She has traditionally given to Republican candidates and PACs, though Walton donated $353,400 to the Hillary Victory Fund , a joint fundraising committee supporting Clinton and other Democrats, during the 2016 election cycle, according to Forbes. During the 2026 election cycle, she contributed to Republican senators including Bill Cassidy and Tom Cotton, as well as Democratic Sen. John Hickenlooper, according to Federal Election Commission data compiled by FundVoter . And she bought a two-floor condo on New York City's Park Avenue for $25 million in 2014. Park Avenue, New York City. Stockyme/Getty Images The condo, which had been owned by late financier Christopher H. Browne, has 52 large windows overlooking Central Park and the city, as well as a media room and a library. Walton was active in the horse-breeding scene in Texas, but in 2015, she said she would devote more of her time to Crystal Bridges. Alejo Benedetti talks with Alice Walton at the KAWS Director Reception at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in March 2025. Wesley Hitt/Getty Images "I've been stretched in too many directions, and I want to get focused," Walton said, according to the Fort Worth Star-Telegram in 2017. "I've got a house in Fort Worth, so I'm moving to town." In 2017, she sold her ranch in Millsap, Texas, for an undisclosed amount . The Rocking W Ranch had an initial asking price of $19.75 million but was later reduced to $16.5 million. Walton also listed her 4,416-acre Fortune Bend Ranch in Texas in 2015 for $28.7 million. Alice Walton in 2015. D Dipasupil/Getty Images She also cut its listing price to $22.1 million . In 2021, the Alice L. Walton School of Medicine was founded. Alice Walton speaks onstage during the Getty Medal Dinner 2022. Stefanie Keenan/Getty Images for The J. Paul Getty Trust The school welcomed 48 students in 2025 and welcomed its second class of 48 this year. Tuition was waived for these students and will continue to be for the next three cohorts. It is for students "devoted to transforming the health of medically underserved and rural communities in Arkansas, its surrounding states, and beyond," the school website says. The Alice L. Walton Foundation and Mercy are building a healthcare campus in Bentonville. Bentonville, Arkansas. Larry Fleury/Getty Images/iStockphoto Its first building, a 709,000-square-foot specialty care center , is expected to open in 2029. events.title: Brickmaker’s woes deepen the UK housebuilding gloom
events.summary: Ibstock has issued a thumping profits warning, with sales 22% below expectations in the third quarter W ith John Healey’s Your First Home scheme on the way, is the mood improving in the housebuilding sector? A couple of the builders have results later this week, so can speak for themselves. In the meantime, though, here’s a thumping profits warning from Ibstock, the country’s biggest brickmaker, to spread a little more gloom. Demand hit a brick wall in the summer, as the company could have put it. Industry data, said Ibstock , show UK brick market volumes down 17% year-on-year in July and August. For the whole of the third quarter, it said, sales were 22% below expectations, forcing a one-fifth cut in its production volumes versus plans set out as recently as August. Cue an 11% fall in the share price to virtually its lowest level since the firm relisted on the stock market in 2015. Top-line earnings for the whole of 2026 will be “in the mid-£40m range” versus a figure close to £60m expected by the City. The short moral from Ibstock’s woes is that the sector’s slowdown is pretty entrenched. Across the board, we’ve heard shareholder-friendly vows from housebuilders of “financial discipline”, corporate-speak for saying expansion is off the table and the job is about hammering away at costs. Berkeley Homes, focused on the south-east of England, even said six months ago it will stop buying new land and hiring new staff . Everybody knows one deep cause: the turnaround in interest rate expectations with the Iran war. The Bank of England will probably raise rates this week (finally); then we’ll be on to wondering how many more increases will follow. In addition, housebuilders complain about costs of regulation that are harder to lose when the prices of new houses are going sideways. So is Healey’s Your First Home a reheat of Help to Buy, a gamechanger? From the point of view of housebuilders, the scheme is clearly welcome – they had been lobbying for action for ages. But there are a couple of caveats. First, the caps on the size of the transactions means it is not a copycat scheme for the very good reason that Healey can’t be seen to be adding too much inflationary pressure at a time like now. Second, it will only be launched next April, the chancellor said in his budget last week. The delay “may weigh on demand in the intervening period”, Ibstock chief executive Joe Hudson said, echoing others. He is surely right: for many qualifying buyers, it will make sense to wait five months for the discounted loans. Healey also said there will be no more changes to building regulations in this parliament (except where critical for safety), a nod towards the sector’s other grumble. On the other hand, he’s not proposing to remove existing regulations. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning So one suspects 2027 – a year of 1% growth in the economy, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts – is probably not going to move housebuilding volumes meaningfully. Your First Home should be “modestly helpful”, reckons Peel Hunt, but “lower interest rates remain key to a pickup in sector activity”. Yes, it all comes back to borrowing costs. And the upturn, when it comes, will surely be too late to save the government’s ambition of 1.5m new homes this parliament . The target isn’t officially rubble, but it may as well be.

events.title: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war
events.summary: Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war. Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs. Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing. “Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA. Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets , so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen. On Monday, US vice-president JD Vance reported that there had been “a number of good conversations with the Iranians” and that he was feeling good about the prospects of a “negotiated settlement”. Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week but the White House has offered few details about the contents of that correspondence. Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress. “The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections. But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.” The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.

events.title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
events.summary: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired. Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business. Some key findings from the report include the following: Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses. Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights. Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context. Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive. Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. SpaceX is looking to buy Boost Mobile from EchoStar, according to a report from The Washington Post. If the deal goes through, it would help the Elon Musk-owned company build a hybrid cellular-satellite network that could help catapult it into fourth place among the top U.S. wireless providers. The space-launch company has been dabbling in cellular connectivity, rolling out satellite access to T-Mobile’s subscribers in 2024. Last year, SpaceX bought $17 billion worth of wireless spectrum from EchoStar for cellular services, which could help the company’s Starlink service reach inside buildings, for example, something it currently struggles with. “This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America,” Musk said on X at the time of the spectrum acquisition. Yet, if Musk is still looking to buy access to terrestrial networks, it apparently wasn’t the last piece. Elon Musk, SpaceX’s CEO, reportedly spoke directly with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen in October about acquiring Boost Mobile, the mobile virtual network operator. EchoStar has about 7.5 million customers between Boost Mobile and Gen Mobile, its other mobile service offering. Musk has also approached AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon about buying capacity on their networks. All three rejected Musk, and they may still have a say in a SpaceX acquisition of Boost Mobile. Boost doesn’t operate its own towers, instead leasing capacity from AT&T and T-Mobile, which might need to approve such a deal. Sources speaking to The Post said that network leases are usually nontransferable. The big three providers each have over 100 million subscribers, dwarfing Boost Mobile. But while the acquisition would give SpaceX an immediate bump in subscribers, the true value of the deal would be giving the company access to terrestrial cellular networks. Gaining access to towers leased to Boost Mobile would expand coverage significantly — Boost currently covers most of the 48 contiguous states in the U.S. — allowing Starlink to cover devices when they’re outdoors and relying on cell towers to handle devices when Starlink signals can’t reach them. events.title: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack
events.summary: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shops Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why? Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France. Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg , the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked. The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”. The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros. A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”. An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”. The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters. The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit. It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.” A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries. Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets. “We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.” He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode. The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops. A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day “It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly. Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result. In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected. At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster. “This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.

events.title: Villa Vie residents made a 'Hail Mary' effort to buy the Odyssey. Read the letter confirming the plan is dead.
events.summary: A drone view of the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship docking at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port. SOVEIT YARN/Reuters A resident-led effort to buy the Villa Vie Odyssey has failed. Villa Vie's "never-ending" cruise came to a halt in Cambodia last Tuesday. One resident called the bid a "Hail Mary." Two days later, a letter confirmed it was over. A last-ditch attempt by residents of Villa Vie's Odyssey to buy and operate the ship is dead in the water. The Odyssey's final months were marked by signs of Villa Vie Residences' financial distress , culminating in the ship's abrupt halt last week in Cambodia. Residents — who bought cabins for between $119,999 and $439,999 in the hope of living permanently at sea — were given just eight hours to disembark on Tuesday. Paul Montoya, a member of the ship's seven-person Resident Council which was involved in securing resident pledges for the buyout, described the bid on Thursday as a "Hail Mary." Two days later on Saturday, a resident-backed group calling itself Sagar Capital told residents that the effort had ended, according to a letter reviewed by Business Insider. Three residents confirmed the letter's contents. The letter said the group had spent two months trying to negotiate a deal, but had been unable to do so. Montoya said in a call with Business Insider on Monday that the group had agreed to contribute a "fair amount" of capital toward the buyout to "get things rolling," while other residents were invited via WhatsApp or in person to pledge matching funds. Cambodian authorities said that 203 residents were on board when the ship docked in Sihanoukville. According to the letter, 169 residents made pledges, but the amount pledged was insufficient. "We were a little bit short, but we were pretty close," Montoya added, declining to say how much residents had pledged. He said that no money was collected from residents. In its letter, Sagar Capital cited a number of reasons for ending the bid, which several residents said was their only hope of keeping the Odyssey sailing. These included: An inability to reach an agreement with the ship's lender; Villa Vie having more debt than anticipated; Potential legal exposure; The cost of bankruptcy proceedings; The financial risk to residents' savings. "It was probably more exploratory than anything to see if the support would be there," Montoya said on Monday. "I think for the most part the support was there, but it would have been probably very tenuous in trying to move forward with those problems." In an interview with Business Insider on Friday, Petterson said the company was doing everything it could to keep the ship afloat after a potential deal with Oneil Khosa, the former CEO of Margaritaville at Sea, fell through earlier this month. Petterson said Villa Vie's focus was on recapitalization. "Preferably, we need an operational partner that can come in with a stronger hand and a bigger pocket," he said. Earlier last week, Petterson told Business Insider that the company was considering bankruptcy . Villa Vie, Petterson, and the company's cofounder Kathy Villalba did not immediately respond to requests from Business Insider for comment for this story. The resident-led effort was a final push to save the ship , Montoya said. Now, he said, residents are relying on "even more of a long shot," such as a "benevolent soul" stepping in. Cheryl Ethrington, a resident who had planned to pledge toward the buyout, said: "I haven't completely given up hope that someone will pick up the baton and run with it. If not, life goes on." You can read the letter from Sagar Capital to residents in full below: A Letter to our Fellow Odyssey Residents October 31, 2026 Dearest fellow residents and cherished friends, It is with profound sadness that we write sharing the difficult news that Sagar Capital has ended its efforts to lead residents in purchasing and operating the Odyssey. Sadly, this decision is final. Out of respect, we want to share a clear and candid explanation. Why we are bring this to a close: No agreement with the lender. We negotiated with the ship's lender for two months and could not reach terms. We understand the lender, with Columbia Ship management, has now taken control of the ship and intends to sell it at auction. More debt than we expected. We were given access to Villa Vie's records only last Saturday. Our review found substantially more debt than we had anticipated. Legal exposure. Taking over Villa Vie and changing its management would have exposed Sagar to significant liability from current and future lawsuits. The cost of bankruptcy. A Chapter 11 process would cost about $3 million for the first 60 days alone and could take much longer if lawsuits were filed. The risk to your savings. We could not find a monthly fee that both covered the ship's operating costs and stayed affordable. We could not in good conscience ask anyone to put their savings at risk on a plan that might not succeed. What we set out to do Our only aim was to keep the ship sailing for the people who call it home. It was never our intent to sell anything to anyone, or to press anyone into a decision. We tried to give you the facts as we learned them, and we are sorry the facts did not allow us to succeed. Profound Gratitude We received 169 pledges. To each of you who pledged, and to everyone who answered surveys, joined calls and offered ideas: thank you for your trust and your commitment. Your pledge: no money was collected. What we have learned over these months belongs to this community. If residents with the financial means to carry an effort forward ever come together, we will enthusiastically join in. We are bound together by this remarkable, unlikely adventure and will forever remain your neighbors and friends. We know this is a tender moment, and need to lean on one another for emotional and practical support. With that on our hearts, we would want to gather virtually in the coming days so we can share, reflect, and support each other as a community. The newly elected interim Resident Council is willing to serve or assist where needed. Though this chapter is closing, our community remains strong. Please reach out to one another as we always have, whether to talk, share resources, or navigate next steps together. We have been and will remain in this together, and we will continue to support one another. With respect and gratitude, Sagar Capital LLC Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Home Depot wants your AI agent to show some ID first
events.summary: Home Depot's CIO shares how she's thinking about AI agents, cybersecurity, and Anthropic's Mythos. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Have an AI agent? Need a hammer? Home Depot is thinking about how to make that palatable for the retailer. Angie Brown, the company's CIO, spoke to Business Insider about agents, the PHP cyber scramble, and AI fixes. She also talked about Home Depot's use of Anthropic's Mythos, and early attempts to join its Project Glasswing. Home Depot wants to roll out the welcome mat for your AI agent — so long as it's wearing a name tag and acting on your behalf. During a sit-down interview with Business Insider, Angie Brown , the company's executive vice president and chief information officer, said the retailer wants to support AI agents that can search and buy products on a customer's behalf. But Home Depot needs to be sure of two things first. "We want to know you're not a bot, and we actually want to know if it's you," she said. "That's something that Muse is working on right now, to self-identify." Her comments are the latest glimpse into how legacy retailers — and their tech staff — are thinking about the possible next generation of online shopping. Recently, several Silicon Valley companies have launched consumer-focused AI agents, such as Meta's Muse and Spear Street Technology's Instinct AI . They promise agents capable of scanning the internet, comparing products, filling carts, and buying items with little to no intervention from the person who sent them. Their rollout has been met with varying levels of resistance and buy-in from online retailers. Amazon barred Muse from shopping on its marketplace, saying the bots didn't properly identify themselves. Several other retailers — including Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora, and Shopify — have announced integrations or openness to AI agents. In October, Meta announced that it co-developed a personal agent protocol with Sierra AI to standardize AI agent identification. Brown said Home Depot is open to the idea of AI agents, but the retailer doesn't want to lose its connection with loyal customers. Frequent Home Depot shoppers, such as contractors and remodelers, are part of the company's Pro Rewards platform, where they're eligible for discounts. The retailer doesn't "want to lose contact with the customer," she said. "That's the next evolution," Brown added, confirming that Home Depot is in active conversations with Meta about how Muse should introduce itself to websites. "There's openness on both sides, because they want it to grow." Home Depot is already using AI to defend itself Brown said Home Depot is deploying AI amid a recent wave of cybersecurity worries. Last week, companies around the world raced to patch critical vulnerabilities in PHP , a programming language used in an estimated 70% of websites. The flaws were discovered with help from OpenAI and prompted US cybersecurity officials to urge affected organizations to update their systems or, in some cases, take them offline. Brown, whose remit includes Home Depot's cybersecurity, called the hours after the warning a "little hectic," but said the company's main website was not affected. "We had a couple of operating units — companies we've bought and things like that that are a little bit smaller — that had to plug a few vulnerabilities," she said, including an internal job application system that was taken down "in the middle of the day for about an hour to patch." Otherwise, she said, the company was largely spared from the sudden tech anxieties. Home Depot, Brown confirmed to Business Insider, has access to Anthropic's Mythos AI model, though the company wasn't granted early access via Project Glasswing, "despite our best efforts, and calling a lot of friends." Those slots were largely reserved for banks and cybersecurity firms, not major retailers. The Anthropic models "found a few things" for Home Depot to fix in its code — but the agents also found a few "false positives," Brown said. Home Depot, she said, has long ranked cybersecurity vulnerabilities, but AI is leading the company to rethink its desired time to deploy a fix. "The speed to fix a vulnerability has to be driven down to hours," she said. Update, November 2, 2026 — This story has been updated to reflect that Home Depot has not participated in Anthropic's Project Glasswing initiative. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 42AI comes out of stealth with $62.5M and a world model that can ‘predict human behavior’
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation? Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand. “A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision. 42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks. “When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.” “So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added. The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company uses a separate language model to generate explanations for its predictions.) Ezra said the model is trained to preserve a person’s underlying tendencies during simulations. So if someone is usually risk-averse, but the model suddenly treats them as a risk-taker, “the target is off,” he said, explaining how the model’s training rewards are structured. 42AI spent three years developing this approach, combining psychological research with neuroscience and genetics, as well as advice from experts in psychology and PTSD, and Dan Shechtman, who was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Gal-Or said the team first studied thousands of people via psych assessments and behavioral scenarios, before adding government and biobank datasets covering more than 2 million people. Its customer datasets have since expanded to cover almost 30 million people, he said. In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls. Gal-Or pointed out the system doesn’t need personally identifiable information, arguing that “the model never knows who the person is.” However, it seems the company still creates individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity. In predicting market trades, 42AI claims its model achieves 98% accuracy, but Gal-Or clarified that this is more a measure of whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not if each trade was predicted correctly. He also said the model consistently achieves an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume. (F1 score is a metric in machine learning that measures how well a classification model can balance correct predictions against false alarms and missed events.) And it’s not like the model can work everywhere, given it’s still a machine in a box. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said. Ezra explained that the system’s accuracy also suffers when it misses important situational context, like if someone chooses to change their trading choices based on advice from a friend or a colleague. Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure. The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number.

events.title: OPay’s US IPO withdrawal casts shadow over African fintech
events.summary: The News OPay’s abrupt withdrawal of its $304 million US IPO on Friday cast a shadow over one of Africa’s most ambitious fintech listings, after an undisclosed foreign regulatory inquiry derailed its New York debut. On Friday, OPay had priced its American depositary shares at $19 each, the bottom of its target range, valuing the company at just over $4 billion. But trading never began: OPay and its underwriters terminated their agreement around 3.30 pm New York time, saying it was no longer prudent to proceed with the offering. OPay, which primarily operates its payments service in Nigeria, did not identify the regulator or specify the subject of the inquiry. It described the jurisdiction involved as “immaterial to its core business” and said it expected the inquiry to be “concluded satisfactorily in the near future.” The withdrawal represents a setback for Nigeria’s fintech sector and the wider African startup ecosystem, which has spent years trying to persuade global investors that its young companies can scale into major, publicly listed businesses that return funds to investors. Know More OPay, which launched in 2018 as a payments company, also outlined plans for a secondary listing on the Nigeria Stock Exchange after the NYSE debut to give local investors an opportunity to buy into a business that drives nearly nine-tenths of its revenue from Nigeria. But the F-1 filing warned investors that shares traded in Lagos may not be exchangeable for the New York-listed American depositary shares, potentially limiting liquidity and allowing prices to diverge. A key part of the IPO is a broader strategic relationship with Standard Bank Group, Africa’s largest lender by assets. Its subsidiary, Stanbic Africa Holdings, has agreed to invest up to $200 million, subject to a formula that caps its stake at 4.99% of OPay after the offering. Standard Bank’s Africa head Lungisa Fuzile is expected to join OPay’s board following the IPO. The two companies have also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to explore partnerships spanning payments, merchant acquisition, lending, remittances, and the distribution of selected banking and financial products. OPay suggested in the filings that it will use Standard Bank’s infrastructure, regulatory expertise, and presence to expand across Africa.

events.title: DoorDash enters the restaurant value wars with a $12 meal deal
events.summary: DoorDash is offering $12 meal boxes in some cities. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images DoorDash is offering $12 meal deals in some cities. The value boxes include full meals from local restaurants — and no delivery fees. It's the latest entrant into the restaurant value-deal wars. DoorDash is getting into the meal deal game . The delivery service is offering $12 meal boxes in "select areas across more than 20 cities" including Atlanta, Chicago, and Philadelphia, it said on Monday. The meals will be filled by local restaurants and include a protein, vegetable, and carbohydrate. They also don't include a delivery fee and come with "reduced service fees," the company said. The boxes aren't just cheap eats. Like many value-priced options, they're meant to draw customers to restaurants, hoping to get them to order other items or come back later. "Meal Boxes are designed to drive a steady stream of everyday orders and introduce restaurants to new customers," DoorDash said in its statement. The deal is the latest value option for diners. Restaurant chains from McDonald's to Chili's have revamped their meal-deal offerings in recent years as food inflation has squeezed many consumers. Many customers have continued to order food for delivery while cutting their spending in other areas, despite added costs such as delivery fees and tips. DoorDash's $12 boxes might be an acknowledgment that some diners are seeking budget-friendly options and convenience simultaneously. Do you have a story idea about DoorDash? events.title: Ryanair CEO anticipates European airfare prices up as much as 20% next year
events.summary: The CEO for Ryanair expects European airfare prices may climb as much as 20% next year as jet fuel prices rise The CEO for Ryanair expects European plane ticket prices may climb as much as 20% next year with the conflict in the Middle East ongoing. “So we’re facing 2027 where we have much higher oil prices... I think they’re going to get passed on in significantly higher airfares,” CEO Michael O’Leary said in a Monday interview on CNBC. The price of jet fuel has been extremely volatile after the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran . Jet fuel has risen even faster than oil during the war, reflecting both higher crude prices and tight supplies of the refined fuel that is one of the largest operating expenses for airlines. Carriers have cut some less profitable flights and raised fares and baggage fees, although major U.S. airlines said higher passenger revenue initially covered only part of their soaring fuel costs. Globally, jet fuel averaged about $99 a barrel on Feb. 27, the day before the war began , according to the International Air Transport Association’s Jet Fuel Price Monitor. Prices more than doubled to $209 by early April, fell for nearly three months and reached $195 a barrel in mid-September following their renewed ascent, IATA said, citing data from S & P Global Energy Platts. The global average jet fuel price is currently hovering around $196 a barrel. 3 appear in court accused of causing Athens gas explosion by stealing copper piping Attack on Colombian military base kills 4 civilians, including a 2-month-old A brief ceasefire opens a perilous escape window from Kherson’s riverside kill zone Since diesel and jet fuel are closely related products that compete for space at refineries, shortages of one can put additional pressure on the price and availability of the other. The IATA expects fuel to account for nearly one-third of airline operating expenses this year, up from about a quarter in 2025. Ryanair said Monday that it doesn't expect European short haul airfares to fully offset anticipated increases in its fuel bill for next year, so it is reviewing its costs and may have to impose temporary pay freezes, lower crew ratios and use more artificial intelligence to get further productivity for back office and support functions. events.title: China rolls out support measures to aid struggling stocks
events.summary: China reels from sluggish consumption and property sector debt crisis. China rolled out support to steady weak stock markets after the CSI300 fell 8.5% in October, its worst month since early 2016. The PBOC will use swap operations to inject more than 100 billion yuan, and cut the buyback lending rate to 1% from 1.25%. The CSRC urged big index and tech firms to buy back shares, while the Shanghai Composite rose 1.1% as investors welcomed the measures. BEIJING/SHANGHAI – Chinese regulators have rolled out a handful of measures, from conducting swap operations to upgrading a lending facility for stock buybacks by listed companies, as part of efforts to stabilise struggling capital markets. The authorities also prodded index heavyweights and leading tech firms to try to stabilise their share prices, and are studying plans to ease margin rules to increase market liquidity. China’s central bank and securities watchdog made their announcements on Nov 2 after the benchmark CSI300 Index slumped 8.5% in October, its worst month since early 2016. Persistent weakness in the world’s second-largest economy, reeling from sluggish consumption and a prolonged property sector debt crisis, and sharp falls in tech stocks have hit investor confidence. Local media first reported that regulators had met financial institutions on Nov 2 to discuss tools to support capital markets. Share prices regained ground on Nov 2 in expectation of supportive policies. As part of the measures, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) said on Nov 2 it would conduct swap operations with financial institutions on Nov 2 that could inject more than 100 billion yuan ( S$19.19 billion ) into the stock market. It will be the third time the PBOC has used the liquidity tool, created two years ago to allow brokers, insurers and fund companies to obtain liquidity for stock purchases. The PBOC also said a re-lending scheme designed to fund share buybacks and purchases would shift from a temporary arrangement to a long-term mechanism. The interest rate of the expanded scheme was cut to 1% from 1.25%. In a separate statement, the China Securities Regulatory Commission urged key index constituents and “dragon head” tech companies to “actively buy back shares” and stabilise market value. The regulator will also prod some newly established exchange-traded funds to “speed up building stock positions”, and encourage fund managers to buy shares in a down-cycle. The new round of PBOC swap operations “sends another strong signal of policymakers’ commitment to safeguarding capital market stability and supporting investor confidence”, said Hao Zhou, a Hong Kong-based analyst at Guotai Haitong Securities. He said global volatility and external uncertainties continued to weigh on investor sentiment. The PBOC said bidding under the Securities, Funds and Insurance Companies Swap Facility would take place on Nov 3 . It said 31 brokers and fund companies had already applied for swaps worth more than 100 billion yuan. The central bank previously conducted such operations in October 2024 and January 2025, injecting a combined 105 billion yuan into the market. The Shanghai Composite Index climbed 1.1% on Nov 2 , its biggest one-day percentage gain since Aug 27. REUTERS

events.title: Omen AI adds liquid know-how in $16 million Aquatic Labs acquisition
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. U.S. data centers use 17 to 19 billion gallons of water to cool their hot-running chips each year — and that number is expected to triple in the next five years, according to The Water Foundation. That’s an expensive and politically tricky proposition for investors throwing billions of dollars at the challenge of scaling up AI. One way to use less water is to do a better job monitoring the cooling fluids, a task that currently involves sending samples away to a laboratory for tests in a multi-day process. Omen AI was founded in 2024 to solve that problem. The company is building a real-time sensor to determine whether valves were failing, or if bacteria growth in the system threatened to choke off water flow. After raising a $31 million Series A in June, Omen is now acquiring competitor Aquatic Labs in a $16 million cash-and-stock deal. The deal came together after Omen founder Zach Laberge was introduced to Aquatic Labs’ CEO Allan Adams by an investor in the filtration space. Both startups were building real-time water sensors with complementary technology: Omen’s sensors looked for elements in the water, while the Aquatic Labs sensor tests its alkalinity. Putting those two technologies in the same sensor creates a “much richer picture of the water and the fluid,” Adams told TechCrunch, while uniting their vision of automating what had previously been a slow, manual process. The combination unites two classic species of founder: Laberge dropped out of high school to pursue his first company, which did similar fluid analysis for large construction machines that depend on hydraulics. Adams was an academic, trained as a physicist, who spent much of his career developing advanced ocean sensing technology as an MIT professor and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute researcher before starting his company. Now, with Adams as the company’s chief science officer, the combined teams are working to integrate both technologies into one sensor, which they expect to have on the market by early next year. Omen’s initial sensors will be monitoring chips pulling in 250 to 300 MW of power by the end of the year, worth about $5 to $7 billion, Laberge told TechCrunch, with the hope of being installed on the equivalent of 1 GW of chips by the end of 2027. The added value is in uptime: If the fluid system gets out of whack, data center operators typically choose to dump the water rather than risk damage to their expensive equipment. That means shutting down operations until the fluid system is restored, which costs a lot of money. Monitoring lets data center operators use the same fluid for longer, and minimize the costs of a clean up. Adams hopes to see their technologies have an impact outside of data centers as well, telling TechCrunch that “water goes into data centers, and then it comes out and gets dumped into municipal water, and you want that whole process to happen in a way that’s as safe and responsible as possible — and that means you got to measure stuff.” AI companies once estimated as much as $4 trillion would be spent on AI infrastructure by 2030, but some investors have grown skeptical of the buildout , sending hyperscaler stocks plummeting in recent days. Omen’s team isn’t worried about shifting sentiment though, since their work comes after a data center has been built. “We’re working customers on stuff they’re building today or have already built, and so it doesn’t really affect us because all of those projects were financed 12 months ago,” Laberge said. “Our view is, if there’s tightness, this is still going to be the biggest market in human history, even if you sliced it in half.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Ninja’s first-ever microwave just replaced two of my kitchen appliances at once
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. I never thought I’d get excited about replacing my microwave, but the Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer has made a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one. Combining a microwave with a built-in air fryer, it’s designed to speed up everyday cooking, give leftovers their crunch back and, perhaps best of all, free up some valuable kitchen counter space. Priced at $449.99, it’s certainly not a budget-friendly microwave. But this is no ordinary machine for heating leftover soup. Ninja has paired a 1,000W microwave with a 1,700W air fryer system, powered by its FusionCrisp technology, which combines the speed of microwave cooking with the golden, crispy results you’d typically expect from an air fryer. Think leftover pizza, chicken tenders, fries, and all those foods that tend to turn sad and soggy in a traditional microwave. Instead, the idea is to get food that’s piping hot and juicy on the inside, with a deliciously crisp, golden finish on the outside. In other words, no more choosing between speed and texture. Of course, microwave and air fryer combinations aren’t entirely new. Brands such as Smeg have already explored the concept, while plenty of modern microwaves come with a range of additional cooking functions. What makes the Ninja Crispi Microwave particularly interesting, however, is its FusionCrisp technology, which is designed to bring both cooking methods together rather than simply offering two separate functions. It comes with a 5.5-quart glass cooking dish and a nonstick crisper plate, which sits on top when you want to air fry and crisp up your food. Another part that makes it stand out is that there isn’t a rotating plate inside, opening up a lot more space to cook more dishes at once. It’s not just about reheating leftovers. For example, if you want to make a pasta bake, the microwave can cook the pasta, while the air fryer crisps up the cheese on top. There’s one thing to consider before buying it, though. Measuring 20.3 x 17.56 x 14.1 inches, the microwave is hardly compact. It takes up a fair amount of counter space, so while it could free up room if you’re replacing a separate microwave and air fryer, it’s not necessarily the ideal solution for a small apartment kitchen. Then there’s the $449.99 price tag. That’s a considerable amount to spend on a microwave, particularly when a basic model can handle everyday reheating for a fraction of the cost. But if you’re someone who regularly reaches for both a microwave and an air fryer, the combination could make a lot more sense. events.title: Tomb Raider’s creators on how the game changed their lives: ‘Skint staff were suddenly pulling up in sports cars’
events.summary: ‘Giving Lara Croft pistols meant we could show off her acrobatics. And when she goes to Peru, we threw in a T rex!’ Paul Douglas, lead programmer and co-creator I joined Core Design in the summer of 1994 and met Toby Gard, who showed me his concept sketches for Tomb Raider . He’d already come up with the title and drawn a mock-up box cover with a woman holding two pistols. I was working on a golf game called The Scottish Open when Toby persuaded me that we should pitch his idea to Jeremy Heath-Smith, Core’s co-founder, who gave us the go-ahead to make a prototype. If I had stuck to the golf game, I would have had a much easier life. We had a couple of brainstorming sessions, and settled on the game’s four main pillars: platforming, puzzles, combat and story. Combat was always the weakest element but we didn’t have time to improve it. We also came up with the plot and level themes, and whittled a long list of interesting archaeological locations, including Petra and Angkor Wat, down to four: Peru, Greece, Egypt and Atlantis. Lara was originally Latina and her appearance was more realistic, almost androgynous. We felt that more stylised movement would play better, so her physique changed to reflect that. She became a British mercenary and then, thanks to scriptwriter Vicky Arnold, an aristocrat who tracks down historical artefacts just for fun. Toby and I came up with the movement metrics by measuring out a hopscotch grid in the car park. Lara was three paces tall and each block in the game’s environment was four paces. All of the gameplay systems grew from those measurements and constraints. It was brutal getting it delivered on time. I took just three days of holiday in two years. Toby and I were in the office until 2 or 3am every day, including weekends, for the best part of a year. Toby made himself sick with the stress. We were on the cusp of 3D games going mainstream and the action-adventure focus made us somewhat unique. Then the marketability of Lara thrust Tomb Raider into the stratosphere. The game’s publisher, Eidos Interactive, took the character and ran with it. I like to think the quality of the game spoke for itself, regardless of the way Lara was sexualised. We never imagined Tomb Raider would blow up in the way it did. It was the right time, right place, and it was different from the competition. We showed that ideas that go against conventional wisdom – a female character will never sell! – can uncover new territory and find success. It was gratifying and humbling to see our hard work rewarded by so many people playing the game. We managed to bottle lightning, although I’m still carrying the scars of its creation. We developed most of Tomb Raider in a big Victorian building on Ashbourne Road in Derby. We sat there sweating our guts out in the summer and freezing cold in the winter. I was the only female developer, but that didn’t faze me. I felt respected and was almost seen as a sister by some – the team was like a family. It was a defining time in my life. Toby was lovely. Very eccentric and a bit of a genius. He’d put together a demo that was like a simple top-down version of Prince of Persia, with an Indiana Jones-like character jumping and tumbling from platforms. Although management thought no one would want to play a female character, they went with it. There’s a certain empathy you get from playing Lara. It’s probably the number of times she dies and that awful scream. She was taciturn and mysterious: a loner who played her own game and didn’t answer to anybody. Women hadn’t really been portrayed like that before. Giving Lara pistols enabled us to show off her acrobatic movement. She was mostly pursued by animals rather than people. Hearing a bat, or the growl of a bear, was much scarier than a gunshot. You felt at the mercy of the wild. And we pushed the 3D environment to its limits. We only had so much memory and processor speed, but we were clever with it, giving players the sense that they were in this vast, cavernous space that was actually lots of rooms bolted together. Before designing a level, we always had a team meeting where we’d come up with a rough schematic. We all enjoyed history. We chucked in whatever myths and legends we thought would be fun and interesting. Our imaginations ran wild – to the point where we threw a T rex into Peru! Eidos saw the potential of Lara, rather than the game, so they focused on her. That was the right thing to do, but I think it went a bit too far with what she was wearing or the poses she was put in for some marketing campaigns. They showed a lack of imagination by oversexualising her. I knew we’d made a great game, but it didn’t really sink in until I saw the sales figures. It was life-changing for all of us. People who were skint before were suddenly pulling up in sports cars. I was able to buy a house from the royalties. Lara is right up there with iconic characters such as Mario and Sonic the Hedgehog.
