events.title: Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer: the Amazonian town transformed by a rampant mining boom
events.summary: Mayaya, once-remote, has become a hub for Chinese companies. But critics accuse them of exploitation and illegal exports T he pork belly hits the oil with a sizzle, and a rich aroma of soy sauce and caramelising sugar fills the kitchen. Zhang Changchun, a middle-aged man from China’s Heilongjiang province, is cooking dinner for his friends on a warm evening in Mayaya, a small town in the Bolivian Amazon. “Bolivia is my happy place,” he says in Mandarin as he adds the dish to a table overflowing with pork trotters, duck wings and braised sábalo fish. In this small restaurant, a group of half a dozen Chinese men gathers most nights to eat, drink and play mahjong. Each man plays a critical role in the town’s booming gold business. Some work as investors or miners; others import supplies and equipment. Together, they run most of the town’s mining operations: about 20 open-pit mines and 12 dredge boats, operated by about 2,000 Bolivian and 200 Chinese workers. The table gets rowdy as the men debate their afternoon games over high-end Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer. Almost every conversation revolves around money. In less than a decade, private Chinese mining companies have turned this once-remote Amazonian town into a hub of gold speculation. Mining equipment stores, hotels and Chinese restaurants now line the main street. “We developed this town,” Zhang says between gulps of beer and bites of pork. “Without the Chinese, there would be no Mayaya today.” As record gold prices drive Amazonian deforestation and violent conflict, these small-scale, private mining operations are tightening China’s grip on the world’s gold reserves. The Guardian spent five days with Chinese miners, investors and traders. The Bolivian Amazon has long attracted foreign capital, from rubber and timber industries to North American mining companies in the 1950s. But now, Chinese mining is defining a new era of extraction, as a global network of goods, machinery and labour often thrives illegally under Bolivian law. A 2014 national law limits mining rights to cooperatives and independent miners, state-controlled firms and domestic and foreign private companies. Such foreign firms must have a registered Bolivian office and operate in their own name. The state permits joint ventures, leases and risk-sharing agreements between foreign and national firms, but only through public-private contracts, in which the state is a shareholder. Chinese mining firms operating outside this framework act unlawfully. Under a 2016 law , cooperatives also risk expropriation if they contract, lease or share mining-concession risks with foreign firms. C hinese goldminers first arrived in Mayaya in 2005, but it was in 2017 that a major wave of immigration took place, after China’s national development and reform commission banned domestic small-scale gold mining , citing environmental and national defence concerns. The crackdown sent many miners and investors searching for work globally, and spurred several companies to hire workers from mines closed back home to work at newly opened operations in Bolivia. One of those firms is Shenzhen Vicstar Import and Export, which has operated in Bolivia since at least 2011. Officially, the firm does not carry out mining operations, listing only print materials and manufacturing in a supplier directory. Campaigners say these companies skirt the law, “hiding behind” cooperatives to operate in Bolivia’s mining industry. On paper, foreign investors sign service contracts with local cooperatives, provide capital and machinery. In reality, they control the mines end to end, selecting sites, hiring workers, providing machinery, exporting gold and taking 75% to 80% of profits, says Alfredo Zaconeta, a mining researcher at environmental thinktank Cedla . Behind these contracts, Zaconeta adds, Chinese investors evade legal responsibilities as the state lacks the resources and political will to oversee the mining lobby. He says it rarely, if ever, enforces existing ownership and permit rules. As a result, in Bolivia, an entire economy has emerged to serve this migration, from La Paz lawyers specialising in Chinese work visas to a local phone store that doubles as an informal bank for exchanging bolivianos and renminbi. In some regions, Chinese miners recruit friends and family, forming home town clusters dedicated to the local mining industry. Along Mayaya’s main street, shops sell all things Chinese – from bottled tea and cigarettes to pork intestines. Yang Yanbin, a Chinese investor, says: “As long as you have money to invest, this country welcomes you. We stuff all the money straight into our pockets.” Chang Yuequan, a lifelong miner who has mined gold along the China-Russia border since his teens, is another Chinese investor in Mayaya. In 2017, after verifying Mayaya’s gold quality, he ordered 120 shipping containers from China and began assembling machinery.

events.title: Gulf states united in call for diplomacy to end war

events.title: Poundland's former owner offers to invest as minister prepares to meet board
events.summary: Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm Poundland has been given until Thursday to find a rescue deal, putting up to 12,000 staff at risk. Poundland's founder has said he would invest in the firm and a government minister said she would meet the firm's board amid its administration fears. Steve Smith, who set-up the Walsall-based business, said he had attempted to contact owners Gordon Brothers having been "really surprised" to learn about them filing for administration when sales were up 11% on last year. The BBC understands that Business Minister Kate Dearden will meet with senior Poundland executives later this week to discuss the company's threatened insolvency. US-based Gordon Brothers said it was evaluating interest for the whole business and formal and indicative offers for significant viable parts of it. Gordon Brothers, who bought the firm from Polish retail group Pepco last year for £1, has stopped funding the business and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG). The retailer has given the business until Thursday to find a rescue deal, putting up to 12,000 staff at risk. Steven Smith founded Poundland in 1990 with the help of his father, Kevin Smith It's understood the meeting with Deardon will be predominantly a "fact finding" meeting with government sources conceding there is limited scope for the government to intervene in a commercial transaction albeit one that puts over 10,000 jobs and hundreds of stores at risk. The meeting was first reported by Sky News. There is no current meeting planned between the government and executives from current owners, US private equity group Gordon Brothers. Concerns have been raised that Gordon Brothers have declined an offer from another buyer to keep Poundland afloat in order to ensure repayment of £30 million loan it inherited after buying the company for £1. 'Poundland closure would leave a void in our town' Published 2 days ago How Poundland grew from a market stall to a high street giant Published 3 days ago Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators Published 4 days ago Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government was "ready to support" staff as he also called for answers over why an offer to buy the business had been rejected. Smith, from Wolverhampton and who set up the firm in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, said he contacted the owners over the last three months but had no reply. He had thought that was good news as he assumed the firm must have had offers on the table. "And maybe I was a bit too late, but I'd certainly... with talking to the staff and how Poundland's performing at the moment, I'd certainly, if there's an opportunity, I definitely want to put some money back in there." He said he was still in touch with staff there at levels within the business and "even last week" sales were 11.2 % upon last year. "Although Poundland made a loss last year, they're going to make a good profit this year, so it's just crazy." Staff held a protest outside Poundland's Walsall-based HQ last week He warned that the two or three thousand suppliers to the firm only worked for Poundland so they would be directly affected by its collapse. "This is not just about 12, 000 jobs. I'm estimating more like 20 or 30,000 jobs," he added. The company has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and Smith said it had between four and five million customers a week, so with Poundland not being present on high streets would "cause a lot of other retailers to fall as well". Liam Byrne, chair of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee and Labour MP for Birmingham Hodge Hill and Solihull North, said he felt the company could be saved and "the whole deal stinks to high heaven right now". "Because I think the issue that we've got is, you've got an owner that could well be trying to cut and run, to sell a business that is in fact a going concern in order to maximize their own profits and put in jeopardy 12,000 British jobs on the high street." "Our message today to government and to ministers is, do not leave this to the last minute, which is Thursday... please get on the case now to get everybody around the table to maximize every option to save as much of the business as possible," he added. In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it had not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole". "We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment." Gordon Brothers said: "While Martin Property Group had been identified as the preferred bidder by Poundland's management team, attention must now turn to other active bids." The interest, formal and indicative offers were being evaluated "with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland's people and all relevant stakeholders.

Once the transaction is completed, Constellation is expected to acquire a seed portfolio of aircraft from Avolon with a current market value of $1.4 billion. The sovereign investor said in September that it aimed to diversify its approach across sectors to manage risks. The aviation market is growing amid a continued rise in passenger demand, but airlines continue to face aircraft supply shortages and delivery delays, driving demand for leased aircraft to finance fleet renewal and expansion. In July, plane lessor Dubai Aerospace Enterprise (DAE) partnered with US-based Neuberger Specialty Finance to launch Mustang Aerospace , an aircraft leasing co-investment vehicle targeting up to $6 billion in assets over the medium term. DAE in April also agreed with Blackstone Credit & Insurance to launch a platform that will invest $1.6 billion annually to build a portfolio of commercial aircraft. “Aircraft manufacturers’ order books now stretch a decade or more into the future, and airlines rely on lessors with scale and aircraft delivery slots to grow their fleets,” said Gautam Bhandari, co-founder, managing partner and global chief investment officer of I Squared Capital . “Avolon has one of the largest order books with Boeing and Airbus and thus enjoys significant benefits of scale.” Avolon will retain a minority equity interest in the joint venture and serve as Constellation's exclusive aircraft manager and servicer, the statement said. The transaction is expected to close subject to securing the necessary regulatory approvals. The joint venture will be supported by a syndicated debt facility provided by a group of international banks.

events.title: Singapore manufacturers stay upbeat on AI demand despite geopolitical clouds
events.summary: All clusters except biomedical manufacturing and transport engineering project larger workforces. Singapore manufacturers expect stronger business, jobs and output over the next six months, driven by global AI demand, despite geopolitical and economic uncertainty. The EDB survey found a net weighted 24% expect better conditions, up from 12%, while 72% expect employment to stay broadly similar. Precision engineering and electronics are most upbeat, but chemicals is the weakest cluster. Firms cite high costs, overseas competition, tariffs and crude oil supply worries. SINGAPORE – Manufacturers remain optimistic about the next six months, buoyed by strong global demand tied to artificial intelligence , even as geopolitical developments cloud the economic outlook. A net weighted balance of 24% of firms expect business conditions to be better between October 2026 and March 2027, compared with the third quarter, a survey released on Nov 2 by the Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) found. This is up from a net weighted balance of 12% in the previous survey. A weighted 29% of firms foresee improved conditions, and 5% expect a weaker business situation. On jobs, a weighted 72% of manufacturers expect employment levels in the fourth quarter to remain broadly similar to the third quarter. All clusters except biomedical manufacturing and transport engineering project larger workforces. Overall, the net weighted balance for employment is 14%. By cluster, precision engineering is the most upbeat (+48%), supported by semiconductor-related equipment makers that expect global AI-related investment to keep expanding. The electronics cluster (+42%) also expects a strong outlook, driven by robust orders for semiconductors used in AI applications. Biomedical manufacturing (+14%) and general manufacturing (+7%) are also positive. Firms in transport engineering (+1%) expect broadly similar conditions, and cite rising costs of, for example, materials, fuel and freight, and overseas competition as key headwinds. The chemicals cluster is the most pessimistic (-13%). Firms in the petroleum segment (-28%) remain concerned about persistent uncertainty over crude oil feedstock supply. For the fourth quarter, a net weighted balance of 34% of manufacturers expect output to rise from the previous quarter. Electronics (+55%) and precision engineering (+54%) lead the way. In electronics, the semiconductors and computer peripherals and data storage segments expect higher production to cater to buoyant demand from AI data centres. Precision engineering firms foresee higher output of semiconductor-related equipment, bonding wires and metal precision components. Biomedical manufacturing (+19%) firms expect to produce more active pharmaceutical ingredients and life science instruments. General manufacturing (+10%) is also positive, with every segment except printing projecting higher output. The food, beverages and tobacco segment expects stronger export demand for milk and beverage products. Output expectations in transport engineering (0%) are mixed. While the aerospace and land segments anticipate higher activity, the marine and offshore engineering segment sees lower production of oil and gas-field equipment as geopolitical uncertainties weigh on orders. Chemicals (+5%) is the weakest cluster. On export orders, a weighted 23% of firms anticipate challenges in securing orders in the fourth quarter. The top two factors cited are price competition from overseas rivals, and political or economic conditions abroad, including geopolitical developments, tariffs and inflationary pressures. The EDB survey was conducted in September and October 2026. Of 397 manufacturing establishments surveyed, 83% responded. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
events.summary: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work. Change the economics of repeated use Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows. The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request. Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting. Test the operating model At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%. That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work. Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it. HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships. Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice. Build for adoption, not rationing Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code. As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them. events.title: Greenpeace activists create ‘boulder barrier’ in North Sea to deter industrial fishing
events.summary: Action taken to prevent bottom trawling in the marine protected area and conserve porpoise populations Greenpeace activists have dropped boulders in the North Sea to snag the dragnets of industrial trawlers fishing in a marine protected area. Activists onboard the Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise dropped the giant stones to form an underwater barrier around the Southern North Sea marine protected area (MPA) – the UK’s most bottom-trawled MPA. The Southern North Sea is an area of importance for harbour porpoises , supporting nearly 20% of the UK North Sea population . But despite its MPA status, there are no restrictions on fishing in most of it. Bottom trawlers, dredgers and other industrial fishing vessels scour it daily. Bottom trawlers logged more than 37,200 fishing hours in the protected zone in 2025, an act akin to “a bulldozer tearing through a treasured national park”, Greenpeace UK said. “Hulking great ships prowl the sea day after day, stripping it of fish and killing precious wildlife like porpoises, sharks and sea birds,” said Will McCallum, the campaign organisation’s co-executive director. “With our ship and a movement behind us, we’re doing what the government isn’t: protecting our seas.” The “boulder barrier” had effectively closed 116 sq km (about 45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea MPA to bottom trawling, Greenpeace UK said. Over the coming days, the Arctic Sunrise will patrol the area to deter any other kinds of industrial fishing. The activists have declared the zone an “ocean park”, in the spirit of Britain’s national parks. The Southern North Sea MPA lies along the east coast of England, from north of Dogger Bank to the strait of Dover in the south. It is intended to protect porpoise populations, partly by ensuring the “availability of prey is maintained”. Greenpeace UK’s activists say intensive fishing in the area contradicts this objective. “We announced in June that if the government didn’t act soon, Greenpeace UK would take direct action,” McCallum said. The action coincided with the nationwide premiere of Blue Planet III , the latest BBC wildlife documentary narrated by David Attenborough to focus on the oceans and the human-made threats they face. In 2025 bottom trawlers and dredgers tore through a cumulative 55,600 sq km of MPA seabeds, an area 58 times the size of Dartmoor national park, according to a Greenpeace analysis. The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential A number of notable figures added their names to boulders tipped from the Arctic Sunrise into the North Sea. Among them was the Labour MP Kerry McCarthy, a former climate minister and a member of the all-party parliamentary group for the ocean, who said: “Industrialised fishing is having a hugely destructive impact on our marine environment, yet less than 1% of our seas are protected from it. “[Fishing boats] can legally tear through supposedly protected areas of the ocean, wreaking havoc upon the seabed, precious habitats and the sea life that lives there. Progress is too slow and nature can’t wait, which is why I’ve added my name to one of Greenpeace UK’s boulders. We need a ban on bottom trawling and properly protected ocean sanctuaries, both here in UK waters and right across the Atlantic Ocean.” The government has been contacted for comment.

events.title: The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts. This new era is being called the agentic web. It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process . —Grace Huckins Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide. They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults. Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits. But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes. Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign. Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths . —Sara Kiley Watson This story is the final part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Subscribe to read the other five instalments in our new Impossible issue . The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble Big AI bills and weak earnings have spooked investors. ( BBC ) + The Nasdaq 100 had its worst day since June on Friday. ( NBC News ) + OpenAI has cut its funding target by $10 billion. ( CNBC ) + What even is the AI bubble? ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Hackers have hit Ukraine and Russia’s emergency alert apps Kyiv residents were warned of “nuclear danger.” ( NBC News ) + Russia’s app said nuclear warheads had been launched. ( CNN ) + Ukraine has blamed Russia, which hasn’t yet accused anyone. ( BI ) + AI will transform cyber warfare. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Binance users withdrew $3.6 billion after the largest ever crypto hack The funds moved when the exchange reopened on Sunday. ( Guardian ) + Binance says it’s covered $6 billion of the stolen $6.3 billion. ( Reuters $) + But the industry’s response has undermined its “decentralized” image. ( Gizmodo ) 4 An AI agent injected drugs into a live mouse’s brain It chose the gene therapy and controlled the needle itself. ( Wired $) + We need real-time tracking of AI agents. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Data centres have made utilities a flashpoint in the midterms Americans are angry over rising electricity bills. ( Reuters $) + Virtual power plants could help. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Apple has overtaken Nvidia as the world’s most valuable company Investors are favouring its restraint on AI spending. ( Bloomberg $) + But critics say it’s entering its “slop era.” ( 404 Media ) 7 Supermarket fridges have overheated in a new wave of cyberattacks Stores in Belgium, Sweden, and Luxembourg were hit. ( Politico ) 8 The first chocolate bars made from lab-grown cocoa are here Startups are cultivating chocolate to tackle a cocoa shortage. ( WSJ $) 9 Hackers hijacked digital billboards in multiple countries to show porn They also criticized security flaws and Egypt’s government.( Gizmodo ) 10 A new 3D map reveals instability in interstellar space The discovery could help explain why stars form so inefficiently. ( Quanta ) Quote of the day “It would be great if all this was just a house of cards.” —Kevin Roose, a technology columnist at the New York Times, tells NPR that an AI investment crash would be preferable to the technology permanently upending work and society. One more thing Useful quantum computing is inevitable—and increasingly imminent Last year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang jolted the stock market by saying that practical quantum computing is still 15 to 30 years away. He also suggested that those computers would need Nvidia GPUs to function. But Huang’s predictions miss the mark—both on the timeline and the role his company’s technology will play.  Quantum computing is rapidly converging on utility. And that’s good news, because the hope is that they will be able to perform calculations that no amount of AI or classical computation could ever achieve. events.title: Getting a big head start on holiday shopping can benefit retailers and consumers alike
events.summary: Does it make sense to wait until late December to wrap up, like these California shoppers did in 2023? Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Amazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales as early as October . But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping. As a finance professor who studies how people and companies make financial decisions , I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping. Why retailers get such an early start Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about US$1 trillion to $1.7 trillion in the U.S. Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the Bank of America Holiday Spending survey . But many people like to shop for holiday gifts early – meaning before Halloween . Some do this out of necessity : They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks. For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually . In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping. Retailers are adjusting by getting an early start on holiday sales and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more people to join the early birds . And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season. A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics , since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs. Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory gives retailers more opportunities to sell those items. However, an earlier shopping season does not necessarily increase consumer spending overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October. Early birds could buy these Christmas decorations at a discount on Oct. 17, 2026. Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images Beware of some early-shopping pitfalls To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should read vendors’ fine print and research their return policies . Many big retailers are making their return policies more restrictive by shortening the length of time you can return purchases and adding return/restocking fees. In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, Best Buy’s extended policy takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. Target similarly restricts its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1. Amazon extended its holiday return policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas. The timing of holiday shopping varies whether you buy gifts online or in brick-and-mortar stores. Anchiy/E+ via Getty Images When buying early makes financial sense Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary. For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price. But that doesn’t mean you necessarily need to rush to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out. And you should do some comparison shopping to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items. Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The key is to have a budget , recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping. events.title: Unions gain access to thousands of Google workers after UK employment rights overhaul
events.summary: Prospect to hold workplace sessions and recruit members under agreement with tech company Trade unions are expected to make further inroads into big tech companies in the UK after new rights for unions to access workplaces came into force , with Google UK signing an agreement on Monday. The Prospect union has reached an agreement with Google to begin organising among about 7,000 workers across its UK operations, including YouTube but excluding DeepMind . Google DeepMind is expected to strike a separate agreement, with the Communication Workers Union and the Unite union seeking recognition there. The deal follows a similar agreement between Prospect and Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram and employs about 5,000 people in the UK. The agreements will allow unions to communicate with non-unionised workers and encourage them to join. The union, which represents more than 160,000 UK workers across several sectors, will now be able to run sessions inside Google’s workplaces, including the flagship headquarters in King’s Cross, London. Prospect’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, said: “Prospect has been organising tech workers for many years, and this access agreement is a powerful signal of intent that we can successfully negotiate agreements with even the biggest global tech companies. “Tech workers deserve a stronger voice at work, whether that is over bread-and-butter trade union issues like pay and flexibility, AI deployment or workplace culture. I am pleased that Google has struck this agreement with us, and hope it sends a clear signal to other tech companies that having a relationship with trade unions is the new normal in the sector.” He said workers would have a stronger voice as more employees at Google and Meta joined trade unions. “With our track record of delivering wins for members, I am looking forward to seeing what we can achieve together.” Google said it had signed the access agreement to comply with the new UK workplace legislation, although it maintained that it already had good internal employee relations. “This step builds on our established work with internal employee representative groups, allowing us to fulfil these new requirements while preserving the respectful, direct dialogue our culture is built on,” a spokesperson said. Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary, said last week that he expected a wave of union recognition deals in the private sector over the next year as the “transformative” rules on accessing workplaces came into force. The Employment Rights Act gives unions the right to enter workplaces to meet workers or communicate with them electronically. From January, employers will be required to inform workers of their right to join a union. Previously, unions seeking recognition have sometimes had to organise workers from outside their workplaces – as was the case with the GMB’s thwarted effort to gain recognition at Amazon’s warehouse near Coventry two years ago.

events.title: Singapore factory activity grows at slower pace in October after accelerating since March
events.summary: Singapore’s purchasing managers’ index remained in expansionary territory while falling to 51.4 points in October. Singapore factory activity kept growing in October, but the PMI fell to 51.4 from 51.7 in September. Electronics sector, which accounts for 40% of manufacturing output, also saw its PMI ease. Analysts said there were no signs of a sharp downturn in the manufacturing industry, with AI demand expected to keep supporting exports and investment. SINGAPORE – Factory activity here continued to expand in October but at a slower pace because of factors including a slight decline in new orders. Singapore’s purchasing managers’ index (PMI) – a barometer of the manufacturing industry’s overall health – fell to 51.4 points in October, from 51.7 points in September. The electronics sector, which accounts for 40% of Singapore’s manufacturing output, recorded a PMI of 52.5 points. This was lower than the 52.9 points it posted in the previous month. A PMI reading above 50 indicates growth, while one below that signals contraction. Although the benchmarks remain in expansionary territory, they represent the first pullback in the broader PMI reading in seven months and in the electronics PMI since October 2025, OCBC chief economist Selena Ling noted. Still, she said: “Growth momentum may be taking a breather rather than flagging an outright and imminent reversal of the global artificial intelligence-related capital expenditure boom.” Meanwhile, input prices saw slightly faster growth, and finished goods inventories contracted at a slower rate. The supplier deliveries index contracted much more slowly, indicating that delivery delays have eased. Stephen Poh, executive director at the Singapore Institute of Purchasing and Materials Management, which compiles the monthly survey, also said the readings pointed to a manufacturing sector that was “cooling from a high base, not losing momentum”. He said: “Strong exports, AI-linked orders and elevated backlogs keep electronics the main pillar of manufacturing growth. “However, output still lags orders, and higher input costs weigh. Easing supplier delays help, but renewed Middle East shipping disruption could constrain output.” Other analysts agreed that it was premature to conclude that the manufacturing sector was set for a prolonged slowdown. The moderation in October was driven by slower growth in new orders, with an index tracking the measure declining by 0.1 points from September. However, the new export orders index rose by 0.1 points over the same period, indicating that demand remains robust, said Maybank economist Brian Lee. For the electronics sector, the 0.3-point fall in the output index and the 0.5-point decline in the stocks of input purchases index were more significant, as they “could point to supply constraints”. In China, a recent government survey showed that factory activity contracted in October, marking the third contraction in four months. The reading was weighed down by soft domestic demand for goods and signs of weakness in Chinese exports. Manufacturing activity also slowed while continuing to expand in October in Japan, South Korea and ​Taiwan, according to private surveys. This has raised concerns that the persisting Middle East conflict may be offsetting the benefits from the robust global demand for chips and AI-related goods. Oxford Economics senior economist Sheana Yue said she will be watching developments across the regional electronics supply chain, particularly export performance in Taiwan and South Korea, and global semiconductor sales, in the months ahead. “These provide useful signals of underlying demand for electronic components and semiconductors, which have been an important source of strength for Singapore’s manufacturing sector,” she said. Yue added that she expects AI-related demand to continue to support Singapore’s exports and investment. “We have raised our GDP growth forecast to 5.7% for 2026 and expect growth of 4.3% in 2027. A sustained slowdown in electronics demand would pose a downside risk to this outlook, particularly if it also feeds through to investment and hiring,” she said. Jonathan Koh, senior economist and FX analyst for ASEAN at Standard Chartered, noted that manufacturing activity may continue to moderate over the coming months, as it had a strong run-up so far in 2026. Even so, he added: “We do not currently see signs of a sharp downturn. Electronics new orders remain strong, while finished goods inventories are still contracting, suggesting that underlying demand remains healthy, and that some inventory rebuilding may still be required.” Annabelle Liang is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, where she specialises in trade and macroeconomics.

events.title: Ryanair faces clash with unions as it mulls pay freezes amid soaring fuel costs
events.summary: Airline also weighs up reducing crew on flights and increasing use of AI as part of cost-cutting measures Ryanair has said it is considering implementing pay freezes, setting the scene for a confrontation with unions as the airline tries to offset soaring fuel costs driven by the Middle East conflict . The airline is also considering reducing crew numbers on flights and increasing the use of AI, in a cost-cutting drive. Europe’s largest low-cost carrier said it expected European airlines to raise ticket prices by up to 20% , with its own jet fuel costs forecast to rise by about €2bn (£1.6bn) in its next financial year, which ends in March 2028. “Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair . “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.” Oil prices hit a six-month high on Friday before falling to about $106 a barrel on Monday. Ryanair expects European short-haul fares to “increase materially” next year, as fuel hedging deals taken out by airlines to reduce costs expire. “To help address this, we’re reviewing all costs across group airlines with a particular focus on airport churn negotiations, maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes), lower crew ratios and increased use of AI,” O’Leary said. He said the company had several pay deals that would come up for renegotiation from March. However, the Unite union said it had a multiyear pay deal in place that covered 2027, and in any case was not linked to company performance. “Unite hasn’t been advised of any such proposals and we have a multiyear pay deal in place which covers next year,” said Oliver Richardson, a national officer at the union. “A number of unions across Europe have the same. Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured.” O’Leary also said Ryanair was “slowing down hiring meaningfully” for new pilots, cabin crew and across its training courses. The company said its increased use of AI would focus on improving productivity in operations and back-office and support functions. O’Leary said AI had already been used to increase capacity by 4%. “When you’re running 650 aircraft, it’s too big for a human to be able to do it,” he said. “The machines can actually design the schedules better than we know [how to do], so we are getting more productivity out of the aircraft.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ryanair said 80% of its fuel requirements until the end of March were hedged at $67 a barrel. Twenty-five per cent of its fuel requirements for the subsequent 12 months are hedged at $95 a barrel. “It’s beginning to dawn on everybody that we [the industry] are not well hedged,” O’Leary said. The Irish airline, Europe’s largest by passenger numbers, said average fares fell by 2% year on year in the quarter ending in September. Ryanair added that fares in the final three months of the year were trending “modestly ahead” of the same quarter last year. “The booking window remains closer-in which reduces visibility,” the company said. “[The current quarter’s] fare outcome will heavily depend on the strength of close-in October-November school midterm [holiday] and Christmas bookings.” The airline reported a post-tax profit of €1.61bn in the quarter ending in September, a fall of 6% year on year but in line with analyst expectations. Passenger numbers grew 5% year on year to 64.5 million during the quarter. Ryanair has taken delivery of about 30 aircraft annually over the last two years, but the delivery rate is set to drop to 15 annually for the next few years. The airline said it was to take deliveries of the Boeing 737 Max 10 aircraft in January, which has about 20% more seats but burns a fifth less fuel than its current fleet.

events.title: ‘Bragawatts’ and why all data-center investing isn’t created equal
events.summary: The News For all the talk of AI bubbles and market crashes, Scandinavian private-equity giant EQT says it’s making a bet that regardless of what happens with the frontier labs, AI is still going to need a massive amount of power, energy, chips, and data centers. “All of a sudden, we find ourselves with $100 billion of energy assets, which are really the limiting factor for AI right now,” said Jean Salata, global chair of EQT, which has $400 billion in assets under management. “A lot of people went out and signed tons of contracts with anybody — they call them ‘bragawatts.’ But signing something and delivering it on time, and with power connected, are two very different things,” Salata said. “Sophisticated investors understand that, but there’s a lot of things happening in the public markets where people are investing in things that they really don’t understand.” EQT is a unique animal in an industry where exits have dried up, a generational bet on software companies looks vulnerable to AI, and higher interest rates have broken the math of cheap leverage and multiple expansion. Since 2018, PE firms have asked their investors for $1.5 trillion more capital than they’ve given back, and the industry is sitting on nearly $4 trillion worth of businesses it can’t sell. EQT has largely stayed out of the private credit and insurance boom that has turned its US rivals into asset-gathering giants — a “beta business,” said Salata, an artisanally crafted Wall Street dig. And it has an unusual backstop: The Wallenbergs, Sweden’s most powerful business dynasty, helped found EQT in 1994 and remain its largest shareholder. The family’s patient approach to ownership is close to the long-hold model that much of private equity is now trying to reinvent. Q&A Liz Hoffman: For a long time, private equity firms could borrow cheaply, ride a rising market, and look like geniuses. It feels like the jig is up, and I know you have some thoughts on that . Jean Salata: Our industry needs to remember what we are meant to be doing, which is delivering returns for our clients. If we’re not doing that, we’re going to end up in a very difficult place. There’s been a lot of attention on the growth in assets under management, a business model that has really benefited from the tailwinds of the private credit run of the last five years. But we’re in an environment where the tide is going out and that means you’re going where there is real value being created. There are something like 10,000 private-equity firms out there. What should that number be? The industry already is consolidating and that will accelerate. This year the top 10 firms in the world have raised 50% of the capital. When you raise smaller funds, people don’t see the carry coming in and so they leave and you get zombie funds. EQT has chosen not to chase those credit tailwinds you mentioned. It doesn’t have the big lending business that Apollo, Blackstone, and others have ridden to huge AUM piles. Do you feel good about that decision? I think there’s a role for private credit, but the question is who’s best positioned to deliver that? We’re good at being an equity investor, being really close to the sectors that we invest in, bringing the best operational talent, bringing the technology and the AI capabilities that we have to the company. None of those are really relevant to the credit business. It’s an origination business. It’s a beta business. Best case scenario, you make 8% return on your money. So, the answer is yes, I think we are happy with the decision. But how do you resist the pressures to be a one-stop shop? Eventually there is a feedback loop. Second-quartile [performance] is, maybe, good enough. But when you start talking about third- and fourth-quartile returns, clients will either stop or reduce the amount that they invest with you. It’s hard to take anything public right now that isn’t a giant AI company and private equity’s track record on returning capital has been abysmal . How does the industry get out of this funk? There are a lot of assets for sale that need to find a home and there aren’t that many buyers. At EQT, we’ve been able to take advantage of where there are pockets of opportunity and liquidity. We had $33 billion of distributions to our investors in the last 12 months, and as a result, we’re continuing to attract capital. There’s this strange incentive structure in our industry, where you sell businesses that you otherwise wouldn’t want to sell because of this finite [fund] life. There’s a bit of frustration on the part of sellers that have sold assets because they need to go fundraising, only to see the buyers make like another 3x on it, which is why you’re seeing these longer-hold vehicles like evergreen structures, open-ended structures, continuation vehicles. But then isn’t the market saying that the 10-year closed-end fund is outdated and should probably go away? One of the reasons we bought [secondaries firm] Coller is we think there is a convergence happening between the primary market and the secondary market. There’s a case to be made for the secondary market essentially becoming the private equity market, as it is in the world of listed equities. Remember, the stock market is a secondary market. Yes, you have some IPOs, but the vast majority of the trading is in existing shares. Where we’re heading in private markets is not quite that extreme, but it’s going to be a much bigger part of the industry. There were $250 billion of PE secondaries deals last year. That’s doubled in the last three or four years and it’s probably going to double again in the next five. One other tension in PE right now is that everyone seems to be in the same trade — the AI trade . Are you worried about correlation? There’s no patents in finance. We’re all moving in a similar direction and it’s going to boil down to execution. A lot of this is about talent. There’s a shortage of really good talent that understands technology and AI, and the ability to attract, to afford, that talent becomes a question of scale. Tell me why all this AI investing is not going to end terribly. There’s a lot of noise right now about data centers — ‘it’s a bubble, the market’s crashing.’ But if you look at the fundamentals of what’s going on in the AI buildout with power, energy, chips, data center demand, we think it’s very fundamentals-based and a very, very attractive opportunity. I don’t want to say we stumbled onto it — the team deserves more credit than that — but we found ourselves in the middle of this in a big way because we were investing in power assets and in data center assets for cloud migration. The pre-AI generation of data centers. Yes. So all of a sudden, we find ourselves with $100 billion of energy assets, which are really the limiting factor for AI right now. events.title: Blackstone-backed data center operator tests AI debt fears
events.summary: The Scoop Wall Street is finding out just how expensive things can get in a matter of months. For a look at how much investors’ jitters are reshaping AI-related debt financing, look to QTS, an investment-grade Blackstone-backed data center operator, that just six months ago was weighing a deal to borrow $800 million at a rate of 1.7 percentage points over Treasurys. That deal never went through. And now, that same debt is being shopped to investors at 2.2 to 2.50 points above comparable Treasury yields for a nearly identical offering, according to people familiar with the matter. Both offerings involve the same company, same blue-chip Wall Street backing, and the same collateral — just for a lot more money. Blackstone declined to comment. As debt jitters spread and borrowing gets more expensive, it’s a lesson in just how much sentiment has shifted in such a short amount of time. Know More On Friday, the Financial Times reported that Blackstone told investors it no longer expected Anthropic to get an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its IPO, a reversal of previous guidance about the frontier lab, which is raising billions of dollars to finance its AI buildout. And investment-grade SpaceX’s $40 billion debt launch saw its pricing widen out — reaching an expected 8.75% yield for the riskier portion of its recent debt deal, up from where pricing was discussed just a week earlier, Semafor reported .

events.title: The ANC set to lose South African cities
events.summary: The News The African National Congress is on course to lose control of most of South Africa’s major cities in Wednesday’s local elections, according to polling data, potentially disrupting power dynamics in the national coalition government. Several polls suggest the party’s remaining support is increasingly concentrated in smaller towns and rural provinces as opposition parties make deeper inroads in the biggest cities that drive Africa’s largest economy. The local government vote will decide who runs 250-plus municipalities responsible for basic service provision including water, sanitation, and refuse collection. It is the ANC’s first nationwide test since falling support forced it to share power in 2024 after losing its parliamentary majority — unprecedented in the democratic era. The latest Ipsos poll , conducted between Sept. 12 and Oct. 13, put the ANC’s national support at an “all-time low” of 30%, reflecting just how far its backing in urban areas has fallen. Roughly 30% of respondents in Johannesburg, the nation’s commercial hub, and Tshwane, home of the capital Pretoria, said they would vote for the ANC. And that figure fell to just 10% in the port city of Durban, where the populist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (or MK), which is pressing for sweeping state control of the economy and built around former president Jacob Zuma, is comfortably ahead in polls. Support for the ANC, the party once led by Nelson Mandela, remains near 60% in Limpopo and the Eastern Cape, vast provinces of villages, small towns, and dispersed settlements that remain far less urbanized than Gauteng or the Western Cape, an earlier Ipsos poll showed. “After 30 years of democracy, voting patterns are changing and we are moving into a completely new reconfiguration of the political spectrum,” said Andre Duvenhage, a political analyst at South Africa’s North-West University. The Ipsos survey and several other polls — if replicated on voting day — indicate that most metropolitan municipalities would require coalition governments after the local elections. This broadly matches the assessment of think tank Oxford Economics, which has predicted that voting in six of the eight metros would fail to produce an outright winner, creating the need for coalition negotiations. A poor ANC showing would “upend the power dynamics” inside the national coalition government, said William Gumede, a political analyst and governance professor at the Johannesburg-based University of Witwatersrand. He argued that if the ANC’s share of the vote was close to or fell below the Democratic Alliance, it would force the former liberation movement to treat its junior partner “as an equal power” in policy-making and government decisions. The two parties became governing partners after the 2024 general election for the first time, bringing ideological rivals into the same government where the ANC remains committed to state-led economic transformation policies while the DA has pushed for bigger private investment. Know More Political parties have entered the final stretch of campaigning with failures of local government providing much of the ammunition. Unreliable water supplies, deteriorating roads, corruption, and mismanagement of municipal finances, have left many councils struggling to provide basic services. Companies are increasingly paying for the failures, said Busi Mavuso, CEO of lobby group Business Leadership South Africa, whose members account for nearly a third of the country’s $490 billion GDP. She said businesses are investing in backup water storage, private security, and road repairs to remain operational. “Capital is not sentimental,” she said, warning that investors can redirect money when infrastructure and municipalities fail. That makes the quality of municipal governments formed after the election important to investors, according to Awongiwe Booi, a fixed income analyst at South African lender Investec. “The alignment and performance of the coalition post the election will matter more than the poll results themselves,” she said. South Africa’s eight metros house about 40% of the population and account for an outsized share of economic activity. Tiisetso’s view The theory from an investor’s perspective is that a weaker ANC is better for public finances. That deserves testing. For starters, there is a risk over what the party does to win voters back or retain those largely rural areas, where official data shows that these countryside towns accounted for nearly 60% of the country’s poor in 2023. Under such circumstances the ANC, in its effort to recover voters and shore up support, would have every reason to demonstrate that the government can deliver more on its campaign promises to expand public employment and automatically enrol grant-receiving households for free basic services. The spending pressure is hardly hypothetical, with Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana saying government departments have asked for more than 700 billion rand ($41 billion) in additional spending over the next three years, more than a third of everything the government expected to spend this year. “That money simply doesn’t exist,” he told a local radio station last month. Even so, an electoral decline makes saying no politically harder, creating a longer term political risk. It might just embolden those arguing that a post-President Cyril Ramaphosa ANC should move toward MK Party and Economic Freedom Fighters, a radical left movement advocating for nationalization of mines and banks, and ditch the market friendly DA, which has long struggled to shake off its image seen by many Black voters as a party of white interests. There’s nothing irrational about voters demanding more from a state where a third of the work force is unemployed and ranks highest in the World Bank inequality index. The problem is that political need does not create fiscal space. Room for Disagreement David Omojomolo, Africa economist at research house Capital Economics, said fears about the coalition government stability after the election are overdone, and expects the macroeconomic impact of the vote to be limited, with borrowing costs constraining the recovery remaining on track. His comment rests on the DA, rather than MK or the EFF, picking up the ANC losses, which the polls support in Gauteng. “That should compel the next ANC leader to continue to follow business-and-investor-friendly policies, including the commitment to fiscal consolidation,” he said. Notable Unpaid bills owed to municipalities have grown more than seven-fold since 2011 to nearly 500 billion rand ($30 billion), Investec noted, a measure of the fiscal hole new councils will inherit.

events.title: Snowball fight: Cadbury owner in trademark row over festive chocolate treat
events.summary: Mini Snow Balls’ maker Mondelēz is demanding vegan brand Moo Free remove its White Choccy Snowballs from shelves Toblerone owner sues British vegan chocolate brand over chunky shape The owner of Cadbury and Toblerone has demanded that a small vegan chocolate brand remove its products from shelves in a trademark dispute over the use of the word snowball. Mondelēz International has written a legal letter to Moo Free accusing it of trademark infringement by selling its White Choccy Snowballs – gluten-free biscuit-flavoured rice balls covered in dairy-free white chocolate. Cadbury Snowballs first launched in the UK in 1966, and have been sold in their current form as packs of Mini Snow Balls since 2023. The brand registered use of the word Snowball and Snowballs for use in chocolate confectionery as a trademark in 2001. Its Mini Snow Balls are made from Dairy Milk chocolate covered in a crispy shell of white icing sugar. The legal fight has emerged just days after Mondelēz launched legal action against another small vegan chocolate brand, Catherine’s Originals, accusing it of copying the famous chunky shape of Toblerone with its O’bar. Moo Free, which has products stocked in several major supermarkets and online, said it had been selling its Snowballs for about two years before Mondelēz demanded it immediately remove the items from sale just ahead of the busy Christmas period. Mike Jessop, who co-founded Devon-based Moo Free in 2010 when he and his wife could not find allergen-free chocolates for Easter or Christmas, said they began selling online before being picked up by Waitrose and then other supermarkets. He said he had “never even heard of” Cadbury Snow Balls and was lactose intolerant so couldn’t try one. He was surprised Mondelēz had been so “heavy-handed” in its letter and questioned whether it could be possible to trademark an apparently generic term. “It’s a snowball, it is not like we are making a Freddo,” he said, referring to Cadbury’s famous frog-shaped bar. In a letter to customers, Moo Free wrote: “Moo Free takes intellectual property concerns seriously. However, we do not accept that any infringement has been established and have responded accordingly … We are disappointed to find ourselves in this position, and we stand in solidarity with Catherine’s Originals as it addresses its own situation. We hope to resolve these matters appropriately.” A spokesperson for Mondelēz International said: “ Cadbury Snow Balls are one of our most popular Christmas products, enjoyed by households across the UK. No legal action has been taken, but we have been in touch with Moo Free to make them aware of our trademark. We are open to reaching an amicable resolution.” It is not the UK’s first snowball fight. Tunnock’s and Lees of Scotland won legal action against HMRC in 2014 after proving they did not have to pay VAT on their coconut-covered confections, as they were deemed sufficiently similar to a cake for an exemption. Snowballs made by these two suppliers – defined as “a dome of marshmallow coated in any combination” of chocolate, sugar strands, carob, cocoa or coconut – were subsequently given their own VAT-free status .

events.title: Ryanair says it may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares
events.summary: Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran. The airline said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict. Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be €2bn (£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and its boss, Michael O'Leary, said airfares would have to rise by "double-digits" to help cover the cost. But the firm said that was unlikely to be enough and it is looking into pay freezes. Unite, the union representing Ryanair staff, said it had not been told of "any such proposals". O'Leary also said the company would slow down hiring as airline's costs rise. The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to €2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to fuel costs jumping by 15%. The company said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" – in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices – the cost of the remainder was elevated. O'Leary reiterated forecasts from earlier this year Ryanair would "need a 20% fare increase" to cover the cost of jet fuel. "I'm not sure we'll get to 20%," he said. "But we're certainly looking at double-digit fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027." Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere. Ryanair also said it was weighing up whether to freeze pay, as multi-year wage deals with unions come to to an end. The policy could be implemented from April next year. Oliver Richardson, national officer at Unite, said the union "hasn't been advised of any such proposals and we have a multi-year pay deal in place which covers next year. A number of Unions across Europe have the same". He said: "Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured." Ryanair also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions. Meanwhile, Ryanair has cut back on winter flights and said on Monday there would be more to come. It said this was happening across the airline industry, particularly with short-haul carriers. O'Leary said: "We believe those cuts will continue into the summer of 2027. Over the medium term, we expect short-haul capacity will remain constrained out to the early 2030s." events.title: UAE oil exports surpass prewar levels despite Hormuz disruption, energy minister says
events.summary: UAE oil exports surpassed prewar levels “at a certain time” as the Arab world’s second-largest economy continues to work as reliable supplier to the world, despite Hormuz disruptions. “At a certain time, we did better than prior because of our continuous work,” UAE’s Minister of Energy and Infrastructure Suhail Al Mazrouei told delegates at the Adipec conference in Abu Dhabi on Monday. He did not disclose the timelines or the volumes the UAE exported, but said [we] "did our best to make sure that the prices of commodities do not go very high”. The Emirates shipped 3.94 million barrels per day of crude and condensate in June, the highest monthly total in the past year, and a sharp reversal from March, when the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz cut exports to a record low of 2.13 million bpd, Kpler data showed. “We feel the pain on those consumers, and we understand that if prices go too high, that's going to strike the demand in years … the pipeline helped us a lot over there. Our readiness through the fleets and the ships have helped us tremendously," Mr Al Mazrouei said. The UAE's Habshan–Fujairah pipeline, often referred to as the West–East crude oil pipeline, has the capacity to transport up to 1.5 million bpd of crude oil, representing a substantial share of the country’s total oil exports. In May, the UAE announced the expansion of the West-East crude oil pipeline to be completed by 2027, with the project expected to double export capacity through Fujairah . Mr Al Mazrouei said the UAE was able to “fill in the supply gap” as supplies from other countries reduced due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. “Sometimes even we have filled in the gap ... we managed to oversupply to those countries because there was a significant reduction from many countries.” The country must also be ready for worst-case scenarios since it “cannot predict what’s going to happen", he added. Oil prices volatile Oil prices have remained volatile since the Iran war broke out on February 28, with prices rising to more than $120 per barrel in March as the Middle East war escalated, with Iran hitting energy infrastructure in the region and ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz coming to a virtual halt. Prices fell in subsequent months amid peace talks between the US and Iran to end the conflict and reopen the strait, but surged again amid concerns that the US is preparing to restart the Middle East war and attack Iran. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, is trading close to $110 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at about $100 per barrel on Monday. “When I think about what happened over the last eight months, it's really quite stunning the level of disruption to the global energy system. Crude oil, natural gas, products have all been disrupted. The thing that stood out is how resilient the system has been,” Meg O’ Neill, chief executive of BP, said in a separate panel discussion at Adipec. “If you went back to the start of the conflict, people would have said that oil should have been $150 a barrel by June, and that didn't happen. People said that natural gas prices should have spiked, and they really didn't until the last month or so.”

events.title: Sales slump at UK’s largest brickmaker as housebuilding downturn deepens
events.summary: Ibstock, which has cut production by a fifth, criticises government for delay in help for housing sector Sales at the UK’s largest brickmaker plunged by more than a fifth over the summer, as it criticised the government for not introducing fresh help for the housing sector faster. Leicestershire-based Ibstock said on Monday that sales slumped by 22% below its expectations in the three months to the end of September, prompting it to slash production levels by a fifth. Ibstock issued its second profit warning this year and said UK brick market volumes declined by 17% year on year in July and August, with weak market conditions continuing through September and October. “Trading conditions deteriorated sharply during the third quarter, with weakness continuing into October,” said Joe Hudson, the chief executive of Ibstock. “We have responded by reducing production to manage inventory, taking further cost action and maintaining tight control of cash. These production decisions create an additional near-term earnings headwind but are necessary to align output with demand.” The warning by the company, which now expects full-year profits to be “materially below” previous expectations, comes days after the Office for Budget Responsibility cut its forecast for the number of new homes that will be built by 2031 by 190,000. Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, has said there is only a “slim chance” the government will meet its goal of building 1.5m new homes this parliament, amid estimates that the target could be missed by a third. Ibstock also criticised the government’s decision to delay the start of a support scheme that is designed to help first-time buyers in England buy a newbuild home with a 2.5% deposit. “The introduction of the Your First Home support scheme represents a welcome and potentially meaningful intervention for the UK housing market, with the potential to improve affordability, stimulate new-build demand and strengthen confidence in future housing supply,” the company said. “While the announcement reinforces confidence in the group’s medium-term market outlook, the delay to its introduction until April 2027 is disappointing and has put additional pressure on near-term demand.” Ibstock said it now expected full-year profits to be in the mid-£40m range, well down on analysts’ previous consensus of £59m. events.title: Demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments
events.summary: We have seen demands being made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries as a way to avoid tax. HMRC has sought to tackle this tax avoidance through what has been termed the loan charge and published guidance for those affected.Questions have been raised about the regulatory status of these loans and whether they were ever intended to be repaid.Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they’re unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.Some consumers are, however being sent legal letters threatening potential court action and asking for immediate repayment of the loan. Repayment is being sought after these disguised remuneration loans were sold by the original provider to a third party.Those seeking payment may ask the FCA to agree to a Validation Order. This is the formal permission needed before the loans could be enforced. We would consider any request carefully and our agreement is by no means guaranteed. If a Validation Order is required and not granted, the debt would remain unenforceable.Anyone who receives a demand for repayment of a disguised remuneration loan, and is unsure whether they are liable for the amount claimed, should consider carefully whether to make any payment. We’d encourage them to look at the HMRC guidance and consider taking legal advice.Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.If you are experiencing any difficulties, whether they are health, money or other difficulties, or if you don't understand what is happening, you should raise this with those contacting you.
