events.title: I’m a wealthy Californian. The billionaire tax is a win for everyone | George Zimmer
events.summary: I’m a wealthy Californian. The billionaire tax is a win for everyone The measure would ease inequality and bolster healthcare – without draining our coffers or triggering a billionaire exodus On Tuesday, California voters will decide whether to enact Proposition 40 , a one-time, 5% tax on the net worth of about 250 California billionaires . In recent months, a number of California billionaires and their apologists in the media and in government have come out swinging against the ballot measure. I’m not a billionaire, but I’m a Californian wealthy enough to know that they have no valid reason to fight the proposition. For multimillionaires like me, paying a 5% tax would not change our lives materially, and if we can afford this as people well below the billionaire line, certainly those at the very top can too. Prop 40 would enact the first tax on billionaires anywhere in the world, with organizers estimating it would raise roughly $100bn in revenue, most of which would be directed to healthcare to make up for federal cuts from Trump and Republicans’ 2025 tax bill. Six Nobel Prize-winning economists said it would “kickstart a movement to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals in other states – and eventually at the federal level and in other countries”. Opponents’ primary objection to Prop 40 is that it will spark an exodus of the state’s billionaires, who would run for the hills of lower-tax states. They further claim this would blow a hole in the state’s tax base and kill the Golden state’s “ golden goose ”, or its trove of innovative minds. For one thing, numerous studies have failed to find evidence that wealthy people flee en masse when their taxes are raised, which suggests that Prop 40 critics’ fears of a billionaire exodus are overblown. After Massachusetts and Washington state raised taxes on high earners in 2022, both states actually experienced an increase, not a decrease, in their millionaire populations. A 2023 study also revealed that, despite being a relatively high-tax state , since 2011, California has had the second lowest out-migration rate among households earning more than $200,000. As a person of wealth, I can choose to live wherever I want, no matter the tax rates. Like so many of my rich counterparts, I choose to live in California because I love it here. I don’t intend on leaving anytime soon. I will never be able to get enough of our beaches, our forests, our piers, our cable cars, our universities, and everything else in between. I’m willing to pay higher taxes than I would elsewhere to maintain (and improve) all of these wonderful things that make California the Golden state that it is. To avoid the tax, billionaires would have had to move by 1 January 2026; from what we know, only six of them did. Between 2019 and 2025, California billionaires’ wealth grew an average 15% per year, but they paid just 0.26% of it in state income taxes. They pay so little in taxes as it is that, even if they were all to leave, it would take 25 years under current California law for the loss of their tax payments to exceed the $100bn that Prop 40 would raise. Taxes should be based on the principle that our government should be financed based on one’s ability to pay. When 250 billionaires have the means to pay more, it is their civic duty – just as it is mine – to do so. There is also no reason to believe innovation in California will end if Prop 40 passes. Wealthy entrepreneurs like me are the brains behind a lot of products and services that have enhanced countless lives, and our state has become the place to be for aspiring industry leaders. California’s industries attract top talent and intelligence. A 5% one-time tax will not deter people from pursuing a livelihood in entrepreneurial epicenters. So far in 2026, amidst all the buzz about the ballot measure, no less than 80% of all new venture capital funding found its way to California. In short, Prop 40 will not trigger a billionaire exodus, it will not drain our coffers, and it will not spell the end of Golden state innovation. What it will do is add some progressivity to our state tax code , put a check on the power of the richest among us, and raise significant funds that will prevent hospitals from closing, millions from losing their healthcare coverage, and thousands of healthcare jobs from being cut. I want less inequality because my family and I will be better off in a society with less inequality. That should be a win in every Californian’s book, rich and poor alike. events.title: Could the US midterms cause a surprise stock market rally?
events.summary: Investors have a lot on their plate. Oil, inflation and interest rates are climbing, while tech stocks are volatile amid growing fears of an AI bubble . Throw in US President Donald Trump's unpredictability, mounting government debt, regional wars and stretched stock valuations, and it’s all getting a bit much. Now comes another challenge: Americans go to the polls on November 3 for the midterm elections , which will determine control of Congress and the direction of Mr Trump's presidency. Yet here’s a curious twist. History shows that midterm elections have typically been followed by a strong run for Wall Street. JP Morgan Asset Management’s analysis shows the S&P 500 has risen in the 12 months following every midterm since 1950. Might history repeat itself? If so, stock market bulls have plenty to look forward to, says Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell. “The past is no guarantee, but the third year of a presidential term is, on average, the best one for the US stock market.” The average third-year gain across postwar presidencies is a stellar 16.1 per cent. No other presidential year averages a double-digit gain, he says. One theory is that presidents have an incentive to boost the economy ahead of the next election. Another is that the midterms often deliver a lame-duck president who struggles to pass legislation, allowing businesses to operate without interference from Washington. Markets are often volatile before the vote, but when the result is known, investors can focus on policy rather than polling, says Jason Hollands, managing director at Evelyn Partners. Gridlock could boost stocks Mr Trump looks on course to lose control of both the House and Senate. If that happened, it could actually help stocks. “A divided Congress would make major new legislation harder to pass. That could limit the prospect of sweeping changes to areas such as tax and regulation,” Mr Hollands says. But investors shouldn’t assume divided government means quiet government. Aliasgar Tambawala, co-chief investment officer at Klay Group, warns that political gridlock brings problems of its own. “A divided legislature may lead to greater disruptions around issues such as the debt ceiling and government funding.” Mr Trump's executive powers, including tariffs, would remain largely intact, while the President retains his veto. Mr Tambawala expects political volatility to persist, but says GCC investors face bigger concerns, notably the situation in the Strait of Hormuz . “A durable resolution would augur well for the region.” Despite recent volatility, the S&P 500 and tech-focused Nasdaq are up around 12 per cent this year, says Tony Hallside, chief executive of STP Partners. Further gains depend on earnings. “Getting the election out of the way helps sentiment, but it does not create earnings growth. If inflation persists or profits fall short of expectations, the historical election pattern will offer little protection.” AI is another concern. Can the technology justify the huge sums being invested by generating sustainable revenue and profits? “Political clarity will not compensate for disappointing commercial results,” Mr Hallside says. Reality checks for investors Madhur Kakkar, chief executive of Elevate Financial Services, warns that markets face formidable headwinds. Brent crude has hit $117 a barrel, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September and may do so again in December, while 10-year Treasury yields are approaching 5 per cent. “Higher Treasury yields give investors a competitive income alternative at a time when US equity valuations remain demanding,” Mr Kakkar says. The S&P 500's Shiller price-to-earnings ratio ended October at 40.88, a level exceeded only during the dot-com boom. On October 29, Alphabet shares plunged 13 per cent, wiping $500 billion off its value after heavy AI infrastructure spending contributed to negative quarterly free cash flow of $9.1 billion. Yet the US economy remains resilient, with third-quarter GDP growing at an annualised 3.4 per cent. Mr Kakkar urges investors to maintain balanced portfolios rather than chase a post-midterms rally. Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial, believes AI and interest rates, rather than politics, will determine whether markets finish 2026 strongly. “Easing inflation and a successful Anthropic IPO could still fuel a year-end rally.” For the GCC, the outlook is firmer than headline figures suggest, he says. The IMF expects Gulf output to shrink 4.8 per cent this year because of the Iran war, before rebounding 9.1 per cent in 2027. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are shipping substantial oil volumes around the Strait of Hormuz, while high crude prices bolster revenue. Non-oil activity remains strong, but a full recovery depends on the strait reopening, which the IMF assumes will begin in March 2027. Mr Mould remains cautious. Inflation is sticky, interest rates may rise, the Middle East war could drag on, oil and equity valuations are high, and the AI boom could end in an investment bust. History suggests the midterms could unleash another Wall Street rally. But with so many risks stacking up, investors may discover that this time, history really is bunk.

events.title: Resilience of Gulf oil infrastructure has its limits
events.summary: Amena’s view The drums of war are beating again, and the oil-exporting states are bracing “for the worst,” as the UAE’s presidential advisor Anwar Gargash recently put it. Eight months into the US-Iran war, one lesson is clear: There is no amount of operational resilience that can shield energy infrastructure from an unresolved political conflict. Renewed strikes will put more of the region’s oil supply at risk. Saudi Arabia and the UAE have demonstrated exceptional levels of resilience, activating contingency plans, carrying out repair works in record time, and keeping customers supplied. Their bypass pipelines have proven the value of planning for the shift from the “just in time” model to the “just in case” approach. The UAE’s 1.8 million-barrel-per-day (bpd) pipeline from Abu Dhabi to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman was once questioned as an investment. Its cost was recovered after just one month of conflict, according to people familiar with the matter. A second link with similar capacity is expected to be completed by July 2027. Saudi Arabia is considering expanding its larger East-West Pipeline and may bring in countries like Iraq and Kuwait that don’t have shipping outlets outside the Gulf. Within the industry, there’s a growing consensus that the pre-war oil flows will not return. More investment will be earmarked for contingencies, reflecting in part the view that reaching a diplomatic resolution to the Iran war is unlikely anytime soon. So far, the global energy system has performed better than expected. Gulf exporters kept their oil flowing despite the risks faced in Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, inventories were released, and some demand was curtailed, all of which combined to limit the oil price spike. But this resilience should not be mistaken for future security of supply, especially as this potential escalation comes at a time when global inventory levels have been drained by around 1 billion barrels. Brent is trading above $110 a barrel, of which perhaps $40 could be attributed to geopolitical risk. While much of the focus is on guessing what US President Donald Trump is planning, the reality for the oil industry is that higher prices may have eroded around 3 million bpd of demand, according to energy industry executives. This assumption is even more pessimistic than the IEA’s forecast of demand declining by around 2.6 million bpd this year. Another rise in prices, or oil prices sustained at this level, will only lead to even more demand destruction. This week, ahead of Abu Dhabi’s flagship energy conference ADIPEC, senior executives and CEOs from the energy industry gathered to discuss the challenges facing the industry under the Chatham House Rule. There was frustration about the lack of policy support, especially from European governments, for investment in the upstream sector and the construction of refineries. Over the past two decades, around 25% of Europe’s refineries were shut down, mainly as a result of policies related to the energy transition. Today, energy executives from European oil majors are pressured to address rising prices of oil products without having the facilities needed to deliver the energy to consumers. If there’s one silver lining from this crisis, it’s prioritizing investments in new supply and abandoning the dichotomy between the concepts of “old energy” and “new energy.” At the opening of ADIPEC on Monday, Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, was asked what the biggest challenge facing his industry is. He replied with one word: “energy.” Another round of war will make that energy costlier, and less abundant. Notable The UAE’s race toward its “Zero Hormuz” strategy runs through Fujairah, where investments can be seen in all directions intended to move the fossil fuels and products that would otherwise be trapped in the Gulf, Semafor reported.

events.title: Prediction market bettors are the new political pundits. Why are we listening to them? | Judith Levine
events.summary: Prediction market bettors are the new political pundits. Why are we listening to them? Sites like Kalshi and Polymarket offer faux populism as elites reap the benefits – and voters risk being misled Online betting is a bit like Donald Trump. The prediction markets – platforms where users bet on whether events will occur – pretend to be populist, pushing the nabobs aside and representing the “wisdom of the crowd”. “This data is bottom-up, not elites-driven,” a Kalshi ​spokesperson told Reuters . But in fact, the markets are controlled by a few, skillful traders. Their users are led to believe they can strike it rich. But like gamblers everywhere, most of them lose most of the time, while enriching the casino and bankrolling the winner’s takings. The markets pretend honesty and transparency, but they open the door to fraud and insider trading. Like opinion polls, they affect voters’ expectations of the outcomes of elections but make them no smarter about whom to vote for. Fundamentally, the assumptions projected by the prediction markets are Trumpian. The companies suggest that their results are improved by the financial stake customers have in them. “Prediction markets are a way to see what people are saying when there’s money on the line,” said the Kalshi spokesperson. When money talks, in other words, its message is more authentic and valuable than mere political speech. The prediction markets made a better collective call on the 2024 elections than conventional polls and pundits, particularly in the swing states. But why? The authors of a much-cited 2025 study from Vanderbilt University infer that their results – that Polymarket was more accurate than polls – were “in alignment with research on the ‘Wisdom of Crowds’ theory, which suggests a large group of people are often accurate in predicting outcomes, even if they are not necessarily experts or closely aligned with the issue at hand”. But more recent analyses suggest that the betting masses are not so wise after all. A new working paper from scholars at the London Business School and Yale University looked at publicly available trading data from Polymarket. Whereas almost every wagerer’s outcomes were no better than chance, they discovered, the “accuracy comes from a minority of persistently skilled traders, around 3% of accounts”. The crowd “generates most of the volume but little of the information”. The crowd also furnishes most of the cash but reaps little of it. Analyzing 1.6m Polymarket accounts, or “wallets”, traded since November 2022, the Wall Street Journal found: “Casual traders are bleeding cash while a small number of sophisticated pros – including trading firms with access to vast streams of data – eat their lunch.” What skills do these pros employ? They react quickly to public and financial news, say the London and Yale authors. They gather poll data and buy access to big data streams, which can cost $200,000 annually . They analyze the data using “algorithms to predict price movements and manage risk”, says the Journal, “faster than any human”. Operating at scale and speed, with commensurate information and discipline, the pros can make tens of thousands of trades a day. And the more they trade, the more they earn. In the Journal’s analysis, three-quarters of the profits went to 0.1% of the accounts. Of at least 2.3 million accounts on Polymarket’s site, just 2,000 netted a total of almost half a billion dollars. Meanwhile, the median Polymarket user placed 46 trades across 10 active trading days in 2026, according to Pew Research . And because the few have the skills to trade against the mistakes of the many, the losses of the many bankroll the profits of the few. The traders steering the prediction markets are not PhD pollsters and PBS talking heads. But they are elites nonetheless – the same elites who dominate Wall Street and make economic policy, whichever party is in office. If it were a simply a matter of some people’s money squandered or increased, the problems of the traders would remain with the traders. But the press and the public are listening to them more and more. “Prediction market odds shift voters’ expectations substantially,” a study funded by the Brennan Center found. The same features that rig the markets in favor of the few can distort what we think we know about coming elections. Explained CoinMarketCal , a newsletter serving crypto traders: “A market price reflects trades, liquidity, and available capital, not a representative poll. A well-funded trader can move a thin contract without any change in voter sentiment.” And it’s not just expectations that prediction markets influence. They can also change voter behavior. “Elections have the property that what one believes is going to happen can actually affect what happens if a candidate is thought to be losing momentum or the campaign is flagging,” the Barnard College economics professor Rajiv Sethi told NPR .

events.title: “Chaos” in the Air: Five Ways Voting Could Be Disrupted on Election Day
events.summary: Election workers in Los Angeles County process ballots for the state’s primary in June. Mario Tama/Getty Images As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out. Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting . The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters , an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants. The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats. Help Us Report on Key Election Issues ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something? Send Us a Tip Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens. The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines. Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system. “The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.” “Paper Trail” Podcast Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “ Paper Trail .” In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.” The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.” Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm. Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said. Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds: People arrive to vote early on Oct. 27 in Coral Gables, Florida. Lynne Sladky/AP Images 1. Will There Be Federal Interference? An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls. Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this. He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage . “Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said. It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places. events.title: Pharma's next cash cows could be specialized treatments
events.summary: Pharmaceutical companies facing a steep patent cliff are concluding the key to future profits may be customized treatments tailored to patients' genes and lifestyles — not blockbusters aimed at large patient populations. Why it matters: The pivot could influence which diseases get treated in the decades to come, and how much the health system pays. The stakes are huge. More than $500 billion in brand-name drug sales is potentially at risk from generic competition between 2026 and 2032, according to the consulting firm Evaluate. The latest: The race is on to find new treatments that each generate at least $2.4 billion in global sales, a new Iqvia Institute report finds. They're increasingly specialty treatments, biologics and rare disease drugs — with a small group of flagship products accounting for an outsized share of industry sales. GLP-1 drugs like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Zepbound now define that elite category. The next wave could include "biological missiles" that combine antibodies with chemotherapy to target specific cancer cells. "As precision medicine continues to advance, similar approaches may extend beyond oncology into areas such as immunology, metabolic disease and neurology," the report states. Reality check: It's not clear whether all of the innovation will cure more people, or just make health care more expensive. Novel RNA drugs and cell and gene therapies are expensive, hard to make and target small groups of patients. Challenges identifying eligible patients and getting insurers to pay for treatments have already revealed a disconnect between promising R&D and patient benefit. Widespread concern over high drug prices will force manufacturers to find more unmet needs and build sales more quickly after a drug's launch, according to the report. Context: Top-selling drugs historically were aimed at large patient populations with chronic conditions like high cholesterol. The ulcer drug Tagamet became the first to exceed $1 billion in sales in 1986. Over time, cancer and immunology drugs became major drivers of growth, followed by GLP-1s, which are sparking huge demand for conditions beyond obesity and diabetes but also driving up health costs. Iqvia found that blockbusters on average maintain a dominant market position for 12.1 years before losing market exclusivity, or nearly 80% of their commercial life. Specialty drugs for rare or complex diseases lasted even longer. Yes, but: A substantial number of top-sellers will lose patent protection and face potential competition from generics between 2028 and 2036. Bristol Myers Squibb's blood thinner Eliquis and Merck's cancer blockbuster Keytruda, which are both due to lose market exclusivity in 2028, accounted for a combined $65 billion in global sales in 2024. Follow the money: The search for new blockbusters is playing out in a highly charged environment. Drugmakers and biotechs not only have to figure out how to grow outside of crowded categories but also how much payers value new classes of drugs, Evaluate says . There's also uncertainty over China , where Western drug giants have invested tens of billions of dollars to bolster their product pipelines. Evaluate predicts that only autoimmune disease drugs will come close to rivaling GLP-1s, because of their potential to treat dozens of conditions. One example is AbbVie's injectable Skyrizi for plaque psoriasis, arthritis, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, which could find more uses and generate more than $33 billion in sales in 2032. Iqvia identifies RNA therapeutics as a potentially important middle ground between traditional "small molecule" drugs for chronic diseases and highly specialized genetic treatments. These drugs can target disease-causing mutations across many genes and conditions, with applications for central nervous system, cardiovascular and kidney disease, as well as rare conditions. The bottom line: The success at innovating while also making sure patients have access to the new treatments "will ultimately determine whether the growth in blockbuster medicines observed over the past 25 years can continue at its extraordinary pace," Iqvia concludes.

events.title: JP Morgan boosts UAE presence with wealth management branch at DIFC
events.summary: JP Morgan Chase has expanded its private banking offerings in the Middle East with the opening of a dedicated wealth management branch at Dubai International Financial centre . Regulated by the Dubai Financial Services Authority, the DIFC branch will enable JP Morgan Private Bank to better serve clients across the UAE and the wider region, it said in a statement on Monday. In the 12 months leading up to the final DFSA approval, JP Morgan more than tripled the size of its Dubai-based private banking team to build capabilities before launch, it said, without specifying the number of bankers added. The team in Dubai is led by Selim Elgen, UAE market head and senior executive officer, and Karim Rekik, regional head, Middle East at JP Morgan Private Bank, the lender said. “JP Morgan Private Bank’s expansion into DIFC reinforces Dubai’s position as a global hub for private wealth,” said Arif Amiri, chief executive of the DIFC Authority. JP Morgan is the latest among major global financial institutions that have expanded in the UAE this year despite Iran war-driven uncertainty and economic headwinds. HSBC, Barclays as well as several Swiss wealth managers have also boosted their operations in the country to leverage the rapid growth of domestic wealth as well as the migration of global capital into the UAE. In October, Dubai and Abu Dhabi were ranked among the top 10 destinations for next-generation wealth despite the fallout from geopolitical tension. Dubai was ranked eighth and the UAE capital was 10th among favoured cities for the $84 trillion of wealth expected to be transferred between generations over the next two decades, consultancy Savills said in a report. Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility, according to Boston Consulting Group data. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at an annual growth rate of 10.6 per cent, the consultancy said in a report last month. Long-term relations JP Morgan Private Bank said its dedicated money management branch is the latest chapter in the bank’s five-decade relationship with the UAE. Over the past 20 years, the company has also used DIFC as its regional base for corporate and investment banking and, more recently, broadened its activities with authorisation to provide asset management services through JP Morgan International Advisers. "The UAE and the broader Middle East represent a significant and growing opportunity for us as a business and for our clients,” said Mr Rekik.

events.title: "Arrogance": 3 GOP Senate candidates blasted over costly red-state rescues
events.summary: Republicans are burning tens of millions of last-minute ad dollars to try to rescue three red-state senators who they say ignored months of warnings that their campaigns were in danger. Why it matters: Senate races in Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi are normally GOP layups. This year, Republicans have diverted resources from swing-state battles to defend them. The frustration with Sens. Roger Marshall (Kansas), Darline Graham (South Carolina) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (Mississippi) comes amid broader GOP finger-pointing as polls show a nationwide backlash against President Trump . "Democrats may win these seats in a wave ... but not a blue wave. It's the wave of arrogance [and] laziness ... that washed over these GOP incumbents and made them think they were invincible," said a national GOP operative involved in several key Senate races. By the numbers: National Republicans have spent $33 million in Kansas, $21 million in South Carolina and $2.4 million in Mississippi, according to data compiled by campaign finance expert Rob Pyers. Trump also has spent valuable campaign time in all three states. Behind the scenes: Republicans say the three senators ignored warnings to raise more money and build stronger campaign operations. National Republican Senatorial Committee chair Tim Scott warned all GOP senators in February 2025: "We do not need to spend time and money in places where races should not be competitive." Trump's political operation also warned Senate Republicans that they would need to pull their own weight. The most complaints center on Marshall, who has raised just $7.5 million compared with $19 million for his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton. Republicans blame his strained relationship with the banking and credit card industries — major GOP donors — and a lack of outreach to K Street. Republicans describe Marshall's campaign as overconfident. About a month ago, his team told aides to other GOP senators that the race would be effectively over within 10 days once it released opposition research on Hamilton. It wasn't. Strategists blame chief of staff Brent Robertson for Marshall's weak campaign operation. The campaign only recently tapped veteran Trump operative Chris Grant as part of a last-minute rescue effort. Alex DeGrasse, another veteran strategist recently hired to help Marshall, pointed to millions in spending by national Democrats and said the senator has made "hundreds of stops across all 105 counties in Kansas" and continues to "work hard for the people of Kansas." In Mississippi, Republicans have long viewed Hyde-Smith as a political underperformer. In 2020, she ran six points behind Trump. She has raised just $6.5 million despite warnings that Democratic megadonors, including George and Alex Soros, were preparing to spend heavily against her. Democratic groups have poured $13.7 million into the race. Republicans also fault Hyde-Smith for holding too few campaign events and underestimating her Democratic opponent, district attorney Scott Colom. Hyde-Smith's campaign did not respond to a request for comment. In South Carolina, Republicans fault Graham for failing to tap her late brother Lindsey Graham's donor network and showing little interest in soliciting contributions. In the first two weeks of October, Democrat Annie Andrews outraised Graham $4.2 million to $570,000. Graham spokesperson T.W. Arrighi said the senator "has faced unprecedented headwinds since losing her brother three months ago, and has risen to the occasion." Some Republicans are sympathetic to Graham, a political novice thrust into the Senate after her brother's death who faced a grueling primary and little time to campaign. They blame Trump for pushing her to run. Yes, but: Republicans point to Idaho Sen. Jim Risch, whose campaign required no spending from national GOP groups, as an example of an incumbent who took the political environment seriously. What they're saying: Representatives for the NRSC and the pro-GOP Senate Leadership Fund super PAC didn't respond to requests for comment. What's next: Top Republicans say the party needs to rethink how it deals with complacent incumbents in 2028 — and make clear that its campaign organizations can't be treated like a charity.

events.title: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it
events.summary: Exclusive: Gap between NHS claim and trusts’ comments described as ‘very misleading’ by senior health official More than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited from Palantir’s medical data platform are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology, the Guardian can reveal. The 29 hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as “realising benefits” from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official. It comes as the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, which aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements. Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”. The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”. NHS England has previously faced scrutiny over how it has used data to defend the Palantir contract, which began in 2024. It claims 117,539 more operations were carried out by trusts using the FDP in a year , but this summer it conceded it could not prove cause and effect, and the Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) watchdog ran an investigation. Asked about the claim of NHS Trusts “realising benefits”, the OSR said it will now be “taking this forward under our casework function”. The contrast between the number of hospitals the NHS claims realise benefits from Palantir’s technology and the statements of the hospitals themselves emerged from more than 100 freedom of information requests. NHS England states on its website that 137 trusts are “live” with the FDP, but of those described as “realising benefits”, 29 responded that they were either not using the system or its apps. Epsom and St Helier said it was “not using FDP at the moment”, Kent and Medway said the trust “has been focused on other priorities … the FDP is not currently live”, Mersey Care said they had “not yet gone live with the FDP”, Nottingham University Hospitals said “no implementation timeline has been agreed”, and University Hospitals of North Midlands said: “FDP is not live. We do not intend to roll it out in the future.” Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology committee, said: “If many NHS trusts don’t see the value of the FDP, serious questions need to be asked about whether the hype surrounding Palantir’s products matches reality.” She called on the government to activate the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s contract and launch an open competition for a UK-owned and based supplier to handle patient records. The Commons health select committee is also calling for ministers to pull Palantir’s deal. The FOIs were obtained by Medact, a medical charity campaigning for Palantir to be ejected from the NHS , and shared with the Guardian. Medact spokesperson Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne said: “Our NHS institutions are meant to work in the interests of public trust and evidence-based healthcare, not use creative accounting to justify a deeply controversial contract. There is no good reason for the government to continue this failing project. We now have to ask, if ministers are using these flawed claims to make their decision, are they being misled?” Asked to respond, NHS England insisted nearly 140 trusts “have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform, helping staff join up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.” It has previously said that its list of hospital trusts reporting benefits includes those using the tools for back office data analysis and submission rather than to support patient care. It is understood trusts that say they do not use the FDP may use a small part of its functionality to help calculate treatment costs. For example, Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust said it is “not currently operationally using the FDP” but NHS England records it as “live” because infrastructure is in place “to support data submission, rather than active operational use of FDP apps.” Palantir has been hitting back against criticism of its deal and last month hired Labour’s former deputy leader and member of the House of Lords Tom Watson as a full-time senior lobbyist. Watson this week has been posting videos on X aiming to debunk “myths” about Palantir, including concerns that public services will become “locked in” to its systems.

events.title: America's changing power grid faces a powerful El Niño
events.summary: A powerful El Niño could bring major shifts in electricity supply and demand across the U.S. this winter, posing new challenges for utilities. Why it matters: The U.S. power grid has far more solar, wind and battery storage than during the last major El Niño, and the ongoing event could reveal whether that changing energy mix has made the grid more resilient or left it vulnerable in new ways. Driving the news: A very strong El Niño is strengthening in the tropical Pacific and is expected to continue into spring 2027, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says. NOAA's latest outlook favors wetter-than-normal conditions across California , the Southwest and much of the southern U.S. this winter, while the northern Rockies and parts of the Great Lakes lean drier and much of the northern U.S. leans warmer. The intrigue: El Niño doesn't affect every electricity resource the same way. A March study found that previous super El Niños were associated with reductions in potential solar power output of nearly 5% in parts of California over 12 months — and more than 10% in the state's north during winter. Vincent Tidwell, chief scientist at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, says a wetter California winter could boost hydropower, while reduced precipitation or snowpack in the Pacific Northwest could cut generation there. Erik Smith, a climate scientist at the Electric Power Research Institute, tells Axios the Southeast is another region to watch for reduced solar generation as El Niño favors cloudier conditions. California now has more than 21 gigawatts of battery capacity , giving the grid another tool to manage fluctuations in electricity supply — one it barely possessed during the last very strong El Niño. The Columbia and Snake river basins accounted for roughly 62% of Western U.S. hydropower generation between 2001 and 2020, according to a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory analysis . Tidwell tells Axios that the Western grid is accustomed to shifting electricity between regions when hydropower conditions differ, helping compensate for shortages. Federal water managers, states and utilities use seasonal forecasts to plan for potential hydropower availability at Hoover and Glen Canyon dams on the Colorado River, Tidwell says. Zoom in: Tidwell expects natural gas to play a larger backup role if El Niño reduces Pacific Northwest hydropower and California solar generation this winter. Other resources, including wind, geothermal and nuclear power, provide additional options, though he says El Niño's effects on wind generation remain poorly understood. The big picture: A very strong El Niño could actually ease some pressure on the electricity system, Smith says. Warmer-than-normal conditions across the northern U.S. could reduce winter heating demand, potentially offsetting some of the pressure from changing electricity supplies elsewhere. Yes, but: Even a very strong El Niño doesn't guarantee specific weather impacts. A severe cold outbreak could still stress the grid despite a warmer-than-average winter, while a few major storms could radically alter regional rainfall and snowpack, Smith says. The bottom line: "We have a lot of confidence in how the averages are going to play out, but we don't have a lot of confidence in the day-to-day, week-to-week, particular weather events that could drive those averages," Smith says. events.title: ‘No room for debate’ over human control of AI, says Sam Altman
events.summary: People, not artificial intelligence, must stay in control of the future, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said on Monday. “There are a lot of other things we can debate, but on this one, we think there must be no room for debate,” he said in conversation with The National 's Editor-in-Chief Mina Al-Oraibi. Speaking at the opening ceremony of Adipec in Abu Dhabi, Mr Altman said there “should not be a handoff to AI” and that the technology “needs to be a tool built for people and needs to serve people, not the other way around”. “I can’t believe that this differentiates us from other AI companies, but it does,” he said. “This is a value that we intend to really go fight for. And I wish it didn’t need to be said.” The remarks followed OpenAI's agreements with Abu Dhabi, covering energy, education, investment and government. These include a deal with Adnoc and Abu Dhabi technology group G42 to use OpenAI’s most advanced models on the energy industry’s hardest problems. Mr Altman’s message was that AI has crossed a threshold. By his account, it has gone from trailing the world’s best scientists at the start of the year to mostly outperforming them. Its demand for power is growing just as fast, he said. “AI was mostly not as smart as our smartest scientists, and now it’s mostly smarter than them,” Mr Altman said, adding that AI could now do “a lot of parts” of many white-collar jobs. He said he believed society would “navigate through this all fine”. But he warned that the industry must show it can prevent harm as its systems become more capable. “How do we guarantee, and how do we give the world comfort with that guarantee, that we are going to avoid serious safety and alignment incidents?” he said. “I think that’ll be increasingly important for our industry to demonstrate.” Energy challenge In a quick-fire round, Mr Altman was asked what challenge he faces today. He answered with one word: “Energy.” He said the energy needed for each AI query had dropped sharply, but demand kept climbing . Six years ago, OpenAI’s heaviest internal user consumed about 100,000 tokens a month. Today, that figure is roughly the global per-capita average, and the top user consumes about 500 billion, he added. Costs could fall “in almost every way, except, you know, atoms are still atoms”, Mr Altman said. He called power “the very dominant factor” in how much AI the world can use. He said he hoped AI would deliver “a net gain for energy availability in the world”. Mr Altman also said OpenAI had solved one of the Millennium Prize problems, a set of unsolved mathematics problems. He said the work used 10,000 agents running an upcoming GPT model for about four days, collaborating with “no hierarchy”. The claim could not immediately be verified independently. He praised the UAE as “consistently the most forward-looking country in the world for AI adoption”, saying about 80 per cent of young people in the country were using ChatGPT .

events.title: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer
events.summary: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires We cannot let the billionaire class take unprecedented risks with our future A merica is a divided country in crisis. Despite the sunny economic forecast coming from the Trump administration, millions of Americans are struggling to find and keep jobs, getting crushed under the rising cost of living, and losing health insurance when they need it the most. Meanwhile, via corporate consolidation and political corruption, the billionaire class is getting richer faster than ever before: a 40% increase in wealth in just the last two years. Today, the combined wealth of nearly 3,000 global billionaires equals one-fifth of the entire world’s yearly output . Nearly 1,000 billionaires live and do business in the United States. The tools of their domination are tax loopholes, corporate mergers and, in the tech world where many of these billionaires exist, IPOs . When a company goes public, its founders and investors win the capitalist lottery. And instead of paying their fair share of taxes and redistributing resources back into society, most turn around and fund even more corporate consolidation and political corruption to extend their dominion. Elon Musk became an instant trillionaire when SpaceX went public earlier this year, on the backs of workers’ pensions – and is bankrolling the Republican midterm campaigns with a small percentage of his egregious gains. Oracle’s Larry Ellison – currently seventh on the Forbes billionaires list – backed the Paramount-Warner Brothers merger that is destroying the film industry and the livelihoods of the Americans who labor in it. Google’s Sergey Brin spent $100m opposing California’s Prop 40 , a one-time wealth tax that would put the funds toward healthcare and other public services. To pay for essential services, we must tax billionaires, and pass legislation to do so starting in California and New York, but that is clearly not enough. We cannot allow more billionaires – or trillionaires – to be made in this country, further expanding the inequality chasm that’s turning a dignified life into a luxury in this country. We must also block the impending tech IPOs and preserve what’s left of our economy and our society. The Trump administration and tech investors have positioned IPOs as market success stories: when a company goes public, US investors could gain from their valuations. But regular Americans also shoulder a company’s risks – and risk their own futures when that stock ends up in their retirement accounts without consent. Problems with a private company or its products become problems for everyone invested in that company once it goes public, whether they’ve made the choice or not. And when the speculative investment bubble pops – such as with the 2008 crisis – regular people end up holding the bag. It’s no secret that the AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI are intending to go public in the near future. Both of these players also had major security flaws exposed recently, and openly acknowledge mind-bogglingly huge amounts of debt. If these companies are allowed to go public, their cofounders and investors – some of whom are already billionaires – will rise to whole new strata of private wealth. Americans, meanwhile, will be financially crushed if the technologies fail or if these companies prove unable to make good on their extravagant financial promises. Already, the 10 most valuable public companies are in tech, which means the country’s economy depends on the stability of a single industry, one with an undeniable history of bubbles, crashes and, in extreme cases like Theranos, outright fraud. June’s highly contentious SpaceX IPO already carries great risk for regular investors. If more speculative tech companies with staggering risk profiles are allowed to follow suit, the results will become too much for the market to bear. If and when the AI bubble bursts, it will take all of us with it, investors or not. Recessions level lives indiscriminately, and globally. The one exception will be the billionaires, who will have sufficient resources to walk away from the wreckage relatively unscathed. We cannot let the billionaire class take these kinds of risks with our future. To stop these reckless IPOs we must stand together, take collective action, and push for real change. We must find legal and legislative avenues to stop the new tech IPOs from minting new billionaires and transferring the AI industry’s enormous risks onto us. The first step is passing wealth taxes on billionaires to keep them in check. Today, let’s send a message to the billionaires that Americans will not lie down and let them bulldoze working people and the environment on their way to the bank. Tax the billionaires. Block the IPOs. Naomi Klein is a Guardian US columnist and contributing writer. She is the professor of climate justice and co-director of the Centre for Climate Justice at the University of British Columbia.

events.title: I tested Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo. It's a fascinating experiment, but the price is hard to justify.
events.summary: I've spent the past week trying to figure out whether Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo is the future of smartphones or just an expensive way to do things I could already do on my regular iPhone. The answer, unsurprisingly, is a bit of both. Why it matters: Apple wasn't first to the folding smartphone party. Samsung, Google and others began making them years ago. But Apple's arrival in a category has a way of reinventing it. The big picture : The most exciting thing about Apple's first foldable iPhone isn't necessarily what it can do today but what it can become. Already, it's inspiring developers to explore possibilities that could reshape how we use our devices. Old habits die hard One of my first surprises was how little I initially used the Duo's biggest selling point: its folding screen. While other reviewers talked about endlessly opening and closing their devices, I found myself mostly using the smaller outside display. After years of conventional iPhones, it was a mix of instinct and muscle memory. Zoom in: Over time, though, I found reasons to unfold it. Watching sports was one of the clearest advantages. I pulled out the Duo at Starbucks to watch the 49ers with my son and later followed a tied World Series game in a doctor's waiting room. At the WNBA Finals, having forgotten my laptop, I managed some quick edits to a story about Anthropic's IPO . I wouldn't want to write a full article that way, but it was reassuring to have the option. Playing the New York Times' Spelling Bee alongside its Spelling Bee Buddy helper was a small but delightful example of multitasking without constantly switching apps. Between the lines: The Duo's advantages aren't always about more screen space. Sometimes they're about what you can physically do with a phone that bends. I tried watching Netflix with the phone unfolded, propped up like a tent and partially folded into a miniature laptop. I also used the Duo's ability to stand on its own to capture wide shots of the WNBA Finals from a press-box ledge without needing a tripod. Other experiences were less seamless, including getting the orientation right when trying FaceTime's option to use multiple camera views. The developer wild card Perhaps the biggest difference between the Duo and the Android foldables is the enthusiasm Apple's device has sparked among independent developers. Zoom in: Some of the early experiments are more entertaining than useful, including apps that turn the Duo into a virtual cassette player or a grilled cheese toaster . My favorite was Tiny Computers , which let it simulate a semi-functional 1984 Mac, Windows 95 PC or candy-colored iMac. Nearly two decades after the App Store debuted, we aren't all using our iPhones as virtual cigarette lighters. And I doubt we'll all be making imaginary grilled cheese sandwiches on our phones 20 years from now. Zoom out: But these early experiments offer glimpses of what might be possible when developers start thinking beyond a conventional rectangular screen. The question isn't whether today's novelties become hits. It's whether all this experimentation eventually produces genuinely new ways of using our phones — the kind of breakthroughs that make today's smartphones feel indispensable. The $2,000 question For all the fun I've had with the Duo, its price is an insurmountable obstacle. At $2,000, it's simply not a purchase I could justify for myself, much less recommend broadly. The catch: There are other compromises. I missed Face ID, occasionally fumbling for the side-mounted Touch ID sensor until I started wearing an Apple Watch to make unlocking the phone easier. And when I needed to accomplish something quickly, I often instinctively reached for my familiar, traditional iPhone. What I'm watching: On Friday, I tried putting the Duo away to see if I missed it. I didn't find myself longing for it the way I sometimes felt when I only had the Duo only and missed having a better camera. The bottom line: The Duo is a fascinating glimpse of where smartphones could go next. But early buyers are paying a steep premium to participate in an experiment whose biggest rewards may still be years away.

events.title: Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right.
events.summary: Quitobaquito Springs, a rare Sonoran Desert oasis imperiled by border wall construction, is located within 200 feet of the U.S.-Mexico border in Organ Pipe National Monument outside Ajo, Arizona. Anna Watts Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors. “People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said. Fifteen days later, her fears were realized. ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors. The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said. The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted. “The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural practices.” Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe, and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will disturb more sites. “​​Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.” Hia-Ced O’odham elder Lorraine Eiler stands in the shade of a giant saguaro cactus in Organ Pipe National Monument in 2022. Roberto “Bear” Guerra Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a saguaro cactus that was still standing. In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this location to date.” The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as the Las Playas Intaglio , that was believed to be at least 6,500 years old. (CBP said the incident was accidental .) Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica recently reported, DHS has responded by deploying masked federal agents as escorts for its work crews and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border.” Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it was necessary. “When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members — whose remains are being desecrated.” U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.” James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the field. While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.  Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained, and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the land.” “Work in the immediate discovery area must remain suspended for at least 30 calendar days,” he wrote, while the park service consults with tribal representatives “to determine the disposition and physical treatment of the remains.” Workers clear desert flora to make way for construction of a double border wall in Organ Pipe National Monument. Anna Watts In a region as rich with archaeological sites as the American Southwest, the inadvertent disturbance of Native American remains occurs with some regularity. What sets the discovery in Organ Pipe apart are the extraordinary powers the Department of Homeland Security wields to expedite wall construction in the borderlands. Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Real ID Act, which included a provision empowering the secretary of DHS to waive any law that might slow border wall construction. In the two decades since, DHS has invoked its powers 66 times, with 60 of those instances occurring under President Donald Trump’s two administrations. events.title: Banking on innovation for a more connected future
events.summary: At Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026, Hang Seng Bank will showcase AI-enabled innovation and partnerships designed to enhance customer experiences while supporting Hong Kong's development as an international innovation and technology centre [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Hang Seng Bank will bring AI-powered wealth management, digital banking, investment innovation and an interactive table tennis experience to Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026 as it makes its debut with a dedicated exhibition booth at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre on November 2 and 3. Six interactive experiences will showcase innovation across Retail Banking and Wealth Management, Commercial Banking, Markets and Securities Services, Hang Seng Indexes and the bank's partnership ecosystem. One example is Hang Seng's e-Passbook, Hong Kong's first service of its kind, launched in April 2026 with the needs of elderly customers in mind. Another demonstration is a Proof of Concept exploring the potential of bond tokenisation to make fixed-income investments more accessible to retail investors. Tokenisation holds the potential to enable fractionalisation of an underlying bond into smaller digital tokens, lowering the minimum investment required. It may also help streamline transactions and enable faster settlement. Visitors can follow a simulated demonstration investment journey, to experience the conversion of traditional bond into digital tokens. Elsewhere at the booth, visitors can take on a humanoid table tennis robot as part of an AI-wealth management experience. The game introduces visitors to AI-powered personalisation already available through the Hang Seng Mobile App, which provides tailored financial insights and suggestions based on customer profiles and preferences. Its Wealth Overview page and Goal Planner also help customers review their finances and plan ahead. The table tennis connection draws on Hang Seng's more than 35 years of support for local sporting talent. Supporting businesses and investment decisions Hang Seng will also showcase digital services designed to support businesses at different stages of development. An interactive installation takes visitors through an SME owner's journey, with three steps triggering videos covering remote account opening and daily operations, business expansion and wealth management. The bank's capabilities include digital payment solutions, a cross-bank cashflow analysis platform, Hang Seng SME Business Loan, Hang Seng TradePay, alternative data-backed financing and business mobile investment trading.Investors, meanwhile, can explore ThemeFinder, a Gen-AI-enabled solution co-developed by Hang Seng Indexes with an AI innovator from Cyberport's community. The technology identifies thematic investment trends and accelerates index development, improve the efficiency of identifying listed companies and processing relevant data by up to 5 times. The solution also helps maintain consistency across index operating processes and supports data traceability. Visitors can experience how thematic investment themes can be identified in the markets, create simulated personalised indexes and compare their performance against the Hang Seng Technology Composite Index. The showcase will also feature the Hang Seng Technology Index Family and HK-US index series, which combines Southbound Stock Connect-eligible Hong Kong tech stocks with major US-listed tech companies. Connecting Hong Kong's innovation community Its Living Lab programme with HKSTP, for example, launched a second cohort in April 2026 focused on AI applications in retail and commercial banking, providing technology ventures with opportunities to test solutions in banking environments. Such collaborations can move ideas from exploration and pilot programmes towards safe deployment, turning technological advances into solutions that can benefit customers at scale. With deep roots in Hong Kong, Hang Seng is connecting people, ideas and expertise to make banking more accessible, personalised and responsive to changing customer needs.

( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) More than 400 positions are expected to be affected at Mater Pathology in Brisbane and Springfield as the hospitals transition to an external pathology provider. A spokesperson for the healthcare provider blamed rising costs for the decision. More than 100 positions will be lost in the next two months, with most of the remaining positions ending in 2027. Mater has outsourced its pathology services in a move that will affect more than 400 staff. The announcement was made today, just a month before Christmas. The healthcare provider has blamed rising costs, saying Medicare subsidies have not kept pace with increasing financial pressures over the past decade. Mater says the transition to external pathology providers will affect more than 400 part-time, full-time and casual employees over the next 12 to 18 months. A spokesperson said the change will have no affect on patients. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) Under the new model, pathology services at Mater's Brisbane and Springfield hospitals will be delivered through specialist providers, including Sullivan Nicolaides Pathology and Pathology Queensland. The change will not affect Mater hospitals in Townsville, Mackay, Rockhampton, Bundaberg or the Gold Coast, which already rely on external pathology service providers. A Mater spokesperson said the decision would have "no impact on the high-quality care Mater patients receive". "The pathology model Mater is adopting is used by private hospital operators across Australia and will allow more resources to be directed to the clinical care of our patients. "We are deeply grateful to our Mater Pathology people," the spokesperson said. "This decision is not a reflection on their capability, professionalism or commitment." events.title: Election ‘war rooms’ enter the AI age
events.summary: Both OpenAI and Anthropic will have “war rooms” dedicated to ensuring their platforms provide accurate information about the midterm elections, a first for both companies. The concept of a tech platform “war room” dates back to 2018, when Meta stood one up for the first time amid concerns about the proliferation of election-related misinformation. The AI age has supercharged those threats, which now include deepfake videos and AI-powered search results spreading incorrect information. Case in point: Last week, Google’s AI Mode wouldn’t respond to a query about who won the 2020 election, which the company said they were working to fix . “Teams across the company work year-round on strengthening our election-related safeguards and enforcing our policies. Ahead of the election, we have a dedicated war room monitoring our platform for misuse and ready to quickly respond to any incidents,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Semafor. These efforts will be made more difficult by AI’s unpredictable nature, recent cybersecurity issues, and the tendency of AI search tools to reflect back results users want to see. Former Meta director of public policy Katie Harbath told Semafor that war rooms are “built for dealing with the things we can’t necessarily predict going wrong and you need a quick, established process in terms of triaging.”

events.title: Leading progressive wants Democrats to think big post-midterms
events.summary: A leading progressive lawmaker says his party colleagues need to think big and dare President Donald Trump to veto Democratic bills if they take the majority. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, is pushing for votes on bills to tackle “price gouging, that crack down on utility rates going up, that crack down on politicians profiting off their jobs” — and though he acknowledged some might become law, “if Donald Trump vetoes them, then that’s exactly the platform upon which we beat JD Vance or whoever else in 2028.” House Democratic leaders have sketched out some early priorities for their potential majority, like restoring lapsed health insurance subsidies or reversing cuts to Medicaid; the path beyond that is fuzzier. But the scope of House Democrats’ ambitions will depend on how many seats they pick up, and on Senate control, too. Casar bristled at recent comments by Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who said that Democrats should table bigger policy questions until the 2028 campaign, since Trump is still in the White House and likely to veto their legislation. He argued that pushing the envelope was necessary for Democrats to prove to voters they care. “I don’t want to waste our majority by negotiating down to Trump’s level,” Casar said. And if Democrats take the Senate as well on Tuesday, party-line legislation to circumvent the filibuster should be on the table, Casar said. “We should do a reconciliation bill, or multiple reconciliation bills, and dare Trump on those issues. We should also push for policies that are 80% popular across the country and dare Senate Republicans to vote against them,” Casar added. Some incoming progressive lawmakers have threatened to withhold votes for Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries in a speaker election unless he commits to progressive policy goals. Casar sidestepped a question on that prospect. “I’ve worked very regularly with Leader Jeffries, and I am a supporter,” he said. “Everybody’s vote, of course, is their own, and I would let each member speak for themselves on that question.”

events.title: How Trump's iron grip on the Republican Party put the Senate in play
events.summary: The News Americans are angry about war and prices, and a president’s second midterm is always difficult — but a series of decisions by President Donald Trump has made Republicans’ Senate majority ever-more vulnerable. The mark Trump made on the midterms began in the summer of 2024, when he selected former Ohio Sen. JD Vance as his running mate. Since then, the president’s personnel and political decisions have reshaped the Senate battleground from what looked like an impenetrable red wall into a toss-up. His decision to pick Vance opened up a special election in Ohio that will by the end of this week cost the GOP hundreds of millions of dollars and potentially a Senate seat. Trump’s party-boss mentality in North Carolina, Texas, and South Carolina has further contributed to the yawning battleground. He endorsed Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia’s Senate race against Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff — a contest that never really got off the ground after Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, whom Trump tried to take down in a primary in 2022, passed on the race. Ossoff is favored to win. And party insiders blame Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran for creating a volatile Senate map that has left seats in red states like Nebraska and Kansas vulnerable. Republicans could hold the chamber — or lose as many as a half-dozen seats on Tuesday. “Every negative for the GOP this cycle is a downstream effect of Iran,” said a person close to the White House. Republicans can lose up to three seats and still keep Senate control. Trump’s zeal on the campaign trail is undeniable and he helped direct huge sums of money into the midterms, albeit later than many Republicans would have liked. He spent the last weekend capping off a breakneck fall campaign schedule stumping in Iowa and Kansas, two places where the GOP was strongly favored to win a few months ago but now is struggling. “President Trump has a 97% endorsement record and he remains the best turnout machine for our base voters,” said Republican National Committee press secretary Natalie Baldassarre. Trump is hosting nearly 20 tele-rallies in the last days of the campaign, in addition to his almost-daily travel for rallies over the past month. The White House has sought to emphasize the administration’s accomplishments on issues like the border, crime, and US investment and manufacturing, as they look to encourage low-propensity voters to turn out for Republicans. “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle said. But his moves to reshape the party in his image over the past two years also often showed little regard for conventional political risk assessment. Trump created two special elections with decisions to put Vance as his vice president and Marco Rubio, a popular former Florida senator, as his secretary of state. On Tuesday, Democrats are underdogs in Florida after nominating democratic socialist Angie Nixon to face appointed GOP Sen. Ashley Moody. The race is more competitive than expected but not a five-alarm fire like Ohio, where Vance’s replacement, Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is in a precarious position. The longtime preference of Husted, a former lieutenant governor, was to run for governor, according to multiple people familiar with internal party deliberations. He was instead appointed to the Senate and Vivek Ramaswamy ran for governor; Ramaswamy now trails Democrat Amy Action. A campaign spokesperson for Husted said that he “is completely focused on retiring Sherrod Brown once and for all this Tuesday.” “Public polls in the national media have gotten Ohio wrong every election cycle since 2016,” one Ohio GOP operative argued. drama in the south A year after selecting Vance, Trump tangled with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., over healthcare cuts included in the tax cut law, prompting Tillis to retire. Tillis told Semafor afterward that Trump’s backing might not have helped anyway: “I’m not sure that his endorsement would have helped me in a general election in North Carolina next year, to be quite candid.” Trump quickly cleared the field for former RNC Chair Michael Whatley, avoiding a costly primary, but Whatley’s candidacy crumpled against his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said in an interview last summer that Tillis was “established” and “knew how to run and win in North Carolina,” while also praising Whatley as a candidate who could win with Republicans united behind him. In recent weeks, however, Republicans essentially ceded the race as the battleground map expanded to places like Texas. Thune and many sitting GOP senators had hoped to convince Trump to back Sen.
