events.title: The agentic web is here
events.summary: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.  At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus.  They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight.  As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not. How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.” Building a web for agents There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers. When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces. The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are naturals at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not. PINGNAN LU So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do. Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. For example, if you open up Claude, ChatGPT, or Muse, you’ll find an option to add a wide variety of “plug-ins” or “connectors” that your agents can use: Gmail connectors allow your agent to triage your inbox, and Instacart plug-ins let your agent do your grocery shopping. events.title: Asian shares are mixed and US futures advance, while oil prices retreat
events.summary: Asian shares are mixed ad oil prices have retreated, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran HONG KONG -- Asian shares were mixed and oil prices retreated Monday, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran. U.S. futures advanced after U.S. stocks fell Friday to their worst day since June as investors dumped technology- and artificial intelligence-related stocks. Japan’s Nikkei 225 gave up early gains, slipping 0.3% to 63,081.86 as some major technology companies fell. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index rose 2.2% to 5,859.08. Samsung Electronics added 1.8%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 3.8%. Technology stocks have been volatile as investors worry that the AI buildup may prove to be a bubble. Apple is due to report its latest earnings results later in the day. Last week, earnings reports from Google parent Alphabet Inc. and Amazon rattled markets and raised fresh questions over whether their massive AI-related spending will bring profitable returns as quickly as hoped. While recent developments do not necessarily mean that the AI boom is beginning to unravel, the debate is entering another phase, Sunil Tirumalai at UBS Global Research wrote in a recent note. Investors have become “distinctly more nervous about a handful of companies with weaker balance sheets or bigger financial commitments,” he said, rather than the technology sector as a whole. “Some cracks have appeared,” said Tirumalai. “Increasingly, the question will be whether all the money being spent on it can generate adequate financial returns.” Over the past month, the Nikkei 225 has fallen more than 7% and the Kospi dropped more than 16%. Taiwan’s Taiex was 0.7% lower, with leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., shedding 1.7%. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.5% to 23,411.49. The Shanghai Composite index was up 1.1% to 3,638.03, despite China reporting over the weekend that its factory activity returned to contraction territory in October indicating that the economic momentum may have slowed. China’s central bank and its securities regulatory body met with financial institutions Monday to discuss ways to support the markets, according to Chinese media reports. The Shanghai Composite index has fallen 14.6% in the past year. In Australia, the S & P/ASX 200 lost 0.6% to 8,856.50. On Friday, Wall Street’s benchmark S & P 500 fell 1.8% and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite declined 2.9%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 1.1%. Investors are watching for the outcome of Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections . Voters across the political spectrum have shown increasing concerns about AI and data centers , along with inflation and other key issues. Oil prices dropped more than 2% early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, down 2.8% to $110.24 per barrel. Benchmark U.S. crude gave up 3.1%, to $100.85 a barrel. Iran’s top diplomat said in an interview shared on his Telegram channel over the weekend that Iranian negotiators were in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. meets several conditions. However, he said no direct talks were being held with the U.S. The final outcome of the diplomatic efforts to avoid a return to all-out war depends on answers provided by the United States to the “Iranian questions,” he said. In other dealings early Monday, the U.S. dollar rose to 157.83 Japanese yen from 157.49 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1186, up from $1.1160. events.title: Asia’s factories lose steam as AI glow meets war’s economic chill
events.summary: Manufacturing activity slowed in China, indicating the drag from Iran war may be offsetting gains from robust global demand for AI chips. Asia’s factory growth slowed in October, especially in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, even as chip and AI demand stayed strong. The Middle East war is lifting fuel and food prices, hurting spending and confidence, while China’s price competition is also pressuring exporters. The IMF warned Asia’s growth may ease in 2026 and 2027, and Japan’s central bank said an AI slump could hit exports, production and financial markets. TOKYO – Factory activity across Asia continued to expand in October, but growth slowed in major chip exporters, private surveys showed on Nov 2, suggesting the AI boom may be losing momentum as markets start to question the sector’s profitability. The data points to growing strains on export-led economies, as prolonged conflict in the Middle East keeps fuel and food prices elevated, hitting consumption and business confidence, even as demand for chips and artificial intelligence-related goods remains resilient. Manufacturing activity slowed in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, the surveys showed, indicating the drag from the US-Israeli war on Iran may be offsetting the benefits from robust global demand for chips and AI-related goods. “Strong chip and AI demand had masked soft spots in Asian and global economies. But that’s becoming hard to sustain with the Middle East war dragging on for so long, pushing up fuel and food prices,” said Toru Nishihama, chief emerging market economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute in Tokyo. “High inflation is hurting Asian consumption. Intensifying price competition from China is also weighing on rival exporters like Japan and South Korea,” he said. The RatingDog China general manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI), compiled by S&P Global, stood at 52 in October, exceeding the 50-mark that separates growth from contraction but falling from 52.1 in September. The reading followed official data released on Oct 31 showing China’s factory activity shrank in October, marking the third contraction in four months. “The PMIs suggest that China’s economic activity lost momentum in October following September’s pick-up. Manufacturing softened a touch, but foreign demand still looks resilient,” said Nguyen Hoang Nam, China economist at Capital Economics. “More worrying was the sharp reversal in construction activity and expectations, suggesting that firms have become less confident that fiscal support will provide a substantial boost over the rest of the year.” Japan’s PMI eased to 53.3 in October from 54.1 in September, a survey by S&P Global showed, marking the slowest expansion in seven months as output and new orders lost momentum. South Korea’s factory activity grew in October at the slowest pace in eight months on weaker output and demand, with the PMI falling to 51.3 from 53.9 in September. Taiwan’s PMI stood at 54.9 in October, down from 56.7 in September. Other economies showed factory activity expanded in October at a faster pace than the previous month, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia. India’s manufacturing growth slowed in October as domestic demand eased and hiring weakened, though a surge in export orders helped cushion the slowdown. Asia has outperformed many other regions as manufacturers benefitted from brisk demand for chips and AI-related goods. But the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected Asia’s economic growth to moderate in 2027 , and warned of heightening risks from the Iran war-induced energy shock and a potential correction in the AI boom. The IMF said it now expects Asia’s economy to grow 4.8% in 2026 and 4.4% in 2027, higher than projections made in April but still slowing from a 5% expansion in 2025. While Japan has been among the beneficiaries of the AI boom, the central bank warned the technology also poses risks to the country’s long-term economic outlook. “If growth expectations for AI decline substantially, a tightening of global financial conditions, accompanied by a rapid repricing of stocks and a sharp slowdown in the race for AI development, could significantly hurt Japan’s economy through a plunge in exports and production,” it said. events.title: Al Habtoor Group board approves sale of all assets and investments in Lebanon
events.summary: Dubai-based Al Habtoor Group said its board of directors had approved the sale of the company's assets and investments in Lebanon , after it ceased operations there. The company, which has hotels, commercial and residential properties in Lebanon, said in January that it was ceasing operations and would terminate its employees in the country due to "prolonged instability" and an investment dispute. The conglomerate, which made investments across hospitality, retail, leisure, real estate and banking-related activities in Lebanon, said at the time that it suffered losses exceeding $1.7 billion. "Following careful consideration, the board has determined that the complete divestment of the group’s Lebanese assets represents the most appropriate course of action, consistent with its commitment to responsible investment management, capital allocation, and the protection of its interests," Al Habtoor Group said on Monday. The company said it intends to undertake the divestment "through a structured and commercially driven process, with each asset evaluated on its individual merits and transactions pursued in accordance with appropriate market conditions and valuations". In February, Al Habtoor Group said it also appointed law firm White & Case to begin arbitration proceedings against Lebanon in the US. The case is based on the dispute resolution mechanisms provided under the UAE-Lebanon bilateral investment treaty, Al Habtoor Group said at the time. The group established its presence in Lebanon with the opening of its first hotel in 2001. It said it "has made substantial investments" since then and has remained committed to the country through successive periods of economic and political uncertainty. The board’s latest decision "reflects a considered shift" in its investment strategy and its plan to concentrate resources on markets "offering greater long-term stability, investment certainty, and sustainable growth opportunities", it said. Al Habtoor Group will announce further details regarding the divestment process, it added. Lebanon has been mired in an economic crisis since 2019, one of the worst in modern history, according to the World Bank. The lender expects Lebanon's economy to contract by 6.4 per cent in 2026. The country, which is heavily reliant on imports, is also struggling from the fallout of the Iran war, as it is more exposed to shocks such as the disruption to shipping and energy supplies. The International Monetary Fund said last month that it was advancing discussions with Lebanon as part of broader efforts to support vulnerable countries in the Middle East and North Africa.

events.title: Alstom shares plunge after it cuts guidance, plans overhaul in second warning
events.summary: Alstom’s anticipated positive free cash flow was revised to an expected cash burn of €1.5 billion (S$2.1 billion). Alstom cut full-year guidance after delays in German projects hurt margins. It now expects about 1% adjusted Ebit margin and a €1.5 billion cash burn. Problems in Coradia Max orders caused penalties and a “domino effect” across other projects. Chief financial officer Bernard Delpit said the project’s gross margin is now negative. The company will review its organisation, cut costs, and seek about €2 billion of debt reduction through more asset sales. It reports full results on Nov 17 and a capital markets day in 2027. Alstom cut its full-year guidance and announced a deep overhaul after delays in key German projects led to penalties and hurt margins, plunging the French train maker into a fresh crisis. Its stock slumped as much as 27% in early Paris trading on Nov 2, after the company slashed its profit margin, cash flow and train car production targets for the fiscal year. The shares have lost more than half of their value in 2026. Alstom now expects an adjusted Ebit margin of about 1% for the fiscal year, down from 6.5% previously, it said on Nov 2 . An anticipated positive free cash flow was revised to an expected cash burn of €1.5 billion (S$2.1 billion). Alstom also downgraded its train car production target for the period to about 4,000 units from as many 4,500. The latest warning is tied to the Coradia Max orders, a series of projects including regional trains ordered by German states such as Baden-Wurttemberg and Lower Saxony that were meant to be the company’s biggest ramp-up in 2026 . The delays in one of the Coradia Max projects, caused by problems in the final development phases, had a “domino effect” on other German projects, leading to penalties that weighed on margins, chief financial officer Bernard Delpit said on a media call. The Coradia project’s gross margin is now negative, according to Delpit. The problem was detected after chief executive officer Martin Sion, who took the helm in April, sent out teams to deal with struggling projects, Delpit said. The CEO found that “not only were there engineering issues, but the organisation surrounding project management was neither efficient nor effective”, Delpit said. Alstom is now tackling a broader review of its organisation to improve execution and accountability, to lower costs and to make processes simpler. It also will carry out a new plan to slash debt by about €2 billion, which will include further divestments. “We have identified the assets and are beginning the process,” Delpit said on the call, when asked about the group’s possible future divestments. He declined to elaborate on details, saying it was too early. The company already stunned markets in April by withdrawing its financial guidance due to slow progress related to various projects, prompting a share slump. The group has been seeking to shore up its balance sheet after the troubled US$5.5 billion (S$7.03 billion) acquisition of Bombardier’s rail business in 2021. The group’s former CEO, Henri Poupart-Lafarge, had completed a previous €2 billion plan to slash debt. Alstom is due to report full fiscal results on Nov 17 and hold a capital markets day in the second quarter of 2027. BLOOMBERG

China’s top three airlines are heading for full-year losses as surging jet fuel costs, weak domestic fares and typhoon disruptions hit third-quarter results. Air China, China Eastern and China Southern all posted sharp profit falls, with China Southern swinging to a loss and all three losing money in the first nine months of 2026. Analysts said airlines remain under heavy pressure because fuel costs have more than doubled, competition is intense, and profits may stay weak into the fourth quarter. BEIJING – China’s three biggest airlines are on track for full-year losses after posting far weaker third-quarter results than in 2025 as surging jet fuel costs, weak domestic fares and typhoon disruptions hit what is normally their most profitable period. Air China and China Eastern Airlines are heading for a seventh consecutive annual net loss since the Covid-19 pandemic, according to analyst estimates compiled by LSEG. China Southern Airlines, which returned to the black in 2025 for the first time since 2019, is also set to slip back into the red, the estimates showed. Air China’s third-quarter net profit fell 92.6% from a year earlier to 270.6 million yuan (S$52 million). China Eastern posted a net profit of 64 million yuan for the quarter, down 98.2% from 2025. China Southern swung to a third-quarter net loss of 609 million yuan from a net profit of 3.84 billion yuan in 2025. All three airlines reported losses for the first nine months of 2026, a period in which they were profitable in 2025. The third quarter, which covers the peak summer travel season, is traditionally the strongest for Chinese airlines and set a high base for year-on-year comparisons. But all three carriers said the steep rise in jet fuel prices had a negative impact on their results. The price of jet fuel has more than doubled since the United States and Israel launched a military campaign against Iran in late February. Chinese airlines hedge far less of their fuel than many Asian and European peers, leaving them more exposed to swings in oil prices. Domestic fares were weak in the third quarter amid intense competition, including from high-speed rail. Huatai Securities estimated Air China’s yields, a proxy for airfares, fell 5% during the period, leaving it unable to recoup higher fuel costs. “Chinese airlines are expected to remain in net loss into the seasonally weaker fourth quarter given the impact of spiking jet fuel,” said Nathan Gee, head of Asia-Pacific transport research at BofA Global Research. Gee said third-quarter earnings had come in slightly better than “very low expectations”. Checks suggested domestic fares were rising at double-digit rates year-on-year after the October Golden Week holiday, as airlines kept a lid on capacity. But fuel “remains the big headwind”, he said. “Chinese airline margin remains under extreme pressure from spiking jet fuel and soft consumption demand,” Gee added. Airlines are trying to boost flying hours per plane to control costs, but big cost cuts will be difficult, he said.

events.title: Investor scrutiny of the AI spending boom is rising, but Big Tech is unlikely to give up
events.summary: Given that the bulk of chip manufacturing capacity is in Asia, the AI boom’s fate has the potential to redefine the region’s economic outlook. Investor scrutiny is rising over Big Tech’s huge AI spending. Alphabet fell 13% after reporting US$51.4 billion capex and negative free cash flow, despite 25% revenue growth. Big Tech says it must keep buying compute and chips to stay competitive. Scaling Laws, custom silicon and lower compute costs are driving more data centre and chip investment. Asia’s chip exporters are watching closely because AI demand supports trade and growth. Analysts say spending should stay high, with supply still tighter than demand and more sell-offs possible. SINGAPORE – As tech titans continue pouring massive amounts of money into data centres and equipping them with ever more expensive chips, growing investor scrutiny on the AI build-out is pulling down stock prices and pushing up borrowing costs. The selling pressure isn’t just pounding hard on Big Tech; their most consequential partners in the global AI supply chain, semiconductor chipmakers, have also suffered. Hence, investors and policymakers in Asia’s top chip-exporting nations, including Singapore, are watching Wall Street’s attempt to reset the AI trade with measured trepidation. The International Monetary Fund recently noted that global trade rose 8.3% between 2023 and 2025 – a figure that would be closer to 4.6%, or nearly half, without AI-related products. The Monetary Authority of Singapore’s latest Macroeconomic Review said Singapore’s technology-related sectors accounted for around 75% of overall year on year GDP growth in the third quarter of 2026. On the face of it, the question investors are asking seems plain: Can Big Tech afford the AI buildout? The market evidently doesn’t think so. Google’s parent, Alphabet, for instance, saw its stock drop by as much as 13% , erasing US$500 billion (S$639 billion) in market capitalisation, following its third-quarter 2026 earnings report released on Oct 28. Even as Alphabet posted strong revenue growth of 25% and a doubling of Google Cloud revenue, its stock was hammered after it reported US$9 billion in negative free cash flow, driven by a massive US$51.4 billion in capital expenditure, mostly on AI infrastructure. Free cash flow is the money left with a company after paying day-to-day operations and maintaining or expanding physical assets. So why aren’t companies that are leading the charge on AI giving in to the demand for fiscal discipline? For tech firms investing in AI infrastructure, including computing and memory chips, sufficient compute capacity is a must. This capacity is the single most important driver of AI capability, speed and competitive advantage. In the tech world, the concept is known as Scaling Laws. A framework of predictable mathematical relationships in AI that shows how a large language model’s performance improves – it gets smarter and makes fewer mistakes – as the resources driving it increase over time. According to the Center for Governance of AI, a non-profit research organisation, compute capacity is also the primary gatekeeper of AI diffusion, acting as the bridge that transforms elite lab research into affordable, ubiquitous commercial tools. Economic experts refer to this process as compute deflation, which reflects the rapid, sustained drop in the cost per unit of processing power, memory and AI inference. As the falling cost of compute replaces the cost of labour and production, it exerts downward pressure on the general price of software and tech-enabled services. That’s why some AI hyperscalers are also designing their own high-performance AI accelerator chips – specialised semiconductor hardware designed to process AI, machine learning, and deep-tech learning workloads much faster and more efficiently than standard chips. Big Tech is also investing in chips The shift towards custom silicon is reshaping the entire cloud computing industry. To break free from Nvidia’s hardware monopoly and drastically lower operational costs, all major cloud hyperscalers – including Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure – have aggressively built out their own proprietary chips. Alphabet disclosed in its third-quarter earnings report that more than 100 significant Google Cloud customers – including Anthropic and Apple – are now running AI using Google’s own tensor processing units, an alternative to Nvidia’s AI chips. Consumer tech platforms are also designing custom silicon – Meta’s MTIA, or Meta Training and Inference Accelerator, chip family, for instance – to power their internal AI tools and ad engines. This competition in semiconductor chips and devices aims to break old hardware monopolies and force down pricing.

events.title: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack
events.summary: Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history. The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets. Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack . The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack. Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion." There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added. Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance. The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack. Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed. Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back. "We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme. "The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added. AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened Published 22 October The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them. The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets. Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions. The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue. Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said. Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices. Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally. events.title: MAS sets aside $30m to help insurers build expertise in funding major projects
events.summary: MAS is also proposing changes to the capital insurers must set aside against investment risks, reducing requirements for investments where the risks justify this. MAS will set aside $30 million to help insurers build skills in financing major projects such as power grids and data centres, using funds from the Financial Sector Development Fund. It also plans lower capital rules for some project investments, if risks are lower. The public consultation runs from Nov 2 to Dec 18. At the Singapore reinsurance conference, industry players launched a data centre insurance scheme and an AI risk handbook, showing new growth areas and new risk concerns. SINGAPORE – The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will set aside $3 0 million to help insurers build expertise in investing in major projects such as power grids and data centres. The central bank is also proposing changes to the capital insurers must set aside against investment risks, reducing requirements for investments where the risks justify this. Minister for National Development Chee Hong Tat announced the measures o n No v 2 at the 2 2nd Singapore International Reinsurance Conference at Sands Expo and Convention Centre. The event, organised by the Singapore Reinsurers’ Association (SRA), drew more than 4, 300 delegates representing 85 countries and territories, according to the association. Reinsurers provide insurance to insurance companies. Chee, who is also MAS deputy chairman, said insurers could play a bigger role in financing Asia’s growth, alongside protecting businesses and communities against risks. The $30 million, from the Financia l Secto r Development Fund , will help defray the costs of building dedicated investment teams, training staff and engaging professional services to establish and expand these investment activities in Singapore. Across ASEAN, more than U S$200 billion (S$256 billion) is needed annually for projects ranging from roads and ports to renewable energy and telecommunications networks, Chee said. Yet, past studies put such investments at only around 1 % to 2% of insurers’ assets, although this share has been growing. “High-quality infrastructure assets can generate stable, long-term cash flows that align well with insurers’ long-dated liabilities, particularly those of life insurers,” Chee said. This means income from these projects can help insurers meet payments owed to policyholders years later. MAS proposes extending lower capital requirements to qualifying debt investments in these projects that have credit ratings, subject to conditions. Investments with features that reduce risk, such as stable contractual revenues, could qualify for further reductions. MAS also proposes lower requirements for certain rated investments backed by pools of assets, subject to conditions including repayment priority, ease of trading and structural safeguards. The public consultation runs from Nov 2 to Dec 18. Chee said industry players are developing a Singapore-based insurance facility for data centres, with US $200 million in initial capacity. An insurance facility is a pre-arranged agreement where several insurers join their underwriting ability to cover particular types of risks. Participants include MSIG, Gallagh er Re, SCOR, Samsung Re and the Cybersecurity Association Singapore. The facility is expected to cover construction, operational, supply chain, design and cyber risks. Separately, SRA launched a handbook at the conference to help reinsurers assess risks associated with artificial intelligence. The guide addresses issues including the reliability of data and AI decisions, dependence on external providers, and how AI affects decisions on insurance coverage and claims. Minister for National Development and deputy chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore Chee Hong Tat speaking at the Singapore International Reinsurance Conference on Nov 2. SRA ch airman Glen Rid dell said: “AI is creating new opportunities across the insurance value chain, while also introducing new considerations for the risks insurers and reinsurers assume.” Reinsurers need to understand how AI affects the risks they cover and claims outcomes, he said. “This handbook provides practical, principles-based guidance to help reinsurers assess these considerations and incorporate them into reinsurance decision-making.” The conference runs until Nov 5, with discussions covering geopolitical and economic shifts, disaster protection and the skills needed as technology changes the insurance industry.

( Supplied: Environmental Protection Authority Tasmania ) Tasmania's EPA says it has "disrupted an interstate waste tyre operation" it alleges unlawfully collected an estimated 4,000 to 5,000 tyres from local businesses. The operation posed as legitimate controlled waste transporters, making $50,000 in 10 days. The EPA says investigators have located six shipping containers filled with the tyres collected from businesses under false pretences. Tasmania's Environment Protection Authority says it has disrupted an interstate waste tyre operation that unlawfully collected thousands of tyres from Tasmanian dealerships and mechanics. The EPA's investigation began last year, after it received reports that an unlicensed company was approaching businesses posing as "legitimate registered controlled waste transporters" approved by the EPA and Tyre Stewardship Australia. At least 30 instances of unlawful tyre collection involving around 20 Tasmanian businesses were identified. The unlawful operators made approximately $50,000 in 10 days. Investigators located six shipping containers filled with waste tyres, four in Bridgewater and two in Launceston. ( Supplied: Environmental Protection Authority Tasmania ) Investigators uncovered a tyre network that had been operating in various Australian states over recent years, using rented vehicles, short-term shipping container leases and false credentials to collect the waste tyres. In June, six shipping containers filled with waste tyres, four in Bridgewater and two in Launceston, were located, with an estimated 4,000 to 5,000 tyres having been collected and stored across the state. The EPA said the investigation resulted in enforcement action against one operator, with warning notices issued to "retailers who should reasonably have recognised and acted on suspicious activity." Call Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 Report anonymously via the Crime Stoppers website Evidence gathered across the investigation included alleged breaches of the Environmental Management and Pollution Control (Waste Management) Regulations 2020 and potential fraud offences. EPA chief executive and director Catherine Murdoch said the investigation would assist other jurisdictions in tackling the unlawful activity. "The EPA undertook its largest proactive industry-targeting exercise in response to organised environmental crime to date. events.title: 'Impossible to get ahead': ACT inflation rate rises above national average
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Small businesses feel the pinch as ACT inflation rate rises above nation's average Casey Johnston said her business had been avoiding passing on costs to consumers. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Household inflation has risen to 4.7 per cent in the ACT, with the national average being 4.3 per cent. Canberrans are continuing to curb their spending, with small businesses seeing declining foot traffic. An economics lecturer says inflation is not expected to come down anytime soon, with another rate increase on the horizon. The ACT's inflation rate jumped to 4.7 per cent in the 12 months to September this year, and now sits above the national average of 4.3 per cent. And with the RBA expected to lift the cash rate again tomorrow to 4.85 per cent — the highest rate since the 2008 global financial crisis — many households are doing all they can to curb their costs. But for some Canberra business owners that means sales are down, with no end in sight. "Nobody's out and about eating and obviously that hurts us," Casey Johnston, who runs a burrito business in Tuggeranong with her partner, said. Ms Johnston said she was used to business "fluctuating" in the hospitality sector, but sales were "a lot lower" than past years. "I feel like our foot traffic, people walking along the street just to find somewhere to eat for dinner or lunch, is definitely declining," Ms Johnston said. As the cost of living continues to bite, Canberrans are cutting back on their discretionary spending. ( ABC News: Mark Moore ) Ms Johnston said they were also absorbing rising business costs including products and rent, rather than passing those costs onto customers. "[It] is a hard battle because we can't increase our prices for our consumers, but we're definitely taking the hit of our products being more expensive ourselves," she said. "We can't always afford wages and that kind of thing. "If people aren't here then the employment is not necessarily needed all the time, and that can make things really tricky." Interest rates projected to rise again Dr John Hawkins said interest rates were predicted to continue rising. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Senior lecturer in economics at the University of Canberra Dr John Hawkins said global oil prices were the main driver for rising inflation rates. In the ACT specifically, the biggest drivers were fuel, electricity, childcare and school fees, new housing builds, and furniture, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. "You get these variations that are quite random," Dr Hawkins said. "Our inflation's lower than Hobart, Darwin, and Adelaide, but it's a bit higher than Sydney and Melbourne." Dr Hawkins also warned the Reserve Bank of Australia was likely to once again hike up interest rates. "There's an 80 per cent chance that [homeowners] will probably be paying 0.25 per cent more on their mortgages from tomorrow, and the financial markets think if the Reserve Bank doesn't move tomorrow, they'll probably move in either December or early next year," he said. "Raising interest rates will lower inflation because it will slow down the economy. Hairdresser Elanor said people tended to spread out their appointments these days. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Elanor, a hairdresser, said she has personally already cut down "literally everything" when it comes to discretionary spending. "So no coffees out, no more expenditures," she said. "Holidaying, going away, just being able to eat out — so not going out to restaurants, even though we've got all these beautiful restaurants and everything around us — no, I don't spend on that anymore." Elanor said her workplace's clientele base had largely remained the same, but people were booking hair appointments less frequently than they normally would. events.title: Christmas donations gift demand up, charities say
events.summary: The Christmas Sparkle appeal said demand for toys has gone up in recent years Charities giving Christmas presents to struggling families say more children need their help - but they are getting fewer donations this year. The Chard Christmas Present Appeal said it was having to deal with a high-than-normal demand this year, and blamed the problem on more people struggling financially. Martyna Lee, founder of the appeal, said a lot of families were worried about affording presents for their children due to the cost of living crisis and have "tears in their eyes" when the charity can help them. She added: "We are getting more referrals and less donations because of cost of living, so we do struggle. Cost of living is going to get harder and harder." Song urges builders to talk about mental health Published 19 hours ago MP facing voice loss after surgery shows recovery signs Published 1 day ago Bid launched for 410 new homes near motorway Published 1 day ago Lee started the appeal by herself in 2019 from her living room as part of the Lord's Larder food bank in Chard. They rely completely on donations and do not receive any funding. The Chard Christmas Present Appeal said more families need their help this year "With one family, the social worker asked the children what they would like for Christmas and they asked for pencils and a colouring book," Lee said. "That broke my heart. They weren't asking for expensive gifts. "So I made sure they had a large gift package, including board games." She added that another family she remembers had a fire at their home just before Christmas and they lost "nearly everything". "We managed to get them fantastic gifts and a Christmas tree and decorations," Lee said. Meanwhile, Taunton's charity appeal Christmas Sparkle said their demand has risen sharply over the last couple of years, with 500 presents given out in 2015 to 10,000 last year. They said they are expecting even higher demand this year. Gill Harrison, founder and manager at Christmas Sparkle, said she believes the cost of living crisis is increasing the demand for their services. "When we started the project in 2015, we gave out 500 individual gifts. Last year, it was around 2,300 parcels, that's about 10,000 individual gifts," Harrison said. "We are expecting possibly even more requests this year. That's mostly because of the cost-of-living crisis." Harrison said they work with schools, social services, police, women's refuges and community nursing teams, which have all increased their referrals to Christmas Sparkle over the last few years. events.title: Christmas shoebox appeal launches to help children
events.summary: The boxes will be available in supermarkets for shoppers to pick up and pack before they are passed on to school and charities for distribution. Children across Staffordshire who might otherwise go without a Christmas present are set to receive gift-filled shoeboxes through a new appeal encouraging residents to donate locally. The initiative, organised by World Give, is asking people to pick up empty shoeboxes from supermarkets, fill them with gifts and return them for distribution to families through schools, charities and Staffordshire County Council. Trustee Adam Contoret said the appeal was launched after the charity recognised growing levels of hardship closer to home. "We look around the shops, we see everyone going about their business, but you don't see the people that aren't there," he said. School children gave feedback on what sort of items could be included so that a list could be prepared to help shoppers understand what to put in the boxes. "There's people that would be buying Christmas presents, but they can't because they haven't got the money." Over the past 20 years, the charity has helped more than 100,000 children across the world by sending shoeboxes full of gifts. This year, however, it has turned its attention to supporting children and families in Staffordshire. "It's apparently one in seven children who won't get a formal gift-wrapped Christmas present under the tree at Christmas," Contoret said. "This year we're turning around. Charity begins at home. The boxes are being done in Staffordshire for Staffordshire kids." People will be able to collect empty shoeboxes from participating supermarkets, fill them while doing their shopping and return them to be distributed through schools and local charities. The appeal comes as a Family Action survey of 2,000 parents and carers found one in five had considered cancelling Christmas because they could not afford it, while one in nine said they would not be able to afford a Christmas present for their child. Adam Contoret has previously sent shoeboxes over the world but this year after seeing the statistics, wants to shift the focus closer to home Contoret said schools and local charities were best placed to identify families who could benefit from the scheme and ensure gifts were distributed discreetly. "The schools know the families and they're the best place to hand those gifts over at the right time in a discreet and respectful way," he said. Students supporting the campaign said the shoeboxes could have a significant impact on children at Christmas. Noah said he would include practical items alongside gifts. "I think it's good to give things to everyone and relate it to the age groups," he said. "I would give them notepads, pens, calculators and a stationery set, for example pencil cases, rulers and protractors." Steven said the appeal could help children enjoy the festive season. "Christmas is a festive season of merriness, so if you don't have any presents, you don't feel that giving and love and you won't feel that much merrier," he said. Isabelle said receiving a gift-filled shoebox could help children feel valued. "They might feel special because they know someone actually put thought into putting stuff in the box for them, so they know that someone cares for them and they feel loved," she said. events.title: Dr Sultan Al Jaber urges energy security overhaul as nearly billion barrels drawn from oil markets
events.summary: The disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has drained nearly one billion barrels from global oil inventories, exposing the need for a fundamental rethink of energy security, the Adipec conference in Abu Dhabi heard on Monday. “Simply put, the world has eroded its supply buffers,” said Dr Sultan Al Jaber, UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc. “But, trust me, supply is only half the story. The other half is delivery." During the event's opening ceremony, Dr Al Jaber called for greater investment in supply infrastructure and artificial intelligence to help the energy industry withstand future shocks, warning that securing production was no longer enough to guarantee that supplies reach consumers. Referring to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, who attended the ceremony, Dr Al Jaber said, “Sam, from the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI. And now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy.” He spoke as Adnoc announced an agreement with OpenAI and G42 to become the world's first energy company to deploy OpenAI's Frontier platform, with plans to transform the Abu Dhabi energy company's field development, well management and commercial operations. The partnership, guided by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, would make Adnoc's systems smarter, safer, more secure, more resilient and more productive, Dr Al Jaber said. The Iran war severely disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz and exposed weaknesses in global supply chains, he added. “For years, our industry optimised for just in time,” Dr Al Jaber said. “And to tell you the truth, we got very good at it. This year we got the bill for just in case.” Diesel stocks in some markets have fallen to their lowest seasonal levels in 35 years, while others face a 600 billion cubic feet gap in LNG supplies, he said. Shipping and logistics costs, which accounted for less than 5 per cent of the cost of a barrel before the disruption, now exceed 30 per cent. “Energy security is not only measured at the point of production. It is now also measured at the point of delivery,” Dr Al Jaber said. He outlined five priorities for strengthening energy security: accessible supply, routes to market, operational intelligence, investment confidence and people. He also called for intelligent energy systems capable of anticipating risks, improving performance and reducing costs. On investment, Dr Al Jaber said: “Capital follows confidence. Policy must create it … finance must accelerate it … and insurance must keep trade moving.” He said the UAE would continue to advocate dialogue, diplomacy and political solutions to support stability in energy markets and the global economy. “Talent stayed. Capital stayed. Investment kept coming … and the economy kept moving,” he said. “That is the UAE model, pressure-tested and proven by results.” Dr Al Jaber said Adnoc's preparedness had been developed years before the disruption. “We did not write our resilience playbook during this disruption. We wrote it years before,” he said. “Energy leadership is not measured by what you produce in good times. It is measured by what you deliver in hard times.” “Because when it counts the most. You can count on the UAE,” he added.

events.title: Land of the free, home of the bill shock. This is life in Trump's America
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rising cost of living to hit heavily at US midterms as bill shocks rattle Americans The decaffeinated coffee beans at a US cafe sum up how its customers feel about the rising cost of living. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) It's a quiet Sunday morning in Lansing, Michigan. The low autumn sun lights the interior of the Hob Nob cafe, illuminating a table of young regulars, including the flat-cap-wearing Nicholas Kolacz. He's just bought his weekly coffee. "After a tip, because I always like to tip, it's $US10," Nicholas says. "I used to come in here … probably three or four days a week. Now I come in once every Sunday because I don't have the money to spend," he says. Nicholas Kolacz rarely buys coffee out now due to the higher prices. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) Nicholas makes $US17.50 per hour as a delivery driver. After rent and bills, there is no spare cash. He stopped buying beer long ago and looks at every discretionary purchase through the prism of his wage. "When I do buy things, I look at like, 'Oh, how many hours am I working to get this?'" Once, America felt affordable. Now, the land of the free is also the home of the bill shock. I felt it myself at a bagel cafe on New York's Upper West Side. Twenty years ago, when I lived in Manhattan, my regular breakfast was a bargain: coffee, orange juice and a bagel with lox for $US5. This week, at a no-frills diner, the same breakfast cost me $US31 ($44). The owner of the Hob Nob cafe in Lansing, Trisha Kosloski, says her expenses have gone through the roof. She estimates her delivery costs have increased 50 per cent as shippers pass on fuel costs. But her biggest expense had nothing to do with petrol, or the US and Israel-led war with Iran. The price of coffee beans shot up just after Donald Trump was elected and announced a suite of tariffs on a number of nations where coffee was grown. The average price of coffee in the US is now $US9.33 ($13), the federal minimum wage is $US7.25 ($10.22) . "I'm an import business. We do not grow a lot of coffee in America, as much as we want to pretend that we do," Trisha says. "When we saw those first round of tariffs that were just like blanket tariffs when he first got into office, all of my coffees went up at least 30 per cent. Trisha Kosloski has passed on the cost increases to her customers. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) In July, Donald Trump announced 50 per cent tariffs on goods from Michigan's neighbour, Canada — which also hit the coffee industry . "A large amount of the beans roasted in America … are actually roasted in Canada. So we had to pay those tariffs to get them," Trisha says. All the extra costs have put pressure on her business. "There is no profit margin," she says. Coffee might be a discretionary purchase, but for many Americans there has been no way to avoid the most painful price increase. Petrol — or "gas" as it's known the US — is hovering at about $US4.30 per gallon ($6.10 for 3.8 litres or about $1.60 a litre), about $US1 more expensive than it averaged in 2025. That is still cheaper than Australian prices, but Americans aren't used to paying anything like this. Big cars are standard, and long journeys are unavoidable in sprawling mid-western communities like Lansing, Michigan. The city is the home of the Michigan State University Spartans college football team, and for many, a lively Saturday morning tailgate begins before dawn. The parking lots around Spartan Stadium are filled with gleaming, oversized SUVs and "trucks", like Ford F150s and Chevrolet Silverados. It's costing Americans more to fill up the tank of their big cars. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) "Gas is the number one thing that used to not be so much," MSU student Samson Sprague says. It's not only students feeling the pain. It's Parents' Weekend at MSU, where there are two and sometimes three generations of Americans here today. "My daughter goes to University of Kentucky, so when we drive down to see her, gas is a lot more expensive. It's almost more reasonable to fly to Kentucky than drive to Kentucky right now because of the price of our gas," Michelle Krebill says. Michelle Krebill (right) says it's costing her more to visit her daughter interstate. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) Tara Lukaart is another struggling with the cost of filling up tanks. Her husband operates a plumbing business with several trucks on the road. "For a small business to be able to afford that kind of increase in gas price has been a big deal," she says. Elizabeth Madigan believes the current situation should lead to political change.

events.title: Sheng Siong shares continue last week’s slide, fall over 9% to hit one-year low
events.summary: Sheng Siong reported a modest 1.9% year-on-year increase in Q3 net profit. Sheng Siong shares fell as much as 9.4% to a one-year low after Q3 net profit rose only 1.9% to S$44.6 million, despite revenue growing 6.2% to S$441.5 million. Management said fierce supermarket competition, heavy promotions, rising labour costs, and the upcoming RTS Link could pressure sales and margins, so the group will adjust its strategy. DBS expects slower earnings growth in Q4 because of a high base, the Thomson Imperial Court store closure, higher utility prices, and staff costs; it kept a hold rating and S$3 target price. SINGAPORE – Shares of supermarket operator Sheng Siong continued to fall, dropping as much as 9.4 per cent on the morning of Nov 2, after the group reported a marginal 1.9 per cent year-on-year increase in third-quarter net profit on the evening of Oct 29. The stock had closed down 4.6 per cent or 13 cents at $2.67 on Oct 30. The counter opened on Nov 2 down 7.1 per cent at $2.48 as at 9.01am, before slipping to $2.46 as at 9.16 am. It fell further to $2.42, down 9.4 per cent, as at 10.44am. This is the lowest level the stock has reached since Nov 3, 2025, when it hit S$2.33 in intra-day trade. Some 7.4 million shares changed hands as at 10.44am on Nov 2. No married deals were reported, according to data from ShareInvestor. The mainboard-listed supermarket operator reported a net profit of $44.6 million for the three months ended Sept 30, up from $43.7 million in the corresponding year-ago period. Revenue for the quarter rose 6.2 per cent to $441.5 million, from $415.5 million a year earlier. The group attributed the increase to a larger store network in Singapore, as well as improvements in comparable same-store sales. The stock’s decline also comes after management said during its third-quarter results briefing that the grocery retail landscape remains competitive, with sustained promotional activity potentially putting pressure on revenue and margins. Competition could intensify further with the upcoming Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link, which is expected to begin operations in February 2027. The link could encourage more cross-border shopping and heighten price competition for selected packaged groceries and household products. Sheng Siong said it would adapt its strategies as developments surrounding the RTS Link unfold, in order to address the potential impact on its business. Beyond competition, the group also flagged rising labour costs as another challenge. These include wage increases under the Progressive Wage Model and the National Wages Council’s guidelines for 2026 to 2027. The group had raised the salaries of its retail workers in September last year to meet Progressive Wage Model requirements for the retail sector. DBS analyst Chee Zheng Feng said in a note on Friday that he expects Sheng Siong’s earnings growth to moderate further in the fourth quarter, as it comes down from a high base boosted by SG60 vouchers. Another potential factor is the full-quarter impact of the Thomson Imperial Court store’s closure on Sept 25, while higher utility prices and rising staff costs could also weigh on the supermarket chain’s profitability, he added. The brokerage maintained a hold and unchanged target price of $3 for the counter. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Adnoc becomes first energy company to deploy OpenAI Frontier
events.summary: Adnoc has signed an agreement with OpenAI and G42 , to become the first energy company to deploy OpenAI’s Frontier technology as it seeks to expand AI use across its operations. Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, met OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman on Monday and witnessed the agreement, signed by G42 through its subsidiary Inception42. “Abu Dhabi and the UAE are setting a bold, global standard for AI integration across both the public and private sectors to make sure the benefits of AI reach everyone,” said Mr Altman, who is in Abu Dhabi to attend Adipec . “We are proud to support the UAE’s ambition, anchored in a shared commitment to safety, accessibility and responsible innovation.” The project will integrate advanced AI capabilities across Adnoc’s operations, enabling more connected operational, investment and commercial decision-making to improve efficiency and productivity. The technology will run on OpenAI’s GPT models using inference infrastructure based in the UAE. OpenAI launched Frontier on February 5 as an enterprise platform for building, deploying and managing AI agents. HP, Intuit, Oracle, State Farm, Thermo Fisher and Uber were among its first adopters. The Frontier deal is one of four agreements signed between Abu Dhabi-based entities and OpenAI, spanning the government, energy and investment sectors. The Abu Dhabi government and OpenAI also launched what they described as the world’s first AI native Machine-Readable Government initiative , part of the emirate’s goal to become the world’s first fully AI-native government. The initiative converts government policies and regulations into a format AI systems can read, to help officials carry out routine compliance assessments, such as issuing permits and certificates. Officials retain oversight of the processes, and accountability for final decisions. Led by the Department of Government Enablement, its first pilot is already running with the Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority and focuses on food imports. Mubadala , Inception42 and OpenAI signed an agreement to apply AI to investment analysis, opportunity identification and risk assessment. Inception42 and OpenAI also signed a five-year agreement to support the adoption of frontier AI across government, enterprise and education in the UAE. Adnoc has been building its AI capabilities for several years. In 2019, it agreed with G42 to set up a joint venture to develop and commercialise AI products for the oil and gas industry. The venture, AIQ , was 60 per cent owned by Adnoc and 40 per cent by G42. The agreements build on OpenAI’s long-standing ties with the UAE. G42 and OpenAI first partnered in October 2023 to apply the US company’s generative AI models in sectors including financial services, energy, healthcare and public services. In May last year, the two companies announced Stargate UAE , OpenAI’s first international deployment of its Stargate AI infrastructure and the start of its OpenAI for Countries programme. The 1-gigawatt cluster is being developed by G42’s Khazna Data Centres within the 5-gigawatts UAE-US AI Campus in Abu Dhabi, with OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco and SoftBank as partners. OpenAI said at launch that the first 200 megawatts were expected to go live in 2026 . Abu Dhabi has also invested in OpenAI, with MGX among the co-leads of OpenAI’s $122 billion funding round, which closed on March 31 at an $852 billion post-money valuation.

events.title: Oil prices slide more than 3% as Trump signals more time for Iran diplomacy
events.summary: Oil prices fell on Monday morning amid hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough between the US and Iran , easing concerns about further supply disruption. US President Donald Trump reportedly said he wants to give diplomacy with Iran more time before considering renewed military strikes after Tuesday’s US midterm elections. The two key benchmarks slid more than 3 per cent in morning trading. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's crude, was trading at $110 a barrel at 7.55am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, dropped to $100.90 a barrel. Mr Trump reportedly told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a phone call that he wanted to give diplomacy with Tehran more time before considering further strikes, Axios reported, quoting sources. CBS News reported that Mr Trump said he believed the US would soon end the war with Iran, "one way or the other". The US President was speaking to Right Side Broadcasting Network before a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday, according to the report. "We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other," Mr Trump was quoted as saying. "Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it … The job we've done is amazing." On Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said no decision had been made on renewed strikes and that Mr Trump preferred a diplomatic resolution. On Sunday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said it received a report that a ship had been struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz , after an attack on a liquefied natural gas tanker on Friday. The UKMTO also reported a vessel was struck east of Ras Al Khafji, along Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast. An Iranian delegation was in Qatar for discussions with mediators on Saturday, according to a Bloomberg report. Fears of US strikes on Iran have maintained upward pressure on crude, keeping supply risk premiums elevated. Oil prices started sliding on Monday after hitting a six-month high last week on Hormuz strikes and a US threat to hit Iran. Over the past week, both Brent and WTI increased by about 0.8 per cent. On a monthly basis, the benchmarks surged by about 15 per cent and 12 per cent, respectively, to hit their highest levels since April. Meanwhile, Swiss lender UBS said in a report recently it expected Brent crude prices to remain elevated, near $110 a barrel at the end of the year, as Middle Eastern supply remains volatile and geopolitical uncertainty persists. "Record freight costs, constrained tanker capacity, and recovering Chinese imports are other factors likely to keep oil prices high," UBS commodity analyst Giovanni Staunovo said.

events.title: Alterra's investments designed to hedge against AI bubble, says chief executive
events.summary: Alterra, the UAE's $30 billion climate vehicle , has designed its artificial intelligence investment strategy to protect it against a much talked about bubble in the sector, its chief executive has told The National . The fund's focus on investing in energy systems powered by AI and not directly into the technology is serving as a “hedge” against any potential bubble that may burst in the booming industry, Majid Al Suwaidi said. “We're investing in the only place that our portfolio touches the AI story – through the energy systems. What is great with our investment thesis is that we don't invest directly in AI infrastructure,” he said in an interview. “Those energy systems, regardless of whether it's powering AI or powering a factory, homes, schools, or hospitals, that power will still be needed. So, in a way, Alterra and the investments we make are a really good hedge against a bubble in AI.” Mr Al Suwaidi's comments come as Abu Dhabi-based Alterra gives a vote of confidence to the technology by partnering with one of Europe's biggest sovereign AI companies. On Monday, Alterra announced that it had partnered with Milan-based Domyn to develop a proprietary climate intelligence system that the former will own and control, which will pave the way towards becoming an AI-native company, Mr Al Suwaidi said. “Once we've built that core system, we can then extend that to other aspects of the business and truly become an AI-native organisation,” he said. The system, which will be developed in phases, will “come into the fore” next year, he added. “To pick up these technologies and apply them very early in our development means that we will be able to use AI or our analytics to … take advantage of the power of this technology.” Alterra did not disclose the value of its partnership with Domyn, which was formerly known as iGenius and founded by former Apple employee Uljan Sharka. Domyn has raised $1.1 billion in debt financing over the past two years and is valued at about $2 billion. In June, the European Commission chose Europa, a project led by Domyn, to develop an open-source AI model covering all 24 official languages in the EU. “The way we're designing the system is that it can be evergreen in the sense that as new models are being built or as new developments happen within the technology that they can be plugged in immediately and we can upgrade our system,” Mr Al Suwaidi said. The partnership with Domyn mirrors his confidence in the AI sector, where the bubble debate is hot. Recently, two of the biggest names in asset management, Citadel chief executive Ken Griffin and Blackstone president Jon Gray, gave negative and positive views, respectively. Mr Al Suwaidi acknowledged that there is a bubble “in some ways”, but managing expectations and doing due diligence to make sound investment decisions will help contain potential ill-effects. “Any time you have a new asset class, a bubble is developed … and bubbles can be good if managed and bad if they burst … it just remains to be seen how long it will continue to grow and whether we can manage it in a prudent way so that it doesn't burst with negative consequences,” he said. “We know for sure that this technology is going to be critical to our future economic development, and how we use it becomes increasingly important, and we're discovering that, so there's going to be winners and losers in that process.” Alterra's mandate is to raise $250 billion globally by 2030 to create a fairer climate finance system. Its chairman is Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc. It is less than three years since Alterra's launch at the Cop28 climate conference hosted by the UAE. Since then, Alterra has grown into three funds – Acceleration, Transformation and Opportunity – with five global investment partners: Brookfield Asset Management, BlackRock, Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, KKR and TPG. It also has more than 60 direct and indirect portfolio companies across more than 40 countries, supporting more than 100GW of renewable energy capacity. Alterra's capital activity is also accelerating. More than $51 billion in expected equity capital across its fund and co-investment activities has been mobilised, with preliminary mobilisation ratios of more than 10 times for its Acceleration Fund and over four times for the Transformation Fund, excluding Alterra's own capital and deal-level debt. Recent investments also show the breadth of Alterra's expansion, including Inkia in Peru, Wireless Logic alongside General Atlantic, and Jeppesen ForeFlight with Thoma Bravo. “What Alterra has shown through our success in the climate realm is that you can achieve the same goals, but in an economically prudent way,” Mr Al Suwaidi said. “Something that is very unique, and very underreported is how successful we've been in our model.”

events.title: US economy under Donald Trump in five charts
events.summary: A nervous US electorate is heading to polling stations across the country for Tuesday's midterm elections , and their personal finances could determine which way control in Congress swings. Recent polling suggests President Donald Trump 's shifting tariff policies, war with Iran and overall handling of the economy will be major issues this week for voters, who say they have been affected by higher prices at the petrol pumps and on grocery shelves. Half of registered voters rate the economy as “extremely important this year”, with health care costs and the war in Iran also top among 11 issues rated in an October 29 Gallup poll. Roughly four in 10 voters rate income and wealth distribution (44 per cent) and petrol costs (42 per cent) as extremely important. Forty-seven per cent of registered voters said the cost of living would be the single most important factor in their votes this week, according to an Ipsos poll conducted in August. Only 17 per cent approve of Mr Trump's handling of the cost of living, while an AP-Norc poll found 26 per cent approve of his handling of the economy overall. A Chicago Council poll also found 71 per cent of Americans think US tariffs on imports have been bad for the economy, and 81 per cent said they have been bad for their cost of living. Although not a particular macroeconomic data point, the Consumer Confidence Survey measures attitudes, buying intentions and holiday plans, inflation expectations, and where people believe stock prices and interest rates are heading. In this way, it can offer a key insight into perceptions on the economy. Fergus McCormick, senior economist at the Conference Board, said “consumers continued to express frustration with rising costs” in October, with most references pointing to the high cost of goods, groceries and petrol. Easing petrol prices saw some recovery in the Consumer Confidence Index, which rose 7.5 points to 91.7 in October, although confidence remains on a long-term and persistent downwards trend. Moreover, consumers are planning for less spending on services and goods over the next six months, reflecting enduring inflation. Despite this anxiety, consumer spending rose at a 3.4 per cent pace in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department data, showing the US economy has remained resilient amid the energy price shock caused by the Iran war. Strong business spending also accounted for US GDP to grow at a 3.4 per cent annual pace in the July to September period. US inflation has significantly eased since peaking at 9.1 per cent in 2022, and fell to 3 per cent when Mr Trump began his second term in office in January 2025. Headline inflation fell as low as 2.3 per cent in April that year. But inflation picked up again after he imposed a sweeping set of tariffs on nearly every trading partner. The disinflation process now appears stalled, and the Iran war has led to surging energy prices couple with AI-driven investment. Petrol prices accounted for nearly half of the all-items increase in September, when CPI inflation clocked in at 3.7 per cent. Even after stripping away food and energy, inflation still gained 0.3 per cent on a monthly basis and 2.6 per cent year on year. It has been nearly six years since CPI inflation registered at 2 per cent. Seventy-nine per cent of Americans agreed that prices at the pump were higher now compared to 38 per cent in February, a dramatic shift in perceptions since the Iran war began, according to an Ipsos poll conducted in September. The prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the world's energy supplies, has pushed up global energy costs. Even the US, the world's top crude producer, has not been fully insulated. Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries have exacerbated rising costs for diesel , which powers the lorries that transport food and other goods. The average driver is currently paying $4.20 for a gallon of petrol today, an increase of $1.17 from the same time last year, according to automotive group AAA. Of the six “swing states” in this year's midterm election cycle, only Georgia's petrol prices are below the national average. Diesel prices have also soared to $6.32, compared to $3.68 a gallon a year ago. The Federal Reserve was in the middle of an easing cycle when Mr Trump returned to office last year. While the Fed's announcements on short-term interest rates grab headlines, they also influence the 10-year Treasury yield through market expectations and the inflation outlook. The 10-year Treasury is the global benchmark for interest rates, car loans, corporate borrowing and consumer mortgages. Energy-driven inflation, the massive AI buildout and heavy government debt issuance have weighed on the bond market in recent months, with yields on the 10- and 30-year Treasury at levels unseen in nearly a quarter century. At the same time, the Fed has begun a new tightening cycle and has raised expectations it will raise rates further before the year ends. This combination of factors has plagued the housing market, where fixed 30-year mortgage rates climbed as high as 7.4 per cent before pulling back slightly to 7.24 per cent, compared to last year at 6.17 per cent. That means a homebuyer refinancing or purchasing a home would face higher borrowing costs on their monthly payments. Mr Trump frequently uses the stock market as an economic barometer. After suffering brief dips during last year's tariff row and the early days of the Iran war, Wall Street's major indices have surged. The S&P 500 has climbed more than 10 per cent this year and hit a new record-high of 7,818.93 on October 6, though disappointing earnings reports are fuelling a new wave of investor concerns over the AI buildout and the massive investment powering it. AI investment has been cited as the major driver behind the surge. The Magnificent Seven stocks – Nvidia, Alphabet, Apple, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Tesla – make up 34 per cent of the S&P 500. This leads to what economists classify as a K-shaped economy, in which high-earners who own assets such as stocks see their wealth climb while workers relying on pay cheques fall behind as living costs increase.
