events.title: Gold climbs back from one-year low as dip buyers arrest slide
events.summary: Gold was finding some immediate support from long-term investors who see the current price as cheap, said Justin Lin, a strategist at Global X ETFs. Gold rose after hitting a one-year low, as cheaper oil eased inflation worries and buyers stepped in after last session’s 3.7% fall. The metal remains under pressure from Middle East war risks, tech stock sell-offs, and forced selling to cover losses elsewhere. Analysts said gold is at “precarious levels”; a move back above US$4,000 is needed to improve the short-term outlook. NEW YORK – Gold rose, as lower oil prices offered some respite from inflationary pressures and dip buyers were drawn by the metal’s slide on Oct 30 to the lowest in a year. Bullion gained as much as 0.7% to nearly US$3,900 an ounce, clawing back some losses after a 3.7% slump in the previous session that rounded off the worst October for the metal since 2008. Oil dropped ahead of the Oct 27 US midterm elections, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying that US President Donald Trump would prefer a diplomatic resolution to the Iran war. Still, bullion remains vulnerable to any escalation in fighting in the Middle East. Trump has repeatedly threatened to resume strikes on Iran after the US midterms, while Tehran threatened wider retaliation and several Persian Gulf states expressed concerns that another attack could unleash an even more destructive war across the region. A global rout in technology stocks is also adding pressure to precious metals. Recent sell-offs have prompted investors to liquidate bullion to meet losses elsewhere, and stocks were set to fall again on Nov 2, tracking a rout on Wall Street fuelled by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade. “We are likely to see some dip buying in the Asian session today as investors, and possibly central banks, cautiously add to positions,” he said. “But gold is undoubtedly sitting at precarious levels.” For now, liquidity concerns and technical selling were overshadowing the metal’s longer-term investment appeal, Ole Sloth Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank AS, wrote in a note. Oct 30 is close below the key technical level of US$3,886 an ounce “leaves gold vulnerable to additional downside pressure”, he said, adding that a recovery to above US$4,000 would be needed to restore “a more neutral short-term outlook”. Spot gold climbed 0.6% to US$3,899.39 an ounce at 7.45am in Singapore. Silver gained 1.3% to US$49.76 an ounce, having dropped nearly 6% on Oct 30. Platinum and palladium also gained after big declines in the previous session. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was marginally higher. BLOOMBERG

events.title: More MAGA than MAGA: How the Daily Caller turned on MAGA and Trump
events.summary: The News When Tucker Carlson co-founded the Daily Caller in 2010, it was to be the Republican Party’s answer to The New York Times. A few identity crises later, the publication has followed Carlson into a hard turn against Donald Trump’s war in Iran, and against Israel — choices that have injected into the publication the digital energy of the new online right, and cost it the support of some of its backers. “I’ve had some of the most aggressive donor pressure over this — the single most aggressive donor pressure over this, of anything I’ve seen in journalism in 20 years,” Daily Caller publisher Neil Patel told Semafor. He wouldn’t detail the cost of lost financial support to the Caller, which includes both a for-profit firm and the nonprofit Daily Caller News Foundation, but acknowledged that there had been costs. The Caller has been a pillar of Washington’s conservative media scene since its launch, an important voice in internecine Republican conflicts and a pipeline of journalistic talent whose alumni include employees of both conservative and mainstream outlets. Now it’s at the vanguard of a Republican civil war that Carlson has helped unleash. “The Iran war is a huge turning point for the conservative movement,” Editor-in-Chief Amber Duke told Semafor on Friday. Nowhere has that shift been clearer than in the outlet’s X feed since the United States went to war with Iran in February. The organization has taken to tweeting the price of diesel every day, emphasizing the war’s cost on drivers, and posts screenshots of Trump’s posts about the war in Iran, adding spicy commentary. “What if instead of “banning” a term, we stopped spending endless amounts of money on foreign wars?” the outlet wrote of Trump’s command that AI be referred to as “super intelligence.” The Daily Caller has similarly gone after Israel, questioning its decisions in the Middle East. It has blasted Benjamin Netanyahu and his policies, and repeatedly highlighted Israeli settler violence, particularly against children . The criticism has gotten the attention of pro-Israel hawks, who have accused the publication of antisemitism and crudely implied it is pro-Islamic propaganda. “Daily Caller means Al Jazeera in Arabic,” Fox News host and commentator Mark Levin wrote . The fissures at the Caller — and in the broader conservative movement — began widening when the activist Charlie Kirk was assassinated last September, according to most of the nine current and former Caller employees who I spoke to over the last week. The movement that had united around Donald Trump devolved into a frenzy of unfounded conspiracy theories, many blaming Israel for Kirk’s death. The podcaster Candace Owens drove those theories, infuriating her former employer, Daily Wire founder Ben Shapiro. Shapiro laid into Owens for perpetuating what he said were antisemitic conspiracy theories, attacked podcaster Megyn Kelly for not condemning Owens, and criticized Carlson for what he described as a cozy interview with self-proclaimed white nationalist Nick Fuentes. The Daily Caller, long a younger and slightly edgier outlet than other right-leaning publications like the Washington Examiner, The National Review, or even Breitbart, followed that online energy. Some on staff noted that former editor Dylan Housman left the publication the Friday before the Iran war started, and the tone shifted significantly following his departure. Duke, a former Caller staffer, replaced him and encouraged the publication to adopt an aggressive posture on social media. Employees also said they sensed that Patel seemed to side with Carlson, Patel’s longtime friend and business partner. While Carlson has long been unaffiliated with the outlet, Patel retains business connections with Carlson, while Carlson’s brother Buckley Carlson has served on the Daily Caller nonprofit’s board. Patel told Semafor he is not involved in day-to-day operations at the Caller, on which he defers to Duke and others, and stressed that Carlson’s stances had no bearing on the outlet. Still, he said he encouraged the Caller’s leaders to remain independent and reflect the publication’s values. That reality for average Americans, he said, has turned against Trump. “Things just aren’t going that well today. I think if you’re at all looking at this objectively, it’s hard to make the case that things are going great in a lot of areas. And so if our coverage has changed, I think it’s changed just to reflect that,” he said. Right vs. Right The concern, of course, is whether it could go too far. Some former Daily Caller staff told Semafor they are worried the publication has drifted a bit too close to the “groyper” wing of the right, whose criticism of Israel reflects its antisemitism. In October, Semafor reported that the Daily Caller tweeted a cartoon of Bill Gates and the devil posing with disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein wearing an Israeli flag Speedo. The post was quickly deleted, but not before it caught the attention of Republicans who have grown increasingly concerned about the Caller’s anti-Israel turn. The publication told Semafor that while the post didn’t meet the publication’s standards, it hadn’t been posted with any “malicious intent.” Other Caller alumni suggested to Semafor that the recent pivot could threaten what in the last decade has become an important talent pipeline and incubator for the right. The Daily Caller has brought up some of the most prominent young political media figures in America, some of whom have left the conservative media sphere (like CNN’s Kaitlan Collins and Semafor’s Shelby Talcott), and others who have built major franchises in independent media (like Breaking Points’ Saagar Enjeti) or moved into positions within the Republican Party apparatus. The previous generation’s crowd is clearly uneasy with the new crop. Max’s view The Daily Caller is clearly positioning itself for a landscape not just post-midterms but post- Trump, and for a bitter and intensifying intra-party media battle. The issue of how each side talks about Israel and the war in Iran has played out in both parties, as was clear on Sunday when Rep. Haley Stevens, the former Michigan Democrat Senate candidate, endorsed the Republican in the race over the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, citing her view that he had not done enough to condemn antisemitism. While Israel has garnered much of the attention, the Caller has taken stances against Republican Party orthodoxy on other issues. The publication has published critical pieces about the impact of artificial intelligence and the coziness between business interests and the Trump administration. It recently feuded with The Daily Wire, mocking the company for defending Kalshi. “I’ve always said the best thing we can do for young men is introduce them to crippling gambling habits. events.title: Metrocon chairman resigns after charge over unlicensed worker dormitory that was discovered in January
events.summary: Catalist-listed construction engineering company Metrocon Holdings was formerly known as Hatten Land. SINGAPORE – Metrocon Holdings chairman Alvin Lim Yee Hong has resigned after being charged with allegedly allowing an unlicensed foreign worker dormitory to operate, the Catalist-listed company said on Nov 2. The construction engineering company, formerly known as Hatten Land , also disclosed that Lim and another director had not informed its board or sponsor about earlier dealings with the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) regarding the matter, including interviews conducted during investigations. The case concerns LBD Engineering, Metrocon’s controlling shareholder, where Lim, 35, also serves as general manager. Neither Metrocon nor any of its subsidiaries has been charged. LBD faces one charge of operating a foreign employee dormitory at 58A Sungei Kadut Loop without a valid licence between July 2025 and January 2026. Lim faces a separate charge alleging that he knew LBD did not have a valid licence, but allowed it to continue operating the premises as a dormitory. The first court hearing took place on Oct 29, with lawyers attending on behalf of Lim and LBD. The next hearing is scheduled for Dec 17. Lim intends to contest the charge, is seeking legal advice and has told the company that he needs to devote substantial time and resources to personal matters arising from the case, leading to his resignation as non-executive and non-independent chairman effective Oct 29. However, Lim has indicated that he wishes to be considered for reappointment to the board after the proceedings conclude. Metrocon said any return would be subject to the nominating committee’s assessment and applicable regulatory requirements. In its Nov 2 announcement, Metrocon set out the sequence of events based on information Lim provided to the board on Oct 29. Its statement said MOM had inspected the Sungei Kadut dormitory on Jan 6, and informed LBD by e-mail the next day that the company was operating the premises without a licence under the Foreign Employee Dormitories Act. LBD was then directed to relocate all occupants by Jan 9, which it did. On Aug 5, MOM requested that Lim attend an interview on Oct 2, after which he was released on bail. Metrocon’s non-executive and non-independent director Charlotte Tay Tingyin was also interviewed by MOM on Aug 7 to assist with investigations arising from the January inspection. Tay had served as an LBD director from Dec 17, 2025, to Feb 13, 2026. She subsequently acted as Lim’s bailor on Oct 2. The board said it understood from Tay that she was only assisting with investigations, had not been charged and had received no further contact from MOM since Oct 2. Explaining why the board and sponsor were not informed earlier, Metrocon said Lim and Tay did not consider the inspection and interviews to give rise to disclosure obligations because they concerned LBD rather than the listed group. They therefore “inadvertently omitted” to notify the board and sponsor, the company said. Apart from Lim and Tay, no other Metrocon director or key management personnel had been ordered or asked to assist with MOM’s investigations, according to the announcement. The chairman’s position will remain vacant while the nominating committee identifies and evaluates a suitable candidate. In the interim, board meetings will be chaired by lead independent director Kenny Sim Mong Keang or a director elected by those present. The board said it does not expect the recent developments to have a material impact on the group’s operations or financial performance for the year ending Dec 31. Lim confirmed that the charge did not restrict LBD from continuing its construction business and that its projects were proceeding in the ordinary course. Meanwhile, Metrocon’s business transactions with LBD remained ongoing and unaffected, the announcement said. Metrocon listed on Catalist in September via a $28 million reverse takeover (RTO) of embattled Hatten Land, a Malaysia property developer whose shares had been suspended from trading since August 2024, when it entered judicial management. Under the proposed terms, the acquisition was to be paid for through about 107.7 million new shares issued at 26 cents each to LBD. It now holds about 64% of Metrocon after purchasing additional shares following the RTO.

events.title: How a Kansas City vlogger captivated New York society
events.summary: The News On Oct. 10, an unhappy billionaire, Amy Griffin, confronted a former host, Billy Bush, at a celebrity wedding on the Hawaiian island of Lanai. Guests included Demi Moore and Tobey Maguire. It was the sort of thing that delights the entertainment media, even if you won’t often read about it in this column. But this meltdown didn’t break on Vanity Fair or TMZ. Instead, New York and LA society discreetly tuned in to the Instagrammer known as KatyinKC , who cited “multiple” sources at the wedding. When I wrote about Griffin , the wife of a hedge-funder and author of a bestselling memoir, last week, I repeatedly heard that the wealthy and powerful figures in her social world are obsessed with KatyinKC. Her name is Katy Hoffman, and she is a 33-year-old registered dietitian and mother of two toddlers who works from the sofa in her comfortable Midwestern home. Over the course of this year, Hoffman has become the chief inquisitor of Griffin’s story of abuse during a superficially perfect childhood in Amarillo, Texas. Hoffman has unmasked pseudonymous characters from her book, discovered key audio files, and given a hard-edged voice to the skepticism about Griffin’s account first raised by The New York Times . Hoffman’s Instagram account is the thing “women in the ballrooms and the Upper East Side and the Palisades and Brentwood are listening to, but not following,” said Bush, who was fired from in 2016 for a 2005 hot mic exchange with Donald Trump on , and who now hosts the podcast . Social convention dictates that you not be caught liking Hoffman’s posts or following her yourself. But she is “the internet version of Nancy Grace,” Jolie Hunt, the CEO of a New York marketing and communications consultancy, told me. Hoffman’s videos across TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram offer regular glimpses of her own life. Sometimes she dances. Once she defended a local pizza joint from another influencer’s criticism. Her home is on display, too, a well-kept place with a wood-paneled den you’d immediately rip out in the Hamptons. She doesn’t, one person I spoke to noted, seem like the sort of person who would be found on Lanai. I called up Hoffman Friday to ask how she’d become part of a new generation of social media sleuths, why she was so focused on Griffin, and, of course, her decor. Courtesy of Katy Hoffman Hoffman got on the video call Friday wearing a T-shirt featuring the lovers in the TV show . She had just dyed her blond hair red. She grew up in the well-off suburbs of Des Moines — her family loves to travel and she’s been all over the world, if not Hawaii. She attended Iowa State, where she put her energy into her sorority and personal training (and certainly not journalism). She moved to Kansas City to start her career counseling people with eating disorders, but also developed a set of hobbies that, along with fishing and hunting, includes poking around public records. “I’m just a nosy lady,” she told me. She’d be the one to tell her friends that the neighbor down the street had a lien on his house. She recalled being in a nutrition office at a local hospital where colleagues were talking about local radio personalities’ messy public divorce, and she looked up the court documents. She also closely followed the messy drama between the actors Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni; like many on social media, she grew skeptical of Lively’s well-publicized claims and was persuaded by Baldoni’s responses. She posted to a tiny audience about them, and was briefly featured in an Atlantic article last April that asked: But Hoffman had long harbored this generation’s great American dream — to be a “content creator.” She had experimented with posting recipes and talking about her professional expertise, nutrition. One TikTok about Ariana Grande has 7.2 million views. But she also edged into original reporting. When a process server in the Lively-Baldoni case was arrested trying to get into Kansas City Chiefs star Travis Kelce’s property to reach his wife, Taylor Swift, Hoffman drove to the nearby police station to get court records, posted them online, and watched the news spread. She became one of a pack of traveling social media analysts and partisans, attending hearings in New York in January and April. The Griffin case, however, has been Hoffman’s breakout moment, and it has thrust her a little closer to the world of professional journalism than she expected. “It wasn’t until this case that I’ve really figured out being an investigative journalist a bit without any of the training or whatever,” she said, adding that she wasn’t sure how to feel when she noticed New York Times and Wall Street Journal reporters sign up for the Patreon where she distributes the court documents she’s turned up. She said she felt “intimidated” by the professional journalists who have started calling her up to swap notes. Ben’s view Hoffman, who sometimes works from a small swivel chair in her children’s room, has followed a path from social video into the center of the swirling news cycles of true crime and celebrity. Her rise has echoes of podcaster Ashley Flowers and blogger Jessica Reed Krauss — media outsiders who tapped into deep veins of public interest. But she’s also an obsessive researcher whose focus and work ethic remind me a bit of CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski, were his focus celebrities rather than politics. She has gone to elaborate lengths to follow hints in Griffin’s book through high school yearbooks and long-forgotten high school sporting events. Hoffman also noticed a link in a legal filing to a redacted audio recording of Griffin’s 2021 call to the Amarillo police department and posted it; later, she posted the unredacted audio, but wouldn’t tell me how she’d obtained that. In other ways, she is pure social media. In one recent short video, Hoffman dances to a pop song, Nina Nox’s , and closes by giving a middle finger to the camera and lip-syncing. It’s been a disorienting year, she said. She’s made enough money from her content to pay for court documents and a little travel, but her day job and her husband’s (he’s an engineer) still pay the bills. “I don’t know what to do with it, I’m kind of stuck in this crossroads,” Hoffman said. “I can see how someone can grow and build this — but do I want to do that?” She was amused to hear that New York’s elite were making fun of her Midwestern life. “Put their direct quotes about what they think about me so I can rip them apart,” she suggested. My New York interlocutors, sadly, declined to go on the record — though one asked that I stress that any class-inflected mockery was delivered “with love.”

events.title: New creator brand Magnet Originals launches
events.summary: Megan Cunningham, a media and marketing industry veteran and founder of Magnet Media, is on Monday launching Magnet Originals, a brand to help established personalities grow their media empires and to incubate the next generation of stars. Former TikTok executive Dustin Goot and former Vice exec Subrata De are both joining in senior roles, alongside media operators Alexandra Zaslow and Brannan Goetschius. Magnet Originals will provide advice and production support for media personalities, including Justin Tranter, Boyz II Men’s Shawn Stockman, and former NBA star Byron Scott. It will also build on its own original franchises. The company said it is launching with a docuseries from the poet and critic Hanif Abdurraqib and a music show hosted by Billboard executive editor Lyndsey Havens, both co-produced with Live Nation, as well as , a show co-hosted by comedian Sam Jay, Olympic gymnast Jordan Chiles, and broadcaster Ari Chambers. The company is also hoping to build a business around training the next generation of creators. Its Top Creator Academy will offer courses and one-on-one consulting with professionals. Cunningham told Semafor that she saw the program growing into a seven-figure business on its own. “Documentaries can’t count on distribution, and newsrooms keep closing because their business model is in jeopardy. … I was watching a generation of entrepreneurial, brilliant storytellers build podcasts, YouTube channels, and newsletters on sweat equity alone,” Cunningham said. “A consultancy would have reached a handful of clients at a time, and it didn’t excite me.”

events.title: How Canada’s resource wealth makes it a strategic partner for the UAE and Europe
events.summary: “Worthy Canadian initiative” is a common joke for the world’s most boring headline. But, threatened by the US, Canada is launching initiatives that could be more world-shaping than worthy. The UAE and the EU have become two vertices of the triangle including this northern resource giant. The Canada-EU summit concluded in Montreal, one of the most European cities in North America, on Friday. Though Prime Minister Mark Carney’s hopes of “associate membership” may not be granted in so many words, a much closer relationship is on the cards. And on Tuesday, the UAE signed a comprehensive economic partnership with Ottawa . The UAE committed $50 billion of investment in the country last year. This has a strong energy component: Abu Dhabi’s renewable energy champion Masdar concluded a co-operation agreement with federal agency Natural Resources Canada. Simultaneously, Dubai’s DP World is discussing developing the northern port of Churchill, on Hudson Bay, with access to the Arctic and Atlantic oceans. Rail connects it to the Pacific. Canada’s official Latin motto translates as “From Sea to Sea”, and some have proposed amending it to “From Sea to Sea to Sea” to respect the northern ocean. Churchill’s operator suggests it could be part of an Asia-Europe trade corridor that would be as fast and more secure than traditional routes through the Red Sea. The fast-warming Arctic, itself a warning of dangerous climate change, is opening up new shipping routes through previously ice-choked straits. These moves span four global trends. First, the need for other great and middle powers to build alliances and lessen dependence on an increasingly erratic US, a revanchist Russia and a potentially overbearing China. Second, the creation of alternative transport routes as maritime security comes under threat . Third, the construction of new trade architecture while other countries try to demolish it. Fourth, the search for reliable providers of critical resources. Resource superpowers The UAE and Canada may not have much in common geographically, but they are resource superpowers. While the UAE’s bounty concentrates mostly on hydrocarbons, the northern nation has those, plus many others. At nearly 6.2 million barrels per day, it is the fourth-biggest oil producer in the world and, depending on your view of Venezuela, the second or third-largest reserves owner. It is fifth in gas output, and its shale resources ensure plenty of room to grow production. The Shell-led LNG Canada in British Columbia began exporting liquefied natural gas (LNG) last June, with an ideal geography to supply Asia. LNG Canada is set to double capacity by the early 2030s, and two other projects are due to start in 2027 and 2028. Bloomberg last month suggested that Adnoc’s international unit XRG was interested in taking a stake in LNG Canada. The company already bought Calgary's Nova Chemicals in a $13.4 billion deal last March. Canada is first in the world in extracting potash, a crucial fertiliser, second in uranium mining , and fourth in gold, platinum and nickel mining and aluminium smelting. And it is an agricultural hothouse, with huge exports of wheat, oilseed, livestock, wood and other crops. For the new strategic minerals, as well as nickel for batteries, it is a growing producer of lithium and natural graphite. It has important deposits of titanium and vanadium, crucial metals for aerospace and defence technology. In the famous and geopolitically sensitive rare earths , it has no commercial mines today, but holds large resources, and several projects are being developed. Finally, its cool climate, open land and abundance of cheap, zero-carbon hydropower – where it is the third-biggest generator in the world – make it a good site for data centres . This commodity wealth makes it tremendously attractive as a partner to the EU: a stable, Western, free-market democracy, and closer than the similarly advantaged Australia. It is further from the UAE, but many of the same attractions apply. In turn, Canada needs good friends. Seventy-six per cent of its exports go to its overbearing southern neighbour. The EU, China and the UK are each of similar weight, with about 4 per cent to 5 per cent each. This dependence makes Canada vulnerable to the US's arm-twisting with tariffs. While Canada will no doubt expand trade with China, that brings its own political exposure. A recent preliminary referendum on independence for the hydrocarbon heartland province of Alberta, backed by right-wing voices in the US, was heavily defeated. But Canadians are not amused by “51st state” taunts. They saw how their Arctic neighbour, Greenland , was intimidated by the White House, which eyes enviously its rare earths and possible oil. New routes, new partnerships Transport barriers mean Canada does not earn full value for its resources. American natural gas producers might complain about low prices, currently $2.86 per million British thermal units. Europeans’ wallets are emptied, and their energy-intensive industries hollowed out by paying around $30, as they suffer from the cut-off of LNG from the Gulf. But the wholesale price in Alberta, Canada’s main producing region, is just $1.40 per MMBtu. It is a similar story for oil. With only one pipeline to the Pacific, Albertan producers are hostage to the US market. Western Canadian crude usually sells at about a $12 per barrel discount to the US’s West Texas Intermediate. That differential has now widened to $31 per barrel. Mr Carney has sought to promote new pipelines, to integrate the national electricity grid, and in general to recharge the Canadian economy by diversifying exports and slashing inter-provincial trading barriers. Broadening its transport infrastructure is a crucial element and needs deep-pocketed investors with a long time horizon. Full development of the Churchill port and rail corridor alone will cost $57 billion. It will not replace Suez or Panama, but the current war in the Gulf shows how valuable back-up plans can become. Like Western countries in general, Canada also struggles less with mining critical minerals and more with processing them. Investors are deterred by high costs, lack of access to proprietary technologies, and the tendency of China to undercut competitors. This may be a fruitful area for triangular UAE-EU-Canada co-operation, whether investing in metals refineries in Canada or in the Gulf, as part of an integrated supply chain. Diversification – of allies, trading partners, transport routes and commodity providers – seems like a good policy today. Although technically hydrocarbon competitors, the UAE and Canada have much to complement with Europe. A new geography mingles the warm waters of the Gulf with the chilly north.

events.title: "Petty, selfish, unhinged": Haley Stevens' staff and colleagues erupt at her "betrayal"
events.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) faced fierce backlash from fellow Democrats, party officials and her own staffers after endorsing Republican Mike Rogers for the U.S. Senate on Sunday. Why it matters: It's a stunning reversal in standing for Stevens, who came within a few percentage points of being her party's nominee for Senate in Michigan just months earlier. "Pathetic, petty, selfish, unhinged," Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) told Axios of her endorsement of Rogers. "You run out of words." Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-Calif.) said of the video Stevens posted to social media announcing her endorsement and her joint press conference with Rogers: "I've seen more pleasant self-immolations." The latest: CNN's Anderson Cooper repeatedly pressed Stevens on why she changed her mind during an at times testy interview, asking whether she still wanted Democrats to win control of the Senate. "I absolutely do. I'm just casting this vote in my own way," she replied. When Cooper pointed out that she was "publicly casting your vote," Stevens responded: "I'm just one person." State of play: Stevens' endorsement of Rogers came after her long-running feud with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed reached a boiling point over the weekend. El-Sayed, a leftist who narrowly defeated the more moderate Stevens in the Senate primary in August, said in a statement on Friday that Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago." Stevens had been pressing El-Sayed to more forcefully condemn an ad from an outside super PAC that suggested U.S. aid to Israel was partly to blame for rising prices. Stevens, in her video endorsing Rogers, said that El-Sayed "said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign, and that I should stay away," adding, "He's right. ... I don't belong in Abdul's campaign." What they're saying: Stevens' Democratic colleagues met her endorsement with shock and fury. "I am lost for words," Rep. Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.) told Axios. Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.) said in a text to Axios: "I'm shocked that Haley would do this ... right before the election." "I JUST SAW THIS BULLSHIT," Rep. Emily Randall (D-Wash.) texted. "There is too much on the line for BS like this." "What the fuck is she doing?" another House Democrat said. "This election is not about her, and this will not age well." Zoom in: "I'm dumbfounded that Haley told me one thing last night and changed her mind today," said Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who had previously said Stevens told him in a phone call she was "voting straight down the line on the Democratic ticket." Raskin told Axios in a brief interview: "There is a great sense of betrayal for this to happen at the last minute before such a critical election." Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.) told Axios: "Stevens showed her true colors and Michiganders could see right through her. It's why she lost the Democratic primary." "I'm sincerely worried about my friend," Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.) said. What we're hearing: Several of Stevens' staff members resigned shortly after her announcement on Sunday, a former staffer familiar with the matter told Axios. Her former chief of staff Justin German said in a statement that he was "shocked and heartbroken" and that "many members of our team have resigned, including myself." Curtis Hertel, the chair of the Michigan Democratic Party, said in a post on X : "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future." The other side: "This is what happens to the far left when they go against the centrists," a centrist House Democrat told Axios. The lawmaker added: "I don't think I would have done what she did. But this is what the far left needs to understand when they burn bridges." Another centrist House Democrat told Axios that El-Sayed "created this mess," adding: "He should have just condemned the ad and invited her to church." Stevens did not immediately respond to Axios' text seeking comment. Editor's note: This story has been updated with more comment from Democrats.

events.title: Haley Stevens faces push for removal from House Dem caucus
events.summary: Some House Democrats want Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) expelled from their caucus after she crossed party lines to endorse Republican Mike Rogers for Senate on Sunday. Why it matters: It would be an extraordinary step that reflects the deep internal resentment towards Stevens within her own party. "I hope she doesn't return to work on Tuesday," Rep. Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.) told Axios, saying Stevens should be removed from the caucus. "Agreed," Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas) told Axios, arguing the endorsement "doesn't accomplish anything except hurt[ing] Haley" and that "she got bad advice." "I'd support that," Rep. Emily Randall (D-Wash.) said of removing Stevens from the caucus. Driving the news: Stevens infuriated colleagues on Sunday by endorsing Rogers over Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Stevens in the Senate primary in August. Stevens, a pro-Israel moderate, had been urging the more left-leaning El-Sayed to more forcefully denounce a super PAC ad partially blaming U.S. aid to Israel for rising prices. Stevens said the ad claimed "Jews are responsible for America's economic woes." El-Sayed pushed back in a statement saying Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago." Stevens attended church with Rogers on Sunday and released a video to social media endorsing him. The two also held a joint press conference. What we're hearing: There has been private discussion about moving to oust Stevens, a senior House Democrat said, telling Axios, "That's what people want." Stevens was also removed from several House Democratic text chains, the senior lawmaker said. A second House Democrat told Axios: "I've heard people invoking the rule about not endorsing against Democrats." "Endorsing a Republican in a tipping point state is ridiculous, especially from a Democrat ... She should be removed from our caucus altogether," a third House Democrat said. Yes, but: Not everyone is on board with the idea — even those frustrated at Stevens. The senior House Democrat told Axios that, at the very least, "we need to wait and have the discussion after Tuesday." A fourth House Democrat said it's "too bad she chose to throw her career in Congress away so easily" but that the caucus "might still need her vote in the final two months before she's gone." Several lawmakers noted that Stevens is retiring anyway and that if El-Sayed wins, the point likely becomes moot. Stevens did not immediately respond to a text requesting comment on this story. The bottom line: "[I] am not letting it distract me from the work between now and Tuesday at 8pm," Randall told Axios.

The Star Market 50 Index, which is dominated by the nation’s biggest chipmakers, rallied 3.1 per cent, and Shenzhen’s ChiNext gauge of tech start-ups surged nearly 2 per cent. Speculation was swirling that China would bolster a 300 billion yuan (US$45.1 billion) relending facility, introduced in 2024 as part of a package to stabilise the stock market. The People’s Bank of China was set to convene a meeting with regulators overseeing the stock market and the financial sector on Monday morning to improve the programme that finances stock buy-backs by listed companies and key shareholders, according to local media reports.

events.title: Bourke filmmaker takes over reins of Indigenous film festival in Paris
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bourke filmmaker named director of Indigenous film festival in Paris In conversation with Allan Clarke on Speaking Out. ( Supplied: Michael Fairbairn ) Filmmaker and former journalist Allan Clarke will take on the role of artistic director of Europe's only Australian First Nations film festival. The Festival du Cinéma Aborigène Australien is a celebration of First Nations film on an international stage. The festival will run from December 4-6 at the Cinémas l’Arlequin et Reflet Médicis in Paris. Growing up in far-west NSW, Allan Clarke struggled to identify with "overwhelmingly negative" depictions of Indigenous people in the media. "I remember from a very young age in Bourke looking around and going, 'I can't reconcile those kinds of tropes and stereotypes and negativity with my actual loving community,'" he said. Now living a world away in Paris, the Muruwari and Gomeroi filmmaker, writer and investigative journalist wants to challenge and subvert those tropes as the artistic director of Europe's only Australian First Nations film festival. "The conversations I've been having since living in France are providing context to people and saying that a lot of those stories aren't authentically us," he said. Allan Clarke is an award-winning journalist and filmmaker. The 11 th annual Festival du Cinéma Aborigène Australien will take place in Paris this December, with this year's theme Kinetic — Tradition in Motion: Cinema in Revolt. Festival founder Greta Morton-Elangué said the festival specifically identifies First Nations cinema and takes it to a global audience. "There literally was no existing platform in France or Europe," Ms Morton-Elangué said. "There are many great films coming and they often get selected in high profile [film] festivals like Cannes and Berlin and Toronto but in terms of a whole festival, there really was nothing anywhere." Mr Clarke has directed documentaries The Dark Emu Story and The Bowraville Murders. This year's program will feature films by acclaimed First Nations filmmakers Warwick Thornton, Wayne Blair and Danielle MacLean. "Coming in sort of fresh, I really wanted to highlight our filmmakers who are really challenging the status quo and who are consistently subverting and bending genres to tell our stories," he said. Mr Clarke said the festival can expand the European perception of First Nations Australians. "There is a view that we are not modern and that we're not making a huge contribution to the international cultural landscape," he said. "Largely what they have seen, whether that's in film or TV about us, has been made by non-Indigenous people." Allan Clarke will be the artistic director of the 11th edition of the film festival. ( Supplied: Instagram ) Head of First Nations content at Screen Australia, Gillian Moody-Ardler, said international audiences were eager to connect with First Nations cinema. "It's really important for us to be sharing our stories to a broader audience than just domestically," she said. "A lot of people haven't travelled to these desert regions that some of our stories come from, "They haven't experienced the stories that we have from our coastal territories as well." Mr Clarke said that in recent times, he has seen a shift with First Nations cinema turning to genres such as romantic comedy and horror. "We are taking these very well-established genres and subverting them," he said. Ms Moody-Ardler became the head of First Nations content for Screen Australia in 2025. ( Supplied: Screen Australia ) Ms Moody-Ardler said Mr Clarke was a good fit for the role. "He's done some really amazing films that have highlighted some terrible parts of history and he's done it in a very empathetic way but also not shied away from the hardness of those projects," she said. This is the first year that Ms Morton-Elangué will not be in charge of programming Parisian film festival. "In a sense, it is like handing over a baby," she said. Ms Morton-Elangué said she bonded with Mr Clarke over their shared love of First Nations cinema and had regularly invited him to join the festival's speak events, including with Tiwi screen celebrity Crystal Love Johnson. "We were able to have this really animated discussion about naughty Tiwi Sistergirl humour," she said. Ms Morton-Elangue and Mr Clarke bonded over their love for cinema. ( Supplied: Greta Morton-Elangue ) Mr Clarke was simply grateful for the opportunity to show an international audience the breadth of Indigenous cinema.

events.title: ‘Dumbfounded’: Democrats’ chaos in Michigan exposes party's divides
events.summary: The News Democratic party leaders have found themselves unable to stave off an embarrassing schism in Michigan’s must-win Senate race, a crisis that may offer a glimpse of internal battles to come. Days of frantic shuttle diplomacy and attempts to organize a joint appearance by erstwhile Senate primary rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens culminated in Stevens’ surprise Sunday endorsement of Republican nominee Mike Rogers. Stevens appeared with Rogers at a Black church in Detroit less than 24 hours after vowing to colleagues that she would back El-Sayed, winning praise from President Donald Trump and calls for her eviction from the House Democratic Caucus. But perhaps the most stunning aspect of the crackup was how hard senior Democrats had worked to avoid it. Party leaders like Reps. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., and Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., were pushing hard to get El-Sayed and Stevens on the same page for a show of unity going into Tuesday’s critical elections. Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., said on national TV hours before Stevens’ defection that she had personally assured him on Saturday night she’d be backing El-Sayed. Raskin told Semafor in an interview Sunday: “I was blindsided, and I feel dumbfounded by the whole thing.” While the Senate race remains very close, it’s not clear how much Stevens’ turnabout will affect the final balloting. She has, however, laid bare deep divides within the party — principally over Israel and the establishment’s relationships with the left wing. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ statement backing El-Sayed after the flap did not mention Stevens, a member of his caucus, by name. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who had initially favored her as a better general election candidate than El-Sayed, called her endorsement of Rogers a “ despicable betrayal .” Many in the party believe leaders were powerless over Stevens: “I certainly don’t think it’s somebody else’s fault, other than Haley Stevens,” said a Michigan Democratic operative. Yet Michigan, where El-Sayed was struggling to win over some Jewish and Black voters even before this week, is now set among the first-in-the-nation Democratic nominating states. And the party’s inability to come together during the final week of the election is likely to haunt it well into the 2028 primary. what happened Stevens kept her allies and staff in the dark through the whole process as she privately insisted she would keep backing Democrats, including El-Sayed. As she and El-Sayed squabbled publicly over the last week, a few of her staff reached out to her discouraging her from endorsing Rogers, according to a source who’d worked on her race. Stevens’ response, according to the source: “Omg why would you think I would do that?!!” By Sunday, many of her staff had resigned, slamming her Rogers endorsement. “She lied to the people that she says she respects,” said the Michigan Democratic operative. El-Sayed, who had implored Stevens not to campaign with him last week, brushed aside the news. “None of this matters,” he told reporters in Detroit. Michigan party chair Curtis Hertel Jr. said Sunday on X Stevens was expelled from the state party. Meanwhile, national party leaders across the board were united in saying they supported El-Sayed. what happens next Stevens faces rough waters ahead. She appears to have violated House Democratic caucus rules banning campaign activity for non-Democrats, and some in the caucus want to punish her. It’s not immediately clear whether Jeffries and Stevens have talked. The Stevens-El-Sayed crackup had been building in the months since she lost to him in the primary. Stevens and other Michigan Democrats kept their distance from El-Sayed over his association with controversial streamer Hasan Piker and his positions on Israel. The feud accelerated over the closing weeks of the campaign when Cenk Uygur’s Rebellion PAC began running the anti-Israel ad that would eventually convince Stevens to endorse Rogers. Uygur says he never imagined that outcome when he aired it. “It wound up creating the perfect storm because it caused two weather fronts to collide,” Uygur told Semafor. “The establishment hated it with a passion and the internet loved it with equal passion. That’s what caused this explosion.” Nicholas and David’s view Democrats are closing their campaigns this cycle with fairly unified, populist messaging about “affordability” and “corruption” that helps the super-rich stay wealthy. Underneath that messaging is a feud between the party’s left flank and centrist arm that’s bound to erupt after Tuesday’s results. If El-Sayed loses, there will be a fight over blame between Democrats who spent tens of millions of dollars to support him and progressives who’ll argue that the party establishment can’t be trusted when leftist candidates win a nomination. This is in the air already, given Andrew Cuomo’s decision to run a third-party campaign after losing the Democratic primary to democratic socialist and now-New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. But if El-Sayed wins, his faction of the party will be able to say he did it in spite of the opposition of pro-Israel Democrats. That will weaken pro-Israel Democrats’ ability to say, as AIPAC does, that their agenda is “good policy and good politics.” That’s in the air too, with Democrats already gearing up to challenge Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., who’s stopped campaigning for other Democrats after feuding with pro-Palestine activists.

events.title: Homeowners facing thousands in costs to upgrade from gas to electric
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ATCO gas shutdown to force Albany architect onto bottled gas after building dream home Michael Roberts says he would have designed his house with electrical appliances if he had known Albany would lose its gas network. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) An architect spent thousands on gas appliances for his new home only to find out gas was set to go. Eight thousand of ATCO's Albany customers will need to change to electricity, or use gas bottles. The WA government is offering up to $2,000 for conversions, but experts say it will barely cover it. After years designing dozens of buildings in the coastal city of Albany, architect Michael Roberts finally built his dream home. The avant-garde house in Middleton Beach, about 450 kilometres south of Perth, was built connected to the city's reticulate liquid petroleum gas network, with gas appliances for heating and cooking plumbed in. But Mr Roberts is now facing a bill in the tens of thousands to refit the home after ATCO Australia announced it would decommission its Albany gas network over the next three years. "I've had a look at the compensation packages that have been put on the table," he said. "I don't know whether they've all been agreed or signed off yet, but the whole thing has come as a surprise." Michael Roberts says it will cost up to $12,000 to convert his new home from gas to electric. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) The $31 million package, which includes $5 million from ATCO, will cover the cost for customers moving to bottled gas, while those going electric will be compensated up to $2,000. Mr Roberts said the compensation would only cover a fraction of the $10,000 to $12,000 he estimated it would cost to swap his appliances from gas to electric. "We'll probably tough it out with bottles, but had I known earlier I would have made the decision and gone straight to electric," he said. The architect said ATCO's decision, and the timing of its announcement, had affected several of his firm's clients. "It's disgraceful that as design professionals, as architects, we were designing projects for people and they're making selections to use gas in good faith … that we weren't told; they weren't told," he said. ATCO and the state government faced renewed criticism last month after documents obtained by the ABC found they discussed the decommissioning of the network eight months before customers were told. Amber-Jade Sanderson says the government tried to persuade ATCO to remain in Albany. ( ABC News: Armin Azad ) Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said following unsuccessful discussions to keep ATCO in Albany, it was her preference residents move off gas entirely. "It's not going to be the long-term fuel for Western Australia," she said. "It's a transition fuel, and ultimately, we want the residents of Albany to electrify." Rising costs approaching 'scary' levels for WA home owners One-year-old dies in house fire south of Perth Western Australia experienced a roller-coaster of weather in October Country town reliant on backpackers warns visa changes will cripple business Energy analyst Ray Wills said the transition from gas to electric was the right move, but the package needed to be larger to entice people away from gas bottles. "No longer burning gas should be an incentive in itself," he said. "However, if you've got to spend six or eight or 10 grand to convert your house … it's still reasonably dear." Professor Wills said a business case should determine the exact price, with the government subsidising 50 per cent of the cost. Albany residents who want to keep gas appliances will need to transition to gas bottles. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding ) He said the main concern with the package was that customers would stay on gas as the rest of the state electrified. "We can draw a metaphor … the Rio Tinto board tried to electrify, it didn't quite get there because they were getting free money from government for their diesel, so they stuck with it," he said. "This is kind of the same thing. It's about having a lower cost option being the one that's still burning stuff, and the higher cost option is going electric, which is what the state is trying to achieve." Greg Stocks says the package will not encourage all residents to go electric. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding ) City of Albany Mayor Greg Stocks said the package was not enough to achieve the state government's goal of electrification. "This transition package is about gas bottle, reticulated gas to gas bottle, the budget's not big enough for electrification," he said.

events.title: United Arab Emirates says military solutions offer no quick off-ramps to crisis with Iran
events.summary: The United Arab Emirates hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations to prevent a new confrontation between the U.S. and Iran MANAMA, Bahrain -- The United Arab Emirates’ presidential adviser said Sunday that his country hopes a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations is possible to avert a new round of confrontation between the U.S. and Iran. The Iran war , which began on Feb. 28 with joint strikes by the U.S. and Israel followed by attacks by Iran on the Gulf nations, has made it “a watershed year” for the region and the world, UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said at a security forum in Bahrain. “We don’t really want to see another round of confrontation in the region,” Gargash told the audience at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security summit in Bahrain organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, or IISS, that brings together regional and international state, defense and foreign-affairs officials and experts. Iranian negotiators are in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz soon, according to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. He said that no direct talks are being held with the U.S. and that the final outcome depends on answers provided by the United States to the “Iranian questions.” In an interview shared on his Telegram channel, Araghchi said Iran hoped that the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.” He said Iran was ready for both defense and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality.” A possible escalation cast a long shadow over the three-day security forum in Bahrain's capital, Manama. Gargash, the UAE adviser, said that the current crisis requires “a lot of wisdom, with political tools being our main tools, and the understanding that military solutions will only complicate the current very complicated scene that we have and will not actually bring any quick off-ramps.” Gargash, however, acknowledged that “the rules of logic” show that the U.S. and Iranian stances are far apart. “If these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst,” Gargash said. He said it's not in the interest of the region or Iran to withstand another round of war. It was a sentiment echoed by other Gulf and Arab officials at the forum. Egypt's foreign minister Badr Abdelatty, a day earlier, told the gathering: "The second round (of escalation) will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere.” But Gargash added that his country and the region are braced for the possibility of escalation. Before a ceasefire was reached in April, the UAE faced the largest number of airborne attacks from Iran, with more than 3,000 drone and ballistic missile attacks targeting airports, military and oil facilities, according to IISS. Most of those attacks were intercepted. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Since then, Gulf nations have spent billions of dollars to boost their defense capabilities. Gargash said that the war has solidified U.S.-UAE relations, making them “even more important” and at the heart of the UAE’s ability to defend itself. At the conference, Bahraini Foreign Affairs Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani said that his country also welcomes “every effort to reduce tensions, prevent escalation and create opportunities for dialogue.” Al Zayani said that Iran has shown what he called a pattern of attacks or threat of attacks threatening the region’s and the world’s stability and prosperity by targeting sea, air and data facilities. He said Iran has continued to do so even after a ceasefire was reached and as recently as last month, threatening underwater data cables. He described the attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels on neighboring Saudi Arabia as part of the pattern. “These attacks are part of one continued pattern,” he said. “The hands may change, the approach doesn’t.” Iran fired 500 drones and nearly 200 ballistic missiles toward Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, at the height of the war, according to IISS. The attacks hit the naval base, residential buildings, the financial district and a water desalination plant. This summer, Houthi rebels have escalated their attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and airports, saying they were a response to Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa airport. The Houthis have hit critical oil pipelines and disrupted air traffic in the kingdom. Another issue that prevailed over the forum was the lack of a coordinated defense response among the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and Oman. At the height of the war with Iran, the response from the Gulf countries that bore the brunt of Iranian strikes was at the national level, each working with U.S. command and control centers in the region.

events.title: Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson prepare for the return of war as localized ceasefire ends
events.summary: Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson region are preparing for the end of a localized ceasefire KHERSON, Ukraine -- Civilians in Ukraine’s southeastern Kherson region prepared Sunday for the end of a localized ceasefire that has marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began nearly five years ago. The White House said that U.S. first lady Melania Trump helped to broker the limited truce , which began early Tuesday and is expected to end Sunday evening. The pause in hostilities allowed besieged residents in the front-line city of Oleshky to be evacuated in a rare joint operation that ended Saturday. “The ceasefire across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack," Trump said on social media. "Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace.” An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of evacuating to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. For the safety of those who have stayed, exact numbers weren't released after the evacuation. At the Ukrainian border Saturday, family members waited for a glimpse of their loved ones, while residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet the humanitarian convoy. But Moscow and Kyiv have continued aerial strikes elsewhere, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying Sunday that Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy systems before winter. Hundreds of thousands of families were left without power overnight as Moscow sought to exploit Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses, Zelenskyy said in a post on social media. “The intensity of the strikes is extremely high, and the Russians are trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said in a post on X. Residents in the Ukrainian city of Kherson remained calm Sunday, despite knowing that the quiet of the localized ceasefire would soon end. “Don’t be afraid, keep holding on,” Oleksandr Knyha, head of the Mykola Kulish Kherson Regional Academic Music and Drama Theater, told the audience as he opened a concert. The theater performs every Saturday and Sunday. This weekend’s shows fell during the ceasefire, but the company plans to perform next weekend as usual, even as local officials warn that Russian forces have brought in more weapons and personnel and some residents expect shelling to intensify. “Of course, we want peace to finally come,” Knyha said. But “we’ve been working on the front line for four years,” he added, referring to Kherson itself, and the theater has never canceled a performance. “Whatever happens, the show is not canceled,” he said. The company now performs in a basement and is equipping an additional bomb shelter. About 100 of the theater’s 120 staff members work in Kherson, and none has evacuated. Costume maker Alla Vasylenko, 58, said that the silence of the brief truce still frightens her. “Nothing will change,” she said. “Everything will go back to how it was before the ceasefire, because believing the Russians means not believing yourself.” “I have 10 dogs, so I can’t leave,” she said. “They urge us to leave, but you need somewhere to go and the means to get there.” Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say The trip alone would cost 30,000 to 50,000 hryvnias ($650 to $1,080), a significant sum for her, she said. “Until we liberate the left bank, we have no certainty this will end,” Vasylenko said, referring to the Russia-occupied part of the region. For many in Kherson, a city that itself lived through Russian occupation, that belief is the reason they stay. Knyha is from Oleshky, on the occupied left bank, and used to commute from there to work in Kherson. He hasn’t given up hope of returning home. “That’s also what keeps me here,” he said. On the last day of the ceasefire, the theater staged a concert built around a “musical map of Ukraine,” with songs from the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014, to the Carpathian mountains in Ukraine's southwest. “This is also our job — to unite people and give them hope,” Knyha said. Elsewhere, a Russian attack killed three people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Ukrainian region of Vinnytsia when a drone hit the grounds of a vocational school, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. Four others were wounded, including two 5-year-old girls and a 16-year-old boy.

events.title: Don't get caught out by new Buy Now Pay Later rules
events.summary: If you've bought something via Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) since the summer, then you'll have been tested to see if you can afford it. BNPL has always been a type of loan, usually paid back in instalments, but it's only been officially regulated since July. This means stricter background checks on your ability to repay. If you fail, then your purchase via BNPL will be blocked. If there's a chance of this happening to you, here are some ways to approach the situation. BNPL lenders - such as Klarna, Clearpay and others - must now have regulator approval to operate, giving shoppers more access to refunds and independent rulings on complaints if things go wrong. But new affordability checks on each BNPL transaction could also leave you blocked from services for the first time. There are different affordability checks for different purchases, partially based on how much is borrowed. But, with the expensive festive season approaching, here's how to avoid being blocked when time and finances are tight. events.title: Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers amid Michigan Democratic feud
events.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) made a stunning last-minute endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, two days before Michigan's closely watched Senate election . Why it matters: Her endorsement gives Rogers a striking photo op as his party tries to peel away Black and Jewish voters in a tight race that could determine control of the Senate . Driving the news: Stevens appeared Sunday alongside Rogers at Detroit's Perfecting Church, where she praised his support for Black-owned businesses. Stevens later posted an endorsement on X. In a video, she said Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed told her she was no longer welcome in his campaign. "And he's right, and that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today," Stevens said. Stevens' appearance with Rogers was arranged at the last minute after the two spoke Sunday morning, per a person familiar. She had previously planned to attend a Detroit church service with El-Sayed and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.). How it happened: The dispute escalated last week after Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, announced he would vote for Rogers. Stevens demanded El-Sayed condemn an outside group's ad linking U.S. support for Israel to higher grocery prices and remove a campaign ad featuring Tucker Carlson. On Friday night, after El-Sayed's campaign said Stevens would not be welcome at his events, Rogers called Stevens and told her he would welcome her support, according to a person familiar with the conversations. The next day, El-Sayed explicitly rejected the outside ad's contents, prompting Stevens to publicly welcome his remarks. On Sunday morning, Stevens called Rogers back to say she would endorse him, the person said. She told Rogers she remained a Democrat and believed the party would still win a Senate majority. The intrigue: A video posted by Detroit journalist Sam Robinson showed Stevens entering the church and praising Rogers . Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), who helped organize the original planned appearance with El-Sayed, told CNN she asked Stevens not to attend because the dispute had become distracting. Stevens narrowly lost the August Democratic primary to El-Sayed but endorsed him afterward. The other side: A person close to El-Sayed argued Stevens' endorsement could actually help him by reinforcing his anti-establishment appeal. "It's good for Abdul," the person said, portraying Stevens as a symbol of the Democratic establishment, Congress and support for the Israeli government. The endorsement "shows Abdul is the candidate of change and for the people of Michigan," the person added . What she's saying: Stevens told Politico that El-Sayed had made clear she wasn't welcome in his campaign. " Abdul has run a magnificent campaign," she told Politico's Adam Wren. "He just was clear that I wasn't a part of it. I mean, I respect him. I wish him well. He very well could win. It's a close race. I mean, I'm voting for the other guy, and maybe some others are too." What he's saying: President Trump welcomed Stevens' endorsement in a Truth Social post Sunday afternoon, calling it "BIG" and praising her "bravery." Trump said Stevens has a huge following and "virtually unparalleled" respect among Michigan's Black and Jewish voters. "Haley said what few people are willing to say," Trump wrote, calling the endorsement an act of loyalty to Michigan. Trump said at an Iowa rally later Sunday: "I'd love her to join the Republican Party. Actually, I think that could happen maybe." Flashback: In August, Trump called Stevens a "Radical Left Socialist" during the primary vote count. What we're watching: Michigan voters choose between Rogers and El-Sayed on Tuesday, with Democrats facing a crucial test of whether they can reunite their coalition. events.title: Where Dems eyeing the White House are putting their midterm chips
events.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro 's chances of being a presidential contender in 2028 are riding on his winning reelection in a landslide Tuesday. New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez 's future hinges on whether a fellow progressive can carry a swing state, for once. California Gov. Gavin Newsom has to show that his congressional redistricting gambit worked for Democrats — and he needs to beat back a state wealth tax proposal supported by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). Driving the news: Democrats eyeing White House runs have spent the past year preparing to emerge from Tuesday's midterms with momentum, and an argument for a 2028 candidacy. They want Democrats to do well — but to each, some races are especially important. Some have focused their time and money on particular contests for ideological reasons, or a desire to show strength in their home states. Others have hedged their bets across the nation, so that Tuesday is unlikely to be a huge victory or a significant defeat. Here's how the top potential Democratic contenders for president have placed their bets in this week's elections — and what success or failure will look like for them. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez A great night: AOC has wagered just about everything on the Senate race in Michigan, where she's said that a win by progressive Abdul El-Sayed would "break open the entire political calculus in America" and show that "anybody can win anywhere." She's weighing whether to run for president or the Senate, and much of her electability argument for a national campaign hinges on an El-Sayed victory. Progressives are desperate to establish that one of their own can carry a presidential battleground state. Ocasio-Cortez has contributed $1 million to help El-Sayed and stumped for him at several events. An El-Sayed victory "would prove to the country, and the world, that competent, courageous progressive populists can win in the most competitive swing states in America," said Bhavik Lathia, a left-wing strategist from Michigan. "The implications for 2028 would be enormous." AOC would get bonus points Tuesday if other progressives she's supporting — such as House candidate Randy Villegas in California and Senate candidate Angie Nixon in Florida — win their swing-seat races. Worst-case scenario: If El-Sayed loses, many progressives think AOC would be less likely to run for president. That's why she's widely viewed as having more on the line Tuesday than any other potential Democratic contender for president, followed by Shapiro. Josh Shapiro A great night: Shapiro needs to win so big Tuesday that it makes Democratic presidential primary voters see his technocratic "get shit done" brand of governing as the party's best bet to take down the GOP in 2028. Shapiro is less known nationally than many 2028 hopefuls, and that has been by choice. He's largely focused on Pennsylvania this year, even as would-be rivals for president crisscrossed the country. A blowout in America's biggest swing state could help him stand out. A good night for Shapiro would be defeating Republican Stacy Garrity by double digits and carrying three Democratic House candidates — Janelle Stelson, Bob Brooks and Paige Cognetti — across the finish line to defeat Republican incumbents. He'd have a great night if his coattails were so long that he pulled a fourth Democratic House hopeful, Bob Harvie, to victory — taking down GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who's known for surviving difficult electoral cycles. Shapiro would get extra credit if he helped Democrats win a trifecta in Harrisburg for the first time in decades by flipping control of the state Senate. Worst-case scenario: If only one or two Democrats in his state flip House seats or he wins by less than 10 points, Shapiro's setup for 2028 would fall short. Andy Beshear A great night: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who moonlights as chair of the Democratic Governors Association, put his chips this year on helping his party take control of a majority of the nation's governorships. Beshear would earn bragging rights if Democrats flip the two governors' seats needed to do that. He's eyeing the races in Iowa, Ohio, Georgia and Nevada. "I am laser-focused on these governors' races," he told us, arguing that the results will help determine what's possible in the 2028 presidential contest. "Rob Sand wins Iowa, Iowa's in play. When Amy Acton wins Ohio, Ohio's in play," Beshear said. Worst-case scenario: Beshear made enemies among some Latino Democrats this year when the DGA rebuffed calls to invest heavily in Gina Hinojosa's campaign for Texas governor. If Hinojosa loses to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott by a razor-thin margin or pulls an upset, Beshear's decision-making will come under heavy scrutiny — and he could have a problem with some Latino leaders in a 2028 campaign. Gavin Newsom A great night: Newsom won over many MS NOW moms and "resistance" liberals across the country when he responded to President Trump's push to create more GOP House seats in other states by fighting back with a successful voter proposition to do the same in California. His goal has been to gain five Democratic seats from the change to help Democrats take back the House. That's his bar to clear Tuesday. Some political insiders now think Democrats could gain 20 or more House seats across the country, so Newsom's contribution might not be as decisive as once thought. Newsom would score a political win if a proposed billionaire wealth tax on the ballot in his home state, which he opposes, fails. Worst-case scenario: If California voters approve the tax or Democrats flip fewer than five House seats there, it would diminish Newsom's California clout. Jon Ossoff A great night: A long-running knock against Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff has been that he won his seat in 2021 by riding his fellow Peach State Sen. Raphael Warnock's coattails. Ossoff has the chance this year to prove he doesn't need Warnock, who isn't on the ticket. He's on his way to doing just that, with polls showing him comfortably leading GOP challenger Mike Collins. But to have a truly great night, Ossoff needs to show that he has enough sway in his state to help pull Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms to victory. Worst-case scenario: If Bottoms were to lose, Democrats say, Ossoff would be even less likely to leave the Senate for a presidential run, since Georgia's governor has the power to make a temporary appointment if a senator steps down. Ossoff, for his part, has said he has "zero interest" in a 2028 bid. But Barack Obama made similar comments before jumping into the 2008 race. Kamala Harris A great night: Former Vice President Kamala Harris has rallied voters to fight back against GOP redistricting and a recent Supreme Court decision on the Voting Rights Act that threatens Black representation in Congress. events.title: AI trade falters after disappointing tech earnings
events.summary: Some investors are dialing back their expectations for US economic growth, as warning signs flashed red over the sustainability of the country’s breakneck AI buildout. The tech-heavy Nasdaq slid into correction territory on Friday as investors unwound their AI bets. Intel stock plunged 29%, the chipmaker’s biggest single-day selloff since the 1970s; concerns mounted over hyperscaler spending after disappointing Amazon and Google earnings; and S&P Global revised Meta’s outlook to “negative,” citing its high capex . Earnings misses are generating “ sober questions ” about the AI investments powering the economy, a strategist told Bloomberg. “You can’t find the growth slowdown in any of the economic data,” a portfolio manager told the Financial Times. “But… a reassessment of AI means a reassessment of growth expectations .” — Brendan Ruberry

AI threatens to supercharge North Korea’s cyber activities, an expert told the Financial Times: “AI has given hackers wings. events.title: Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering stroke
events.summary: Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) had a stroke Saturday and is being treated at Johns Hopkins Hospital, his office said Sunday. The big picture: Murphy is one of the Senate's more visible Democrats and has been traveling the country campaigning ahead of Tuesday's midterms . Driving the news: Murphy, 53, began experiencing numbness in his arm while attending his son's hockey game Saturday, according to a statement from his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt. He was taken to a hospital where doctors determined he had a stroke and transferred him to Johns Hopkins for monitoring. "The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery," Herwitt said in a statement. What they're saying: President Trump told reporters Sunday afternoon that he had just learned of Murphy's hospitalization and would reach out to him "at the right time." Sen.
