events.title: Insurance unaffordable for flooded homes almost two years on from disaster
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Insurance unaffordable for north Queensland homes flooded almost two years ago Michelle Yates said her home was still being repaired after flooding in February 2025. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) Home owners are struggling to obtain or afford insurance in north Queensland which is still recovering from devastating floods in early 2025. Policy holders in the town of Ingham say their insurance was not renewed after the event or had substantial premium increases. The Insurance Council of Australia says the floods generated $327 million in insured losses, and some claims were still being negotiated. Michelle Yates still hasn't finished rebuilding her kitchen or replacing water-damaged floors in her farmhouse near Ingham nearly two years after devastating floods struck north Queensland. A 15-month payout negotiation with her insurer and ongoing trades shortages have slowed the recovery. Another wet season is looming over the region and bringing a new challenge with it. The north Queensland town of Ingham flooded in the first week of February 2025. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) "We have no insurance," Ms Yates said. "Sure Insurance cancelled our policy altogether because we were flooded." Michelle Yates lives on acreage in the Hinchinbrook Shire north of Townsville. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) It is one of several instances where Sure Insurance sent a non-renewal notice to policy holders who were flooded during the 2025 event. The 2026 notices, viewed by the ABC, stated that Sure Insurance had changed its underwriting guidelines and would not offer insurance if a property made a flood claim in the past five years or had a risk of damage in a one-in-20-year flood. A spokesperson for Sure Insurance said it provided cover to one-in-four insured Ingham properties and that underwriting guidelines were reviewed regularly. "To determine our ability to provide ongoing cover at a price that is fair," they said. Ms Yates, who owns her home, says she's still looking for an affordable alternative. Without insurance home owners like Ms Yates would endure the entire cost of rebuilding or repairs in the event of damage to her property. Ingham broker Kieran Volpe says many residents are struggling to afford rising insurance premiums. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) Ingham-based insurance broker Kieran Volpe said some providers were not offering cover to high-risk properties while others "priced themselves out". "We are seeing, quite commonly, quotes coming in at $10,000, $15,000 or even $20,000 in those high-risk flood areas," Mr Volpe said. Matthew Porter says his home insurance increased 72 per cent in 12 months. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) Matthew Porter bought a home in Ingham after the 2025 floods knowing it had suffered superficial flood damage in the lower, unoccupied level during the event. When his Allianz Insurance policy was due to be renewed this year the premium increased by 72 per cent. "We thought that was quite expensive and there would be something cheaper," Mr Porter said. "To our shock it was at the cheaper end." He said he opted to stay with the policy but found the increase "ridiculous". A spokesperson for Allianz said the frequency and severity of weather events in Ingham had increased in recent years and so had the cost of claims. "Premiums must reflect the genuine cost of insuring a property against these risks to ensure we can continue to pay claims when customers need us most," they said. The 2025 north Queensland floods generated $327 million in insured losses. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) The Insurance Council of Australia said anyone who had received a non-renewal notice from their insurer or a significant premium hike should ask for an explanation, shop around or speak to a broker. "Insurance remains available in Ingham, but in areas exposed to repeated, severe flooding premiums will reflect that risk," a spokesperson said. "The most effective way to bring them down is to reduce the underlying risk, that requires greater investment in flood defences, house raising and more resilient homes." The spokesperson said the council remained involved in individual claims discussions from the 2025 floods and that trades shortages and steep cost increases had delayed recovery. Hinchinbrook Mayor Ramon Jayo said the insurance market was failing in north Queensland. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) The Hinchinbrook Shire Council has released new data from a community survey on insurance that heard from 305 respondents. The survey found most households within the shire maintained some form of insurance, but that underinsurance was an issue locally.

events.title: Lifelong renter now living in tent with dog after Tasmanian housing struggles
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Salvos Street 2 Home service searches for rough sleepers, amid surging demand for help The only homelessness outreach program in southern Tasmania is a team of just three people who search for rough sleepers and connect them to essential services. Street 2 Home used to operate statewide but had to close in the north and north-west because of insufficient funding. Street 2 Home is pushing for more funding to cater to what it says is a growing number of Tasmanians sleeping rough. It is eight degrees on a chilly Tuesday morning, and the Salvation Army's Street 2 Home outreach team has driven along an off-road dirt track in southern Tasmanian bushland. They are looking for Effie*, a woman living in a tent with her German shepherd, Gus. Annie finds camps of unhoused people. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) Street 2 Home is the only homelessness outreach program in southern Tasmania that searches for people sleeping rough, asks if they need help, and connects them to essential services. The program says it is struggling to keep up with demand, as the numbers of people coming onto the street outpace those coming off. With extra funding, it said the program could expand state-wide, having recently closed both its north and north-west operations for financial reasons. Between 2016 and 2021, the number of homeless Tasmanians increased by 45 per cent. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) Rental rejections led to the street With a life of renting under her belt, Effie* was not worried about finding somewhere to live after being evicted from her home. "I was unsuccessful for every house that I applied for," she said. Street 2 Home says it is struggling to keep up with demand for its services. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) She said the difficulty of finding a home or emergency accommodation with a dog meant she had no choice but to pitch a tent and was soon noticed by a passer-by who contacted Street 2 Home. They have visited her regularly since. "I've got the hand warmers and body warmers … my darling friend from [The Salvation Army] brings me those," Effie said. Gus watches from inside a car. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) Burden on homeless to find services themselves For a region with roughly 2,500 people experiencing homelessness, the Street 2 Home team of just three people is stretched to capacity. Program lead and outreach worker Chris Allen said many other homelessness services were based online, and this put the burden on the individual to seek out help themselves. Chris Allen is the team leader of the Salvation Army's Street 2 Home and Beyond the Wire programs. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) "[People sleeping rough] might not have heard about a lot of the programs and a lot of the services that are designed to actually help them," he said. "Most of them won't know how to use a phone, or they don't have internet. They don't know how to look up those services and find them." People who sleep rough are often not aware of the services there are to assist them. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) Success stories few and far between What used to be a state-wide operation was scaled back to the south due to a lack of funding. In September last year, the program shut its doors in northern Tasmania, and in June this year, the north-west met the same fate. Street 2 Home says many people have complex mental health issues, addictions, low literacy and other barriers to securing housing. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) There is no limit on the number of cases or people the team supports, but this leaves it stretched thin. "The more people we come across, the less time we can spend with each individual," Mr Allen said. He said success stories were becoming rarer over the years. "We've had fewer [people getting into housing] this year than we had last year," he said. Housing waitlist times in the state have reached roughly 1.7 years, as of August this year. Mr Allen said the focus was on making it as comfortable as possible for the person experiencing homelessness, while they worked to help them find housing. In Tasmania, people deemed priority applicants can wait up to two years for public housing. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) "If our details are attached to [an application], we'll go out, we'll get [the person] on the phone … and we'll make sure they make it to those appointments, so they don't miss that property," Mr Allen said. Homelessness Australia director Catherine Robinson said outreach services offered "critical" human connection that online services lacked.

events.title: Trump has frank call with Netanyahu about next move in Iran war
events.summary: President Trump had a candid phone call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu Saturday about the state of U.S. negotiations with Iran and how quickly to return to combat, according to one Israeli and one U.S. source. Why it matters: The sources said Netanyahu is pressing Trump to strike Iran immediately after the midterm elections on Tuesday. But Trump, for now, wants to let negotiations play out — a strategy Netanyahu is concerned about. The Israeli source said the call was "tough," while the U.S. source described it as "direct." The White House and the Israeli prime minister's office declined to comment. Driving the news: As he did before Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in February, Trump is pursuing dual tracks — trying to reach a deal to restart peace talks while also preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations after the midterms. Last week Vice President Vance sent a letter to Iran's national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about the possibility of restarting negotiations . It was the most senior-level outreach by the U.S. to Iran in several months. Trump told reporters on Saturday that negotiations with Iran are "going fine" and noted he is not "in much of a hurry." While the Iranians want to make a deal, the president said they "are not very reliable. ... They make a deal and then they back out." At the same time, Trump said the U.S. still has to "take care" of one or two nuclear sites in Iran. "We can do that in 10 minutes. We have that planned. You can look at Pickaxe Mountain. We need to take care of that. We can do that very quickly," Trump said, referring to a suspected nuclear site built into a mountain. The Wall Street Journal first reported the Trump-Netanyahu call, but did not describe its contents. State of play: Qatari mediators met with Iranian officials on Sunday for the third consecutive day in an effort to reach a deal to restart direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that there is no agreement yet and stressed that a deal depends on the U.S. answering Iran's questions. "We are making every effort in this regard and hope that the other side will demonstrate enough rationality to choose diplomacy over other paths," he said.

events.title: Super funds issued with legal warning following regulator's damning report
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Super funds failing members on retirement savings, regulator says Superannuation funds are being urged to listen to their members. ( ABC News: Alistair Kroie ) Australia's corporate regulator warns that super funds are failing to deal with complaints properly. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission says the ombudsman is better at detecting industry-wide issues than the funds. It is threatening legal action against super funds that don't step up. Australia's corporate regulator says superannuation funds are failing their members in managing their retirement savings, warning that those who do not step up could be staring down future legal action. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission's (ASIC's) latest review looked at 45 superannuation trustees, covering $1.6 trillion in benefits for more than 12.8 million members. It found that superannuation members were more likely to get resolutions to their complaints if they went to the financial ombudsman rather than raise it directly with their super fund. It has prompted ASIC commissioner Simone Constant to hand down a blunt warning to the funds that "blaming customers is not a complaint strategy". Simone Constant is calling on super funds to do better. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) ASIC has long been critical of how super funds handle member complaints over death benefits and disability insurance claims payouts and alleged fraud and misconduct. If you have more information about this story, please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com In March last year, it called on funds to overhaul the way they dealt with death benefit claims, noting excessive delays, poor customer service and ineffective claims handling were leaving Australians worse off at some of the most vulnerable times of their lives. In October last year, it criticised superannuation funds over the way they communicated with retirees. Payouts impact people's lives: commissioner Ms Constant said superannuation trustees managed $3.4 trillion in Australians' retirement savings. She said they were dealing with payouts that affect people's lives and the retirement savings they had worked hard to build. Most Australians have not made a legally binding death benefit nomination to ensure their superannuation goes to who they want it to when they die. "Super funds must listen to what complaints are telling them," she said. "When trustees fail to learn from their complaints, small problems left unidentified, unattended or unresolved can snowball into widespread failures. "That expose[s] members to harm and erode[s] trust in the superannuation system." Super funds that don't step up could face legal action. Funds not analysing their complaints data ASIC's inquiries across the industry found close to one quarter of trustees were not analysing complaints data to identify systemic issues on a regular basis. More than half of trustees reviewed (24 out of 45) identified fewer than five systemic issues from complaints over a two-year period. Of these, 14 trustees failed to identify a single issue. "We see low levels of systemic issue identification as a potential red flag, not evidence of better performance," Ms Constant said. "Alarmingly, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority [AFCA] appears better at picking up issues than industry. According to AFCA, superannuation complaints rose sharply in 2025–26, with the financial ombudsman receiving 8,755 complaints, up 42 per cent on the previous financial year. Cathy was compensated just $29 for super fund's death benefit delay Australia's corporate watchdog calls on superannuation funds to overhaul the way they deal with death benefit claims. AFCA said complaints about super funds refusing to pay claims rose by 80 per cent. ASIC said during July 1, 2023 and June 30, 2026, more than 19,400 complaints were made to AFCA about superannuation concerning the 45 funds that were part of its whole-of-industry review. "When comparing the two years of data we collected, AFCA identified systemic issues from superannuation complaints it received at almost twice the rate all trustees identified from the complaints they received," Ms Constant said. ASIC also found several trustees blamed members when they made complaints. Several of them attributed more than 60 per cent of recorded complaint causes to members. events.title: Thousands of public EV chargers may be unusable
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Thousands of public EV chargers are coming, but they could be unusable This kerbside charger in Bondi is used about once a week, as it's usually blocked by non-EVs. ( Supplied: Plugshare ) A program targeting high-density areas will more than double the number of public EV chargers. But many of the power pole-mounted chargers could be inaccessible to EV drivers. Data shows chargers without dedicated parking are often blocked by petrol and diesel cars. Many electric vehicle (EV) drivers know the frustration of rolling up to a public charger and finding a petrol car parked in the way. Getting "ICEd" by an internal combustion engine (ICE) car means expensive charging infrastructure goes unused and EV drivers waste time finding the next available plug. Now, neighbourly conflict over blocked chargers may be coming to a street near you. From 2027, the federal government's Accelerating EV Charging Program will see about 14,000 EV chargers installed on power poles in high-density areas in cities where residents have limited access to off-street parking. Pole-mounted chargers installed under the program will fully charge a typical EV in about eight hours. ( Supplied: Ausgrid ) Under the program's rules, installers aren't required to negotiate with councils for dedicated EV-only parking. Many in the EV industry expect the vast majority of kerbside chargers will be "undedicated", meaning they won't have EV-only parking. Data shared with the ABC suggests many newly installed chargers, partly funded through households paying higher power bills, will end up being obstructed and remain largely idle. As a result, the program's modelled emissions reductions may be wrong. Tension over parking and EV charging in congested areas About a quarter of motorists don't have off-street parking, making it difficult to charge an EV at home. In inner-city areas, the proportion is much higher. But setting aside precious parking for public EV charging can be unpopular, with EVs only accounting for about 3 per cent of cars on the road. Tensions created by high EV uptake and lack of off-street parking are already apparent in Sydney's eastern suburbs. This undedicated EV charger on Curlewis St, Bondi, has been used four times in the past 12 months. ( Supplied: Plugshare ) In the Waverley, Woollahra and Randwick council areas, more than half of residents live in apartments and EV ownership is more than three times the state average. The area has 320 public charging ports, of which 90 are undedicated and sit mostly unused due to obstruction, Anthony Weinberg, program manager for the EV charging program across the three councils, told the ABC. "Utilisation of these spots is about 5 to 10 per cent of the dedicated spots," he said. A dedicated charger on Ocean St, North Bondi, has had 988 sessions over the past year. A kilometre away, on Glenayr St, an undedicated charger of similar power has racked up 40 sessions. Another, on nearby Curlewis St, has had just four charging sessions in 12 months. "A lot of the dedicated ones are getting between two and three sessions a day, and the undedicated ones are getting a session every two days," Mr Weinberg said. "We won't install an EV charger now unless it has dedicated parking." Other councils report a similar pattern. Sydney's Inner West Council found its 78 chargers with dedicated parking were used four times more than the 68 chargers without, according to an internal report tabled in May. The report recommended "Council gradually transition non-dedicated EV charging spaces to dedicated charging spaces". Inner West Council did not respond to requests for comment. Questions over program's modelled emissions reduction The Accelerating EV Charging Program will support emissions reductions of 9.8 million tonnes of CO2, worth $802 million in value, according to modelling by the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW). The idea is more EV chargers will drive EV ownership, which will mean fewer ICE vehicles on the roads. The modelling estimates the program will fund about 14,000 new chargers, and each charger will support 30 EVs, or about 420,000 EVs in total. Most of Australia's existing 11,000 public chargers have dedicated parking, like these at Bondi Beach. ( Supplied: Waverley Council ) This estimate could be overly optimistic, according to a separate analysis of charger utilisation in the Waverley, Woollahra and Randwick council areas by Ross de Rango, director of Vehicle Charging Solutions Australia.

events.title: India's opposition parties stage new protest against the country's election chief
events.summary: It's the latest display of public dissent against PM Modi’s government. NEW DELHI -- India’s opposition parties on Sunday renewed calls for the resignation of the country’s election chief , staging a new protest in the latest display of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government. The protest, called by opposition bloc INDIA , drew tens of thousands of demonstrators, some carrying musical instruments and waving various flags, as they chanted slogans against the central government's policies. Several opposition parties of the alliance, formed in 2023 to unseat Modi, mobilized their cadres from different states for the protest. The demonstration came weeks after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi. Led by Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, and backed by the youth “Cockroach” movement , the protesters called for the safeguarding of India’s democracy while demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a contentious voter roll revision. The protesters gathered at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling public square in New Delhi, after police last month withdrew Jantar Mantar from the list of officially designated venues for demonstrations. The historic observatory had long served as the capital’s main protest site. Addressing the rally, Gandhi said that India has faced vote theft for years. “I am telling every citizen and every youth of India that Gyanesh Kumar will have to relinquish his position. Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail,” he said in Hindi. Gandhi also accused the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the ideological parent of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, of tightening its grip on state institutions, from the education system to investigative agencies. “Because of this, farmers, laborers and youth are being denied their rights,” he said. Authorities deployed thousands of police and paramilitary soldiers and mounted extensive surveillance, with more than 200 security cameras, drones and body-worn cameras at the venue and along the protest route, officials said. The ongoing review of voter lists has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say The Election Commission and Modi’s administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries. Human Rights Watch on Thursday said that the accusations over the voter roll revision raise “serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections.” “The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services,” said Elaine Pearson, the group’s Asia director, in a statement. For weeks, the call for Kumar’s resignation has been a rallying cry for opposition parties and supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP. Opposition parties, mainly the Congress, say the governing BJP has undertaken systemic manipulation of the electoral process, accusing the party of “vote chori,” or vote theft. Modi hasn't publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchists” and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers. In July, protests led by the youth “cockroach” movement forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister , a rare setback for Modi, who has been in power for more than 12 years. The movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India’s chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Suresh Sharma, a protester from northern Haryana state, said that the country’s system needed reform because democracy was being throttled. The process of voter roll revision needs to be scrapped, Sharma said. “We demand that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign and be arrested,” he said. events.title: Virgin Media O2 set to cut thousands of jobs to reduce costs
events.summary: Thousands of Virgin Media O2 staff are facing redundancy as the telecoms firm attempts to save money in the face of billions of pounds of debt and tougher competition. The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be cut but it is likely be a sizeable chunk of its 16,000-strong workforce, the BBC understands. Virgin Media O2 has billions in debt on its balance sheet and is tackling both smaller providers as well as giants like BT, which has agreed a deal to acquire rival TalkTalk, which Virgin Media O2 has firmly opposed. The company declined to comment. Prospect, a union which represents Virgin Media O2 staff, said the cuts were "disappointing and very unsettling". Noel McClean. deputy general secretary at Prospect, said the union was "committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected". The majority of the affected staff are in roles that are not customer-facing and a number of senior leadership changes are already under way, the BBC has been told. Virgin Media O2 is also expected to review its use of contractors and suppliers in conjunction with the job cuts. As of 30 June, Virgin Media O2's total liabilities stands at £27.2bn while it holds assets worth £45.9bn, according to the firm's latest accounts. Meanwhile, the company is dealing with fierce competition from cheaper "altnets" like Hyperoptic, Community Fibre, Gigaclear and YouFibre. Virgin Media O2 had attempted to respond to this growing threat by buying altnet competitor Netomnia for £2bn via nexfibre, a joint venture owned by Virgin Media O2's owners. However, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) has provisionally found competition concerns in the deal , external , with a final decision to come in December, sparking anger from Virgin Media O2. In October, Virgin Media O2 called the BT's agreed takeover of TalkTalk a "stitch-up" that had allowed its rival to "tighten its grip" over the market. BT said its deal provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers as their broadband provider faced collapse without the takeover. On Friday, BT's share price jumped 7% after the Financial Times reported Virgin Media O2 was close to agreeing a deal , external to use its rival's fibre broadband network. The BBC has been told the deal was very close and that Virgin Media O2 was highly likely to announce it will stop all investment in fibre in its results on Tuesday. Do you work for Virgin or O2? events.title: Global energy giants gather in Abu Dhabi as Adipec prepares for record exhibition
events.summary: Some of the world's biggest energy companies will converge on Abu Dhabi on Monday as Adipec prepares to stage what organisers say will be its largest exhibition yet, bringing together industry leaders, ministers and investors amid heightened concerns over energy security and global supply disruptions. The four-day event, running from November 2 to 5, is expected to feature a record 2,260 exhibiting companies, including 54 national and international energy companies, as well as more than 40 government ministers. Organisers expect more than 239,000 attendees from more than 170 countries, with all 16 exhibition halls at Adnec Centre Abu Dhabi booked, prompting them to build additional structures and relocate the opening ceremony to accommodate demand. BP, Shell, TotalEnergies, Eni, ExxonMobil, Chevron and Occidental Petroleum are among the major energy companies listed as exhibitors, alongside technology and industrial groups including Siemens, IBM and Microsoft. “The industry's commitment to Adipec is clear,” Christopher Hudson, president of organiser dmg events, said. “We have a record-breaking 2,260 exhibiting companies, with the exhibition venue fully sold out and additional structures built to accommodate demand.” The gathering comes as governments and companies reassess energy supplies, infrastructure investment and trade routes following months of disruption to global oil and gas markets. Energy security, AI, electricity demand and the financing of new infrastructure are expected to dominate discussions. Energy giants showcase new technology Several major companies have independently confirmed their participation, outlining plans to demonstrate technologies designed to improve operational efficiency, strengthen infrastructure and reduce emissions. US oilfield services company Halliburton said it would showcase advanced drilling and completions technologies, production optimisation systems and AI-powered tools. Its chairman and chief executive, Jeff Miller, is scheduled to address the conference on Tuesday, discussing how energy companies can navigate volatility while maintaining profitability. Industrial automation group Emerson has also confirmed its attendance, with plans to demonstrate AI-enabled software, autonomous operations and advanced instrumentation aimed at improving reliability and project execution. GE Vernova, the US energy equipment manufacturer, said it would showcase advanced gas turbines, electricity grid modernisation and carbon management technologies. Schneider Electric, meanwhile, will focus on autonomous operations and AI-driven technologies. Research released by the French company ahead of Adipec found that 76 per cent of surveyed Middle East energy leaders had increased investment in autonomous technology over the past year. SLB, another major US oilfield services group, plans to demonstrate AI-enabled drilling, reservoir management and digital technologies aimed at improving production efficiency. Industrial software company Aveva will showcase digital twins and connected industrial intelligence, while Honeywell is expected to demonstrate AI-driven autonomous upstream operations. The technology focus comes as energy companies increase their AI spending , with an Adnoc and Microsoft study finding that 89 per cent of surveyed energy leaders had raised investment over the past year. However, the industry's growing reliance on AI presents challenges of its own, with a separate Adipec survey finding that 81 per cent of energy executives believe electricity demand from AI will exceed existing forecasts. Abu Dhabi's Enersol, the energy technology investment platform jointly owned by Adnoc Drilling and Alpha Dhabi Holding, will also highlight technologies developed and manufactured in the UAE. Asia's growing influence Asia will send its largest delegation yet , with 353 companies and six national pavilions representing China, India, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore and South Korea. Participants include China's Sinopec, CNPC and CNOOC, battery manufacturer Catl, Malaysia's Petronas and Japan's Inpex and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. The record Asian presence follows major disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil and gas supplies. Before the war, nearly 90 per cent of crude oil and condensate shipments passing through the waterway were destined for Asia, according to the US Energy Information Administration, with China accounting for 38 per cent. The disruption to shipping earlier this year triggered what the International Energy Agency described as the largest supply disruption in oil market history. For Asian energy buyers, Adipec offers an opportunity to engage with Gulf producers on supply security, infrastructure investment and long-term partnerships. “Asia is at the centre of global energy demand growth,” Abdulmunim Al Kindy, chairman of Adipec 2026, said last month. Mr Al Kindy has also highlighted how Adnoc's contingency planning helped maintain production during the Iran war. The opening day's programme will feature an address by Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc. Adipec 2026: Opening ceremony A ministerial discussion on energy security will bring together UAE Energy Minister Suhail Al Mazrouei and his counterparts from Germany, Turkey and Egypt. Other executives scheduled to speak include BP chief executive Meg O'Neill, Siemens chief executive Roland Busch, Baker Hughes chief executive Lorenzo Simonelli and Inpex chief executive Takayuki Ueda. The exhibition also follows Adnoc's announcement of Dh60 billion in manufacturing opportunities for UAE suppliers, aimed at strengthening domestic supply chains and reducing dependence on imports. Commercial agreements will also be in focus. Last year's Adipec recorded 49,131 agreements worth $53 billion, according to organisers, with further announcements expected during this year's event.

events.title: Guarding the Gates of Knowledge
events.summary: A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion. Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must. Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “ I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper ,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses. “He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.” Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it. Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions , Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools. “Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.” If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty . Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity. Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

events.title: Behind the Curtain: OpenAI's post-election power play
events.summary: Right after Tuesday's midterms, OpenAI will unleash a policy and PR blitz to try to get in sync with the new Washington, including an effort to rebrand data centers as "AI compute campuses." Why it matters: After two years of a friendly White House, AI companies will face a harsher Washington after Tuesday, when Democrats will likely win the House. OpenAI also aims to help frame the AI debate for the big field of 2028 presidential contenders that'll start forming on Wednesday. "You can try to chase the moment, or seek to inform the moment via the power of ideas," OpenAI chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane tells us, calling Tuesday an "electoral portal from one era to the next." Since August, Lehane and his team have been stockpiling policy proposals, some new and some repackaged, to drive urgency and steer the AI debate. It'll all start during the lame-duck session of Congress — the awkward but often consequential weeks between the election and the swearing-in of new members and senators on Jan. 3. This year's lame duck opens Nov. 9. The big picture: Other tech companies are also positioning themselves for a potential blue wave. Meta is taking steps to strengthen its ties with Democrats, Axios' Sara Fischer scooped Saturday . Other big AI and tech players can be expected to do the same. Tech titans who enjoy close relationships with President Trump will be top targets for Democrats, who are eager to ramp up scrutiny and regulatory pressure on the industry. OpenAI's plans, being revealed here for the first time, all involve control — trying to send the message that AI is being built for people, not to displace people. The proposals include: Speed limits: Building on earlier proposals , OpenAI plans to unveil new ideas for mandatory safeguards for the most powerful AI systems — speed limits for AI that will allow humans to keep their hands on the wheel. This'll include a more aggressive congressional drive. "You're going to see us talk more and more about the concept of speed limits," Lehane said. "Our belief is people should always remain in control of this technology. AI should be built by and for people, and people should have more control over how the technology shapes their lives and communities." Data centers: OpenAI hopes to stem the nationwide, bipartisan backlash by offering new community compacts and commitments to smooth the way for future data centers. In addition, the company will try to set a new industry standard by proposing state legislation that gives people a meaningful say in how projects are built and what benefits they receive. In an intentionally provocative rebranding effort, OpenAI will argue that the infrastructure it's building, in contrast to legacy data centers, should be called "AI compute campuses" that can economically transform host communities. OpenAI points to its role in developing a huge data center project that promises to bring thousands of jobs to Pike County in Ohio's Appalachian region. "We think the conversation is good and healthy," Lehane said. "It's democracy in action. Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects." Economic opportunity: OpenAI is developing ideas to help more people see AI as empowering for their daily lives and on the job, including supporting workers through disruption, widening access to education and training, and making it easier to start and grow a business. International cooperation: OpenAI will push for the U.S. to shape global standards with AI built on democratic values. Between the lines: OpenAI is trying to stake out a human-centered "third path" in a debate that often defaults to an artificial binary of doomers vs. accelerationists. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, speaking to the UN Security Council in September, called for an AI approach that leads to a "new Renaissance of creativity and discovery." What we're watching: OpenAI's overtures are aimed partly at 2028 presidential hopefuls, who'll be increasingly vocal about their plans starting Wednesday. "AI is going to be the issue in 2028," Lehane said, calling the midterms a "bit of a movie trailer for what you're going to see in 2028." "I don't think it's going to be good enough just to say 'AI bad,'" Lehane added. "The public gets that this is a much more complex, nuanced conversation. They're going to be looking for whoever their FDR or Lincoln is who's actually going to want to try to lead them through this journey." Lehane said candidates should ask: "How do we start to think about trust? How do we think about the incredible anxiety that exists in modernity? How do we think about the fact that people are profoundly unhappy with where their social contract is, where the American dream is?" The bottom line: The plans for the coming months are just the beginning of OpenAI's effort to inject more urgency in Washington and push the industry on frontier safety. Remember: Every day, AI models get more powerful — and tougher to corral. "Our policy priorities — and urgency, especially on frontier safety — are about meeting the moment in response to the rapidly advancing capabilities," Lehane said. "And we expect that to continue as a new Congress ramps up." Axios' Bradley Olson contributed. Disclosure: Axios has a content licensing and technology agreement with OpenAI, emphasizing expansion of local news coverage. Go deeper : "AI governing the AI world."

events.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
events.summary: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday. The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday. In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack. It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack. The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services. Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits. Speaking to reporters on Saturday night, US President Donald Trump said , external the US is still unsure who the culprits are. "We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," he said. Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury. All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said. From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible. North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks. Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach". Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism". On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners. The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance. Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide. Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers. events.title: Australia nears 'largest property downturn in 40 years' as prices plunge
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'Largest property downturn in 40 years' in sight as house prices fall for seventh time Bidders are nervous at auctions. ( ABC News: Ben Cocklin ) The median value of Australian homes has dropped $63,400 since March. The decline is tracking faster than any past downturn over the past 40 years. Experts predict it will be some time until interest rates start to fall and the market turns. National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, with the speed of the decline in home values tracking at the fastest pace seen over the past 40 years, according to property research group Cotality. Its latest national Home Value Index (HVI) was down 1.2 per cent in October and is now 6.7 per cent below its March peak, equivalent to a decline of about $63,400 in the value of the median Australian dwelling. The index shows the median national house price now stands at $884,855. Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said the speed of decline was tracking faster than any previous downturn over the past 40 years, with capital city values down 8.1 per cent in seven months. Virtually every suburb across Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide has recorded a drop in values over the past three months as buyers have struggled to get loans because of higher interest rates. Investor demand has also been waning because of the federal government's budget changes to property tax breaks. "This is really a demand-led downturn," Mr Burg said. "That's reduced the borrowing capacity of households, but also increased the repayments for people to make on a mortgage, and it's pushed a lot of buyers to the side." Gerard Burg says house prices will fall further. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) Mr Burg is among many economists anticipating higher rates for longer and further house price falls. "The previous record was 2017 through 2019, which stood at 8.2 per cent [falls] across the combined capital cities. Now, at the moment, as of October, the downturn that we've seen over the past seven months is 8.1 per cent, so it looks like we're easily going to push past that mark." Mr Burg said the downturn should be considered in the context of a steep rise in prices before the decline. "But a city like Melbourne has comparatively little further to go and I think we're already seeing that in the dynamics of Melbourne values at the present." People with established mortgages in some cities will be particularly insulated. "However, given the magnitude of the upswing prior to the downturn, most home owners in these cities are likely to be sitting on a significant equity buffer," Cotality said in its release. "For example, a 20 per cent drop in Perth home value from their record high would take the market back to levels recorded in around mid-2025. "Home owners in Melbourne and Sydney aren't in as strong an equity position, with Melbourne home values 7.3 per cent lower than five years ago and Sydney values 1.5 per cent below October 2021 levels. ACT values are virtually unchanged from five years ago." How much further will house prices fall? Home sales have dropped sharply as demand weakens. Cotality puts the number of home sales over the past three months 23 per cent lower than a year ago and 18 per cent below the previous five-year average. With fewer buyers, selling homes has become harder. Auction clearance rates across the combined capitals are consistently tracking below 50 per cent, while private treaty metrics have also weakened. The median time on market, at 39 days, is the highest since August 2020, while vendor discounting, at 4.7 per cent, is the largest since May 2019. Mr Burg said buyers would hold back until the Reserve Bank of Australia indicated a different direction on rates, and that likely would not happen until the latter half of 2027. "The eventual recovery that we do see in the housing market is likely to be more subdued than we've seen in previous episodes," Mr Burg said. "It [the RBA] doesn't necessarily require rates to come down, but [give] the clear signal that that is the direction that they are going to take." Domain's chief economist Nicola Powell said rate cuts might not be on the agenda until well into next year before. "We need something to change to improve buyer confidence. And that isn't going to come at least until we have the discussion of a potential rate cut. And that's unlikely to happen until the latter part of 2027." Nicola Powell says it could be well into next year before rate cuts are on the agenda.

events.title: Why Florida Republicans are "white-knuckled" about Tuesday
events.summary: Florida Republicans aren't panicking about sluggish turnout for the midterms , but in the words of one GOP elder: "We're white-knuckled." Why it matters: Florida once looked like a much safer Republican bet for the midterms. Losing any statewide race would stun and embarrass its elite Republican residents, starting with President Trump . "I don't necessarily want to be the bearer of bad news, but I don't think the turnout is as strong as we would like to see," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis fretted last week. The biggest GOP concern is U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds' campaign for governor, though most polls show him narrowly leading Democrat David Jolly. Donalds has raised $176 million; Jolly just $28 million. Zoom in : The GOP's jitters are rooted in early turnout data. Republicans led Democrats in early ballots cast by 3 percentage points as of Sunday morning. That's much lower than in the past two general elections — and it's despite a much-bigger Republican registration advantage over Democrats: 11 points. Republican turnout is weakest in parts of the conservative Panhandle and rural North Florida, including many of the 17 counties Donalds lost in the Republican primary. In those 17 counties, GOP turnout is 3.2 points below 2022, compared with 1.1 points below in counties that Donalds won, University of Florida political scientist Michael McDonald found. Between the lines: Republican turnout is made up of more habitual voters, while Democrats and independents are banking ballots from people who don't always show up. That could benefit Jolly if polls underestimate those voters. Democrats already have surpassed their entire 2022 early and mail-in vote totals in 15 counties, compared with four counties for Republicans. Nearly every poll shows independent voters favoring Democrats by double digits, so Republicans need a heavy turnout advantage. About two-thirds of Florida voters typically cast ballots before Election Day, making the early and absentee margins critical. Among voters who waited until Election Day in 2022, roughly 60,000 more Republicans than Democrats have already voted this year, Democratic strategist Steve Schale found. That means some voters Republicans rely on for their Election Day surge in 2022 have already cast ballots — potentially shrinking their usual Tuesday advantage. The big picture: Donalds could enter Election Day down by as many as 500,000 votes, according to internal Democratic and GOP estimates shared with Axios. To overcome that deficit, Donalds could need to win the Election Day vote by a 2:1 ratio. It's a tall order, but Republicans have delivered huge Election Day margins before, notably in 2022. By the numbers: Black and Hispanic voters, who are leaning more toward Democrats this year in Florida polling, are making up a growing share of the early electorate, accounting for a larger share of newly reported ballots. Across racial and ethnic groups , Democrats are voting at higher rates than Republicans. Among active Democrats, 50% of white voters, 39% of Black voters and 34% of Hispanic voters have cast ballots, compared with 35%, 21% and 28% of Republicans in those groups. Young voters show another substantial gap: 25% of active registered Democrats under 30 have voted, compared with just 9% of Republicans. Yes, but: Florida Republicans still outnumber Democrats by 1.5 million, with a larger pool of reliable voters. Florida's GOP is better funded and organized than the state's Democratic Party. Even in 2018, when a blue wave flooded the nation, Florida's red wall held. By razor-thin margins, DeSantis won the governor's race and then-Gov. Rick Scott was elected to the Senate. "We always win Election Day, and we know how to do this," state GOP chair Evan Power said. "A lot of the nerves here are because the last time we had a close election was eight years ago, and people forgot what a close election looks like here." Zoom out: Republicans face a different political climate than in 2018, when Trump was ascendant in the GOP and the economy was improving. Today, Trump's approval with Republicans is lower and gas prices are higher. Republicans worry they could lose 10 to 15 state House seats, jeopardizing their supermajority. In Miami's 27th Congressional District, voting patterns are flashing warning signs for Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar in her race against Democrat Eliot Rodriguez. As for the three statewide Florida Cabinet posts (attorney general, chief financial officer, agriculture commissioner), "no one should feel safe, but there's reason to feel OK," said a Republican involved one of the races. Nationwide , the atmosphere is so bad for the GOP that Texas, Kansas, Alaska, Ohio and even South Carolina look in play. Behind the scenes : The early voting data sent a chill through Republican ranks in Tallahassee last week: What if the polling assumptions about stronger Republican turnout were wrong? "Just a few weeks ago I didn't think I would be feeling like this," a top consultant for one of the statewide races said. "It's not panic. At least not yet." Republicans remain more confident about Sen. Ashley Moody's race against state Rep. Angie Nixon, who's widely seen as too progressive for the red state's voters. Friction point: Republicans have quietly fretted that racism could hurt Donalds just as it may hurt Nixon. Donalds and Nixon are Black. "We're about to run the biggest experiment to see how racist some of our voters are," a longtime Republican consultant said, calling the counties Donalds lost "more culturally Confederate" than the rest of Florida. "During the primary, he underperformed in the Panhandle and if people think skin color didn't play a role in that, they are naive," MAGA influencer Laura Loomer posted Saturday on X.

events.title: Opec+ holds December oil output targets steady as Iran war disrupts supply
events.summary: The Opec+ bloc kept its oil production targets unchanged for December, maintaining September's required production levels as the war in the Middle East continues to disrupt global energy supplies. The group's seven core members – Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Algeria, Russia and Kazakhstan – decided during a meeting on Sunday to “maintain September 2026 required production for December 2026” after reviewing global market conditions and the outlook, a statement said. The group finished unwinding 1.65 million barrels per day of voluntary cuts from 2023 in September. It is keeping a further two million bpd of cuts, agreed to in 2022, in place until the end of the year. It is also reviewing members' production capacity to set quotas for 2027. The seven Opec+ countries “reiterated their collective commitment to achieve full conformity with the Declaration of Co-operation”, the statement said. The producers will continue holding monthly meetings to review market conditions, with the next scheduled for November 29. The joint production targets for the seven members amount to about 31 million bpd for December, unchanged from September, October and November. Saudi Arabia has the largest allocation at 10.478 million bpd, followed by Russia at 9.949 million bpd and Iraq at 4.431 million bpd. Kuwait's target is 2.676 million bpd, Kazakhstan's at 1.628 million bpd, Algeria's at 1.007 million bpd and Oman's at 841,000 bpd. But most members are producing below their targets because of the war. The group reaffirmed its commitment to market stability, although the statement did not announce any additional production adjustments or provide a timetable for increasing output. The Strait of Hormuz , which carried about a fifth of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas, has been effectively shut since fighting between the US and Iran started on February 28. The conflict, now in its ninth month, has no clear endgame in sight. Fears are growing that the US might resume hostilities on Iran after the midterm elections, with President Donald Trump saying the war “will be wrapped up soon”. Israeli media reports, meanwhile, claim that the country's military is preparing for the possibility of another round of conflict with Iran, although Mr Trump has yet to make a decision on launching a new military campaign. Attacks on commercial vessels in and around the strait reached their highest monthly level in the Iran-US war in October, with at least 35 attacks reported, according to maritime incident tracking data. Increasing attacks from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia have also added to regional tension. On Saturday, Riyadh said its air defences had “intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone” in the Saudi capital. That followed dozens of Houthi strikes on Saudi assets over the past weeks. Oil prices settled up more than 2 per cent on Friday to hit six-month highs and post a fourth straight monthly gain. Brent was up 2.4 per cent at $117.64 a barrel, after briefly touching $118, while West Texas Intermediate gained 2.08 per cent to settle at $104.12 a barrel.

events.title: Trump's election probes find an opening in Georgia
events.summary: On the eve of midterms, President Trump is facing setbacks left and right in his push to investigate alleged election fraud . But in Georgia, he has an opening. Why it matters: Six years ago, Georgia was at the epicenter of Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election. Now the state's own election board has invited his administration to investigate its voting system. Georgia features two high-stakes statewide campaigns: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) against Rep. Mike Collins (R) for Senate, and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) against businessman Rick Jackson (R) for governor. The big picture: The Justice Department disclosed in court on Friday that the administration has sent letters to officials in California, Washington, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Nevada, asking some states to segregate mail-in ballots from suspected noncitizen voters. A federal judge on Friday issued an emergency order that blocks federal officials from threatening to charge election officials who count ballots from voters the DOJ claims are ineligible. In October, a federal judge restricted the Department of Homeland Security's investigations into suspected noncitizen voters. But Georgia is different . "We've managed with duct tape and bubble gum to be able to bootstrap our way through one last round, but that's not a way of running elections," a Georgia election official told Axios. Georgia's State Election Board asked the Justice and Homeland Security departments to review and potentially investigate the state's voting system and handling of election data. The Sept. 30 letter cited outdated software, threats to ballot secrecy and QR-code ballots it says may violate the Help America Vote Act. A DOJ spokesperson said in response to the letter: "We take seriously allegations that election officials have failed to adequately maintain election equipment and otherwise comply with federal law. We are evaluating the request and will investigate and, if appropriate, bring an enforcement action consistent with federal law." The other side: Georgia State Election Board Chair John Fevrier , appointed by Gov. Brian Kemp (R), opposed the letter and told Axios that a majority of the board now believes it "far exceeded what was in the resolution." Michon Lindstrom, senior director of communications for Georgia's secretary of state, said: "It's unfortunate that the state election board sought to inject chaos in the 11th hour of the election." In 2020, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger rebuffed Trump's efforts to overturn Georgia's presidential election results. Friction point: Georgia has spent years debating how to address vulnerabilities in its voting system. The secretary of state's office said Georgia's machines haven't been updated since they were purchased in 2019. The state said it's starting a procurement process for new machines for the next election cycle. The state's legislature passed a law in 2024 to move away from a QR-code ballot system to hand-marked paper ballots. This transition was supposed to be implemented by this July, but lawmakers passed a deadline extension. A software glitch on the state's tabulators that could impact ballot secrecy has been known to the state since 2022. But an available fix hasn't been installed. Between the lines: "There are no clean hands in this," the Georgia election official told Axios. "The secretary of state could have fought harder for the funding... [The] legislature could have funded it when the secretary of state asked for it. But ... they all have pissed each other off so much." In 2025, Raffensperger urged lawmakers to reconsider a $47 million voting-machine upgrade, proposing a software update costing less than $15 million or delaying any purchases until the existing contract expired. In 2026, Raffensperger told legislators that there wasn't money for any election upgrades. No upgrades were funded. What they're saying: "Money allocation is ultimately the function of the legislative branch, and any questions about why they did not deem it necessary to fund 'election infrastructure improvements' should be directed to the legislature," Lindstrom told Axios. Fevrier told Axios: "I blame the legislature. If the legislature thought it was an issue, they would have fixed it, and they didn't." The Department of Homeland Security didn't respond to Axios's request for comment. The bottom line: The Trump administration suffered a setback in California on Friday, with an appeals court rejecting its demand to set aside mail-in ballots. But the dispute in Georgia shows that the fight over federal intervention in state elections is far from over.

events.title: Dems and GOP quietly bankroll dozens of third-party spoilers
events.summary: More than 40 third-party candidates in pivotal House and Senate races across the country are receiving support from outside super PACs, many of which have ties to the two major parties, an Axios analysis has found. Why it matters: The sums being thrown around, which total more than $16.5 million, are far greater than virtually any of those candidates have raised or spent on their own. The super PACs have spent an average of $375,000 more than the third-party candidates they are supporting. More than half of the 43 candidates haven't filed any financial paperwork with the Federal Election Commission. While it is a comparative drop in the bucket for a midterm that has already seen billions in ad spending nationally, the money will likely play an outsized role in races that are set to be decided by razor-thin margins. Those races, in turn, will help decide the balance of power in Congress next year. Data: Federal Election Commission; Note: Heikes is a self-identified Republican, but Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is the Republican Party-endorsed candidate in the race; Table: Andrew Solender/Axios The top spenders nationwide have been a pair of obscure groups which, like many of the other "pop-up" super PACs in this story, were formed this month and therefore won't have to disclose their donors until after Election Day. Buckeye Freedom PAC has reported spending more than $3.8 million on ads in Ohio's U.S. Senate election supporting Libertarian Bill Redpath and opposing Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who is in a tight race with Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown. Alaska Values PAC has disclosed spending $3.8 million backing Gerald Heikes, a self-identified Republican running on Alaska's ranked-choice U.S. Senate ballot with Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. Between the lines : Third-party candidates in Alaska are facing national scrutiny after the New York Times reported that Heikes and another self-proclaimed Republican on the ballot, Dan J. Sullivan, were recruited into the race. Republicans have long accused Dan J. Sullivan of being a spoiler meant to siphon votes from the incumbent senator by confusing voters with their shared name. The "double-Dan" case is unique in that it reportedly included direct involvement from a political operative working with the Peltola campaign, who allegedly used pseudonyms as part of the effort. The Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied recruiting any third-party candidates into the race. Enough Promises Ohio is another huge spender, putting $2.6 million behind supporting independent Senate candidate Greg Levy in Ohio, per its FEC filings. The group's mailers encourage voters to "join the revolution" and "send a worker to the Senate" by voting for Levy, a member of the Party for Socialism and Liberation who has disavowed the support . The group's FEC filings offer hints as to its partisan affiliation: It shares vendors with several Republican candidates and groups including MAGA Inc. Principled Patriots PAC has reported spending over $600,000 on digital ads supporting right-leaning and Libertarian candidates in 15 battleground House and Senate races, according to FEC filings and Google's Ad Transparency Center. The group's vendor for its ads, Movement Labs LLC, has primarily serviced Democratic clients, filings show. It touts itself as working for "progressive change everywhere." "Washington is spending money it doesn't have. Republicans raised the debt limit $5 trillion. Darline Graham is one of them," says a Principled Patriots' ad in the South Carolina Senate race — part of a $110,000 ad buy. Constitution Party candidate Mark Hackett, the ad continues, "lives here, works here, owes party bosses nothing. Not a Democrat, not a Republican. He'll end the waste, cut spending." "I have spent no money and asked for no help in my campaign," Hackett said in an email to Axios. He said of the PACs supporting him: "I still don't know who they are." Hackett said he will "remain" in the race and suggested he is not concerned about being a spoiler for Graham "since neither Graham nor Andrews have made defunding the wars in Ukraine and Iran an issue." Progressive Champions PAC , a group Republicans used to boost their preferred Democratic primary candidates in several battleground House districts, has quietly resurfaced in a pair of hotly contested general elections. In Virginia's 2nd District, the group has reported spending over $480,000 supporting independent Matthew Baker. One of its mailers, reported by the New York Times , highlights Baker's liberal positions on issues such as abortion. Baker, a self-described "radical centrist," told the Times the mailer makes him "mad as hell" because the group is "only telling half my story" and "trying to use me to trick people." Progressive Champions PAC also spent more than $500,000 on texts and mailers boosting Green Party candidate Shafina Barnett in Michigan's 4th District, according to filings. Our Heritage Matters has reported spending nearly $3.7 million to support third-party candidates in more than two dozen House and Senate races, per FEC filings. Most of the candidates are Libertarians. The group's mailers advertise the candidates as the conservative alternative to the Republicans in each race. Much of its spending is also listed in FEC filings as being in opposition to the GOP candidates. The Nebraska Senate race has seen easily the most separate instances of super PACs boosting third-party candidates — somewhat ironically, given Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts' chief rival is independent Dan Osborn. Outside groups have reported spending more than $450,000 supporting Robin Richards of the Working People Party and $115,000 boosting Mike Marvin of the Legal Marijuana Now Party. The group supporting Marvin, High Time Nebraska, shares a treasurer with a Republican House candidate in California, per filings. One of the other candidates, Chuck Conboy of the America First Party, is supported by Principled Patriots PAC. The intrigue: Axios reported last week that the House Democratic campaign arm put messaging guidance on its website laying out how to boost third-party candidates in several key races. It may have come in handy. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's page on VA-02 — known as a redbox — says white, college-educated men should see that Matthew Baker is "a staunch supporter of the 2nd amendment." Our Heritage Matters began spending for Baker on Wednesday with an initial $18,000 digital ad buy, according to filings. The redbox on Nevada's 2nd District says Republican women in the district should be informed Independent American Party candidate Lynn Chapman "has spent decades fighting for conservative values." events.title: Hundreds of thousands of young protesters take to the streets across France
events.summary: Thousands of young protesters take to the streets of France for a third weekend. PARIS -- Hundreds of thousands of protesters inspired by frustrated high school students took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education. Youth-led protests were also held elsewhere in Europe , including in Germany and Portugal. France's protests were overwhelmingly peaceful, with whimsical Halloween costumes lightening the mood, but gatherings in Paris and other cities ended in clouds of tear gas and scattered fires set by small groups on the margins. About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country after French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Paris marches were rerouted to the capital’s edge to protect stores, government buildings and touristed areas in the city center. France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew 550,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers’ turnout estimates are higher. Authorities in France reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred marches the previous two Saturdays. In the main Paris march, each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living. Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where “there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats.” An information technology worker protested in solidarity with the students and her mother, who was struggling with a minimum wage job. A gray-haired woman carried a sign reading ‘’The Old are Fed Up Too.'' Halloween costumes reflected the mood. Cléo Farenc, a 30-year-old gallery assistant, came dressed as a beheaded Marie-Antoinette. “It’s about embodying a figure of power who was brought down by the people,” she said. “It’s a very strong symbol in French culture.'' The rallies in France were started last month by high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at the leadership of President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands. On Saturday, the crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, avenues that ring the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city. Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell. Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris. While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Police use tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries . Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement. In Germany, a youth initiative called “Gen Z regelt” — roughly “Gen Z’s got this” — rallied in more than 30 cities “for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life,” and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
