events.title: Fight over race questions intensifies ahead of 2030 Census deadline
events.summary: A fight over whether the 2030 Census should stop asking about race and ethnicity has drawn more than 100,000 public comments, according to advocates tracking the federal docket. Why it matters: The change could weaken the nation's most complete snapshot of race — data used in civil rights enforcement and redistricting — just as America grows more multiracial. Catch up quick: The Census Bureau proposed in September to stop asking Americans about their race and ethnicity on the once-a-decade census. The Census Bureau says a shorter form could encourage more people to respond, while greater use of existing government records would reduce the need to ask certain questions. The proposal wouldn't end federal race data: Census could obtain demographic data from government records and other sources and ask about race and ethnicity on the American Community Survey (ACS) and other surveys. But civil rights advocates say that would give the federal government more power to determine people's race and ethnicity , rather than the respondents, leading to inaccurate data. State of play: Census extended the comment deadline from Oct. 13 to Nov. 2. An outside analysis of 52,424 published comments through Oct. 16 found 86% opposed the overall proposal, while 88% addressed removing race and ethnicity questions. This week, an advocacy alert citing Regulations.gov said the docket had topped 108,000 submissions . These comments are not meant to be treated like a survey or poll, but show that people who feel strongly enough to comment tend to be opposed. What they're saying: "If you've ever fought for political maps or explained why race or data matters...it is vital that you tell the Census Bureau what losing that information is going to mean to your work and to your community," said NC Counts Coalition executive director Stacey Carless. The big picture: Race has appeared in some form in every decennial census since 1790, but how Americans identify themselves has changed dramatically. The number of Americans reporting two or more races rose from 9 million, or 2.9%, in 2010 to 33.8 million, or 10.2%, in 2020. Census says improvements in question design, coding and processing accounted for a substantial share of that increase, along with demographic change. The bottom line: The Census Bureau hasn't explained how it would produce detailed racial population counts without asking Americans to identify themselves. The agency already combines information from government and other records to determine people's race and ethnicity when working with administrative data. But its proposal doesn't say whether that system would replace people's own answers in the 2030 Census.

events.title: Hackers pushed freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to 122 degrees. Now the Pentagon is asking whether the same thing hit U.S. military bases
events.summary: The Pentagon’s criminal investigators are leading a joint probe into freezer failures at U.S. military commissaries in August, and four officials told Reuters this week that the Pentagon is treating them as a possible cyberattack. It comes weeks after hackers took over the refrigeration controls at hundreds of French supermarkets overnight. There’s no proof yet that the two are connected, or that the commissary failures were a hack at all. But the same kind of target experienced the same type of outage within about two months of each other, which is enough to raise the eyebrows of Christopher Whyte, an associate professor of homeland security and emergency preparedness at Virginia Commonwealth University.  “You’d be silly not to be suspicious,” he told Fortune .  For the stores, the damage can’t be undone: Two supermarkets, Intermarché and E.Leclerc, reported an estimated €270,000, about $300,000, in combined stock damages , according to local news outlet Sud Ouest . “Refrigerators give an attacker a weirdly direct route…to financial loss that’s, with cyber, unusually irreversible,” Whyte said. “You can’t unspoil food or other products from these freezers. It’s just euros and dollars down the drain.” Napoleon Bonaparte, the French military general who met an infamous defeat in Russia after overextending his supplies, is credited as saying, “An army marches on its stomach.” The aphorism, also attributed to Prussian King Frederick the Great, refers to the necessity of food and basic logistics for a military campaign’s success. It’s not surprising, then, that refrigeration may be the next frontier of widespread cybersecurity attacks. Earlier this month, hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets , raising the temperature of their refrigeration and freezer systems overnight to more than 122 degrees Fahrenheit, spoiling food and causing fires. The affected grocery stores included 80 Carrefour locations, about two dozen Monoprix stores, and 150 Intermarché stores. The Paris prosecutor’s office called the outages a “large-scale” attack. Similar outages were reported across Europe. The Pentagon’s investigation—and a partnership with French authorities to probe the French supermarket outages—followed a series of refrigerator outages across several U.S. military commissaries in August. More than a half-dozen commissaries were impacted by the disruption, including in Fort Irwin, California; Holloman Air Force Base, New Mexico; Naval Station Newport, Rhode Island; Little Rock Air Force Base, Arkansas; F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyoming; Robins Air Force Base, Georgia; and Fort Huachuca, Arizona, the Military Times reported at the time. Commissaries typically offer subsidized goods to those living on military bases, costing about 25% less than civilian grocery stores. The Substack Signal and Silence was first to report the possibility that outages were a result of a hack. The Pentagon confirmed the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, the criminal investigative arm of the agency’s Office of Inspector General, is leading a joint investigation into the outages, but said in a statement to Fortune , “For security reasons, we do not comment on ongoing law-enforcement investigations.” Cyber incidents, particularly targeting corporations and government agencies, have been on the rise over the last two decades, including more than a dozen major attacks this September alone, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Cybercrime is projected to cost the global economy $10.8 trillion this year, according to Cybersecurity Ventures, more than triple the $3 trillion it cost in 2015. Rapidly developing AI capabilities have made hacking more sophisticated, while the number of appliances attached to the internet have created more targets. The cold, hard truths of the new era of cyberattacks Cybersecurity experts believe it was only a matter of time before practical appliances like refrigerators became the target of cyberattacks. Nadiya Kostyuk, an assistant professor at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy and Technology, told Fortune it was an ongoing joke among her cohort to discuss when their home fridges would be hacked. “I’m surprised that it took so long,” she said. “A lot of these devices have a lot of really cool features, but the security is not the first priority for them,” Kostyuk added. “Hopefully future inventions will come with more security in mind when it comes to the design, and the existing ones also will be revisited to incorporate all the potential vectors of the cyberattacks.” In the case of the outages in France, the vulnerabilities originated from access to the Danish-made Danfoss AK-SM, AK-SC series remote controllers for refrigeration systems, as well as Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb, according to an alert bulletin published by French authorities, and affected units were running outdated firmware hackers could exploit by accessing the devices through the internet. More broadly, refrigeration systems present vulnerabilities because many of the devices are similar across commercial chains, and identifying an exposure in one means hackers can generalize that exposure to other systems, according to Whyte. Beyond the accessibility of refrigeration systems, the consequences of outages yield practical consequences, which can make them appealing targets for hackers who want to make a statement or take a financial jab at a victim. The U.S. military theater is vulnerable to emblematic attacks on supply stores as well. The U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln , which had a record deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea before it docked in San Diego earlier this month, became a symbol of weaknesses in U.S. military amenities. During its Iran war mission, the crew faced poor morale and mental health, including as a result of food and hygiene supply shortage. Liberté, égalité, réfrigérite  Gregory Winger, an assistant professor of international relations and cybersecurity at University of Maryland, Baltimore County, told Fortune that actors from Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea typically rely on cyber incidents that appear random but are actually connected.  Allied countries have built partnerships for the express reason of identifying and sharing the techniques of hackers, particularly NATO’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) in Mons, Belgium, which is the body’s cybersecurity headquarters. Significant attacks can trigger NATO’s invocation of Article 5 , a collective defense that defines a threat against one country as an effective threat against the body’s 32 members. events.title: Dubai's Dewa steps up global expansion push with Shanghai Electric deal
events.summary: The international arm of Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (Dewa) has signed an agreement with China's Shanghai Electric to explore energy and water investments in global markets, as the emirate seeks to expand its footprint in the international utilities sector. The deal covers potential projects in solar and wind energy, battery storage, desalination, green hydrogen and conventional power generation, as well as electricity transmission and distribution. The agreement establishes a framework for identifying, evaluating, developing and investing in projects, including participation in international tenders. “At Dewa International, we are committed to expanding our presence in global markets and building strategic partnerships that leverage Dubai's pioneering expertise in the utilities sector and the global capabilities of our partners,” said Saeed Mohammed Al Tayer, managing director and chief executive of Dewa and chairman of Dewa International. The agreement was signed by Waleed bin Salman, vice chairman of Dewa International, and Shen Bing, president of Shanghai Electric Power Generation Group. The partnership marks another step in Dewa International's efforts to establish itself as a global energy and water infrastructure developer. DEWA International, the global arm of DEWA, has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Shanghai Electric to explore opportunities to develop and invest in energy, water and infrastructure projects across global markets. In the presence of HE Saeed Mohammed Al Tayer, MD & CEO of DEWA and Chairman of DEWA International, he MoU was signed by Waleed bin Salman, Executive Vice President of Business Development and Excellence at DEWA and Vice Chairman of DEWA International, and Zhao Hui, Managing Director of Shanghai Electric Group in the Middle East and North Africa. #DEWANews — DEWA | Official Page (@DEWAOfficial) November 1, 2026 Dewa established its international subsidiary in June to pursue overseas projects and partnerships, drawing on Dubai's experience in developing large-scale electricity, water and clean energy infrastructure. The company aims to work with governments, developers and financial institutions to identify investment opportunities and participate in projects outside the UAE. At its launch, Mr Al Tayer said global demand for energy and water infrastructure was expected to exceed $20 trillion by 2035, presenting substantial opportunities for international expansion. Dewa also operates the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park, one of the world's largest solar developments, which has helped establish Dubai's expertise in renewable energy. The utility is continuing to expand its renewable energy capacity, with plans for the seventh phase of the solar park, incorporating large-scale battery storage. Shanghai Electric, a major Chinese power equipment and engineering company, brings experience in developing and supplying technology for large-scale energy projects. The two companies have previously worked together on the fourth phase of Dubai's Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park, a Dh15.78 billion project. The latest agreement also covers potential co-operation in green ammonia, concentrated solar power and equipment supply for the oil and gas sector. Dewa has previously invested in green hydrogen production , including a pilot facility developed with Siemens Energy at the solar park. However, the partnership remains exploratory, with no specific overseas projects, investment commitments or development timelines announced.

events.title: UAE updates e-invoicing penalties for businesses
events.summary: The UAE Ministry of Finance has issued new rules to update fines for e-invoicing to support businesses and reduce duplicate penalties. Structured invoices are issued and exchanged digitally between a supplier and a buyer and reported online to the UAE Federal Tax Authority . The latest amendments – following a cabinet decision – aim to provide businesses with greater regulatory certainty and reduce administrative burdens by introducing more proportionate fines. A penalty of Dh5,000 ($1,360) applies for an initial accounting violation, followed by Dh5,000 for each month during which the non-compliance continues. Fines are subject to a maximum aggregate penalty of Dh50,000 for these breaches in any 12 consecutive months. Administrative penalties for the issuer's or the recipient's failure to notify the authority of a system failure have also been removed. This change aims to ensure that penalties are applied more appropriately, taking into account the respective responsibilities of the different parties within the e-invoicing system. The changes support the UAE's wider digital transformation objectives and reinforce the country's commitment to implementing a modern tax administration framework. A pilot phase and voluntary e-invoicing adoption launched in July, with a full introduction planned for October 1, 2027.

events.title: Binance to resume withdrawals after covering 95% of $6.3bn crypto heist
events.summary: Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, is preparing to resume cryptocurrency withdrawals in phases after covering 95 per cent of the $6.3 billion in tokens stolen in what has been described as the world’s largest digital heist . The first phase of withdrawals is scheduled to begin between 6am and 9am GMT on Sunday, covering Bitcoin , ether, BNB, Solana, XRP, dogecoin and other digital assets, Binance said in a post on X late on Saturday. The remaining 5 per cent of the stolen tokens consists of less liquid assets that may take longer to source in the required amounts, the exchange said. https://t.co/pBJaht1UGV — Binance (@binance) November 1, 2026 “Since the incident, our teams have taken precautionary measures to safeguard the platform, conducted security assessments, and worked to verify the readiness of affected services. We aim to restore withdrawals progressively as we complete security and readiness checks,” the Binance post on X said. “Deposit services remain open and are not affected by the incident,” it added. The resumption follows security assessments and precautionary measures taken by the cryptocurrency exchange to safeguard its platform and verify the readiness of affected services. Binance said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than passing the losses on to customers. “As we have said throughout this incident: user funds remain safe,” Binance said. The FBI on Saturday attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit. Members of the group were observed by law enforcement converting the stolen assets into ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected further laundering through related technology. Binance said on X that withdrawals were temporarily suspended as a precaution, “while our teams worked to contain the incident loss, assess its impact, restore affected services and complete security checks”. “We did not take this decision lightly. We understand how important reliable access to withdrawals is for our users. However, our priority was to protect users, safeguard the platform, and complete the necessary security checks before restoring services.” Despite its reputation for robust security, the cryptocurrency industry has suffered several high-profile hacks and collapses over the years. In 2014, the Mt. Gox exchange, then the world's largest Bitcoin trading platform, collapsed after hackers stole hundreds of thousands of Bitcoins, alongside a series of technical and operational failures. Eight years later, FTX, then the world's second-largest cryptocurrency exchange, imploded amid revelations of fraud and the misuse of customer funds. Its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried , was later sentenced to 25 years in prison. More recently, the FBI attributed a $1.5 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit to North Korea, highlighting the persistent security threats facing the industry.

events.title: FBI blames North Korea for stolen billions from Binance in biggest hack in history
events.summary: FBI sys attack was tied to an entity known as TraderTraitor. New York -- The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history , was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday. The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins. It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum. The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and “instant swap services.” Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, President Donald Trump suggested investigators weren't yet certain that North Korea was involved. “I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it," Trump said of the case. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea.” Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was. events.title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
events.summary: Airbnb host Lisa says her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests When Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess. Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage. But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden. "It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes. She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher. Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her property and fears that guests leaving more mess could mean increasing costs But Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site. The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests. Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests. The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins. "We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all." While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal. "It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect." Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides". Krissi says there's a difference between being a respectful guest and being expected to help run the business you've just paid to stay in During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area. "I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says. For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests". Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine. While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says. "If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business." Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two. His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it". Anthony and his husband used to list five of their 12 cabins in North Yorkshire on Airbnb... ... but will now list just two in light of the new rules He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals. "It's common sense and common decency," he says. His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according to data from AirROI , external . Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests. Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect.

events.title: Judge tosses Trump lawsuit against WSJ, Murdoch over Epstein story
events.summary: A federal judge on Saturday threw out President Trump's lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over the paper's reporting on Trump's ties to Jeffrey Epstein, Why it matters: It's the second time this year courts have blocked Trump's efforts to sue the paper over stories about his relationship with the disgraced financier. As with the first one, courts found the president did not clear the high bar set by New York Times vs. Sullivan for allegations of defamation in critical reporting on public figures. Driving the news: Judge Darrin Gayles of the southern district of Florida issued the 20-page ruling Saturday afternoon, finding that Trump failed to prove the paper acted with "actual malice" by reporting on his links to Epstein. Gayles dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice, meaning it can't be refiled. "We're pleased with the court's decision," a representative of WSJ parent Dow Jones said. Zoom out: Trump first filed suit against the paper and Murdoch in July 2025, seeking $20 billion in damages. At issue was a story describing a "bawdy" letter, bearing Trump's name and given to Epstein for his birthday, which the president insisted was fake. Gayles tossed the initial suit last April, but allowed Trump to file an amended complaint — which was the one he dismissed Saturday, saying it fell short of the burden to prove the paper acted maliciously. What they're saying: "Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false," Gayles wrote. For the record: " President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions," a spokesman for his legal team said in a statement. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details. Sara Fischer contributed.

events.title: Tusk defends suspension of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal president as protesters gather again
events.summary: Prime Minister Donald Tusk says his government is acting to restore judicial independence in Poland WARSAW, Poland -- Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Saturday that his government would press ahead with efforts to restore the independence of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, as hundreds of protesters gathered for a second night against the suspension of the court’s president . The pro-European government said the suspension is necessary to restore judicial independence, while critics from the opposition have likened it to a “coup d’etat.” President Karol Nawrocki — who opposes the pro-European government — turned back his plane during a flight to Senegal on Friday evening and returned home. On Friday night, he made his way to the Constitutional Tribunal despite the chaos and said he helped the suspended court president enter the building. Police said they detained three protesters on Friday night after some threw objects at officers and tried to break through the security fence around the court. The dispute over the long-embattled Constitutional Tribunal is likely to deepen political polarization in Poland a year before a parliamentary election, further intensifying the standoff between the pro-European government and the national-conservative opposition party Law and Justice , or PiS. Critics in Poland and the European Union accuse PiS, which led the country between 2015 and 2023, of imposing political control over key judicial institutions. Reforms introduced under the PiS government prompted the EU to impose fines on Poland. Tusk’s pro-European government came to power in 2023 with a promise to restore the independence of the judiciary. Since then, its efforts have been blocked by vetoes from two successive presidents aligned with PiS, including Nawrocki. “Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” Tusk had earlier pledged that his government would ensure the tribunal was again staffed with lawfully appointed judges while acknowledging that his methods may not be to everyone’s liking. The functioning of the Constitutional Tribunal had been impaired for years. The Court of Justice of the European Union, the EU's top court, had said it was no longer an impartial court after PiS appointments. Even after Tusk took power, efforts to balance the court were hampered by Nawrocki and the tribunal's president, Bogdan Święczkowski. On Friday evening, the Constitutional Tribunal’s website announced the suspension of Święczkowski. Shortly after, the protesters — including PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński and far-right politicians — began rallying outside the building. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say The government says Święczkowski repeatedly broke the law and jeopardized the tribunal’s work. Święczkowski became head of the court under the former PiS government. Tusk has accused him of blocking judges elected by the parliamentary majority from taking up their posts at the tribunal. “Since last night, we’re dealing with a massive constitutional crisis in Poland, the result of an illegal, forceful attempt to take over an important institution,” Marcin Przydacz, a top aide to the Polish president, told The Associated Press. Przydacz said that the president had invited all parliamentary parties to talks on Saturday in an effort to defuse tensions and find a solution to the crisis. The government is a broad coalition made up of Tusk's centrist Civic Coalition, the Left, and two more conservative groupings, Poland 2050 and the Polish People’s Party, or PSL. Representatives of Poland 2050 and PSL, along with several opposition parties, met with Nawrocki on Saturday, while Tusk didn't attend. The president’s camp is hoping that the crisis surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal will erode Tusk’s parliamentary majority. “Everything depends on those political parties who supported Donald Tusk so far,” Przydacz said. Speaking on Saturday night, Tusk compared PiS to a man who steals an elderly woman’s purse and then claims to be the victim when police catch him and take it back. PiS' response to the suspension of Święczkowski, including the attempts to forcefully enter the Tribunal on Friday, represents “another stage in the process of destroying the rule of law in Poland” by PiS and the president, Tusk said. events.title: D.C., Virginia sue to block Trump's 250-foot arch
events.summary: The governments of Washington D.C. and Virginia asked a federal court to block construction of President Trump's planned " triumphal arch ," claiming it's unlawfully tall and would snarl traffic for years. Why it matters: It's a last-minute gambit to stop construction before the multi-year project begins, potentially as soon as this coming week. What they're saying: " This project is flagrantly unlawful," the two governments said in a Saturday filing in D.C. federal court, first reported by the Washington Post. "During the three-year period of construction, the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges," they argue. They further claim that the defendants — the National Park Service and the Interior Department — have rushed the project without the proper consultations. The city and state are asking a judge to issue injunctions to stop any site preparation or construction on the project. Zoom out: The proposed 250-foot arch would be one of the largest such monuments in the world, sparking concerns that it could interfere with other national symbols, block views and even complicate landings for pilots at nearby airports. (The FAA found otherwise.) The Park Service's own August report indicated the construction of the arch would have adverse effects on nearby monuments and landmarks. The other side: The administration has argued it will be a major tourist attraction — but also vital to national security, serving as a base for snipers and drones. "The Triumphal Arch in Memorial Circle is going to be one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. What's next: A federal judge held a hearing Friday on a separate challenge to the arch, and indicated she may block construction at least temporarily.

events.title: Binance covers 90 per cent of assets stolen in $6.3 billion hack
events.summary: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said on ​Saturday that ​it has ​been able to cover ⁠90 per cent of the amount stolen in ⁠ an unprecedented hack ​on its platform. In an update on its website, Binance said the amount to cover the stolen funds would come out of three sources: a partial use of the Secure Asset Fund for Users; a portion of the Futures insurance fund; and Binance's own corporate treasury. Users were also invited to check the balances of the first two funds online. The outstanding 10 per cent consists of tokens that are less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. The exchange said withdrawal services for users are expected to resume on November 1, with more details to be confirmed later. What happened? Binance Holdings, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, lost an estimated $6.3 billion to hackers early on Friday, in what has been described as the single biggest theft of cryptocurrency on record, exceeding the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in February 2025 . Funds began leaving Binance's hot wallets, which are connected to the internet to process customer withdrawals, at about 12.24am UAE time on October 30. A single transaction moved about 167,464 Ether, worth about $388 million, along with 63 other tokens, to an address created hours earlier and funded through the Tornado Cash mixing service, according to Etherscan data. Bitcoin shares plunged after the news, and have now fallen to about $76,450, data from CoinMarketCap shows.

events.title: Rising health costs and coverage changes are big concerns for older adults as Election Day nears
events.summary: Rising healthcare costs are a major concern for older Americans, and it's affecting their finances and political priorities WASHINGTON -- Barbara Weigand could not have prepared more for retirement. She stayed healthy and saved diligently for years. This year, though, a shoulder surgery and a bladder cancer diagnosis have really tested her finances. She recently withdrew $4,000 from her retirement account to cover medical expenses associated with her cancer treatment. “On my monthly income, I would not be able to afford my new medical expenses,” says Weigand, 83, who lives in North Canton, Ohio. She is currently on a Medicare Advantage plan and was searching for new coverage as Medicare's open enrollment period began in October. For older adults in the United States, the rising cost of healthcare is hitting where it hurts most — their pocketbooks. With Medicare costs, prescription drug prices and long-term care expenses weighing on household budgets, their concerns could carry significant political weight heading into Tuesday's elections. Weigand is part of a reliable voting bloc; 83% of voters over age 50 say they’re extremely motivated to vote in the midterms, according to an AARP poll conducted in early October. Their concerns over managing healthcare costs put the issue of affordability squarely in the spotlight. Here are some of their biggest healthcare concerns — and how Weigand sees them. THE SITUATION: Open enrollment for Medicare plans began in mid-October, and enrollees are facing a slew of changes that will go into effect in 2027. During the enrollment period, people are considering higher Part D out-of-pocket caps, the end of temporary federal Part D premium subsidies , and new drug price negotiations. Additionally, in some states, insurers put caps on the number of people who can enroll in Advantage plans, pulling out of markets or eliminating plans that people have come to rely on. Juliette Cubanski, director of KFF’s program on Medicare policy, told The Associated Press that the open enrollment period offers enrollees “an opportunity to evaluate the coverage they have and see if there might be better options for them in terms of accessing the care that they need, at possibly a lower cost.” While Weigand is grateful to have the mental acuity to do the research and the spiritual community that she relies on, she worries about other older people who are struggling to plan for the year ahead. “There are so many changes, and a lot of people my age who don’t know where to start," she says. "What do they do?” THE SITUATION: The Trump administration has made lowering drug prices a priority in its effort to show Americans that it is tackling soaring costs. Republican President Donald Trump has struck multiple most-favored-nation drug deals with pharmaceutical companies and has launched the discount drug website TrumpRx , among other steps. In September, his administration said all 50 states would join in on a program set to provide most-favored-nation pricing to some drugs within the Medicaid program, bringing the net price of selected drugs down to prices paid in certain other countries. Still, the cost of prescription drugs prevents some people from filling prescriptions. A KFF survey from March found that about 4 in 10 U.S. adults say they have not taken their medication as prescribed in the past year due to costs. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Weigand is considering rationing her drugs to save money. “I've been thinking — if I could just do this every other day rather than every day to make the medicine last longer," she says. "Isn't that sad?“ The KFF report says about 1 in 5 people surveyed had cut pills in half or skipped doses of medicine in the prior year because of the cost. The costs of receiving long-term care — whether from spouses, home-care aides or friends — have risen steeply for retirees. An AARP report released Wednesday that examines out-of-pocket caregiving expenses finds that family caregivers are spending nearly 60% more supporting a family member or friend than five years ago. They spend an average of $11,508 a year supporting a family member or friend, compared with $7,242 in 2021, according to the report. Nancy LeaMond, AARP's executive vice president and chief advocacy officer, said “we're already hearing from our members about healthcare affordability — its prescription drug costs, caregiver costs, co-pays, premiums," she said. "Not only are we trying to help family caregivers with their finances, but also to get them the kind of information they need to help their loved ones.” These worries are top of mind for older people.

events.title: Iran's supreme leader orders "maximum" response to any U.S. attack
events.summary: Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei told the country's top three military commanders that a renewed attack by the U.S. and Israel ״must be met with an immediate and effective response, without geographical limitations״ in order to achieve "maximum deterrence," according to a statement from his office. Why it matters: This is the first publicly disclosed meeting between Khamenei and all the top commanders of Iran's armed forces since the war began. It comes as President Trump weighs major strikes on Iran after the midterm elections. Khamenei hasn't been seen or heard in public since he was wounded in an Israeli strike on the first day of the war. He has only issued written statements, which raised questions about his condition. The unusual apparent meeting took place a day after Qatari mediators held talks in Tehran for more than 12 hours in an effort to reach a deal to restart direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran and avoid an outbreak of war after the midterms. The discussions continued in Doha, Qatar, on Saturday. What he's saying: "If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Islamic Republic of Iran's Armed Forces and the Iranian nation that determine when and under what conditions those hostilities will end," Khamenei told the commanders, according to the statement. Zoom in: According to the statement, the meeting included armed forces chief of staff Gen. Ali Abdollahi, army commander Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander Maj. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi. The commanders briefed Khamenei on the state of military readiness along the Gulf coastline and around the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf of Oman, and Iran's northwestern and southeastern borders. They also reported "a several-fold increase" in production of various types of ammunition and reconnaissance, support, and combat weapons. Khamenei instructed the commanders that the "target bank" must be updated "so that all types of the American-Zionist enemy's material and non-material assets fall within the reach of the Armed Forces." Khamenei praised "the intelligent steadfastness" of Iran's proxies across the region and stressed "the unity of the different arenas" as a "decisive and strategic" element for Iran. Reality check: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera that senior-level officials have discussed a proposal from Vice President Vance and called the U.S. effort to open talks a "positive step." But he made a strict set of demands for an agreement: lifting sanctions, reducing the U.S. military presence in the region and recognizing a Strait of Hormuz shipping route agreed to with Oman. Araghchi also told Al Jazeera that reopening the strait on Iran's terms could pave the way for direct negotiations. Iran is examining mediators' proposals to address its nuclear program, a bottom-line issue for the U.S.

events.title: When Electric Cars Were for Women
events.summary: At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000. For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place. Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with. Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers , was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations. In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it. Who Invented the Mercury-Arc Rectifier? Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706 , granted to Percy H. Thomas , advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps. The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery. A Carriage Maker Pivots to Electric Cars I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass. This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC. Heritage Museums & Gardens According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago. Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles. Thomas Edison Designed a Bad Battery Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery . Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market. While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5). Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model. Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate .) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling. When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phae

events.title: Election cheat sheet: These early races could tell us where the midterms are headed
events.summary: You won't need to stay up all night Tuesday to spot a big Democratic wave in the 2026 midterm elections . But it could take days — or even weeks — to know whether Republicans have survived a smaller one and held on to the House or Senate. Why it matters: A handful of early results in key states and congressional districts will tell us whether Democrats are headed for a landslide or disappointment. What we're watching: Florida, Florida, Florida. Most polls close at 7pm ET, and the state counts quickly — ready for release when the Panhandle finally calls it a night an hour later. At 8:01pm , refresh your browser and watch FL-14. The great mid-cycle redistricting wars transformed this Tampa-based district from Harris +8 to Trump +11. If Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor survives, Republicans can all but kiss their majority goodbye, according to party strategists. Next up is FL-25. The country's most expensive general election race is playing out in a district that went from Harris +4 to Trump +9. If Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz's race is close — or too close to call early in the night — House Republicans can keep hope alive. While you're at it, this is a good time to check on South Carolina's Senate race, where polls close at 7pm and the state counts relatively fast. If Sen. Darline Graham loses to Annie Andrews in the Trump +18 state, Senate Republicans can say goodbye to their majority. (And they'll be sweating if it's close.) "Underperformance is rarely isolated," said Jason Thielman, executive director of the National Republican Senatorial Committee in 2024. "If you see the GOP underperforming early in the East, it is likely going to continue as you move further West." At 9pm, check in on Virginia: The commonwealth's polls close at 7pm, but historically tight races often aren't called until the 9pm hour. If Democrats flip VA-01, a Trump +5 seat, they're in for a very good night. If they flip VA-05, a Trump +12 seat, they're in for a great night. Between the lines: VA-02 could tell us whether a strong Republican candidate can survive a Democratic wave, and whether Speaker Mike Johnson can keep his job. Trump carried the Hampton Roads district by just 0.2 percentage points in 2024, while Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans won by 3.8 points. The AP didn't call her race until 5:28pm ET the following Wednesday. GOP strategists believe Kiggans has run a nearly flawless campaign. If even she gets swept away in a 50-50 district, other Republicans in a low-single-digit Trump seat should brace for impact. If she holds on, that could bode well for Sen. Susan Collins in Maine and Rep. Ashley Hinson in the Iowa Senate race. The intrigue: Also keep an eye on Kentucky's 6th District. Polls close there at 6pm ET, but the state takes a more genteel approach to counting ballots. If Democrats take the open Lexington-based seat (Trump +15), Republicans will be downing their bourbon. Neat. Moving west: Polls close in Ohio at 7:30pm and Texas at 8pm ET, but Texas counts faster. If Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton holds on, Republicans still have a path to keeping their Senate majority. Iowa polls close at 9pm ET. If Hinson is looking good, the night might not be as bad as many Republicans feared. The bottom line: Don't stay up for the Senate results in either Maine or Alaska. Even a clear win (or defeat) for Collins may not be obvious until Wednesday. In 2020, when she won by nearly 9 percentage points, the AP didn't call the race until lunchtime Wednesday. In Alaska, with its ranked-choice voting, results could take weeks.

events.title: How North Korea perfected the crypto heist
events.summary: The world's biggest crypto heist is the latest feat by North Korean hackers who have spent years perfecting an arsenal of financial theft, social engineering and sophisticated cyberattacks. Why it matters : The suspected North Korean hackers behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft appear to have combined familiar hacking tactics with extraordinary speed and automation — raising fresh questions about how AI could supercharge their already sophisticated operations. Driving the news : Binance said late Thursday that its blockchain partners have frozen at least $3 billion of those $6.3 billion assets on-chain so far, and it believes the hackers gained initial access by compromising one engineer's laptop alongside other "points of breach." Several blockchain investigation firms have tied the hack to TraderTraitor, a group linked to the North Korean government's Lazarus Group collective. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said in a video on social media Friday that the attackers also used a "self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces" as they went, making it more difficult to investigate what happened. "This was a complex attack," he said. The big picture: North Korean government hackers have spent more than a decade carrying out financial heists and disruptive cyberattacks, and they have turned cryptocurrency theft into an industrial-scale operation. In 2016, hackers attempted to steal nearly $1 billion from Bangladesh's central bank, successfully making off with $81 million. In 2017, North Korea was blamed for the WannaCry ransomware outbreak , which disrupted hundreds of thousands of computers across more than 150 countries. In recent years, the country has intensified its focus on pillaging crypto exchanges in part because the digital assets can more easily be transferred and laundered across borders — although those attacks tend to leave more of a paper trail. The same North Korean hacking group, TraderTraitor, also set the last record for the world's largest crypto heist last year when they stole $1.5 billion from the ByBit crypto exchange. Between the lines: North Korean hackers are only getting better and faster at their attacks, experts tell Axios. "They're essentially crowding out other threat actors by stealing the bulk of the value that's taken in any given year," Eric Jardine, head of research at Chainalysis, told Axios. Zoom in : Chainalysis said in a research report Friday that hackers made off with the billions of funds in as little as 20 minutes. The hackers also laundered and destroyed evidence of their operations at an unprecedented speed, suggesting they used automation throughout the heist, researchers found. Researchers at TRM Labs found that the hackers started preparing for the attack just 36 hours before it began. "There were transactions happening with a frequency and a scale that just meant there could not have been someone involved in the approval of these," Jardine said. "It had to have been done by a computer." The intrigue: Social engineering and automation has been hallmarks of the latest North Korean cyberattacks, Vijay Balasubramaniyan, CEO and co-founder of Pindrop Security, told Axios. Advances in AI-powered video and audio tools have allowed North Koreans to vastly expand their widespread IT worker fraud , where American companies are tricked into hiring North Koreans for IT jobs. Balasubramaniyan said last year, North Korean job applicants made up 1 in every 343 applications. This year, across their customer base, these applicants make up 1 in 47. "It is absolutely underpinning everything," Balasubramaniyan said. "It's just not AI, it's the scale of AI — you have so many AI choices that the number of such tools is crazy, the cost is so cheap and it's becoming an ecosystem." What to watch: Law enforcement and blockchain investigators may still be able to recover the other half of the stolen Binance funds if they enter specific exchange infrastructure and operators can move quickly enough to freeze them, Jardine said. "It's still early days," he added. Go deeper: How North Korea's IT army is hacking the global job market

events.title: New Census data reveal a homeowner-renter divide in America's electric-car transition
events.summary: Data: U.S. Census Bureau, 2025 American Community Survey 1-year estimates; Table: Russell Contreras/Axios Homeowners were nearly twice as likely as renters to have an electric vehicle in 2025, new Census data show, revealing a striking divide in America's shift to electric cars. Why it matters : Homeownership is just one factor in EV adoption, but reliable access to charging is critical — giving homeowners with private driveways or garages an advantage over renters, particularly those in multifamily buildings. By the numbers: About 7.3 million U.S. households — 5.5% of the nation's 134 million — reported having at least one EV, according to the 2025 American Community Survey released Thursday. Homeowners reported EVs at a rate of 6.4%, compared with 3.6% of renters. California led the nation at 13.8% overall, more than twice the national rate. North Dakota (1.3%), Wyoming (1.6%) and Louisiana (1.6%) ranked among the lowest. State of play: For the first time, the Census Bureau asked households with vehicles kept at home whether they owned or leased an EV, offering a nationwide snapshot of who has gone electric. The figures cover fully electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids. Our thought bubble: Many factors, including local government policies, can influence EV adoption rates, but ultimately, it comes down to affordability and access to charging, says Axios Transportation Correspondent Joann Muller . Homeowners with higher incomes are more likely to afford EVs, sometimes as a second car. The intrigue: A 2026 study by researchers at the University of Vermont and University of California, Davis, found higher home-charger installation costs at rental properties in Burlington, Vermont. Renters were also less likely to adopt fully electric vehicles, even after researchers accounted for home values and vehicle preferences. Zoom in: Even California, the nation's EV leader, has a sharp homeowner-renter divide, new Census data show. About 17.7% of homeowners reported an EV, compared with 8.9% of renters. Santa Clara County, home to much of Silicon Valley, led the nation at 24.1% of households — roughly 163,000 households. Zoom out: Washington (8.9%), Hawaii (8.5%) and Nevada (8.2%) ranked among the leading states. Outside California, Boulder County, Colorado, and Loudoun County, Virginia, each recorded 13.9%. Yes, but: California renters reported EVs at a higher rate than homeowners nationwide. The Census figures don't track charging access or explain why households choose EVs. With only one year of data, they also can't tell us whether the homeowner-renter gap has grown.

events.title: The $13 billion startup racing to close America’s hypersonic gap
events.summary: The first thing to know about hypersonic missiles is that they’re air-rippingly fast. A hypersonic missile, definitionally, moves at least at Mach 5, or five times the speed of sound; one could cross the U.S. coast to coast in under 45 minutes. Unlike ballistic missiles, hypersonics are maneuverable and unpredictable to watchers, with an uncanny ability to fly low, change course, and skirt radar. The second thing to know about hypersonics is that China and Russia have them, and the U.S. doesn’t—not really. It’s not for lack of trying: Despite years of research costing billions and some successful tests, the U.S. has yet to fully field a hypersonic missile of its own due to testing complications and production issues . The tech’s been around, but it’s been expensive and difficult to produce at scale. That’s the chasm that startup Castelion, valued at $13 billion, is betting it can close, even if the defense giants have so far fallen short. “Humans have done it, just not Americans,” says Castelion CEO and cofounder Bryon Hargis. “I firmly believe it’s doable.” The Torrance, Calif.-based startup has become a darling of the defense tech boom, in part because it encapsulates the movement’s raison d’être: The U.S. must rebuild its industrial base faster, cheaper, and with an eye to scale. The war in Iran has crystallized that bleak reality: The U.S. is firing missiles faster than it can replace them, by an order of years. Castelion was founded in 2022 by three former SpaceX executives: Hargis, Andrew Kreitz, and Sean Pitt. (Hargis started the military-grade satellite network Starshield; Kreitz ran classified finance; and Pitt led sales of Falcon 9s in Europe.) The enterprise got off to an almost comically inauspicious start: In an early Zoom pitch to the Pentagon’s innovation outfit, the founders said they planned to compete with Lockheed Martin at building affordable hypersonics. The room laughed, Pitt recalls. But the tables have turned: Castelion, in less than two-and-a-half years, took its low-cost hypersonic missile Blackbeard from a drawing to progressing reality—and it’s designated as a “program of record,” the elusive and coveted government budget line that makes (and often breaks) defense sector entrants. This places Castelion in direct competition with Lockheed, the maker of hypersonic race favorite Dark Eagle, a program that’s been in process since 2017—and is reportedly three years behind schedule. (“Dark Eagle has successfully deployed in support of Indo-Pacific exercises and completed multiple successful flight-test events,” an Army spokesperson said via email. “The Army continues planned operational assessment activities.”) In September, the U.S. Navy awarded Castelion a contract worth up to $200 million for Blackbeard, which documents say can be made for less than $500,000 each. (In comparison, Tomahawk missiles can cost millions each.) Blackbeards have had successful test flights on fighter jets like the F/A-18 Super Hornet, and the company is currently racing to open its 1,000-acre New Mexico site, which could eventually turn out thousands of Blackbeards each year. “This capability is needed now, and you have to sprint directly at what the country needs,” says Kreitz, Castelion’s CFO. Hypersonics are effective not just as weapons but, even more essentially, as deterrents, Kreitz argues. “It’s really important we have a credible deterrent that we pass down for generations to come,” adds Hargis. Pitt gestures at a Mad Men -esque poster in Castelion’s mid-century office. “Cheesy as it is, this was the first poster we ever made for the company,” he explains. “You can see the tagline was: ‘Win before it begins.’” Of course, deterrence only has a chance if the weapons exist. And recent conflicts have created an unmissable urgency, Kreitz says. “This is the capability that will define warfare in the 2030s and beyond,” he said. “The campaign was basically large, sustained volleys of back-and-forth long-range fires. That’s what the future of warfare will look like.” Build, fly, test, repeat In 2022, as Hargis, Kreitz, and Pitt were just getting started, they presented to the Defense Innovation Unit, the Pentagon’s tech acceleration division. It didn’t go well. “It was the tailish end of COVID,” said Pitt. “So, it was a video presentation, and we explained ‘we’re here to make low-cost missiles.’ They asked: ‘Are you going to compete with Lockheed?’ We said yes, and it was not a little laugh. There were a good number of people laughing.” In venture capital, 2022 was the bizarre era of peak metaverse. Defense tech was a novelty and largely seen as controversial or ignored. (Anduril, defense tech’s greatest hardware success, had a skyrocketing 2022, but there was no sense that breakthrough was imitable.) The three founders are all candid about the impasse of the very beginning. Hargis, who has a forceful warmth and natural deadpan—his father, he says, worked at a nuclear power plant “like Homer Simpson”—doesn’t hold back. “I was using my retirement to fund my living,” he said. “I was messaging these guys: ‘At what point would they have to call it quits if we didn’t make anything?’” Castelion’s co-founders, left to right: Bryon Hargis, Sean Pitt, Andrew Kreitz. Courtesy of Castelion In their first investment contracts, Hargis, Kreitz, and Pitt promised to return the money if they couldn’t raise $1 million. In the end, they cleared that bar through a SpaceX tender offer, in which Hargis and another employee sold shares and invested in the company. Then, in April 2023, Lavrock, a Washington, D.C.-based VC firm, led a seed round of $5.6 million, a shoestring sum for an aspiring missile-maker. But it was enough: The founders went off into the Mojave Desert, near Edwards Air Force Base, to build their first rocket motor. “The early, early days in the desert were threadbare,” remembers Kreitz, a history buff keenly aware of the lines between past and present. “We all wore Tyvek suits and respirators, helped make propellant and assembled parts, and we were getting hardware built alongside the engineers and techs.” It took months, funds dwindled, and it was soon time for a Hail Mary: They found a high-speed cameraman to film a static-fire test. The resulting video, of a rumbling firing motor, drew the attention of the VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, which quickly led an $8.6 million seed extension in Castelion. The race then really began. Building a defense company is an amalgamation of tiny precisions, from the rigamarole of clearances to establishing processes for classified information. The endgame, for Castelion and any defense startup, is selling to the Department of War, a bureaucratic behemoth with labyrinthine fiefdoms. events.title: The AI trade's trick-or-treat earnings season
events.summary: The latest wave of hyperscaler earnings is spooking Wall Street. Bulls and bears alike have evidence to validate their wildest dreams — or their worst nightmares. Why it matters : The market's AI obsession has entered its Jekyll and Hyde era, with the latest earnings from tech giants offering contrary signals about the AI boom. Driving the news : The tech-heavy Nasdaq briefly sank into correction territory, falling 10% from its prior peak, losing $1.2 trillion in value for the month of October, after a slew of earnings reports pointed to AI's big risks. But it wasn't all horror: within the earnings statements, some investors found proof that the AI bet is going exactly as it should. Here are three examples of the AI trade's deepest contradictions — the good and the scary — from the earnings releases and calls of the Big Tech hyperscalers. Google: The scary: AI overviews are cannibalizing Google's core business: ad revenue from search. Yes, search queries are up, but results in AI mode have lower margins. The company has lost more than $500 billion in market value post-earnings, bringing the broader tech sector along with it. The good: Google Cloud is closing in on Microsoft's Azure cloud revenue, a stunning development given that Google was an also-ran in the cloud game only a few years ago. Much of Google's success is tied to demand for its TPU chips, which analysts expect to see massive growth in coming quarters. The takeaway: Google's predicament mirrors the problems of many tech giants, where AI represents a true threat to the golden goose but presents new opportunities if they can move fast enough. Microsoft and Amazon: The good: Both companies had explosive cloud growth, though the market was disappointed Amazon's wasn't higher. Microsoft touted its OpenAI investment and Amazon its Anthropic holdings. The iffy: Those private AI investments can help or hurt: Amazon's net income fell despite soaring operating profits, as it didn't repeat the pretax gain from its Anthropic investment that boosted earnings a year earlier. Microsoft's OpenAI investment boosted its net income slightly, which lifted its profit growth. The takeaway: Check under the hood. Is any given hyperscaler's earnings growth coming from private investments in AI labs, or is it due to their underlying business? Data: FactSet, company filings; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Free cash flow The good: Sure, some of the most asset-light tech companies have turned free cash flow negative to fund their AI ambitions, but they say that's because demand is outstripping supply! You want these businesses to keep investing in infrastructure to meet that demand and turn it into revenue. The bad: If there's a hit to that demand, and these companies poured trillions into creating more supply, that's, well, a recipe for a bit of a popped bubble situation. The takeaway: Watch the demand picture. Jeetu Patel, President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco, is bullish, but told Axios that a major cyber event that hits the core of AI demand could be a downside risk. The bottom line: Tech stocks are broadly under pressure following these results. DeepWater partner Gene Munster says the street is waking up to the risks of an agentic world: How does Google make money without ad search revenue? How does Amazon make money if shoppers are using bots? But those existential issues aren't stopping the AI capex spending spree, for now.

events.title: Meta’s Muse Could Upend All Kinds of Businesses. It Hasn’t Yet
events.summary: Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks , is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average. Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents. Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.” While financial experts have suspected that users may ask Muse to dump unused subscriptions and memberships, fitness chain Life Time Group said it has “seen zero” cancellations from agents. Public Storage and Hartford Insurance Group offered similar data. In India, the delivery app giant Eternal estimated agentic commerce as “close to zero.” The comments leave questions about where users of Muse, Instinct, and other popular AI agents are spending their money. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on his company’s earnings call this month that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. Over 25 percent used it for shopping, more than any other task and above the company’s expectations, he added. Meta declined to comment beyond the earnings call remarks, but pointed to partnerships with 10 retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of them last reported earnings before Muse launched and haven’t shared data about it yet. Across the board, executives acknowledged agents are at an early stage. But immense public anxiety about AI technologies has left companies searching for any lessons they can from the outset. Despite the seemingly slow uptake, some are already hard at work optimizing their websites for agents. Chipotle chief digital officer Arlie Sisson told reporters this week that the restaurant chain discovered agents struggling to complete purchases because of hiccups from applying loyalty discounts or ordering after-hours. Muse’s debut increased agentic orders by a single-digit percentage, she said. So Chipotle is now tidying up its website code to help agents better navigate and satisfy the hungry humans behind them. Similar discussions are underway at Doordash, even though CEO and Meta board member Tony Xu said present hype about agents might be “delusional.” Costco and Extra Space Storage said sales originating from AI chatbots such as Gemini and ChatGPT are surging as the companies optimize their online content for the tools, so they plan to do the same for AI agents. Reliance on agents could be costly. Zuckerberg said Meta plans to charge businesses a fee for transactions facilitated by Muse, and he predicted that this source of revenue would eventually top the company’s massive advertising business. InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf is taking a cautious approach in ongoing talks with Meta. “We haven't come to any conclusions on what an eventual collaboration could look like, if any,” he said. Security issues and errant orders remain top of mind. This week, Bank of America became the latest big bank to warn customers about giving login information to AI assistants. “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access,” chief client care officer Ashley Ross wrote in an email. There’s also the possibility that agents encourage comparison shopping in a way that hurts profits. Executives at many companies dismissed the notion. They suggested product quality, customer service, and brand trust would still factor into purchase decisions despite less human involvement. Stances on agents are evolving quickly. Amazon blocked Muse last month, contending that users would prefer its own Alexa shopping agent . But this week the retail giant acknowledged that it anticipates working with outside agents. Insurance marketplace Insurify also blocked Muse but this week changed its mind after introducing technology to ensure agents could present accurate offers.
