events.title: Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon says the best advice he ever got came from his grandmother in his 20s: ‘Don’t be in a hurry’
events.summary: David Solomon runs one of the most powerful banks on Wall Street, but the best career advice he ever received didn’t come from a mentor in a corner office. It came from his grandmother. “Don’t be in a hurry,” the Goldman Sachs CEO told NBC News’ Christine Romans in a rapid-fire interview about his daily routine and the lessons that have shaped his career. He said she gave him that advice when he was in his twenties. The clip came out of Romans’ wider conversation with Solomon for NBC’s Business in America series. That conversation aired Oct. 23, one day after Goldman launched its Small Business AI Institute , part of a new $500 million commitment to its 10,000 Small Businesses program, with Anthropic, Google, Meta , and OpenAI as partners. In the segment that ran on Nightly News , Solomon said he’s excited about what AI could mean for businesses and for people’s longevity. In the lightning round, though, he talked less about markets and more about how he manages his days and his life. Gym, coffee, and a protein shake before 7 a.m. Asked to name three things he does before 7 a.m., Solomon kept it simple: He wakes up, goes to the gym, and generally has a cup of coffee and a protein shake. He’s in good company. An early workout is a fixture of many executives’ routines, from the Bupa CEO who trains six days a week with his Gen Z son to the many leaders featured in Fortune’ s Day in the Life of a CEO series. The research suggests the habit matters more than the hour. A 2022 systematic review published in the Public Health Agency of Canada’s journal Health Promotion and Chronic Disease Prevention in Canada examined 35 studies. Eleven found morning activity more beneficial; 12 found afternoon or evening activity more beneficial; and 12 found no clear difference. The authors concluded there is no consistent evidence that exercising at one time of day is better for your health than another, and they rated the evidence quality as very low. ‘Stick to the schedule’ Solomon’s best trick for keeping his day on track is unglamorous: sticking to his schedule. “The one thing that we can’t…get back is time,” he said, adding that he tries to be very purposeful with how he spends it. That means making commitments and keeping them, because, as he noted, it’s easy to drift off schedule. The science backs him up, with a twist. A 2021 meta-analysis in PLOS One by Brad Aeon, Aïda Faber, and Alexandra Panaccio found that time management is positively linked to job performance. It was even more strongly linked to well-being, especially life satisfaction. In other words, the payoff from guarding your calendar may show up as much in how you feel as in what you get done. Why slowing down isn’t a contradiction At first glance, “stick to the schedule” and “don’t be in a hurry” seem to pull in opposite directions. For Solomon, they work on different timelines: Be disciplined with the hours in a day, and be patient with the arc of a career. He repeats this message often. In August, he told Goldman’s summer interns at a town hall that taking more time can open up more opportunities, urging them to “try not to be in a hurry and enjoy the ride.” He offered small-business owners the same counsel about AI at the institute’s launch last week, telling them that “the important thing is to get it right, not to get it quicker.” ‘I don’t like to do things halfway’ Solomon’s patience has a limit, and it’s the things he cares about. Asked whether he has any obsessions, he said it depends on what has captured his interest. “If I’m interested in something, I get very obsessive about it. I don’t like to do things halfway,” Solomon said. When something grabs him, he added, he tends to go deep. Psychologists have found that kind of intensity cuts both ways. In a 2007 study in the Journal of Personality , Robert Vallerand and colleagues distinguished between “harmonious” passion, an activity you freely choose that fits with the rest of your life, and “obsessive” passion, which feels compulsive. Obsessive passion predicted deliberate practice and mastery-oriented goals, which supported performance. But it was also tied to fear-of-failure goals that undercut results. Harmonious passion delivered the upside with less of the downside. The takeaway: Going deep can fuel success, as long as the obsession serves you, not the other way around. Not every passion turns into a career, of course. Solomon also named one ambition he’s had to let go of: playing professional basketball. He conceded that one isn’t on the table. events.title: UAE petrol prices defy expectations with surprise drop in November
events.summary: UAE petrol prices will decline in November, the first reduction in four months, defying expectations after global oil markets posted a sharp rise in October amid elevated tensions in the Middle East. The cost of Super 98 petrol will drop to Dh4.16 a litre, down 5.5 per cent, while Special 95 decreases by 5.6 per cent to Dh4.04. E-Plus 91 will fall 5.7 per cent a litre to Dh3.97, while diesel at Dh4.75 is down 1 per cent. Prices are still up by about 80 per cent compared to February, before the Iran war started. How much will fuel cost in October? Super 98: Dh4.16, from Dh4.40 in October Special 95: Dh4.04, from Dh4.28 E-Plus 91: Dh3.97, from Dh4.21 Diesel: Dh4.75, from Dh4.80 The cost of fuel in the UAE has been tied to the global oil market since 2015, when deregulation was introduced. Traditionally, petrol prices have moved in sync with those benchmarks, but not all the time. Several factors influence monthly fuel costs, and, although the mechanisms for setting these prices vary by nation, governments can also help control high prices at the pump. Crude prices on Friday settled at hit six-month highs and posted a fourth straight monthly increase in October. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's crude, was up 2.4 per cent at $117.64 a barrel, after briefly touching $118. The more active January futures contract added 2.37 per cent to $113.43 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, gained 2.08 per cent to settle at $104.12 a barrel. For the week, both Brent and WTI increased by about 0.8 per cent. On a monthly basis, the benchmarks spiked by about 15 per cent and 12 per cent, respectively, for their highest levels since April. Analysts previously told The National that they expected UAE pump prices to rise again in November , saying that the recovery in Middle East oil supplies does not immediately translate into a return to normality for the energy market. Vessel attacks on the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, plus the possibility of the US renewing hostilities on Iran, have kept markets on edge. "Persistent geopolitical risks and higher freight costs support [an] outlook [for higher oil prices], while resilient supply, weaker demand and the prospect of a diplomatic breakthrough could limit further increases," Ahmed Zaheer, a consultant at Dubai-based Qamar Energy, told The National .

events.title: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
events.summary: Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of Binance , the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis. This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted. Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied. Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim. The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives. Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far Published 3 days ago Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea Published 3 days ago Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange. In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency. The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities". The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports. Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups. Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected Much of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain. North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022. In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker. TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme. Binance has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area. The company had initially said it thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider. "Our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said. Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for. If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become – a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper. Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means. In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems. As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before". events.title: Judge blocks DOJ from threatening election workers before midterms
events.summary: A federal judge Friday blocked the Trump administration from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution for counting ballots cast by registered voters the administration claims are ineligible. Why it matters: The emergency order, issued four days before the midterms , prohibits federal pressure to sideline ballots based solely on allegations of ineligibility and forces the Justice Department to walk back threats it already sent to election officials. The big picture: The ruling adds to a series of courtroom losses for the administration, as federal officials intensify election-related investigations and challenges across the country. Judges are warning that federal threats and investigations are driving citizens out of elections and putting lawful votes at risk. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson found that the Justice and Homeland Security departments likely violated the Voting Rights Act's prohibition on voter intimidation and exceeded their constitutional authority over elections. Her temporary restraining order prohibits demands that states remove registered voters, withhold their ballots or stop counting votes solely because the administration claims the voters are ineligible. It also bars threats of criminal prosecution against election workers who refuse those demands or process ballots in accordance with election laws. The judge ordered prosecutors to disclose pending search warrant applications, grand jury subpoenas and other demands related to its lists of allegedly ineligible voters. What she's saying: Thompson found the administration's actions forced election workers to choose between complying with "Defendants' unlawful demands" or risk criminal prosecution for performing their jobs. "In the lead-up to the election," she wrote, "high-ranking DOJ and DHS officials have engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election." Zoom out: The ruling comes amid a sweeping federal campaign to obtain voter records, investigate suspected noncitizen voting and threaten state officials over election administration. Since May 2025, the DOJ has filed 31 lawsuits seeking sensitive voter records. So far, 27 have been dismissed. In July, the DOJ warned election officials in all 50 states they could face criminal charges for knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote. On Thursday, it sent another round of letters nationwide, warning of criminal penalties for violating election-record preservation requirements. The other side: DOJ has defended its election-related actions as necessary to enforce federal prohibitions on noncitizen voting. The department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment, but a spokesperson previously told Axios the government would not wait for a "more convenient time" to enforce election laws. Reality check: Noncitizen voting in federal elections is already illegal. Research finds it is rare. Zoom in: In the final days of the election, the administration has stepped up its legal fights across the country. California: The DOJ sued to set aside ballots from more than 20,000 voters it suspects are noncitizens, threatened election workers and issued grand jury subpoenas. An appeals court rejected its emergency request Friday, warning of "potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system." Washington: Federal prosecutors demanded officials segregate ballots from more than 400 voters. Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said the federal list included U.S. citizens and was unreliable. Arizona: Prosecutors announced Friday evening an investigation into three Democratic-aligned registration groups after a right-wing outlet published an undercover video. The DOJ also requested the state's and Maricopa County's top election officials review registrations. Alaska: The DOJ sued to delay certification if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses reelection and if votes for a similarly named candidate could have changed the outcome. Prosecutors confirmed a criminal investigation Friday into an alleged Democratic effort to recruit the other Sullivan. In a separate ruling Friday, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals left in place restrictions on DHS election-related field operations involving known or suspected U.S. citizens in nine states through Election Day. The underlying order, by Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, found that federal threats had already caused citizens to "withdraw from participating in electoral activity." The appeals court also questioned the timing: "In an operation ostensibly focused on past voter fraud, the government could have aggressively pursued its campaign against non-citizen voting well before these elections commenced."
